11708-abraham-lincoln-a-history-volume-0:
John G Nicolay and John Hay's second volume of Abraham Lincoln appeared in 1890. It opens with Jefferson Davis on rebellion and the conventions of 1856. Congressional ruffianism and the Dred Scott decision follow in the early chapters.

Douglas and Lincoln on Dred Scott, the Lecompton constitution, and the revolt of Douglas come next. The Lincoln-Douglas debates and the Freeport doctrine follow in turn. Harper's Ferry, the Cooper Institute speech, and the Charleston, Baltimore, and Chicago conventions lead to Lincoln's election. The volume ends with beginnings of rebellion and a cabinet cabal.
14227-on-english-homophones-society-for-:
Robert Bridges wrote this Society for Pure English tract in 1919 on words that sound alike but differ in origin and sense. Homophones, he argues, mislead readers and speakers, and delicate vowel distinctions offer no safe cure. Common sense, he insists, needs no proof that such twins cause trouble, and he gives one sharp example in a note.

Sun and son carry the point. A Greek epigram calls Homer a second sun on the life of Greece, but second son in English means a family's second male child, so the line cannot cross languages intact. Lists follow for spelling reformers: core and caw, door and daw, floor and flaw, lore and law, roar and raw, soar and sore. Number matters less than frequency, Bridges adds, and quality of words decides which twins deserve attention first.
2102-history-of-friedrich-ii-of-prussia-:
Thomas Carlyle opens the early story of Brandenburg and the Hohenzollerns in this volume of his vast life of Frederick the Great. Book Two runs from 928 to 1417, before the family rose to rule Prussia. Carlyle spent years on Frederick, and this volume shows his habit of digging into obscure chronicles.

Carlyle begins with Brannibor and Henry the Fowler, and with travellers such as Pytheas who glimpsed the north long before written history. His prose is rough and vivid, and the volume sets the deep roots from which Frederick's kingdom grew. Brandenburg's marshes and forests set the scene, since the land itself shaped its rough early history.
24999-the-strange-adventure-of-james-she:
Louis Becke's 1902 novel, published by T. Fisher Unwin, opens on Tarawa Island in the Gilbert Group, where the narrator keeps a trading station. The night is close and stifling, surf bellowing on the weather side, and the expected rain about to drench the thirsty soil as palms and pandanus wave in the trade-wind. Rising from a bed of cane-work and mats, he walks to the beach, wondering why he took charge of such a God-forsaken place.

Four months of depression and half a year on the island have left him poisoned by malarial fever caught in New Ireland and New Britain, aged before his time at seven-and-twenty. He feels he will not live out his two years' engagement unless he shakes the fever or reaches a cooler climate like Samoa or the Marquesas. The novel that follows is Becke's Pacific at its most personal.
30527-the-works-of-robert-louis-stevenso:
Volume two of the Swanston Edition of Robert Louis Stevenson's works was printed in London in 1911. Its Roman date is MDCCCCXI, and it follows the same limited pattern as volume six: two thousand sixty copies printed, two thousand for sale. An illustration shows The Silverado Squatters, from a drawing by J. D. Strong.

Contents open with The Amateur Emigrant, part one, From the Clyde, tracing Stevenson's emigrant journey. The volume gathers travel writing and early prose in a collected, durable form, with Chatto and Windus, Cassell, Heinemann, and Longmans Green as publishers. It suits Stevenson readers who want his works in a handsome uniform set.
30711-wilson-s-tales-of-the-borders-and-:
Wilson's Tales of the Borders and of Scotland, volume two, is historical, traditionary, and imaginative, with a glossary. Alexander Leighton, one of the original editors, revised it, and it was published in London and Newcastle in 1884. Contents open with A Wife or the Wuddy by John Mackay Wilson, Lord Durie and Christie's Will by Leighton, and Recollections of Burns by Hugh Miller.

Later tales add The Professor's Tales, The Convivialists, Philips Grey, and Donald Gorm by Alexander Campbell. The Surgeon's Tales, The Cured Ingrate, The Adopted Son, and The Fortunes of William Wighton follow. Leighton's revision preserves border lore, humor, and history in stories rooted in Scottish place and speech.
3078-original-short-stories-volume-02:
The Colonel's Ideas opens volume two, with an old beau of the old school. Colonel Laporte, old and gouty with legs stiff as wood, declares a pretty woman could send him anywhere. If she told him to go through the eye of a needle, he says, he would jump like a clown through a hoop. He will die an old beau of the old school, sighing after women. The volume adds Mother Sauvage, Epiphany, The Mustache, Madame Baptiste, The Question of Latin, A Meeting, The Blind Man, Indiscretion, A Family Affair, and Beside Schopenhauer's Corpse.

A scene of a woman on a state chair, unable to move or hide her face, breathing like a horse up a steep hill, shows Maupassant's pitiless eye. The tales range from war to adultery with equal force.
3340-the-wandering-jew-volume-02:
Eugene Sue's vast serial reaches its second volume with Book Two, the interval and the Wandering Jew's sentence. The chapters run from the ajoupa and the tattooing through the smuggler and M Joshua Van Dael, to the ruins of Tchandi and the ambuscade. M Rodin, the tempest, and the shipwreck follow, with the departure for Paris and Dagobert's wife.

The sister of the bacchanal queen, Agricola Baudoin, and the return close the early movement, with Agricola and Mother Bunch among the later scenes. Sue's plot, the Rennepont inheritance and the Jesuit scheme to seize it, gathers force here. Readers meet the novel's wandering outcast and its Parisian schemers in full stride, in a serial built to keep its audience waiting.
3552-memoirs-of-napoleon-bonaparte-volum:
This second volume of Bourrienne's memoirs covers 1797 and 1798, from chapter five to chapter fourteen. Bourrienne describes the preliminaries of peace at Leoben, the fall of Venice, and his own arrival and reception there. Bonaparte wishes to pursue his success and advance on Vienna, but the Directory in Paris opposes him, and the army of the Sambre and Meuse moves on its own path.

The volume then follows Bonaparte to Milan, where he and Bourrienne take up residence and the work of governing conquered Italy begins. Readers see a young general learning to be a statesman, bargaining with old republics and new allies. The book gives the inside view of a career that was already outgrowing its masters.
3569-recollections-of-the-private-life-o:
Constant, Napoleon's first valet, continues his recollections of the emperor's private life in this second volume. Constant served in Napoleon's household for years, dressing him, waking him, and traveling with him, so his view is closer and more domestic than any general's. This volume belongs to the older Project Gutenberg Napoleon series.

Readers meet Napoleon at table, in his study, and on the road, in small scenes that show temper, habit, and kindness beside the public legend. Constant writes as a loyal servant, proud of his place and frank about its burdens. The volume suits readers who want the emperor as a man at home, rather than as a commander on a battlefield.
3582-essays-of-michel-de-montaigne-volum:
This second volume of Montaigne's Essays opens Book One, with chapters one through eight. They argue that men arrive at the same end by various ways, treat sorrow, and ask whether our affections carry themselves beyond us after death. Later chapters consider how the soul discharges its passions on false objects. They ask whether a besieged governor should parley in person, why the hour of parley is dangerous, and whether intention judges our actions.

Montaigne also writes on idleness, which he calls the mother of his book, since retirement gave him time to study himself. The essays are short, personal, and full of ancient examples. The volume suits readers beginning Montaigne, since it shows his method from the start: a small question, a pile of examples, and a modest conclusion.
3763-coniston-volume-02:
Winston Churchill's second book of Coniston follows Cynthia Wetherell and her father William on the road home through Northcutt's woods. A ghostlike neighbor, Samuel Price, warns them that Bijah Bixby of Clovelly has come spying from the state capital. Bixby tends the flock of Jethro Bass, the political boss who rules the district from his store. Cynthia, sharp beyond her years, already senses the web closing around her home.

Later pages bring railroad passes, envelopes from the Truro Railroad, and town talk in the store, as Jethro's machine works its quiet will. The volume shows a village learning that votes, favors, and friendships are traded like goods. Readers who enjoy political fiction rooted in one town will find this middle book tense with small moves that carry large weight.
3902-the-confessions-of-jean-jacques-rou:
Jean Jacques Rousseau devotes his second book to a boy's flight and the dreams that carried him. Leaving relations, resources, and an unfinished apprenticeship, he runs toward inevitable misery with his eyes on independence alone. The vast theatre of the world, he writes, seemed ready to captivate at his merit, with amusements, treasures, adventures, friends ready to serve, and mistresses eager to please at every step.

Remorse soon dogs the dream, as he reproaches himself for the past, excuses the future, and treats each error as the inevitable consequence of the last. It takes more resolution than his age affords to break chains he himself forged. Readers who know the Confessions will find the runaway's pride and shame laid bare, with the famous line about the whole universe taking interest in his concerns.
3915-serge-panine-volume-02:
Georges Ohnet, crowned by the French Academy, continues his novel of money, marriage, and pride in this second volume. The action centers on Madame Desvarennes, a formidable mother, her daughter, and Serge Panine, the suitor whose sweetness and openness win the household. A marriage arrangement takes shape, with Serge proposing that his wife need not leave her mother, so that both women gain and he gains their liking.

Madame Desvarennes, who feared Serge might demand independence, thanks him with relief, reading in his pallor, trembling, and changed voice the depth of a mother's love for her daughter. Ohnet writes in the clear popular style that made him famous. Readers who like French society novels will find a volume of bargains struck in drawing rooms, with affection and interest closely weighed.
3920-the-red-lily-volume-02:
Anatole France's second volume of The Red Lily moves Therese into the world of art and devotion. She rides with Marmet to the Chartreuse convent of Ema, and in intoxication of vision forgets importunate letters and distant reproaches. She thinks only of cloisters chiselled and painted, villages with red roofs, and roads where she saw the first blush of spring.

In the studio world around her, Dechartre models a waxen Beatrice for Miss Bell, Vivian paints angels, and Prince Albertinelli caresses his beard while seeking admiration. Asked about marriage and love, he answers that a woman must choose, and her heart is not quiet with a man whom women love. Readers who like France's Florence will find art, faith, and desire intertwined.
3924-monsieur-madame-and-be-be-volume-02:
Gustave Droz's second volume of Monsieur, Madame and Bebe continues his sketches of Paris married life in the same comic key. A wife reports a visit from a lady who praises her husband as amiable, cheery, and witty, and begs her to bring him along, since it is an honor to have him. The wife answers certainly, without meaning it, and shrugs at the prospect.

Madame de Lyr's house holds too many serious people, she complains, influential perhaps and possibly useful, but no amusement to her. She would rather stay home for dinner, where a bottle of famous Pomard waits for a partridge. Readers who like Droz's domestic humor will find a volume of calls, evasions, and small household pleasures.
5185-kalevala-the-epic-poem-of-finland-v:
John Martin Crawford's English translation of the Kalevala continues in this second volume, covering runes twenty-five through the later songs of the Finnish epic. Its contents include Wainamoinen's wedding songs, the origin of the serpent, the unwelcome guest, the isle of refuge, and the long, tragic story of Kullervo, son of evil, shepherd, and avenger.

The volume also follows Ilmarinen and his bride of gold, carrying the epic toward its later sorrows. Readers meet the Kalevala's heroes in their full mythic range, in a translation that first brought Finland's national epic to English-speaking readers in 1888.
5243-tales-from-the-arabic-volume-02:
John Payne's Tales from the Arabic, second volume, continues his translation of stories from the Breslau and Calcutta editions of the Thousand Nights. It carries on the tale of King Shah Bekht and his vizier Er Rehwan. Inset stories follow a pious woman accused of lewdness, a journeyman and a girl, a weaver turned physician, and sharpers who cheat each other.

Further tales follow a hawk and a locust, a king and his chamberlain's wife, an old woman and a draper, and Selim and Selma, among others. The volume holds only this middle part of Payne's collection. It shows the Arabian Nights method at full stretch: stories nested within stories, each with a moral turn.
5276-tales-and-novels-of-j-de-la-fontain:
Jean de La Fontaine's Tales and Novels continue in this second volume, in English verse translation. Its contents are The Cudgelled and Contented Cuckold, The Husband Confessor, The Cobbler. The Peasant and His Angry Lord completes the set, each tale turning on marriage, trickery, and the gap between reputation and desire.

The opening tale follows a younger brother home from Rome, finding good wine on the road and trouble at home, in La Fontaine's light, ironic manner. Readers get four bawdy, witty stories from the French classic, told with the economy and sting that made La Fontaine famous beyond his fables.
5305-travels-in-the-interior-of-africa-v:
Mungo Park's Travels in the Interior of Africa continues in its second volume. The first volume left him sick and solitary at his first sight of the Niger, stripped of nearly all he possessed, starving himself and riding a starving horse. A kindly chief's bag of cowries helped him on, but in this volume he is soon stripped of all again.

Park presses on through the interior, enduring robbery, hunger, and fever, toward the river's course and a return. The volume completes his first great journey, and it offers readers a harrowing, plainly told account of exploration, in which survival itself becomes the story.
5354-guy-mannering-or-the-astrologer-vol:
Sir Walter Scott's Guy Mannering continues in its second volume, opening at chapter thirty-two with a quotation from King Lear on justice and thieves. Gilbert Glossin, late writer turned Laird of Ellangowan, takes a lively interest in discovering who waylaid and wounded young Charles Hazlewood, a question that drives the volume's opening.

This volume holds only the middle portion of Scott's novel of astrology, smuggling, and lost heirs. It follows the characters through the Scottish border country. Readers following the novel in order will find Glossin's schemes, the law's workings. The mystery of Harry Bertram's fate unfolds chapter by chapter.
5357-the-inside-of-the-cup-volume-02:
Winston Churchill's Inside of the Cup continues in its second volume with chapters five through eight. They are The Rector Has More Food for Thought, Watchman, What of the Night, The Kingdoms of the World, and The Line of Least Resistance. Sunday after Sunday, Hodder looks on the same picture: winter light through emblazoned windows, falling athwart stone pillars, staining the marble of the centre aisle.

The organ rolls out hymns, the white-robed choir echoes among the arches, and Hodder's eye, sweeping the decorous congregation, grows troubled. This volume holds only this early portion of the novel, in which the rector's doubts first take shape against the wealth of his parish.
5366-richard-carvel-volume-02:
Winston Churchill's Richard Carvel continues in its second volume with chapters eight through twelve. They are Over the Wall, Under False Colours, The Red in the Carvel Blood, A Festival and a Parting, and News from a Far Country. It opens with Dorothy treating Richard ill that spring, since tasting power at Carvel Hall, and with her mother refusing Dr Courtenay's plea for assemblies.

This volume holds only this middle portion of the Maryland romance, following Richard through love, disguise, and the stirrings of revolution. Readers following the novel in order will find Annapolis society, family pride, and the Carvel blood asserting itself chapter by chapter.
5375-a-modern-chronicle-volume-02:
Winston Churchill's Modern Chronicle continues in its second volume with chapter seven, The Olympian Order. Lying back in a Pullman chair, Honora watches the Hudson glitter in the afternoon light while her imagination runs riot. The seeming possibilities of life become infinite, drawing nearer at every click of the rails to a great world of country houses.

Susan, reading in the chair behind her, is but a humble representative of that Olympian order, though Providence sometimes makes use of such instruments. This volume holds only this portion of Honora's story, following her widening horizon, a chapter of conquests, and what might have been.
5384-the-celebrity-volume-02:
Winston Churchill's Celebrity continues in its second volume with chapter five, set at Asquith on the northern lakes. No wonder, the knowing said, that Irene Trevor should draw the eye of Charles Wrexell Allen. Her cheeks held the red and tan won by lake breezes, and her step and glance gained ground with the Celebrity.

Little by little Miss Trevor gains ground with the famous man, to the neglect of other young women at Asquith, and an announcement follows. This volume holds only this middle portion of Churchill's comedy of fame, in which a celebrated author becomes the prize of a summer resort.
5389-the-crisis-volume-02:
Winston Churchill, the American novelist, sets this second volume of The Crisis in St. Louis on the eve of the American Civil War. Virginia Carvel, a Southern sympathizer, rides out to visit friends while nursing a sharp dislike for a young Northern newcomer in town. Around her, neighbors, households, and old loyalties are already splitting along sectional lines.

The volume blends romance with political tension, as private quarrels mirror the larger national break. Virginia's pride, her family's standing, and her encounters with Northerners drive the scenes forward. Readers get both a love story and a portrait of a border city pulled apart before the war begins.
5410-the-memoirs-of-count-grammont-volum:
Anthony Hamilton's memoirs of Philibert de Grammont, edited with notes by Sir Walter Scott, continue in this second volume with the Chevalier's arrival at the court of Turin. Hamilton opens by arguing that military glory alone does not make a hero, since love must finish the portrait through daring enterprises and successful courtship. Grammont and his companion Matta test that idea in practice.

The volume follows their time at Turin, where gallantry, wit, and romantic pursuit matter as much as soldiering. Court manners, rivalries, and love affairs fill the chapters. Readers get a lively slice of seventeenth-century court life, told by a man who lived inside it and enjoyed telling the tale.
5440-uarda-a-romance-of-ancient-egypt-vo:
Georg Ebers continues his ancient Egyptian romance Uarda in this second volume the morning after a tense night. Princess Bent-Anat and her followers had knocked at the gate of the House of Seti, and now dawn freshness gives way to heat pouring from a cloudless sky. Fine white dust hangs over the hills enclosing the city as the sun climbs.

The volume follows the princess and her party from that night visit into the day's business, with temple and court life close at hand. Ebers keeps the Egyptian landscape present in every scene: light, dust, and heat shaping how people move. Readers get a vivid continuation of the romance, grounded in place and ritual.
5451-an-egyptian-princess-volume-02:
The guests have all gone when the second volume of Georg Ebers's An Egyptian Princess turns to Rhodopis alone. A drunkard's abusive words have cut down the departing mirth like hail on young corn, leaving her standing in an empty, brightly decorated supper room. A slave extinguishes the colored lamps, and a dull half-light replaces their brilliance.

The quiet aftermath sets the volume's mood: gaiety gone, secrets and regrets surfacing in the gloom. Rhodopis, hostess and courtesan, stands at the center of the scene. Readers get a moody, atmospheric stretch of the romance, where a party's end reveals more than the party itself.
5474-cleopatra-volume-02:
Barine lives in a house facing the garden of the Paneum in the second volume of Georg Ebers's Cleopatra. The house belonged to her mother, who inherited it from her parents, while Barine's father, the artist Leonax, son of the philosopher Didymus, died long before. After her unhappy marriage to Philostratus was dissolved, Barine returned to her mother, who manages the household.

Alexandria's artistic and philosophical circles surround the volume, with family history shaping Barine's present. Ebers sets a young beauty's story against the city's gardens, studios, and learned families. Readers get a graceful stretch of historical romance, centered on a woman rebuilding her life in Cleopatra's Alexandria.
5484-the-emperor-volume-02:
Pontius the architect returns to his work-people with a smile in the second volume of Georg Ebers's The Emperor, after a frowning visit to the steward's room. The steward, a little offended at first, is now a capital friend who will help with the matter of lighting. In the hall of the Muses, Pontius pauses among his work.

The volume follows builders, stewards, and artists in Roman Alexandria, where a great building project depends on favors, quarrels, and reconciliations. Ebers writes about craft and administration with the same care as court intrigue. Readers get a working-day stretch of historical romance, set among workshops and half-built halls.
5495-homo-sum-volume-02:
A draught given by the senator sends Stephanus into sleep early in the second volume of Georg Ebers's Homo Sum. Paulus keeps watch beside him, quite still, his breath held back and any urge to cough stifled, lest he break the invalid's shallow sleep. Well past midnight, after an hour has gone, the aged man rouses and rests awake, eyes open, lost in thought.

He then reflects aloud on selfishness, telling Paulus he had called himself and everyone with him selfish, and that he himself is certainly so. The volume turns on that quiet confession between two desert dwellers. Readers get an intimate stretch of the early Christian romance, where a sickroom talk carries moral weight.
5502-serapis-volume-02:
Karnis and his two companions stay away a long time in the second volume of Georg Ebers's Serapis, while Dada grows dull aboard the boat. She has almost forgotten her wish to see the young soldier again, and plays with little Papias until the quiet becomes intolerable. When the sun sinks and the travelers return, she at once reminds Karnis of his promise to take her for a walk.

The volume follows a troupe of performers and travelers in late Roman Egypt, where restlessness and small promises drive the action. Ebers sets their story against temples, boats, and cities in transition. Readers get a lively, character-filled stretch of historical romance, centered on a spirited young girl.
5509-arachne-volume-02:
In the far northern part of the little city of Tennis, a large plain whitewashed building stands on an open, grass-grown square in the second volume of Georg Ebers's Arachne. Its north side rests on a solid substructure of hewn stone washed by waves, and a protecting wall runs along both sides, keeping water from the open space belonging to it. Archias owns the place.

The volume grounds the romance in Tennis itself, with its waterfront, walls, and plain great house. Ebers describes buildings as carefully as people, making the town a character. Readers get a place-rich stretch of the story, where a house by the water frames artists' lives.
5518-the-bride-of-the-nile-volume-02:
Pangs of soul and doubts of conscience prompted the governor to purchase the hanging in the second volume of Georg Ebers's The Bride of the Nile. He might even have been glad if it had cost him dearer, since the greater the gift, the better his hope of grace and favor from its recipient. Yet he still asks himself whether he acted rightly.

Revenge, the volume notes, is no Christian virtue, even when wrongs cry out for answer. Ebers sets the governor's conscience against the politics of Byzantine Egypt. Readers get a moral stretch of historical romance, where a gift cannot quiet a troubled mind.
5531-a-thorny-path-volume-02:
Crowds now homeward bound fill the road in the second volume of Georg Ebers's A Thorny Path. Their wild, high spirits give no hint that they came from a mournful scene. They take the sea road from the Nekropolis to Eleusis, wandering in glowing moonlight. A great procession of Greeks has been to Eleusis to celebrate the mysteries after their ancient manner.

The volume follows a festival crowd returning through the night, with grief giving way to revelry. Ebers sets Greek ritual against Alexandrine streets. Readers get a moonlit, processional stretch of the romance, where a sacred journey ends in high spirits.
5553-margery-gred-a-tale-of-old-nurember:
Summer wears away in the second volume of Georg Ebers's Margery, a tale of old Nuremberg, as forest oats are garnered and the vintage begins in the vine lands. It is a glorious sunny day, and Margery wonders whether forest life is sweeter in spring or autumn. She can scarcely say, since spring comes gaily into the woods like a saviour of numberless folk, great and small.

The volume follows Margery through seasons in forest and vineyard, with nature setting the mood for family life. Ebers writes the year turning in a young woman's voice. Readers get a lyrical stretch of the tale, where harvest and spring share the page.
5562-barbara-blomberg-volume-02:
The old captain blows dust from a wine flagon and carefully removes its seal in the second volume of Georg Ebers's Barbara Blomberg. His presence stops Wolf from renewing an interrupted conversation. Reflection warns Wolf that sharing a lifeboat with this woman would be dangerous, yet she seemed bewitchingly beautiful in proud superiority and in the agitation of soul stirred by yearning.

The volume follows Wolf's divided mind around Barbara, a singer whose beauty and pride unsettle him. Ebers writes attraction and caution together. Readers get a romantic, watchful stretch of the story, where a young knight weighs danger against desire.
5573-a-word-only-a-word-volume-02:
The magistrate's horses do not reach the city gate from the monastery more quickly than Ulrich in the second volume of Georg Ebers's A Word, Only a Word. As soon as the smith wakes from sleep at the boy's knock and recognizes his voice, he knows what is coming. Silently he listens to the lad's confessions while hurriedly taking out his hidden hoard, filling a bag with necessities, and thrusting his lightest hammer into it.

The volume follows a boy's midnight confession and a smith's swift, silent help, with flight from the monastery at stake. Ebers writes the scene as urgency and loyalty. Readers get a tense stretch of the romance, where a knock at night sets a life in motion.
5579-the-burgomaster-s-wife-volume-02:
A second and third rainy day follow the first in the second volume of Georg Ebers's The Burgomaster's Wife. White mists and grey fog hang over meadows, a cold damp northwest wind drives heavy clouds together and darkens the sky, and rivulets dash into Leyden's streets from steep roofs. Canal and ditch water grows turbid and rises toward the banks, while dripping, freezing men and women hurry past.

The volume shows a besieged city under relentless rain, where weather joins the enemy. Ebers writes Leyden's streets as a place of wet, cold endurance. Readers get a bleak, atmospheric stretch of the siege romance, where rain itself becomes a hardship.
5585-in-the-blue-pike-volume-02:
The ropedancer Kuni really was with the sick mother and her babes in the second volume of Georg Ebers's In the Blue Pike, toiling for them with utmost diligence. The unfortunate woman lives in great distress, since the man who promised to cart her to her native village of Schweinfurt barely supports himself and his family by tricks of trained poodles. He makes them perform their best feats in taverns, under the village's watchful eyes.

The volume follows Kuni's charity toward a poor family, with poodles, taverns, and hard travel in play. Ebers writes kindness amid poverty. Readers get a compassionate stretch of the tale, where a wandering performer becomes a family's helper.
5594-the-story-of-my-life-volume-02:
Georg Ebers tells his own story in The Story of My Life, from childhood to manhood. This second volume covers his introduction to art and acquaintances great and small in the Lennestrasse. The Drakes from his sister's journal are the family of the sculptor to whom Berlin and many German cities owe splendid works of art. A warm friendship bound the sculptor and his young wife to Ebers's mother, and they were kind neighbours to the children.

The volume follows a boy's artistic education among Berlin sculptors and family friends. Ebers writes memory with warmth and detail. Readers get an engaging stretch of autobiography, where art enters a child's life through kind neighbours.
5646-sketches-by-seymour-volume-02:
Seymour's Sketches, part two, offers comic scenes in verse, opening with two urchins out on sport intent. One day they get a pistol, powder, horn, and shot, and proudly set forth, dreaming of shooting a hare to make father stare. Spotting mother Tibbs's tabby cat, Bill cries that a cat's eye is as good a mark as any bull's eye. He calls puss, only for a squall and a head and fist above the wall to announce the cat's mistress.

The sketches that follow mix boys, animals, and scolding elders in short, illustrated jokes. Readers get Victorian comic verse, lively and mischievous, in the tradition of illustrated humor.
5665-the-arabian-nights-entertainments-v:
Volume two of the Aldine edition of the Arabian Nights draws on the text of Jonathan Scott. It was printed in London in 1890, and it carries the frame tale forward through stories told to delay a death sentence. Its contents open with the story of the little hunchback. The telling then passes from voice to voice. A Christian merchant speaks, then the sultan of Casgar's purveyor, a Jewish physician, a tailor, and a barber with his brothers. Each teller speaks to save a life.

The pleasure here is in nested tales, where one story pauses so another can begin, and wit, luck, and quick talk decide who survives. Readers meet markets, courts, and sea roads, and they see how a well-timed tale can turn anger into mercy. This volume works best read in order, since each new narrator picks up the thread the last one left hanging.
5689-the-innocents-abroad-volume-02:
Part two of Mark Twain's Innocents Abroad carries the pilgrims from chapters eleven through twenty, deeper into their European tour. The opening chapter finds them growing foreignized with ease, getting used to stone floors, tidy waiters, and rooms that ring underfoot. Twain records the small shocks of travel: strange beds, new customs, and the slow loss of American habits.

The comedy sharpens as the party stops being startled and starts judging everything it sees. Readers get guidebook sights filtered through Twain's teasing eye, with fellow passengers as comic as any cathedral or ruin. This part works as a portrait of tourists learning to travel, and it keeps the voyage's running joke alive: grand expectations meet plain, funny reality at every stop.
5783-a-tramp-abroad-volume-02:
Volume two of Mark Twain's A Tramp Abroad covers chapters eight through fourteen, at Heidelberg and on the Neckar. Chapters treat the great French duel, mistaken notions, an outbreak in the French assembly, and Twain volunteering as a second, with wills, challenges, weapons, distance, and hearses arranged in comic detail. Theatre, German ideals, opera, and four hours with Wagner follow.

Readers also get lessons in art, a great picture of Heidelberg Castle, the Rathaus, an old robber knight, and a famous turnout of raftsmen on the Neckar. Twain turns student duels and opera nights into satire without losing affection for Heidelberg. This volume suits readers who enjoy Twain's German chapters best, where observation and invention mix most freely.
5904-the-history-of-don-quixote-volume-1:
Day dawns as Don Quixote quits the inn in chapter four of this early installment, happy, gay, and exhilarated at finding himself dubbed a knight. His joy nearly bursts his horse girths, though he recalls his host's advice about the requisites of knighthood as he rides. Chapter five continues the narrative of his mishap, as the new knight's triumph meets the road's first hard lesson.

Readers watch a freshly dubbed knight test his fantasies against innkeepers, travelers, and his own body. The comedy comes from Quixote's exhilaration colliding with ordinary rudeness, while Sancho has yet to join him. This part suits readers starting the novel, since it carries Quixote from dubbing to disillusion in two brisk chapters, with laughter as the true dubbing gift.
6047-works-of-john-bunyan-volume-02:
The second volume of John Bunyan's works, edited by George Offor, gathers experimental, doctrinal, and practical treatises. It opens with The Saints' Knowledge of Christ's Love, or The Unsearchable Riches of Christ. That treatise was one of ten works Bunyan had prepared for press when suddenly summoned, as the editor puts it, to the Celestial City.

Friends in the ministry called the manuscript excellent, fit to help Christians grow in grace and win others over. First published in a folio selection of 1692, about four years after Bunyan's death, it shows deep research and wide usefulness.
6196-cumner-s-son-and-other-south-sea-fo:
The High Court of Budgery-Gar opens Parker's second South Sea volume, camped on a billabong's edge. Barlas kneads damper, Drysdale packs coals about the billy to boil water, and the narrator cooks chops, while hobbled horses pick grass and salt-bush near and Bimbi gathers twigs and bark.

The order of merit runs Barlas, Drysdale, narrator, horses, and Bimbi, then the Cadi alone, given an isolated and indolent place as guest and government representative. Bushmen, skeptical of far-off government, still give its man the lazy side of the fire.
6244-the-right-of-way-volume-02:
Jo Portugais breaks the law of the river, running a little raft downstream at night instead of tying up at sundown. River driver, woodsman, hunter, carpenter, and guide by turns, he has come a hundred and fifty miles down from the nor'west alone, through slides, rapids, and strong currents. The evening Charley Steele meets his mishap, Jo is on the river, defying custom as he has done all his young life.

This second volume carries Charley onward through old debts, a curtain raised, the coming of Rosalie, and a midnight foray by a tailor, ending with the stealing of a cross. Madame Dauphin takes up a mission, and a mark in a paper points to trouble ahead. Parker keeps the river world close, where a man's gifts and his stubbornness decide whether he survives the water and his past.
6602-mysteries-of-paris-volume-02:
Eugène Sue's second volume of Paris mysteries opens in a poor garret, where a lapidary opens his door to two mean-looking men. One, Malicorne, tall and thin with a loaded cane and a mud-stained coat, leads the way, while his short, red-haired mate trails in shabby finery. An execution chapter sets the tone: Paris at its darkest, where the poor are prey.

This volume, the middle of three, follows the threads Sue spun in the first: crime, disguise, and the hope of justice for the lowly. The scenes are vivid, crowded, and fast, with the city itself as a maze. Mysteries of Paris, volume two, is a gripping slice of French serial fiction at its most sensational.
6671-life-of-edward-earl-of-clarendon-vo:
Henry Craik's second volume on Edward, Earl of Clarendon, Lord High Chancellor of England, runs from the Restoration to the triumph of faction. Chapters cover the restored monarchy's prospects, Scottish rule, Irish problems, a marriage treaty, religious settlement, and the Dutch war. Portraits of John Hampden and George Monk, Duke of Albemarle, front the book.

As Clarendon's sway decays, his foes grow bitter and his troubles mount, until faction wins. Craik writes with a biographer's care for politics and character alike. Volume two is a solid, detailed life of a great seventeenth-century statesman in his fall.
6749-voyages-of-samuel-de-champlain-volu:
Volume two of Champlain's voyages, translated by Charles Pomeroy Otis and edited by Edmund Slafter, covers the years 1604 to 1610, with twenty local maps in heliotype. Tall s is turned to plain s, footnotes become endnotes, and old numbers, like 176 and a half and two notes numbered 283, are kept as they stood. The Prince Society imprint frames the work.

A preface notes two poems in Champlain's 1613 edition, tied to his early matter. The voyages that follow trace French settlement, exploration, and Native contact in early Canada. Volume two is a scholarly, vivid record of a founder's middle years on the St. Lawrence.
6760-the-adventures-of-ferdinand-count-f:
Part two of Smollett's Count Fathom opens at chapter thirty-nine, with a new scene of life for the adventurer. He views majesty and its satellites in eclipse, settles one quarrel and fights another with unusual arms, and meets an unexpected turn that changes his affairs. A proverb guides the tale: what's bred in the bone will never come out of the flesh.

Anecdotes of poverty, Renaldo's deepening distress, and Fathom's thickening plot lead to his power over a friend's passions and the art of borrowing. Part two brings the rogue to his reckoning. Volume two is the darker, sharper half of Smollett's great rogue novel.
6771-the-thirty-years-war-volume-02:
Book two of Schiller's Thirty Years' War opens as Ferdinand's new course gives the war a new direction, a new scene, and new actors. From a Bohemian rebellion and the punishment of rebels, war spreads first to Germany, then to Europe. Schiller pauses to survey Germany and Europe, where Catholics and Protestants, unequally divided in land and rights, must each use their own strengths with care.

Neither side, he argues, could stand alone against the other's encroachments without prudent union among its own members. The narrative that follows traces that widening struggle. Book two is the middle opening of Schiller's war history, where a local revolt becomes a continental war.
6777-history-of-the-revolt-of-the-nether:
Book two of Schiller's Revolt of the Netherlands centers on Cardinal Granvella, born Anthony Perenot at Besançon in 1516. His father was a blacksmith's son who rose by merit. He served Margaret of Savoy, regent of the Netherlands, then Charles the Fifth. For twenty years he sat in the emperor's cabinet as privy counsellor and keeper of the seal. Fortune, honors, and state secrets followed.

Granvella, immortalized by his contemporaries' hatred, becomes the face of Spanish rule in the Netherlands. Schiller traces his rise with a historian's eye for power and resentment. Book two is a portrait of a minister whose name became a byword for oppression.
6849-the-prince-of-india-or-why-constant:
Volume two of Lew Wallace's Prince of India continues book four, The Palace of Blacherne, from chapter eleven onward. The princess hears from the world, Lael tells of her two fathers, the Hamari turns boatman, and the princess gains a creed. The Prince of India preaches God to the Greeks, and the tale weighs how the new faith was received.

Lael and the sword of Solomon, a festival of flowers, and castles built for a guest follow, as Constantinople's fate draws near. Wallace keeps the romance vast and the history vivid. Volume two carries the Prince's tale toward the city's fall, with faith, love, and empire in the balance.
6919-darwiniana-essays-volume-02:
Thomas Henry Huxley calls this second volume of collected essays Darwiniana, since its pieces circle the doctrine of evolution. Some treat that ancient idea as rehabilitated and set on a sound scientific footing by the Origin of Species. Others answer the weighty criticisms that fell on Darwin's great work for years after it appeared.

Still other essays record the mark left by Darwin himself on a friend of some thirty years, and sum up his work and its lasting sway over scientific thought. Huxley writes as both champion and witness, defending evolution while recalling the man behind it. The volume stands as a record of a scientific revolution argued in public.
7004-the-antiquary-volume-02:
The second volume of Scott's Antiquary continues the tale in twenty four chapters, with notes to the novel at the close. Illustrations show the funeral of the countess, Lord Glenallen and Elspeth, the Antiquary visiting Edie in prison, and the Antiquary arming for action. The first chapter opens on Wiser Raymondus, pent in his closet, laughing at danger while half his lands go up in golden smoke.

His second hopeful glass is broke, yet he trusts a third furnace may hold, a picture of the collector's hopeful folly. Only this second volume's matter is described here, as old secrets surface and the prison, the funeral, and the arming drive the plot on. Scott keeps the comedy warm even as the mystery darkens.
7024-rob-roy-volume-02:
The second volume of Scott's Rob Roy opens with the hero torn between griefs, as a Burger verse on hurrying riders heads the chapter. He grieves at separation from Miss Vernon, yet less than he might, since his father's apprehended distresses press on his mind. News of Mister Tresham distresses him too, yet less than if it had filled his mind alone.

Scott reflects that man can give only a certain portion of distressful feeling to each cause, and when two press at once sympathy must divide like the funds of a compounding bankrupt. Only this second volume's matter is described here, as the hero rides between love, family ruin, and the outlaw world of Rob Roy. The volume deepens the novel's tangle of heart and honor.
7587-the-caxtons-a-family-picture-volume:
Part two of The Caxtons treats schooling as a forming force, comic as well as serious. The father, who reveres learning, stops trying to rein in his son's mind and lets study run its course. That respect sets the tone: education here is not a chore to be endured, but a passion to be guided. Lytton makes the schoolroom a place where character shows.

The part follows Pisistratus to school, where early success and a return of eager study mark his last two years. Rivalry and a plain wish to do well revive work that had flagged. Dr. Herman, a theorist with learned attacks on every teaching method, adds the comedy, loudest against spelling books. The result is a school story with ideas in it, not just lessons.
7607-zicci-a-tale-volume-02:
Book two of Zicci is the tale's turning point, where a supernatural bargain meets human love. Glyndon faces a night of decision: he must choose, before the first hour of morning, whether to wed Isabel di Pisani or part from her for good. That choice, stated in the volume's old excerpt, gives the book its pressure. Everything else in the part bends toward it.

The book opens in alarm, after Merton and the Italians reach safety at the spot where they left the mules. Only when they recover breath do they think of Glyndon, who does not appear as minutes pass. Merton, good-hearted as most people are, grows seriously alarmed and, by lavish promises, persuades the guide to return and search over ground calm and white in starlight. Rescue and decision thus frame the same night.
7610-eugene-aram-volume-02:
Book two of Eugene Aram is courtship in a scholar's household, tender and ominous at once. Around the engagement moves Ellinor, whose ready temper, household turn, merry laugh, and winning playfulness suit Lester's secret heart even more than her elder sister's graver, higher nature. She gives the household its warmth. Lytton lets happiness gather here before the shadow falls.

The engagement itself is settled in formal and informal ways at once. Aram's affection for Madeline has been formally announced to her father Lester, while Madeline's consent, somewhat less formally obtained, leaves only the wedding day to fix. Lester, forbearing to question Aram about his circumstances, hears the student's frank confession. The chapter heads promise Lester's hopes and schemes, and the truth and fervor of Aram's love, both of which the book keeps in view.
7616-pelham-volume-02:
Henry Pelham, the dandy hero of Bulwer Lytton's Pelham, spends this part in Paris. He dines at the Freres Provencaux, then strolls through the gambling houses of the Palais Royal. The crowd and heat nearly drive him out, until one face holds him.

That face belongs to a man he saw with Thornton that morning, and its stern, ferocious look fixes itself in his memory. Gambling, fashion, and a gathering sense of danger mix here. Pelham's polish hides a watchful mind, and the Paris scenes plant the mystery that later parts pursue.
7625-devereux-volume-02:
Book two of Devereux takes the hero to London. It had just become the fashion for young men of fortune to keep house, giving bachelor establishments the importance once reserved for a married household. Devereux's rooms stand near the court, magnificently furnished.

An anteroom crowds with visitors, and the part savours town pleasure at its height. The chapter heading warns that pleasure is often the shortest road to wisdom, and the earliest. Devereux enters the world early, and the world wastes no time in teaching him. Town life teaches its lessons quickly and without mercy.
7632-the-disowned-volume-02:
The Disowned continues in this part by settling Clarence among new company, where money, manners, and talk all carry hidden meanings. The house belongs to the Copperas family, whose painted shelves hold a small library. Mr. Copperas is a stock-jobber and a wit, his wife a fine lady and a sentimentalist. That household, with its books as furniture and its talk as currency, will test Clarence's manners.

Clarence arrives safely lodged, after a first night whose slumbers are disturbed and brief. Whether the cause is heat or the unease of a strange bed, he sleeps badly. He rises early and finds the parlour being laid for breakfast. The part thus pairs a restless arrival with a settled household, and lets breakfast introduce the people who will matter.
7641-ernest-maltravers-volume-02:
Book Two of Edward Bulwer Lytton's Ernest Maltravers opens at a bright ball in Naples, where crowds gather round Madame de Ventadour, the reigning beauty of the hour. The young hero watches how fame, manner, and mere fashion can crown a woman queen for a season.

Through salons and late talk, Maltravers drifts toward a world of pleasure he half distrusts. He still hears older calls toward beauty, virtue, and great aims, yet the pull of company grows strong. This part charts a gifted youth learning how society shapes, and sometimes spoils, a mind.
7651-kenelm-chillingly-volume-02:
At daybreak Kenelm Chillingly quits his father's house on foot in Book Two of Edward Bulwer Lytton's Kenelm Chillingly. He knows he starts as a copyist, trailing poets and heroes of old, yet hopes something of his own will work free. A skylark over summer corn lifts his heart as he walks.

By nine he reaches a town twelve miles on, where he meets field workers and hears of Tom Bowles. Over beer beneath thorn trees, he listens with grave kindness to Jessie, a girl in trouble. The volume pairs high talk of fable with plain human need on the road.
7660-what-will-he-do-with-it-volume-02:
Lionel Haughton rides five miles of rough parish road to Fawley Manor in Book Two of Edward Bulwer Lytton's What Will He Do With It? Wide commons, beech woods, and no village spire mark an older England, far from the gay river scenes he has left. The place invites rest and plain talk.

There he hears how Guy Darrell and his father Charlie were warm friends as boys, and how Charlie's gay town life and debts broke that bond. A servant's slip opens the old wound, and Lionel presses for the truth. The volume links landscape, family pride, and a quarrel that still shapes the living.
7673-harold-the-last-of-the-saxon-kings-:
Book Two of Lytton's Harold is subtitled Lanfranc the Scholar. It pictures Saxon daily life in plain terms: four meals a day from earl to ceorl, yet food never sweet under servitude. Danish feasts taught Angles to eat and drink to excess, a habit the author deplores.

Against this stands King Edward the Confessor, raised among Normans. He loves sober manners and church rite, and trusts clerks more than earls. The volume follows Lanfranc's rise and William's wrath when a priest bars his wedding. Learning and power meet in a tense court, where church and crown contend.
7686-lucretia-volume-02:
Sir Miles St. John holds court in his state room in the second volume of Edward Bulwer Lytton's Lucretia. The old gentleman, stiff yet hearty, keeps his bed behind a screen in King James's chamber, ringed by Italian curios and faded gilt leather, with a gallery close by for wet days.

Conferences follow: letters grow colder, a boy named Gabriel is pressed to read a poem, and a secret begins to clear at a first glance. Susan loves, though she hardly knows it yet. Through formal talk and household detail, the novel shows how pride and old manners hide young feeling.
7693-a-strange-story-volume-02:
Mrs. Poyntz sends a twisted note to Dr. Fenwick in the second volume of Edward Bulwer Lytton's A Strange Story, summoning him at once. She has spent the evening with the Ashleighs and finds Lilian much altered, weak, and ill treated by Dr. Jones, so she insists on a change of doctor.

Honor holds her back from naming Fenwick outright as suitor, yet her talk points that way. Later Fenwick returns to his own work on knowledge from the senses, after Lilian's departure leaves a void. The volume blends matchmaking, medicine, and a young man's earnest philosophy.
7703-my-novel-volume-02:
Mr. Caxton insists each book needs an opening chapter in Book Two of Edward Bulwer Lytton's My Novel, citing Fielding's rule in Tom Jones. A reader, he says, gains by starting at the fourth page, a boon for those who read only to say they have read.

Pisistratus argues back with good humor, while the tale turns to Riccabocca, a learned Italian whom a widow admires yet fears as Papist and conjuror. Lenny's dislike halts all talk of marriage. The volume mixes literary jest with village courtship and scholarly pride.
7716-the-last-of-the-barons-volume-02:
Young men ride the Strand in Book Two of Edward Bulwer Lytton's The Last of the Barons, subtitled The King's Court. Toll profits have made the road passable, lined by half-fortified mansions toward the river and merchants' garden villas decked with the fleur-de-lis of Agincourt.

They press toward a fair chain of fields, brooks turning mills, and the famous Cross where judges once sat. At court, Warwick the Kingmaker's barge nears a palace gay with awnings below Traitor's Gate. The volume paints London on the eve of the Wars of the Roses.
7729-paul-clifford-volume-02:
Paul wakes in prison in the second volume of Lytton's Paul Clifford. He finds odd comfort there: ladies and gentlemen share his cell. A learned note on human nature says most things bring more pleasure than pain, even to a youth with bleak prospects.

The volume follows Paul through balls and routs in earlier, freer days. Then it returns to confinement, where wit and company blunt fear. Through learned jests and prison scenes, the novel asks how a boy first learns crime: not from nature, but from the company punishment itself provides.
7738-the-parisians-volume-02:
Graham Vane sits absorbed before a writing table in the Rue d'Anjou. This is Book Two of Lytton's The Parisians, weeks after the last chapter, with lime trees greening in the Tuileries. His broad forehead, frank face, and dark auburn hair mark a man of power and honor.

In private theatricals he can change his whole look by forcing his hair to his brows. The volume fills in his parentage and place, showing a youth who lent his mind to debate and stagecraft. It sets an Englishman of principle down in Paris, on the edge of love and politics.
7822-the-attache-or-sam-slick-in-england:
Thomas Chandler Haliburton's The Attache, or Sam Slick in England, volume two, introduces its Yankee hero through a letter dated London, July 3, 1843. The author begs Edmund Hopkinson of Edgeworth to receive his attache, whose politics match his own though his humor needs indulgence.

Contents promise the nose of a spy, the patron or the cow's tail, and Ascot races, among other chapters. Through Sam Slick's quaint sayings and queer views of England, Haliburton turns an American visitor's eye on English manners, with satire that cuts both ways across the Atlantic.
7902-american-historical-and-literary-cu: Part two of American Historical and Literary Curiosities by John Jay Smith and John F. Watson is, in this text file, an editor's note and title page and little else. The editor explains that the series is built from illustrations and page images, with only a few passages suitable for scanning, and directs readers to the HTML version.
8780-the-divine-comedy-by-dante-illustra:
Cary's Inferno continues in this second part, cantos three and four, where Dante actually enters Hell. Over a portal's arch he reads, in dim colour. The terrible inscription: through me you pass into the city of woe, into eternal pain, among the people lost for ever. All hope abandon, ye who enter here. Virgil answers Dante's fear by bidding him leave all distrust behind.

Inside, the neutrals swarm, the ferryman Charon gathers souls, and Limbo holds the virtuous unbaptized and great pagans in a green, sighing meadow. Dante meets Homer, Horace, Ovid, and Lucan, and the noble castle of philosophy. The part moves from terror to a strange, honoured calm, and it introduces Dante's way of judging souls by meeting them, not merely by naming their sins. It is essential reading for anyone entering the poem.
9109-the-project-gutenberg-faq-2002:
Jim Tinsley wrote this FAQ for Project Gutenberg in 2002, when the free book project was still young. It is posted now as a historical record, not as a current guide. Tinsley warns readers to check the live Gutenberg site for up-to-date facts. The file is thus a snapshot of its own time.

Questions cover how to ask for help, how to make a text, and where volunteers talked shop. Answers point to the Volunteers' Board and the gutvol-d mailing list. For students of digital books, it shows how a volunteer army first learned to build a free library.
9400-a-select-collection-of-old-english-:
Volume two of A Select Collection of Old English Plays gathers short Tudor stage works, first set out by Robert Dodsley in 1744. This fourth edition, reworked by W. Carew Hazlitt, sets the plays in time order and adds notes from many scholars. The pieces here come from the 1500s, when English stage art was still young. They mix mirth, moral teaching, and plain stage craft.

Readers meet The Interlude of Youth, Lusty Juventus, Jack Juggler, Nice Wanton, Jacob and Esau, The Disobedient Child, and The Marriage of Wit and Science. Some preach against vice, some poke fun at folly, and some stage Bible tales. A student of early drama gets rare plays in one place, with notes that place each work in its age.
9764-alice-or-the-mysteries-book-02:
Book two of Edward Bulwer Lytton's Alice, or The Mysteries, opens with a meditation on beauty as twice blessed. Beauty, Lytton writes, blesses gazer and possessor at once, and often proves both effect and cause of goodness. A sweet soul speaks through eyes, lips, and brow, the chapter claims. Spenser lines on spring and harvest frame the book's mood.

The book follows the wanderer's return, as Homer's verse promises new trials in Ithaca. Lytton's polished prose weighs looks, virtue, and fate together. A reader gets the second book of a Victorian mystery romance, where beauty itself becomes a moral question.
a-compilation-of-the-messages-and-papers: Andrew Jackson's second term occupies this third volume part compiled by James Daniel Richardson. The volume covers the four years of Jackson's second term together with the four years of Van Buren that follow. Its papers include reports on the bank and other questions of the age. Richardson's compilation keeps the official record of the Jacksonian era in order.
a-modern-chronicle-volume-02:
Winston Churchill's A Modern Chronicle, volume two, continues Book One at chapter seven, The Olympian Order. Honora rides the Pullman along the shining Hudson toward Sutton and the country-house world. Ethel Wing, tall and brilliant in a blue tailor-made gown, embodies that order for her. A Chapter of Conquests and the Vicomte's studies fill the visit.

Honora widens her horizon among the Wing set, whose wealth seems to her a kind of godhood. What Might Have Been turns her toward the marriage market she is entering. A surprise for Mrs. Holt closes the volume's six chapters. Churchill savours the comedy of a provincial girl measuring Olympus at close range. The Olympians prove magnificent, idle, and dangerous in proportion. Honora's education in the world's terms — money, horses, and eligible men — is the real curriculum of Book One's second half.
a-select-collection-of-old-english-plays: Robert Dodsley continues his select collection of old English plays in this second volume, revised and enlarged with notes by W. Carew Hazlitt. Its contents run from moral interludes of youth and wantonness, through a jesting Jack Juggler and the history of Jacob and Esau. A disobedient child and a marriage of wit and science complete the set. Only two or three copies survive of The Interlude of Youth, hailed as the most interesting early-printed moral play of its kind.
a-strange-story-volume-02: Edward Bulwer Lytton continues his strange story in this second volume, opening with a twisted note summoning the narrator, Allen Fenwick, to Mrs Poyntz. She reports an evening with the Ashleighs. Lilian is much altered, very weak, very ill, and very unskilfully treated by Doctor Jones. Bound as Fenwick's confidante, Mrs Poyntz must press for a change of physician without betraying the secret that Fenwick admires Lilian, or naming him as a possible son-in-law.
a-thorny-path-volume-02:
Moonlight leads a festival crowd home in Volume 2 of A Thorny Path, by Georg Ebers, set in Alexandria. Ebers describes Greeks returning from Eleusis, where they had kept the mysteries, secret rites of worship, in the Greek manner adapted to Egypt. Serapis stands in the place of Pluto here, and Greek forms have taken on Egyptian shapes along the road from the city of the dead.

Chapter V stays with the noise and wear of the procession. Torches burn low, ivy and myrtle wreaths hang limp, and the hymn singers lose their ranks. The old cry to the sea still rises, and the call for Iakchos, a name of the wine god, to stay with the crowd. Under the merriment sits the book's real divide: Greek rite, Egyptian god, and a small Christian circle watching both.
a-tramp-abroad-volume-02:
France takes its first insult in A Tramp Abroad, Part 2, by Mark Twain, while Heidelberg gets a second helping. Twain devotes Chapter VIII to the great French duel, a formal affair of honor he reports with mistaken notions corrected and an outbreak in the newspapers. Pistols at dawn, in his telling, become a ceremony so careful that nobody is in much danger except from embarrassment.

The theater and the opera follow, including four hours with Wagner that test the tramp's endurance and his ear. Lessons in art produce his own great picture of Heidelberg Castle, judged with mock seriousness. Then the Rathhaus, an old robber knight named Gotz, and the log rafts and raftsmen of the Neckar carry the party back to the river. Twain's method settles in here: one part genuine admiration, one part tall tale, and no institution left unpricked.
a-word-only-a-word-volume-02:
Volume 2 of A Word, Only a Word, by Georg Ebers, opens on a night flight prepared in silence. Ebers shows the smith Adam woken by Ulrich's knock, grasping the danger at once. While the boy confesses, Adam packs his hidden savings, fills a bag, takes his lightest hammer, and pours water on the glowing coals of the forge in this volume.

Chapter VIII explains the errand: a plot is moving against a Jewish doctor, and word reached Adam through a juggler who hears everything. The doctor is found awake and ready to flee, with no complaint and no hasty gesture. He wakes his wife and his daughter Ruth while old Rahel rushes in, lamenting in a foreign tongue and gathering up bundles. Persecution here arrives as a midnight knock, and friendship answers with a packed bag.
abraham-lincoln-a-history-volume-02: John George Nicolay, with John Hay, writes the second volume of their history of Abraham Lincoln, published by the Century Company in 1890. The contents run from Jefferson Davis on rebellion and the conventions of 1856 through congressional ruffianism and the Dred Scott decision to Douglas and Lincoln on Dred Scott. The Lecompton constitution, the revolt of Douglas, the Lincoln-Douglas debates, the Freeport doctrine, and Harper's Ferry carry the story toward war.
alice-or-the-mysteries-book-02: Edward Bulwer Lytton continues Alice, or the Mysteries with a meditation on beauty as both effect and cause of goodness, in the manner of Spenser and Terence. The second book deepens the heroine's character and the moral questions around love, virtue, and appearance. Its reflective opening gives way to the social scenes and private choices that drive the romance forward.
american-historical-and-literary-curiosi: John Jay Smith's second part of American Historical and Literary Curiosities continues a picture-led series on the American past. Because the work consists of plates and page images, little running text could be digitised here, and the note inside directs readers to the HTML file for the full display. Collectors and students will find visual records of historic papers and portraits.
an-egyptian-princess-volume-02:
Volume 2 of An Egyptian Princess carries Georg Ebers and his historical novel deeper into the court world of ancient Persia and Egypt. Ebers, a German scholar of Egypt, built fiction from close study of old sources. The story turns on Nitetis, an Egyptian king's daughter sent to Persia, and on King Cambyses, whose drinking and pride threaten everyone near him.

Chapter III opens after a banquet at the house of Rhodopis, the Greek hostess at Naukratis whose guests include Croesus and young Persian nobles. Talk turns to Cambyses, his marriage to Atossa, and the sadness of palace life. Sappho and Darius appear among the guests, and private love sits beside public power. Readers get court talk, careful manners, and the slow build of danger around the throne.
arabian-nights-burton-1885-vol-02:
Burton's second volume of the Thousand Nights and a Night appeared in 1885, in step with the first. Shahrazad's nightly bargain with King Shahryar continues: each dawn leaves a tale unfinished, and her life is spared one more day. The stories in this stretch widen the book's world of caliphs, fishermen, and enchanters.

Baghdad under Harun al-Rashid begins to loom large in Burton's pages. Lovers, thieves, and wandering dervishes take their turns inside tales within tales. Burton's English mixes archaisms with street talk to match the Arabic shifts of tone. His footnotes, learned and earthy, run beside the text throughout. Readers who finish volume one meet here the cycle in full flood.
arabian-nights-burton-supplemental-1886-:
Volume two of Burton's Supplemental Nights, issued from 1886 onward, continues the further tales beyond the main ten volumes. Burton gathered them from Arabic manuscripts that the standard cycle left out. Shahrazad's frame still governs, but the store now draws on wider and later sources.

The tales here share the main set's mixture of wonder, romance, and rough comedy. Burton translates with the same literal care and loads the same learned notes. For scholars, the supplement preserves stories that tidier editions never print at all. For readers, it is simply more Nights, told in the established voice. The Gutenberg text is ebook 3446. Burton's appetite for the whole tradition drives every page.
arachne-volume-02:
Storehouse walls open Volume 2 of Arachne, where Georg Ebers surveys the wealth that rules Tennis. Ebers describes a plain whitewashed storehouse at the north end of the little city, set on stone blocks washed by the waves. Its owner is Archias, master of the largest weaving works in town and father of a guest who arrived from Alexandria the night before.

Ships once unloaded flax, linen, and wool straight into the building, but the factories stood too far away for cheap hauling. Archias dug a canal from the workshops to the water and built a second storehouse at its end. Trade detail like this grounds the romance. Cloth money pays for the art, parties, and ambitions that pull the sculptor Hermon and his rivals through the tale.
arxiv-2412-03702:
Behrad Moniri and Hamed Hassani present a study from twenty twenty-four on linear regression when the input traits lean on each other. Standard theory takes the traits as free of each other and bell curved. Real traits often link in space and time and break that mold. The pair model such traits as processes with a space time spread.

They study ridge regression when both sample count and trait count grow in step. A universality claim shows the long run acts the same if bell curved traits with the same spread stand in. That swap lets random matrix tools pin the error down in a fixed point form. Best penalty picks, overfit, and the double descent curve are read in this linked world.
arxiv-2412-05602:
Lasha Otarashvili, Tamilselvan Subramanian, Jason Holmberg, J. J. Levenson, and Charles Stewart build one system to recognize individual animals across many species in a 2024 study. Ecologists identify animals from photos to track populations, but training a separate model per species is costly and starves rare species of data. Shared looks across species also go unused.

The authors assemble a large community-curated data set spanning many species. A single re-identification model trains on all of it at once. Pooling data should help species with few photos while cutting repeated engineering work. The approach lowers the barrier for conservation groups that need individual tracking.
arxiv-2412-13602:
Wenye Lin and colleagues built GAMEBoT in 2024, an arena for testing how well large language models actually reason. Existing reasoning benchmarks are hard to interpret, quickly saturate, or risk leaking into training data. Games offer a cleaner testbed, because strong play demands planning that can be checked step by step against the rules.

GAMEBoT breaks the reasoning inside games into predefined modular subproblems. For each subproblem the designers wrote chain-of-thought prompts that feed the model the relevant domain knowledge before it chooses an action, and rule-based algorithms that compute the correct answer for every subproblem. That makes it possible to grade not only the final moves but the intermediate reasoning itself. The setup also reduces contamination risk, giving a transparent way to compare models' reasoning quality.
arxiv-2412-14002:
Panagiotis Grontas, Anastasios Tsiamis, and John Lygeros build a way that scales for choice tasks with bounds that bulge out, named for Markov. Off the shelf solvers for such tasks work in base rules but scale poor in use. Their first step way rests on a split named for Douglas and Rachford. It splits the move rules of the set from the bounds.

The way swaps steps. One step solves a choice task with a soft add on. The next step casts the result back to the bound set. Both steps are plain to code. The soft add on is built in. It gives last step meet and firm counts with no plain change to the task. When bounds can not all be met, the way spots that fact. It then works out a plan that breaks the bounds by the least sum.
arxiv-2412-18802:
Zhun Gou and colleagues solved a class of leader-follower games under uncertainty in a 2024 math paper. In a Stackelberg game, a leader commits to a strategy first and a follower replies, here with both sides steering a noisy system over time and costs measured in a linear-quadratic way. Extra affine limits tie the leader's choices to the follower's response, which complicates the contest.

Using stochastic Riccati equations and duality theory, the authors derive feedback forms for both players' best strategies. Under a standard feasibility condition, the leader's problem matches its dual, and a checklist condition helps solve it. A new positivity condition secures a unique answer, and two worked examples with indefinite weights support the theory.
arxiv-2412-19902:
Popadiuk and ten co-authors gauge spin waves in thin films of the full Heusler mix Co2FeGe. That mix is a pick for gear that uses spin. Films were grown on magnesium oxide bases in not the same heat states. Light spread named for Brillouin and pull wave tests probed how their pull traits shift and move.

A lay down at room heat and then a bake at three hundred degrees for one hour gave the best mix of traits. That plan gave most pull strength and most swap stiffness. It gave least loss of spin moves, just what fast spin gear wants. The team also saw strong mix of spin waves in the Damon-Eshbach shape. Such mix draws staff who build paths that route facts with waves in place of streams of charge.
arxiv-2501-03802:
Chiara Castello and colleagues studied a family of error-correcting codes built for network communication in 2025. Cyclic orbit codes live in the geometry of subspaces: a single subspace is rotated by a cyclic group to generate the whole codebook. The paper pursues two questions, how to tell when two such codes are really the same, and how close a code can come to the best possible parameters, the quasi-optimality question.

For the first, the authors connect a code's words to a linear set on the projective line, a translation that yields fresh bounds on code parameters. For the second, they isolate one family of near-optimal codes and prove a general existence theorem for quasi-optimal examples in even-dimensional spaces over finite fields of any characteristic. They finish by describing the chosen family's symmetry groups, both geometric and Galois.
arxiv-2501-16002:
Wu and co-authors present ScaDyG, a scalable way to learn from graphs that change over time. Dynamic graphs record ties that evolve, with wide real-world use. Most graph networks pass messages and add time tricks, but growing history makes them hard to scale.

ScaDyG first splits past interactions into time steps, within and between steps. That split allows weight-free, time-aware spreading of features during preprocessing. Fine detail inside steps comes from temporal encoding built on exponential functions. A hypernetwork then fuses each node's history adaptively. The design targets industry-scale graphs where older methods bog down in historical data.
arxiv-2502-01502:
Mohammad Sabri, Marc Riera, and Antonio González addressed a wear problem in 2025: the memory cells inside neural network accelerators wear out. Accelerators built on resistive RAM compute efficiently in place, promising big energy savings over standard chips. But each inference run rewrites cells, and the cells endure only a limited number of write cycles. A chip that dies young is no bargain, however fast it starts.

Their method, Hamun, uses rough computation to prolong the hardware's life. By accepting small, controlled inaccuracies, the scheduler can reduce or redistribute the writes that age the cells. Self-tuning scheduling already adjusts these accelerators to each network's demands; Hamun adds lifespan as a clear goal. Extending service life is what would let resistive RAM accelerators compete honestly with durable standard processors in data centers.
arxiv-2502-03302:
Chand and Jacob build an image fix frame that stands firm near true data. The frame is an energy form with bends at more than one scale. Its dip stands for how apt a scene is in chance terms. A learned net sets the scale weights for that dip. Slope caps keep the dip bent up near the true data cloud. The team calls the frame LC-MUSE in their text.

They use the frame to fix shots from meagre reads. The frame gives one sole best fix for each such task. Paths to that fix come with proof they land there. Small shakes in the reads fail to break the fix by much. On twin-coil MR shots, the frame beat top firm past tools. It tied plug-in and end-trained tools on the same shots.
arxiv-2502-08902:
Chenghao Zhang and colleagues recovered true-scale three-dimensional shape from one photo in a 2025 paper. Depth alone cannot give real size without knowing the camera's internal settings, its intrinsics, which phones and robots often lack. The authors prove depth itself constrains those settings, and the two unknowns hold each other in check, so they can be learned together rather than in sequence.

Their CoL3D framework trains one network to estimate depth and intrinsics jointly, checking consistency at the level of depth, camera parameters, and the rebuilt point cloud. A canonical incidence field prior helps the camera side learn. A shape similarity loss in point cloud space polishes the result. Single-image metric recovery matters for navigation and grasping.
arxiv-2502-09902:
Saikat Banerjee and Piers Coleman take on a paradox in heat reads of many solids: a large heat store like that of free charges, with no like mark in how heat flows. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

At first sight, the clash backs a spread of stuck states in the bulk. The team maps heat flow reads onto charge-like circuits of flow and store. They argue a jam of slow heat paths is apt to arise in both rival views: stuck states, or a sea of neutral free-like parts. The jam comes from the huge gap between how much heat charges store and how much the grid stores. They give a new read of past data that can split the two.
arxiv-2502-13402:
F. Alves-Júnior, A. Lemos, and F. Brito applied the de Broglie–Bohm reading of quantum theory to an anisotropic universe with extra dimensions in a 2025 paper. Quantum cosmology asks how the universe itself evolved from a quantum state; the Bohmian version gives definite trajectories instead of probabilities alone. Their universe is filled with stiff matter and described by a Gaussian wave function depending on momenta and dispersion parameters for each direction, including the hidden extra dimensions.

Solutions show those extra dimensions stabilizing through dynamical compactification. Two patterns appear: dimensions born large at the cosmic bounce that shrink to a small size, or born small and growing to a finite stable value. A special five-dimensional case, where the Wheeler–DeWitt equation degenerates, is treated separately.
arxiv-2502-17102:
Evelia Garcia Barroso, Pedro Gonzalez Perez, and Patrick Popescu-Pampu explain a geometric object called a lotus and show how it can serve as a computing device for curve singularities. A singularity is a point where a curve crosses or pinches in a complicated way, and resolving it takes a sequence of blow-up steps. Earlier work by the group showed that each resolution produces a lotus, a small layered complex built from subdivided polygons, which unifies older tree diagrams used to encode the singularity type. Their paper grew out of a lecture course from twenty twenty-three.

On the lotus, one can read off or compute step by step key numbers of the singularity, including measures of how bad the point is and trees that classify its branches. Three running examples carry the explanations. A final section adapts the method for work in positive characteristic, where the arithmetic differs.
arxiv-2502-17802:
Huaxin Lin proved a stability theorem in 2025 about maps that almost behave like group representations. The setting is operator algebra: a countable, discrete, amenable group, and maps sending its elements to unitary operators on a Hilbert space. An almost representation multiplies correctly only up to a small error on a finite test set, and satisfies a lower-bound condition after passing to a quotient algebra. The question is whether such an approximate object must sit near an exact homomorphism.

Lin's answer is yes. Given any tolerance and any finite set of group elements, a suitable closeness threshold guarantees a true homomorphism within that tolerance on the set. Results of this kind, almost implies near, underlie perturbation theory for operator algebras and some approaches to classifying C-star algebras. They reassure users that approximate symmetries in infinite-dimensional systems are not illusions.
arxiv-2502-18802:
Tatsuya Aoyama and Ethan Wilcox ask why language models stop resembling human readers after a point in training, in a two thousand twenty-five paper. A model's power to predict human reading behavior rises early in pretraining. Past a tipping point, it plateaus or gets worse.

The authors blame a phase transition inside the model. During this transition, specialized attention heads emerge rapidly. Correlational and causal experiments support the claim. Interestingly, the new attention patterns do not directly cause the decline. Instead, the transition changes the model's later learning dynamics. Further training after the transition keeps damaging the human likeness. The finding connects internal model reorganization to an externally measured behavior.
arxiv-2503-01502: Juergen Rossmann proves that the time-dependent Stokes system, the linearized equations of viscous flow, has strong solutions when the flow region is a polygon. The boundary values are prescribed. Corners are the enemy of regularity theory, since solutions can misbehave near sharp angles. Writing in twenty twenty-five, Rossmann works in weighted Sobolev spaces, where the weight is a power of the distance to the corner points. Allowed badness near corners is measured and controlled rather than ignored, and in that setting he establishes existence of strong solutions.
arxiv-2503-05602:
Roberto Florez-Ablan, Marco Roth, and Jan Schnabel deliver unwelcome news for quantum machine learning: tuned quantum kernels quietly become classical ones.
