Quantum kernels promise advantage by embedding data in quantum states, but their signals concentrate and generalization suffers. Bandwidth tuning, rescaling the data, is the standard rescue. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the team shows numerically that optimally tuned quantum kernels closely mimic the classical radial basis kernel. Worse, the tuning's size simplifies them further, toward low-order polynomial kernels. Both fidelity and projected kernel families show the pattern, across encodings and data sets.

A simple analytic model explains the mechanism. The conclusion is measured but firm: with bandwidth tuning doing the heavy lifting, no quantum advantage survives in these setups. The work redirects the search for advantage toward untuned or structurally different kernels.
arxiv-2503-10802:
James Matthews and ten co-authors review, in twenty twenty-five, blast waves and reverse shocks in fast outflows from space objects. Such models are used for gamma-ray bursts, the most fast flows known. They are also used for slower jets from X-ray binary stars. The team asks how the two cases match and where they part.

They show how blast wave size grows with time in the fast case. For set energy, reverse shocks cross the jet much later in slow systems than in fast ones. In X-ray binaries, the cross can take ten to one hundred days. That makes these jets good test beds for shock physics. The authors also weigh shape, spread, and how to tell shock parts apart in real data.
arxiv-2503-12002:
Mark Pustilnik, Antonio Loquercio, and Francesco Borrelli study game-theoretic equilibria in autonomous racing, in a two thousand twenty-five paper. When racing cars share track constraints, their joint behavior is modeled as a generalized Nash equilibrium. The standard way to compute one assumes every player shares identical multipliers for the shared constraints.

That normalized assumption, the authors show, throws away other valuable equilibria. A simple racing example exposes the shortcoming clearly. They then build a method based on the mixed complementarity problem to find non-normalized equilibria. Tests in realistic racing scenarios show richer, multi-modal interactions between cars. The approach widens the set of strategies race planners can consider.
arxiv-2503-13702:
Logan Becker, Francois Baccelli, and Thibaud Taillefumier asked whether faint synchrony explains the hidden stats of brain voltage in a 2025 paper. Neurons sharing a stimulus still fire variably, and their membrane voltages fluctuate far more than free-standing-input models predict. Earlier work showed weak synchrony among inputs could match the size of those fluctuations. This study tests the same idea against richer traits, how voltages in unlike cells move jointly and how lopsided the voltage spread is.

Borrowing fixed-point tools from queuing theory, the authors run a broad moment analysis of conductance-based neurons fed by correlated jump-like inputs. Weak but nonzero synchrony consistently reproduced the gauged covariance and skewness too. One mechanism accounts for three separate test facts.
arxiv-2503-17102:
Thomas Schnappinger and Markus Kowalewski work out how a molecule's response to electric fields changes inside an optical cavity in a 2025 study. When molecular vibrations couple firmly to trapped light, chemistry itself can shift, a field called polaritonic chemistry. Whether the collective coupling reaches down and changes each single molecule's traits is still unsettled.

The authors derive a closed formula for static polarizability under vibrational strong coupling, inside linear response theory. Polarizability gauges how easily the electron cloud deforms, a basic ingredient of reactivity. A clean formula gives the field a testable handle on the local-versus-collective debate.
arxiv-2504-01302:
Han Wang and six co-authors build GLaD, a graphics-chip tool that models both the bend of light by a galaxy and the motion of its stars, in one frame. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

The lag of light from a lensed quasar gives a clean gauge of how fast the cosmos grows. But a warp in lens models adds doubt to that gauge. Star motion gives a free check on the mass that bends the light. The team joins both in one code that runs on graphics chips. On fake data for a known lensed quasar, fine motion data pin the growth rate to a few parts in a hundred. They test what a giant black hole does to that mark.
arxiv-2504-14202:
Zichuan Liu, Liming Jiang, and colleagues present a way to generate images that keep a person's identity in a 2025 computer vision study. Earlier tools bolted identity features onto a trained model through adapters. Prompts also carry text instructions, and the two signals can pull against each other.

Their encoder, FaceCLIP, learns one shared space for a face, the prompt text, and images. Given a reference face and a prompt, it produces a single combined signal that steers a diffusion model. A training procedure aligns that signal with face, text, and image representations. The built system aims for portraits that look like the person and match the words.
arxiv-2504-19102:
Mitra Mansouri and Hadi Salmasian give a pure algebra treatment of a class of functions on groups that mix signs, known as supergroups. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

The functions they study stay the same when shifted on both sides by a sub-group. The team builds them as a part of a dual algebra, cut out by a set ideal. For a broad class of paired super structures, they define how to trim such a function down to a core subspace. They prove that trim loses no facts. For one set pair, they compute a base for the ideal and find a link to two famed count lines.
arxiv-2505-03202:
Xiang-Dong Li carries Perelman's entropy machinery from smooth Ricci flow into the rougher world of metric measure spaces. The W-entropy and the concavity of Shannon entropy power are central tools in geometric analysis. Extending them to super Ricci flows on singular spaces widens where they can be used.

Along the way he proves a Harnack inequality of Li-Yau-Hamilton-Perelman type in the same generality. A headline application shows that, on a class of spaces with synthetic Ricci bounds, volume non-collapsing is equivalent to the W-entropy staying bounded below. The entropy also yields the logarithmic Sobolev inequality with its optimal constant on these flows. The work unifies several strands of modern geometry.
arxiv-2505-15202:
Yu Zhang, Linyu Peng, and Bing-Zhao Li present a study from twenty twenty-five on filling in graph signals that take complex values. A graph signal gives each node a value, like a trait or a reading. In many fields the values are complex, with two parts. Kernel methods can rebuild such signals from samples on a few nodes, but the complex case was near untouched.

Their frame plants the nodes in a high dimensional complex space that hugs a low dimensional shape. Standard kernel tools then stretch to that shape, with tools for its curves and measures. They give both classic kernels and ones built from the graph's own links. Tests on fake and real data beat plain kernel routes.
arxiv-2506-11502:
Mark van der Pas and four co-authors give a reference model and a set of patterns to enrich the event data that plants spew out. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

Firms now log vast data as their work runs across many systems. Joined, those logs can bare new facts for watch and study of how work does. That join is most often done by hand, in a slow, ad hoc way. The model gives a standard way to store and draw out such data. It joins a known trade standard with a graph form for event facts. The patterns list the common draw-out tasks and how each can be run by machine.
arxiv-2506-18702:
Xiao Ma and Michael Cates explored in 2025 what happens when attraction between phases of a fluid refuses to be mutual. Non-reciprocal interactions, where one component chases another that flees it, are among the simplest ways to push a system out of equilibrium, and they produce patterns equilibrium physics forbids. Their minimal model has three separating phases, two interacting non-reciprocally, with the third acting as a spectator that mimics a boundary.

Simulations revealed three regimes sorted by driving strength. In the mildest, droplets settle into a quasi-static state with well-defined non-equilibrium contact angles where the three phases meet. Stronger driving sets the bulk phases rotating endlessly around the contact line in a limit cycle. Stronger still produces travelling waves with persistent directional motion. Linear stability analysis and a wave speed calculation near equilibrium complete the picture, a starter theory of wetting far from equilibrium.
arxiv-2506-20302:
Abbas Anwar and colleagues combined two fashionable techniques in 2025 to clean up damaged photographs. Images shot in poor conditions arrive noisy, blurred, color-shifted, or veiled by scattered light, and every flaw degrades the detection and classification systems that consume them. Their model, TDiR, pairs a transformer, which reads global structure, with a diffusion process, which rebuilds detail step by step, aiming at restoration rather than mere filtering.

The authors evaluated it on three distinct restoration jobs, underwater enhancement, denoising, and rain removal, spread across five standard benchmark sets. Against eighteen competing state-of-the-art methods scored on four quality metrics, their model came out ahead. They argue the pairing is the point: diffusion supplies the generative power to invent plausible detail, while the transformer keeps that invention faithful to the scene's overall layout.
arxiv-2506-22502:
Matvei Anoshin and others stabilize industrial processes by replacing a classic optimizer with two neural networks working as predictor and optimizer. Keeping quantities like temperature steady is a standing problem across industry, and conventional solvers spend heavily on pointwise optimization. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the team reframes the job. An oracle network learns to predict the process, and an optimizer network learns control actions, converting repeated pointwise solving into network training. Once trained, control is read off the networks rather than computed fresh at each step.

On their temperature control tests, the pipeline improved stability about threefold compared with ordinary solvers, while demanding fewer computational resources. The authors present the approach as a general template for steadying time series processes in factories, where both quality and compute cost matter.
arxiv-2506-23402:
Luca Vecchi weighs how a strange quark could contribute to the neutron's electric dipole moment in a 2025 particle physics study. A permanent dipole moment in the neutron would signal new sources of symmetry breaking beyond the standard model. Hypothetical electric dipoles on quarks are one possible origin, and the strange quark's share was unclear.

Vecchi lines up several lines of argument, from perturbative theory and large-number expansions to a fresh look at the simple quark model and an effective field theory calculation. All point the same way: the strange contribution should run near a tenth of the up and down quark parts. In many new-physics scenarios that makes it the dominant piece.
arxiv-2507-07202:
Mohamed Elmoghany and a large team of co-authors survey long-video storytelling generation in a two thousand twenty-five review paper. Today's best video models produce only five to sixteen seconds, and longer clips lose character consistency and scene coherence.

Some methods reach one hundred fifty seconds but with redundant frames and weak temporal variety. The authors study thirty-two papers to find which architectural components and training strategies reliably deliver multi-character narratives with fidelity. They build a taxonomy of existing methods and comparative tables organized by design and performance. The survey maps what cinematic quality, consistency, and length actually require from the next generation of video models.
arxiv-2507-11002:
Kim and co-authors improve a hybrid quantum-neural method for finding the lowest energy state of a system. The earlier method let a neural network adjust a quantum circuit's output. Its non-unitary steps broke normalization and made training unstable. Measurement costs also grew steeply with each added qubit. The new version, U-VQNHE, forces the neural part to stay unitary.

That fix removes the normalization problem at its root. Training stays steadier, and far fewer measurements are needed. Accuracy still beats standard variational quantum methods. The authors frame the design as a step toward methods that scale. Ground state estimates matter for chemistry and materials work.
arxiv-2507-12602:
Ohamouddou and four colleagues classify tree species from LiDAR point clouds with a multi-scale graph neural network. Point density varies enormously between trunk and canopy, yet standard graph methods encode edge geometry the same way at every scale. The authors prove this is suboptimal: normalized features suit high signal-to-noise regimes, raw displacements suit low ones.

Their network uses raw vectors locally and hybrid encodings at intermediate scales, with scale-dependent normalization. Ablations confirm each design choice, including robustness under canopy thinning and noise. On a seven-species terrestrial scanning benchmark it reached the highest accuracy among fifty-six models with a compact parameter count. Airborne data results were also competitive.
arxiv-2507-16102:
Alyssa Chan and Eva Kanso explain why a fish school remembers: not because it can sit in two stable states, but because noise smears a tipping point. Schools switch between polarized swimming and rotational milling. A standard model, with avoidance, alignment, and attraction rules, shows collective memory. Its patterns depend on the group's history. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the pair combine simulations with bifurcation theory. The switch between milling and schooling turns out to be a transcritical bifurcation, where the two states cross and swap stability. Random noise stretches that crossing into a memory effect.

A simple model of the group's polarization captures the essentials: the bifurcation, the lingering transient milling, and the memory itself. The finding resolves a standing ambiguity about the memory's origin. Noise, usually a nuisance, is here the mechanism.
arxiv-2508-12502:
Marta Esteves, writing alone in two thousand twenty-five, builds a logic for what-if thought, based on a gauge of how alike two worlds are. The gauge rests on how long the worlds share a past.

What-if thought is a base topic in both thought and logic. Its core need is a sense of which worlds are near a given one. Esteves sets a distance: worlds that share a long past sit close. She proves the gauge is of a strict kind, which gives a ranked form of nearness. She then builds a logic of that nearness, with many modes, and proves it sound and full for the class of such spaces.
arxiv-2508-17402:
Aleksandar Pramov, Jiangqin Ma, and Bina Patel describe a contest entry that rewrites messy social media claims into clean, checkable statements. Claim normalization feeds fact-checking pipelines, and the CheckThat! 2025 task covered twenty languages, in both familiar and unseen-language settings. Their approach favors simplicity over heavy machinery.

The pipeline first searches the training data for the closest existing normalization and reuses it when possible. Otherwise it prompts a compact commercial model with in-context examples. On the official test set the system ranked near the top in most single-language tracks, winning seven of thirteen. Zero-shot languages exposed the retrieval dependence, and performance dropped there.
arxiv-2508-20302:
Bernhard Haeupler, Yonggang Jiang, and Thatchaphol Saranurak make plain the side by side plans for reach and short paths in graphs with one way links. Plans with near straight work hinge on short cut links that shrink hop counts. Their black box frame lets those plans take the in graph as shallow. That means when a point can reach one more point, it can do so in near the goal count of hops.

That take makes short cut builds much more plain, and gives more plain side by side reach plans. The black box grows in a plain way to hop set builds. From there it grows to short path counts. The team sets the frame out as a join cut that cleans a group of plans that were once hard to track. It is not one new plan on its own.
arxiv-2509-00102: Phu X. Nguyen leads a team with five co-authors who present ECG-Soup in 2025, a study of transformer-based foundation models for electrocardiograms, which are traces of the heart's electric activity. The title frames the work as harnessing multi-layer synergy, which means gains from how the model's layers work jointly. The arXiv record's summary notes that such foundation models have lately reached strong performance in many downstream applications, which are the tasks a general model is later put to.
arxiv-2509-00602:
Salar Nouri, with two co-authors, introduces TranCIT. TranCIT is an open-source Python toolbox. It studies brief causal links in neural signals. Those links can appear and vanish in a short event. Standard methods often miss such short events. Event-based tools also lacked a handy Python version until now.

The toolbox packs a full analysis pipeline for users. It includes Granger Causality and Transfer Entropy, two classic measures of directed influence. It also adds Dynamic Causal Strength methods based on causal models. The team calls those methods more robust. TranCIT captures causality in high-synchrony cases where older methods fail. It also finds the known flow from hippocampal area CA3 to CA1. That flow appears during sharp-wave ripple events in real data.
arxiv-2509-00902:
Written by lead author Cesare Vianello and two co-authors, this 2025 research paper looks at Josephson dynamics beyond the usual mean-field picture. At its core is the phase difference that develops between two linked systems, each large enough to act as a single quantum object.

The authors use a background field method that keeps covariance intact to build a one-loop action involving only the phase. From it they obtain an equation that governs how the average phase moves over time. Tests against exact results for a two-site Bose-Hubbard model show the new formulas do better than standard mean-field theory over many interaction strengths.
arxiv-2509-01302:
One of the most metal-poor stars known, HE 1327-2326, carries a chemical pattern that no model had fully matched. P. Gil-Pons, S. W. Campbell, C. L. Doherty, and M. Lugaro test whether an asymptotic giant branch star, an aging swollen star, could have seeded that pattern. Such stars dredge up processed material and build heavy elements slowly, matching several odd traits of the target star.

The team computed models of giant branch stars with almost no metals and compared their yields with the star's measured abundances. A model of three solar masses matched thirteen of fourteen measured elements, and it also fit the seven elements known only by upper limits. Only oxygen fell short, produced too weakly. The result supports giant branch stars as progenitors of this early star's material.
arxiv-2509-01602:
Equidistribution asks whether a sequence of measures spreads evenly over a space in the long run, a deep question in number theory. Asbjorn Christian Nordentoft and Radu Toma study newforms, special functions on arithmetic hyperbolic surfaces built from quaternion orders. Covers of growing prime level carry these forms, and a Hecke correspondence embeds each cover into a product of the base surface with itself.

The pair conjecture that the measure built from a newform's squared size, pushed forward through that embedding, converges to the uniform measure as the level grows. They prove the conjecture, with an effective rate for the convergence, assuming the generalized Riemann hypothesis. That assumption is stated openly in the work. The result links the fine distribution of automorphic forms to uniform spread, a theme at the heart of modern analytic number theory.
arxiv-2509-01702:
Thomas Hartwell, Daniel Hodgson, Huda Alshemmari, Gin Jose, and Almut Beige argue that light emission can be modeled without sudden quantum jumps. The jump picture says an emitter drops to a lower energy at a random moment and sends out one photon, meaning one particle of light. That picture can mislead work on systems that rely on how light waves overlap far away. Such systems serve in spread out quantum computing and gentle sensing.

The authors show the same behavior follows from a standard wave equation with a local energy rule. No jump step is needed at any point in the math. The approach still agrees with the trusted master equations of quantum optics. Dropping jumps gives modelers a cleaner base for interference based designs.
arxiv-2509-01902:
Igor Filikhin, Roman Ya Kezerashvili, and Branislav Vlahovic study clusters that pair a triply charmed baryon with light nuclei. The baryon holds three charm quarks, making it very heavy. They use the Faddeev formalism, a three body method that sums pairwise forces, in position space. Potentials come from lattice simulations for the charmed pairings and a classic model for the nucleon pair, with electric force set aside.

No bound state appears for the system with two nucleons, meaning the trio does not hold together. Near threshold resonances, short lived near bound states, appear at two spin settings. A heavier system with two charmed baryons also shows no bound state, though a resonance may lurk. Short range behavior of the lattice potential gets close attention.
arxiv-2509-02002:
Pengfei Huang, Georgios Kydonakis, Eugen Rogozinnikov, and Anna Wienhard study symmetric spaces for groups defined over involutive algebras. An involutive algebra carries a flip operation like conjugation, possibly without commuting factors. For symplectic and indefinite orthogonal groups over such algebras, they identify maximal compact subgroups when the algebra is Hermitian. Riemannian symmetric spaces attached to those subgroups are the core objects.

Several geometric models for each space are built, with tangent spaces and maps between models spelled out. The models then reinterpret Higgs bundle data tied to surface group representations. Exact component counts for two moduli spaces follow from subgroup topology, avoiding heavier analytic tools. A factorization of the Hitchin map through norm maps and quotients reduces the algebra needed to describe its base.
arxiv-2509-02402:
Junwei Huang and eight co-authors present a 2025 medical imaging paper for the autoPET IV challenge, which asks computers to outline lesions in PET and CT scans. Hand annotation is slow and varies between experts, so the challenge tests automated tools across centres and tracer types.

The team's pipeline builds on the nnU-Net Residual Encoder framework. They add tracer classification, organ supervision, which teaches the model normal anatomy, and simulated clicks that mimic a human guiding the outline. In fully automatic mode with no guidance, the system stayed robust. When clicks were added step by step, accuracy improved further. The design shows how light human input can sharpen automated cancer imaging without restarting the task.
arxiv-2509-02502:
Chuntai Wu wrote a 2025 conference proceedings paper reporting ALICE experiment measurements of how charm particles flow in lead-lead collisions at the Large Hadron Collider. The collisions create quark-gluon plasma, and elliptic flow measures how strongly particles follow the collision's almond shape.

The study covers several charm mesons, including D-zero, D-plus, and D-s-plus types, split by whether the charm quark came directly or from beauty decays. It also reports charm baryons of the Lambda-c type in this setting for the first time at the LHC. Candidates were rebuilt from their decay products at midrapidity across collision centrality classes. Results are compared with light-particle flow and with models that treat heavy-quark motion and hadron formation differently.
arxiv-2509-02802:
Daniel Cibotaru and Luciano Mari wrote a 2025 geometry paper linking heat flow to a classic law of electromagnetism. The Biot-Savart law gives the magnetic field around an electric current. Its mathematical core is a kernel, a function that spreads influence from each point of a wire or surface.

The authors build solutions by running the heat equation from sharp starting data and adding up the result over time. Careful estimates for very short times let them extend their form smoothly onto a blown-up space, a tool that separates tangled directions near a surface. For the diagonal inside a doubled three-dimensional space, their form recovers the Gauss formula for linking numbers, which count how two loops wind around each other.
arxiv-2509-03002:
Chenhao Wang and 4 co-authors introduced a 2025 method called SOPSeg for outlining tiny objects in images taken from above. Satellite and drone pictures guide city planning, environmental checks, and disaster response. Their hardest targets are small objects, where drawing an exact outline around each one is slow and costly to label by hand.

General tools like the Segment Anything Model lose fine detail on such targets because their internal picture is coarse. SOPSeg magnifies promising regions, predicts edges, and refines outlines step by step. It also accepts the rotated box prompts common in remote sensing work. The authors built a new dataset for this task from an existing aerial benchmark. Their method beat rivals and should speed future dataset building.
arxiv-2509-03102:
Wenrui Zhou and 4 co-authors built a 2025 database optimizer called CARPO. Databases answer SQL queries by choosing an execution plan, a recipe of steps, and a bad recipe can run many times slower. Built-in cost-based optimizers often pick poorly because their cost guesses are rough.

Learned optimizers train models to pick plans, but ranking plans in pairs can produce inconsistent choices. CARPO ranks whole lists of candidate plans at once with a transformer model that sees the full context. A hybrid safety layer spots inputs unlike its training data and falls back to safer choices. On standard benchmarks it picked the best plan far more often than a leading rival. Total run time dropped sharply against a popular open database.
arxiv-2509-03202:
Felix Zahner and 3 co-authors showed in 2025 that magnetism can steer how nanostructures grow on a magnetic surface. Thin film growth usually takes its orders from crystal structure, chemistry, size, and shape. The team asked the reverse question. Can the magnetism of the surface itself direct what grows on it?

They deposited cobalt onto a uniaxial antiferromagnetic surface. On such a surface, atomic magnets alternate in one preferred pattern. Above the ordering temperature, cobalt formed roughly hexagonal islands that mirrored the surface symmetry. Below that temperature, it grew into thin, near one-dimensional forms along set crystal directions instead. Those directions signaled how the antiferromagnetic domains lay beneath. Growth recipes for magnetic surfaces, the authors argue, must reckon with such effects.
arxiv-2509-03302:
Cao H. Nam reported a 2025 mechanism in which curved field space generates a new force among charged leptons. Leptons are light elementary particles like the electron and muon, and their field space is the abstract arena describing their values. Giving that space nonzero curvature, the author finds, produces a force not explored in earlier literature.

The force corrects how leptons couple to electromagnetism, and the correction mixes flavors at the basic level rather than only through loops. Flavor violation, where one lepton type turns into another, is normally extremely rare and tightly bounded. Here the predicted decay rates gain strong amplification, so experiments could probe parameter regions other models cannot reach. The same correction also adds a new type of contribution to the leptons' anomalous magnetic moments, quantities measured with extreme precision.
arxiv-2509-03402:
Zofia Budzik, Matylda Łukaszewicz, and Radosław Poleski reanalyzed the metallicity of the double red clump in the Milky Way's bulge in 2025. Red clump stars are evolved suns with steady brightness, and the bulge shows two such groups. One explanation is two populations with different chemical makeup; another is a single population stretched along an X-shaped bulge at different distances.

The team combined infrared photometry with metallicities, meaning heavy-element shares, from an earlier spectroscopic study. Unlike prior work, they assigned stars to the clumps or the giant branch with a Bayesian method that weighs probabilities instead of drawing hard lines. The mean metallicity difference between the clumps came out positive but with a large statistical error. Because of that uncertainty, the result does not confirm the multiple populations hypothesis.
arxiv-2509-03802:
A 2025 research paper from Prateek Sharma and five co-authors examines the structure of turbulent radiative mixing layers, the churning boundaries where hot diffuse gas meets cold dense gas. Shear-driven turbulence mixes the two into intermediate-temperature gas that cools rapidly by radiating energy away. Such layers are everywhere in the gas within galaxies and around them.

A Reynolds decomposition of three-dimensional simulations separates average flows from turbulent fluctuations. The analysis shows compressive stress, driven by cooling, opens a dip in pressure inside the layer. That dip keeps hot gas flowing steadily into the mixing zone. Enthalpy advection, the transport of heat by the inflowing gas itself, mainly balances what radiation carries away, not turbulent heat flux as often assumed. One earlier claim is overturned directly: in the strong-cooling limit, the cooling rate for each unit of area saturates and stops depending on box size.
arxiv-2509-04202:
Congbo Ma and eight co-authors add extra training examples to improve event spotting on social media in a 2025 computer science paper. Finding and sorting real-world events in posts needs labeled examples, which are slow and costly to produce. Their framework, SED-Aug, expands data in two directions at once. Language models rewrite post text five different ways for variety. Five other tricks nudge the internal feature patterns of posts while keeping their meaning and links intact.

The add-on design plugs into existing detection systems without rebuilding them. On two Twitter data sets from 2012 and 2018, average detection scores rose by roughly sixteen to eighteen percent over the best rival. Social listening tools could track breaking events more reliably.
arxiv-2509-04402:
Tingyou Li and five co-authors reconstruct X-ray images without knowing the illuminating beam in advance in a 2025 research paper. Ptychography scans overlapping spots with an X-ray probe and rebuilds nanoscale pictures from the scattered patterns. When the probe itself is unknown, standard iterative and learning methods lose fidelity, especially with faint signals from low-dose or fast scans. Their framework, PtyINR, represents both the object and the probe as continuous neural networks and fits them together directly from raw patterns.

No prior probe measurement is required, and the method teaches itself from the data alone. Simulated and real experiments beat earlier approaches, holding up remarkably under weak signals. Microscopy fields facing similar unknown-probe problems could adopt the recipe.
arxiv-2509-04702:
Conversational speech in several languages fills a large dataset introduced by Wei Chu, lead author with nine co-authors, in a 2025 paper. OleSpeech-IV gathers audio from English-language podcasts, talk shows, teleconferences, and similar public spoken material. It is multispeaker and multilingual, with diverse topics.

Speaker names, turns, and transcripts came from human sources. A proprietary pipeline then refined them. Timestamps and confidence scores come from that pipeline as well. The dataset is Tier IV in the Olewave series. The authors have also released a subset for non-commercial research use, supporting work on speech recognition and speaker analysis.
arxiv-2509-04902:
Two kinds of flat electronic band can coexist in one layered metal. Hanoh Lee, lead author with eighteen co-authors, report that coexistence in a 2025 condensed matter paper on an ytterbium chromium germanium compound. Its kagome lattice, a pattern of corner-sharing triangles, produces a flat band from frustrated hopping at high temperature.

On cooling, localised ytterbium states hybridise with that band and form heavy-fermion Kondo resonance states. Symmetry protects Dirac crossings of heavy character along certain lines. Topological analysis finds both trivial and nontrivial invariants in the resulting gaps. The authors identify the material as a prototype topological heavy-fermion system.
arxiv-2509-05202:
Boson stars can suddenly grow a scalar field inside theories that modify gravity. Hyat Huang, lead author with five co-authors, study that spontaneous scalarisation in a 2025 theoretical physics paper. Earlier work on neutron stars showed matter-induced scalarisation is mostly tied to a first-order phase transition, where the change happens abruptly.

The authors ask whether boson stars behave the same way. They model the bosonic matter with a repulsive quartic potential, which resists compression. Across their analysis they find only first-order phase transitions. The result extends the phase transition picture of scalarisation from neutron stars to these purely bosonic compact objects.
arxiv-2509-05302:
Drug discovery needs the pockets on proteins to open up before docking can work well, and Raúl Miñán and four co-authors offer a generative fix called Sesame in a 2025 paper. Docking predicts how a drug molecule fits a protein, and it works best with structures captured while a ligand is bound.

Those bound structures are costly and slow to obtain, while unbound ones are common but their pockets sit in less welcoming shapes. Older ways to force the change, such as molecular dynamics, cost heavy computing. Sesame learns to predict the opened geometry directly and cheaply. At scale, that could improve virtual screening, the ranked testing of many candidate compounds.
arxiv-2509-05702:
Alloys that are both hard and magnetically soft are searched for computationally by Mian Dai and nine co-authors in a 2025 materials science paper. High-entropy alloys mix many elements in near-equal shares, and hardness usually trades against soft magnetism, making the joint goal hard to reach by trial and error.

Their multi-objective Bayesian optimisation balances the two goals at once. An ensemble of surrogate models predicts properties of candidate compositions, while a sampling strategy mixing Monte Carlo draws with an acquisition score explores the vast composition space without getting trapped locally. The search found compositions on the optimal trade-off front with improved mechanical and magnetic behaviour. Specific element combinations are highlighted for future synthesis.
arxiv-2509-06002:
Recommender systems as industry actually runs them are surveyed in a 2025 paper by Kuan Zou and Aixin Sun. Academic work on recommenders mostly tunes offline datasets, without live users or giant platforms, which dulls its practical edge. The authors set out to close that gap with a careful comparison of industrial and academic practice.

They contrast data scale, real-time demands, and habits for judging success. Then they sort real-world systems into two families, those built around buying and those built around content, based on item character and recommendation goal. For each family they review how industry teams meet the challenges. Open directions include the often skipped role of user decision-making and importing ideas from economics and psychology. The survey aims to seed stronger collaboration between scholars and industry.
arxiv-2509-06802: Spaces that behave hyperbolically in a complex-analytic sense get new theorems and cases from Hervé Gaussier and one co-author in a 2025 geometry paper. Kobayashi hyperbolicity is a trait of spaces where complex holomorphic maps cannot exist, a strong form of rigidity. The authors work with Riemannian manifolds. They prove a version of the Brody lemma in that setting, a standard tool in the complex case, and they give new cases of Riemannian manifolds hyperbolic in Kobayashi's sense.
arxiv-2509-06902:
Numbers spoken by a language model should carry proof, proposes Aivin V. Solatorio in a solo 2025 paper. Models sometimes state figures that deviate from the data, a failure called numeric hallucination. Retrieval, citations, and uncertainty estimates improve transparency but cannot guarantee a displayed number is right.

The protocol, Proof-Carrying Numbers, works at the presentation layer. Each numeric span is emitted as a claim-bound token tied to a structured claim. A verifier in the renderer checks it against a declared policy, such as exact equality, rounding, aliases, or tolerance. Only checked numbers display as verified; everything else defaults to unverified, so the system fails closed. Solatorio formalizes the protocol and proves soundness, completeness for honest tokens, fail-closed behavior, and monotonicity as policies tighten. The design is lightweight and model-agnostic.
arxiv-2509-07102:
Helena Kolešová and 2 co-authors address theories that copy quantum chromodynamics, the force law for quarks, but with different content in a 2025 paper. Such QCD-like theories matter for ideas about composite Higgs particles and for dark matter made of pions. At low energies, scientists describe them with an effective field theory, a simpler model that keeps only the key features.

The authors work out next-to-leading order formulas, meaning the first level of corrections past the simplest case, for masses, decay constants, and scattering. They fit the formulas to lattice computer data for one gauge theory and extract its low-energy constants. The refined formulas then sharpen the case for pion dark matter that interacts strongly with itself. Getting the corrections right changes which versions of that idea can still work.
arxiv-2509-07202:
Khushiyant, in a solo 2025 paper, designs a system that turns brain signals into text. Electroencephalography, or EEG, records brain activity through scalp sensors, and decoding it into words could restore communication for people with severe motor limits. Past EEG text systems demanded huge data and computing power, which kept them out of reach for many labs.

The design joins a recurrent neural network encoder, a model that reads sequences step by step, with Gemma 2B, a compact large language model, in a classifier-plus-generator layout. Transfer learning, which reuses a model trained elsewhere, keeps data and compute needs low. The author reports performance close to leading methods and about ten percent better overall than current approaches. If the gains hold, EEG typing could become cheaper and more practical for assistive use.
arxiv-2509-07502:
Jackie Liu and 4 co-authors ask in 2025 what happens when AI clones post on social media in our place. A social media clone is an AI delegate built from a person's own data that can interact online as them. Clones promise convenience and comfort, but a mismanaged clone could harm its owner's reputation and relationships. The study sets groundwork for responsible design.

Using a design workbook, the team introduced eight speculative clone concepts to 32 social media users in semi-structured interviews. Users liked the convenience yet worried that clones threaten authenticity and breed skepticism in their communities. Notably, users said they would start behaving more like their clones to reduce mismatches and awkward breakdowns. The authors discuss the findings through identity and impression management research and propose design considerations for future clone products.
arxiv-2509-07602:
James Salsbury's 2025 paper, with 3 co-authors, designs clinical trials that cope with treatments whose benefits arrive late. Trials with survival endpoints are central in cancer research, but immunotherapies often show delayed effects. Delay breaks the proportional hazards assumption behind standard tools like the Cox model and log-rank test, so an early interim look can wrongly suggest the treatment fails and kill the trial.

The framework builds prior distributions for the delayed effect by eliciting them from experts, then adapts the trial as data accumulate. Folding expert knowledge about timing and size of the delay into the design improves efficiency and robustness. The risk of premature termination falls, and real benefits that emerge over time stand a better chance of detection. An example illustrates how the elicited priors enter the design in practice.
arxiv-2509-07802:
Richita Ghosh and 1 co-author explore how higher-order interactions change tipping cascades on networks in a 2025 paper. A tipping point is a threshold where a tiny push triggers a large change. Many real systems act as networks of multistable units. Vegetation patches and infrastructure networks are examples. The units tip one after another in cascades. They are linked in pairs, and also in groups. The group links are the higher-order interactions.

Simulations run on random, scale-free, and small-world networks. They show group interactions can induce cascades at coupling strengths where pairwise links fail. Bifurcation diagrams chart the route into cascades as the two couplings vary. The behavior also appears on real-world social networks. Repulsive higher-order interactions do the opposite. They suppress cascades that pairwise coupling would cause, and they shift the cascade route. Models that ignore group effects may misjudge cascade risk.
arxiv-2509-08202:
Hironori Yamaguchi and 4 co-authors grew a crystal that acts as a chain of magnetic diamonds in a 2025 physics paper. The chain links spin-half copper ions in a verdazyl-based material. Rival pulls between neighbours, plus small twists in the lattice, can break the chain's neat pattern. New quantum phases then appear.

Tests show a clear energy gap at zero field. They also show a flat step in magnetisation at half the full value. A model of paired and single spins explains both facts. Three pair-pair phases are expected as the twist grows. A field-theory map splits them by topology, and one phase is protected by symmetry. Grown lattices let physicists test such ideas on matter they can cool and probe.
arxiv-2509-08302:
Rajendramayavan Sathyam and Yueqi Li survey how foundation models are changing self-driving perception in a 2025 review. The field is moving from narrow models, each built for one task, to broad models trained on huge, mixed data sets. Three flaws still block the road: weak general skill, hard scaling, and poor grace when road scenes drift from the training mix.

The survey sorts the field by four skills a car must have. It must hold broad knowledge. It must grasp space. It must fuse many sensors with grace. And it must reason over time. Each skill is checked against real driving needs. The frame gives engineers a plain test: is this model road-ready, or just large?
arxiv-2509-08502:
Opening a door and closing it look alike frame by frame, and Piyush Bagad with Andrew Zisserman build video representations that can tell such pairs apart in a 2025 computer vision paper. Their new task, chiral action recognition, pairs temporally opposite actions: approaching versus retreating, folding versus unfolding. These actions are everyday, depend on simple visual change over time, and are poorly captured by many video embeddings.

Compact representations must become sensitive to the direction of change in object state, size, position, and count. Latent straightening is the proposed route to time-aware features. Systems that monitor homes, warehouses, or patients need the arrow of time; confusing an opening with a closing is not a small error.
arxiv-2509-09202:
Saddam Hussain and 2 co-authors investigate interacting k-essence dark energy with dark matter in a 2025 paper. K-essence is a scalar field model for dark energy, here with an inverse square potential. Interaction lets the two dark sectors exchange energy.

Two interaction forms are considered, one tied to the Hubble parameter and one built from densities and pressures. Cosmic evolution becomes an autonomous system, a set of equations that runs on its own variables, for phase space study. Many datasets, from cosmic chronometers to supernovae and lensing, test the models. Results reproduce major cosmic epochs and rival the standard model statistically, with late time de Sitter solutions.
arxiv-2509-09302:
Jingtao Zhu and 2 co-authors develop Euler type methods for Lévy driven McKean-Vlasov equations in a 2025 paper. These equations model many interacting particles where each particle's motion depends on the whole group's distribution. Coefficients can grow super-linearly, breaking standard Euler methods.

Projections or nonlinear transformations are built into the Euler step to keep numerical solutions bounded in moments. Tanh, tamed, and sine variants appear as special cases. A restrictive coercivity assumption used in earlier work is removed. Mean square convergence rates arbitrarily close to one half are proved for the particle systems. Numerical examples validate the theory.
arxiv-2509-09502:
Margarida Melo and 1 co-author continue a line of work on tropical trigonal curves in a 2025 geometry paper. An earlier result covered curves with strong links. It tied two traits to each other. One trait is a divisor of degree three with rank at least one. The other is a smooth map of degree three to a rational curve. The map comes after a mild change to the curve.

Here the demand on links is lowered. The new version reaches curves with weaker links. One bar stays in place. The curve must hold no necklace. That is, no cycle built from three or more split points. The wider match helps answer divisor questions through maps. It is a useful bridge in tropical geometry.
arxiv-2509-09602:
Where no doctor certifies a death, health workers interview the family and an algorithm guesses the cause; the guess steers real health budgets. Yiqun T. Chen and 3 co-authors test language models for that job in a 2025 research paper. Verbal autopsy is the standard tool in low-resource settings. Their pipeline, LAVA, mixes large language models with classical algorithmic methods and embedding-based classification.

The team evaluated the approaches on a standard consortium dataset spanning adults, children, and newborns. A leading commercial language model, used off the shelf, beat the traditional statistical baselines by a clear margin. It posted the highest accuracy in every age group. Ensemble combinations were also tested. The authors present LAVA as a proof of concept, not a deployment. Still, cheap language model assistance could substantially improve the cause-of-death statistics that global health planning runs on.
arxiv-2509-09702:
Ninad Bhat and 2 co-authors launch a benchmark for marketing creativity in language models in a 2025 evaluation paper. One hundred brands across twelve categories are paired with three prompt styles, from grounded insights to deliberately wild ideas. Judgements came from 678 working creatives, who compared anonymous outputs in more than eleven thousand pairings, later fitted with Bradley-Terry models.

No model ruled the field: scores bunched tightly, and the best beat the worst only about three times in five head-to-head. The authors also measured how varied each model's ideas were and how reframing a prompt shifted results. Automated judges tracked human rankings weakly and inconsistently, a warning that expert eyes remain essential for creative work.
arxiv-2509-09902:
Saili Keshri and 2 co-authors examine the center of the S0 galaxy NGC 1553 in this 2025 astronomy paper. The galaxy also hosts a gravitational lens, and the team wanted to know how its inner structures formed. High-resolution spectroscopic data from the MUSE instrument let them map how stars move across the galaxy's core in fine detail.

They found orderly rotation with a fast, cooler nuclear disc partly decoupled from the main disc, plus an inner lens and a dense central bulge. Image sharpening revealed a small nuclear bar and faint spirals near the center. The stars there are old and metal-rich. That points to the inner disc and lens forming early from the galaxy's own disc material. Later, inner processes and the group setting shaped them further.
arxiv-2509-10002:
Bhawna Mukhija and 1 co-author simulate what happens to a massive star that suddenly swallows a flood of gas from an erupting partner in a 2025 astrophysics paper. During a giant eruption in a binary, the companion can gain mass fast enough to rewrite its own future. The pair model single stars of twenty and thirty solar masses at three metal contents, feeding each at rates spanning three orders of magnitude.

Slow feeding leaves a star hot, while fast feeding cools and puffs it up, with the switch point differing between the two masses. Metal-rich stars swing their accretion glow more widely at a fixed feeding rate, even though their envelopes start larger. That reversal, against the naive expectation, is the finding the authors stress for interpreting real eruptive binaries.
arxiv-2509-10202:
Alexander Popescu and 2 co-authors design sound tools for neurodivergent listeners in this 2025 paper. Many neurodivergent people have low tolerance for certain sounds, which can cause anything from discomfort to real distress. The team first gathered a list of common trigger sounds from neurodivergent community forums, then built a data set of samples from public sound libraries.

They trained and compared several signal processing and machine learning methods meant to soften only the offending sounds, with very low delay. Dynamic range compression worked best, reliably pulling down trigger sounds in their tests. The authors frame the work as a step toward everyday assistive listening devices that respect the wearer's sound world instead of simply blocking it.
arxiv-2509-10402:
What do programmers actually ask chatbots, and does the code get better as they talk? Suzhen Zhong, Ying Zou, and Bram Adams study developer conversations with large language models in this 2025 software engineering paper. They build CodeChat, a dataset of over half a million real conversations holding 1.7 million code snippets in more than twenty languages, drawn from WildChat.

Web design and machine learning top the topic list, and chats often run long because developers keep switching tasks mid-conversation. Code quality problems are common and language-specific, and they do not reliably shrink even in long exchanges. When syntax errors do get fixed, the winning move is a prompt that names the error plainly and asks for a fix. The authors argue assistants should track shifting intent and watch code quality turn by turn.
arxiv-2509-10702:
Designing a neural network accelerator means choosing hardware and the mapping of the algorithm onto it, together. Charles Hong and four co-authors automate that joint search with DOSA in this 2025 computer architecture paper. Earlier tools explored the two spaces separately, and both are huge and jagged, so the combined problem explodes combinatorially.

DOSA replaces the search with differentiable performance models and gradient descent, sliding through hardware parameters and mappings at once. It beat random search and Bayesian optimization by wide margins on the energy-delay product, the field's combined score for speed and power. The design is modular: adding a learned model beside the analytical one let them optimize a real accelerator's buffers and mappings for another large gain. For chip designers, co-optimization becomes a smooth descent instead of a lottery.
arxiv-2509-11502:
Melissa Anholm and seven co-authors draw new physics limits from potassium-37 beta decay. This 2025 nuclear physics paper varies the beta asymmetry with energy. The asymmetry is measured against the nuclear spin. Letting it vary with the beta particle's energy opens a new window. It gives sensitivity to would-be interactions with a helicity factor.

The team constrains exotic scalar and tensor couplings between quarks and leptons. The sensitivity pairs with the known Fierz term from neutron decay. Their measured Fierz value is small, with stated errors. It matches the Standard Model value of zero. The paper weighs the method against other beta-decay and particle physics tests. It also maps upgrades that could sharpen the method further.
arxiv-2509-11602:
Soichiro Migita, Kyotaro Uehata, and Tomohiro I close a gap in grammar-based string compression. This 2025 theoretical computer science paper treats collage systems. Such systems generalize straight-line programs. Repetition and truncation rules are added. Researchers measure how small a system for a string can be.

A subclass called internal collage systems was known to need room. It needs at least as much as the best two-way scheme. Its size against the unrestricted kind was unknown. The authors prove the two sizes match within a constant factor. Any system converts to an internal one with linear growth. The conversion takes quadratic time. An open question from past work falls as a payoff. A MAX-SAT formula for the exact internal size is added.
arxiv-2509-11902:
Ze-Yu Peng and three co-authors retest a foundational number of cosmology against the newest sky data. This 2025 paper treats the scalar spectral index. It describes how the early universe's density ripples spread across scales. The standard reading sits a few percent below one. A perfectly scale-invariant spectrum would sit exactly at one.

The authors revisit the number through early dark energy models. Those models aim to resolve the Hubble tension. They push the index toward unity. The newest ground-based microwave background data come from ACT and SPT. They reach smaller scales with better precision than Planck. The shift toward one is strengthened and reconfirmed. Solving one tension can rewrite beliefs about the universe's first moments.
arxiv-2509-12002:
Did a neutrino arrive alongside any of the gravitational waves caught in the latest LIGO, Virgo, and KAGRA observing run? L. N. Machado reports a Super-Kamiokande search for exactly that coincidence, covering the O4 run that began in May 2023.

Super-Kamiokande, a huge underground water detector in Japan, watched for neutrino signals timed with gravitational wave candidates from the run's first phase, O4a. During that phase LIGO alone flagged 81 candidate events. The follow-up searches found no significant neutrino signal standing out from background. Rather than a detection, the outcome is a set of flux limits. These are upper bounds on how much neutrino emission could have accompanied those events without being seen. Even so, they still constrain what the sources could have been doing.
arxiv-2509-12102:
Can a chatbot answer mental health questions as well as a therapist? Synthia Wang and five co-authors put that to a direct test in 2025, comparing human replies with output from ChatGPT, Gemini, and Llama on real patient questions.

On the page, the models look strong: their answers run longer, read more easily, use richer vocabulary, and sound more positive, while therapists write in the first person more often. In a survey of 150 users and 23 licensed therapists, model replies were rated clearer, more respectful, and more supportive. Yet both groups still preferred human support overall. The authors read the gap as a design brief: keep the communicative strengths, but answer the trust, privacy, and accountability concerns that hold people back.
arxiv-2509-12302:
Supersymmetry extends ordinary geometry with anticommuting directions. Maps between super Riemann surfaces need their own covering theory. In a solo 2025 paper, Beat Nairz defines super covering maps in analytic terms. These are the branched coverings of the super world.

The maps were already hiding in two active corners of string theory. In one corner, they appear in symmetric product orbifolds of superconformal field theories. There, they let researchers compute correlation functions in a way that keeps supersymmetry manifest. In the other corner, they appear in the hybrid formalism for tensionless strings on a curved background. There, they solve the Ward identities that spacetime supersymmetry imposes on correlators.
arxiv-2509-12402:
Topological quantum field theories turn shapes into algebra. Sergei Gukov and three co-authors propose a new species of them in 2025. Their version is valued in topological modular forms. That is a sophisticated spectrum from homotopy theory. Their construction assigns algebraic objects to closed three-dimensional shapes. It assigns maps between them to four-dimensional cobordisms. Those are the spaces that join one shape to another.

Symmetric bilinear forms supply the building blocks. They come through derived algebraic geometry. Gluing rules are checked. The invariant for unimodular forms lands in the homotopy groups of the spectrum. It is expected to generalize the classical theta function of a lattice. The objects may also distinguish phases of quantum field theories.
arxiv-2509-12502:
A qubit hidden inside an oscillator's motion is the idea behind GKP codes, a leading scheme for error-protected quantum hardware. Jonathan Pelletier and one co-author widen the code's stabilizer group in 2025 to include every operation that acts trivially on the stored information, then exploit that freedom when compiling circuits.

Knowing the full Gaussian stabilizer generators lets them search over physically different implementations of the same logical operation. An algorithm picks the implementation that suffers least from photon loss during the run. In randomized benchmarking tests, the optimizing compiler extends the life of square-lattice GKP qubits compared with a random-walk compiler.
arxiv-2509-12602:
Minyu Chen and Guoqiang Li introduce DaSAThco in a 2025 paper on tuning SAT solvers. SAT solvers test whether logical formulas can be satisfied, and modern solvers depend heavily on internal heuristics, the rules of thumb that guide search. Because SAT problems vary widely, no single configuration works best for all of them.

Earlier automated methods specialized in one problem family but generalized poorly and needed costly re-optimization for new types. DaSAThco instead learns a mapping from instance features to tailored heuristic ensembles, aiming to train once and adapt broadly. A large language model, guided by defined problem archetypes, generates a diverse portfolio of ensembles, and a selection mechanism learns to choose among them. Experiments showed superior performance and robust out-of-domain generalization.
arxiv-2509-12702:
Hongrui Zhao and 3 co-authors present UDON in a 2025 paper on multi-robot mapping under extreme communication limits. Neural implicit mapping lets several robots build a compact reconstruction of a complex setting together. Packet loss and limited bandwidth, however, can degrade the shared map when robots cannot communicate reliably.

UDON introduces uncertainty-weighted distributed optimization for real-time mapping. The uncertainty weighting prioritizes more reliable portions of the map, while the distributed method isolates and penalizes disagreement between single pairs of communicating agents. Broad tests on benchmark data sets and real robot hardware showed greatly better results than current benchmarks. The system maintained high-fidelity reconstructions and consistent scene representations even when communication success rates were extremely low.
arxiv-2509-12802:
T. Nomura, I. Rousochatzakis and seven co-authors report in 2025 what happens in a crystal with spiral magnets when fields grow far past normal lab strength. The crystal can host tiny swirls of spin and links spin to charge, a rare mix in an insulator.

In fields in the hundreds of tesla range, light twist tests show signs of a dense state where spin waves act as one body. That state acts like a tilted magnet and brings a dome-shaped charge shift that makes it visible. The find opens a new high-field phase for study and tests ideas about dense spin states in solids.
arxiv-2509-12902:
Dimitrios Lekkas and Yiannis Petridis count shared upright lines between two closed loops on a curved plane in 2025. The count is a twist on the classic circle problem. Only group cosets by two loop groups are kept.

An exact relative trace form is proved for the count. A large sieve bound from Lekkas and Voskou then caps the error in mean square. The new cap grows as the square root times a log factor. The pair guess this growth is sharp. On the way they give a fresh proof of the known point cap first shown by Good.
arxiv-2509-13202:
Francis Ndikum Nji, Vandana Janaja and Jianwu Wang cluster climate data in 2025 with a two-way time graph transformer at the core. Climate sets mix place, time, and many measures. Classic clusters miss long links and shifting place ties.

A U-shaped autoencoder with memory cells pulls joint place-time traits. Skip links keep fine place detail. The graph transformer at the waist weighs time neighbors both ways. Latent codes then sort into stable groups. Three climate sets show cleaner splits, steadier groups, and closer match to known shifts than top baselines. Insight into variability comes with the clusters.
arxiv-2509-13502:
Carlo Vanoni and 5 co-authors study a one-dimensional model of disorder with a stealthy twist in a 2025 paper. In the Anderson model, random disorder can trap waves in a small region. Stealthy disorder is distinct: its power spectrum is zero across a whole band of wave numbers, so it hides from waves of those scales.

The team work out, by hand and by computer, how far a wave can spread in such a system. For a fixed energy and weak disorder, they find a range of stealth where the spread length tops the size of the whole system. In effect, the wave acts as if it were free, an effect they call effective delocalization. The cause is the long-range links built into stealthy disorder, which set it apart from plain random disorder.
arxiv-2509-13702:
Xiao Zheng, writing alone in a 2025 paper, presents a system for suppressing hallucinations in large language models. A hallucination is false content stated with confidence, and it blocks the reliable use of these models. Retrieval-augmented generation, for one, brings in outside text to correct the model, rather than stopping errors while the answer is being formed.

The new system, called Dynamic Self-reinforcing Calibration, steps in early. It acts while the model decodes its answer one token at a time, the autoregressive way such models write. The idea borrows from dual-process theories of thinking. A small proxy model plays two opposed roles in training. At each step they inject a steering vector, computed in real time, into the generation. In the author's tests on two benchmarks, the system reached state-of-the-art results, with a very high rate of factual consistency among them.
arxiv-2509-14102:
Felicia Nguyen, writing alone in 2025, asks how an online platform should reward new creators who choose their quality before anything is released. Early exposure is scarce, and creators act with their own pay in mind. Her study treats a short test window with a clear pass or fail bar as the core tool.

Nguyen finds that a set payment she calls an implementability bounty can line up what creators want with what the platform wants. Giving promised views early works better than spreading them out. When money and views are both limited, the best rule gives each option equal value at the margin. The work also links real ranking systems to the model, offering a practical way to fix the cold start problem for new creators.
arxiv-2509-14802:
Boyang Ma and four co-authors study how short flashes of light push electrons across tiny gaps in metal, in a 2025 physics paper. Electrons can tunnel through a barrier they could not cross in the classic picture. That effect sits behind tools such as scanning tunneling microscopes. A fast light pulse can drive the flow on very short time scales.

The team uses a quantum method that tracks electron density in time. They find tunneling helped by taking in one, two, or more photons at once. They also track how the barrier, a steady bias, and field strength shift the process from photon-helped flow to direct field emission. Simpler models and fresh lab results help them read what the full math shows.
arxiv-2509-15002:
Shu-Min Wu and five co-authors ask whether excited quantum states can protect their resources near a black hole, in a 2025 gravitation paper. Hawking radiation slowly degrades quantum information held close to a Schwarzschild black hole. Most earlier studies only considered the vacuum and the first excited state of two-mode entangled systems, a narrow slice of what is possible.

The new work allows arbitrary excitation levels in multipartite states, many parties sharing one quantum system. Raising the excitation number reduces entanglement and mutual information under the Hawking effect. At the same time, quantum coherence, a different resource, actually grows stronger. The trade-off matters for anyone designing quantum protocols in strong gravity: excitation sacrifices shared correlations but shields coherence from the black hole's influence.
arxiv-2509-15102:
S Rahul and Giandomenico Palumbo extend a curious band-structure effect into non-Hermitian physics in a 2025 condensed matter paper. Some materials have an indirect band gap, the energy offset between band edges at different momenta, pinned at exactly zero. Such pinning usually needs delicate fine-tuning, yet robust versions were recently found in ordinary Hermitian systems over a finite parameter range.

The authors study a one-dimensional diamond-like lattice with gain and loss, the hallmark of non-Hermitian models. The zero indirect gap in the real part of the spectrum survives those perturbations, and they chart where the stability holds. The gap's appearance coincides with suppression of the non-Hermitian skin effect, where states pile up at a boundary. Links among indirect gaps, exceptional points, and the skin effect point to new experiments.
arxiv-2509-16002:
Quantum learning agents need many qubits as tasks grow longer, and today's quantum chips have few to spare. Thet Htar Su, Shaswot Shresthamali, and Masaaki Kondo offer a design that reuses the same qubits step after step. Their system measures and resets qubits mid-task, so a fixed set of seven serves for any task length.

Good paths through a task are boosted with a quantum search trick so they get sampled more often. Computer tests kept the same paths as a fixed design while cutting qubit needs by two thirds. A run on an IBM quantum chip showed the design works on real, noisy hardware.
arxiv-2509-16302:
Reading the faint polarized glow of the early universe from the ground means fighting bright, shifting air glow above the telescope. Simon Biquard, Josquin Errard, and Radek Stompor test map-making methods that assume as little as possible about that air glow. They lean on paired detectors in each pixel and a spinning plate that modulates the signal.

One method, pair differencing, is shown to follow from sound statistical rules and nears ideal accuracy in clean tests. A rival weighting method could match it only with air models that are hard to get. Spinning the plate also curbs flaws like gain mismatch, which keeps the method robust.
arxiv-2509-16702:
Chen Liu, Haitao Wu, Kafeng Wang, and Weiran Huang build a pet image generator in a 2025 paper. Making an image of a specific animal is hard. Animals vary a lot in shape, and fine marks set one apart. Past tools often lost those marks, so the output drifted from the real animal.

Their system sharpens features drawn from several input types at once. It holds identity better across varied scenes. The team also built AnimalBench, a high-grade dataset for this task. Tests show their method beats strong rivals on identity and image quality. Such tools could help owners and media makers place a known pet in new scenes.
arxiv-2509-16802:
Max Dupre la Tour and Kaito Fujii extend a fairness tool to richer valuations in a 2025 math paper. Discrepancy theory studies how evenly items can be split. Past work assumed values add up in a simple way. Real values often do not. The pair define discrepancy for non-additive values and bound it.

Their main bound holds when the number of groups is a prime power. A second result caps the subsidy needed for an envy-free split. That cap is the first below a quadratic level in this setting. Fair splits matter for estates, chores, and shared resources, where simple added values rarely tell the whole story.
arxiv-2509-16902:
Letian Zhang and co-authors speed federated learning on mixed devices in a 2025 paper. Phones and sensors train a shared model without sending raw data away. Devices vary widely in power, though. Slow stragglers hold up each round for everyone. Their elastic method, FedEL, lets weak devices do less while still contributing.

A tensor module balances local and global importance to fight data bias. Tests show time to a set accuracy fell by up to several fold. Final accuracy held or rose versus baselines. Elastic training could make federated systems practical on the messy mix of devices people actually own.
arxiv-2509-17002:
Aharon Rips and Oron Sabag study messages hidden inside control signals in a 2025 paper. A controller must both steer a system and, in their setup, convey a message to an observer who sees the system's outputs. The control signal thus carries a secret second job. The team ask how much information such a channel can carry for a standard class of systems.

They attack the capacity question with convex optimization. For the vector case, a condition tied to a classic Riccati equation shows when their upper bound is tight. Simulations found the bound tight in every tested case. That hints the bound equals the true capacity for vector systems.
arxiv-2509-17102:
A. M. Mukhamedzhanov, working alone, applies Bayesian methods to a key stellar reaction in a 2025 nuclear paper. The reaction that turns carbon into oxygen during helium burning sets the carbon-to-oxygen ratio in stars. That ratio shapes white dwarfs and supernova yields. At stellar energies, the rate hinges on two near-threshold states and their normalization coefficients.

Mukhamedzhanov builds posterior ranges for the reaction's two main factors at the key energy. Even with published coefficient constraints folded in, the ranges stay broad. Present data do not yet shrink the astrophysical uncertainty. Still, the framework gives statistically sound ranges that stellar modelers can propagate honestly through their simulations.
arxiv-2509-17602:
Giulio Martellucci, Herve Goeau, Pierre Bonnet, Fabrice Vinatier, and Alexis Joly report the PlantCLEF 2025 challenge. Their 2025 arXiv overview concerns quadrat images, the square ground plots ecologists use to sample plant life. A quadrat photo can hold many species at once, and naming them all by hand is slow expert work.

The challenge's new test set holds thousands of high-resolution, expert-labeled quadrat images covering hundreds of species. A vast training set of single-plant images and pretrained vision transformers come with it. The task is multi-label: name every species in a quadrat, learning from single-label data alone. The overview describes the data, the scoring method, the entries, and the results. It measures how far AI has come toward speeding field inventories and widening the reach of biodiversity surveys.
arxiv-2509-17702:
Patrick Schmidt, Vasileios Belagiannis, and Lazaros Nalpantidis sharpen weakly supervised image segmentation with depth cues. Their 2025 arXiv paper serves robots entering new domains, where pixel-level labels are pricey and image-level labels are all a trainer may have. Weak supervision builds pixel maps from those cheap labels, but the maps stay rough at object borders.

Their loss, called DEAL, aligns the predicted segments with depth edges, a signal robots commonly carry. It is model-agnostic, so it can wrap many segmentation designs, and it stacks with other losses for further gains. On PASCAL VOC, MS COCO, and a HOPE onboarding split, the loss lifted mean overlap scores, with the largest jump on the last set. Code is public. The authors frame depth, often treated as a side input, as a direct teacher for where one object ends and another begins.
arxiv-2509-17802:
Qi'ao Xu and 6 co-authors offer a plug-in way to sort medical time data, such as heart or brain traces. Their 2025 paper notes that people differ a lot, so a model trained on some folk may fail on new folk. Past fixes tied to one signal type do not travel well.

Their plan turns a one-line trace into a flat fake image. A pre-trained vision model can then use what it learned from real images. Two contrast steps keep time sense and line the trace up with the image view. On six data sets, the plan beat a wide set of past methods.
arxiv-2509-17902:
Projesh Nath Choudhury and Shivangi Yadav sort the functions that keep a sign trait of matrices when used entry by entry. Their 2025 paper builds on classic work by Schur and others on such preservers. Sign regular matrices have minors whose signs follow a fixed pattern, a trait Schoenberg used in 1930.

The pair give full lists of entry-wise maps that keep sign regularity, in both strict and plain forms. Lists cover rectangle matrices, not just square ones. They also fix a sign pattern and list the maps that keep that pattern too. The trait class holds the known total-positive cases inside it.
arxiv-2509-18002:
M Burak Erdogan, Michael Goldberg, and William Green bound how fast waves spread for a fractional wave operator. Their 2025 paper deals with a Schroedinger operator raised to a non-whole power, plus a fading bump term. Such bounds show that a wave packet thins out over time, not just that it stays bounded.

The team proves point-wise bounds on a key inverse operator for a wide power range. A limit rule with a clean numeric bound comes next. World-wide spread bounds then follow for most dims and a set power window. The tools rest on how the operator acts near the energy of a wave.
arxiv-2509-18302:
Gonzalo Prieto-Lyon leads a large team that sets a base line for Lyman-alpha light at the end of reionization. Their 2025 paper uses ground and Webb telescope spectra of hundreds of galaxies at that late stage. Such a base line is needed to read far earlier galaxies, whose light is scattered by neutral gas.

A first stats map of line widths at that epoch is a key yield. Models for line strength and escape share rest on how bright and blue each galaxy is. About half of mid-bright galaxies pass a set strength bar. Escape shares sit below a bound the team gives.
arxiv-2509-18402:
MRI scans can be sped up by taking fewer samples, but rebuilding the image gets harder. Tingjun Liu and four co-authors present C-MSM, a rebuild method that drops two usual crutches. Their 2025 paper targets multi-coil scans, where each coil needs a sensitivity map. Those maps are hard to get right when samples are few, and clean training images may not exist.

C-MSM learns its scores straight from the raw scan data, with no clean images needed. It estimates the coil maps on its own while it rebuilds. The rebuild draws samples from a spread of likely images, guided by partial scores from the measurements. On a public brain scan data set, quality came close to methods that use clean training data and ready-made maps. The authors say this makes advanced rebuilds usable in more real clinics.
arxiv-2509-18702:
Some graphs reproduce their own structure at smaller scales, and groups can drive that self-similarity. Enrique Pardo surveys self-similar graphs and the algebras built from them in these 2025 notes. The notes began as extra material for a course at a summer school in Argentina. They introduce the algebras from several complementary angles.

Pardo defines the associated C-star algebra, a kind of operator algebra, and works out its basic traits. He then reviews generalizations that appear across the literature. A construction called the Zappa-Szép product gets special attention for its links to the main theme. Recent results on homology and K-theory for these algebras close the notes. The intended reader is a newcomer with some algebra background. As course notes, the piece teaches and surveys rather than proving new theorems.
arxiv-2509-18802:
Robot-assisted surgery gives patients smaller cuts and surgeons a lighter load, but the video it produces is hard to teach machines to read. Garam Kim, Tae Kyeong Jeong, and Juyoun Park present a framework for surgical video understanding in this 2025 paper. Real scenes mix phases, steps, tools, and actions over time. Training data is lopsided: long-term labels cover every frame, while fine labels exist only for key frames.

Their fix propagates the sparse fine labels to nearby frames. Optical flow, estimated from the labeled key frames, carries segment labels across the gaps. That richer supervision feeds a multi-task learning setup. The balance between long-term and short-term information improves. So do accuracy and training efficiency in their tests. Better scene understanding, the authors argue, raises the value of robot surgery data. The method targets the annotation bottleneck directly.
arxiv-2509-18902:
How should chemistry students learn to handle research data well? Alexander Hoffmann and seven co-authors describe a fifth-semester lab course at RWTH Aachen University that teaches data care as a core skill. Students in the advanced inorganic course plan, record, and judge their experiments in digital form. The course uses Chemotion, a free electronic lab notebook tied to a national chemistry data effort.

Old lab notes were often handwritten or saved as plain PDF files, which made them hard to reuse. The new course trains students in the FAIR ideas: data should be easy to find, open to reach, able to work with other data, and fit for reuse. A seminar, training videos, and interactive Moodle tasks support the lab work. The team also shows how the DALIA platform helps students discover learning material on data care.
arxiv-2509-19202:
Alloy designers juggle many input parameters, and seeing how a blend changes as settings slide toward the best known recipe is hard. Benedikt Kantz and five co-authors present a visual analytics tool for that job. Their tool, ParamInter, guides users along interpolations from a starting setting toward an optimal one. A t-SNE map, which flattens high-dimensional data into a readable plot, gives an overview of the path.

Small linked views show each parameter's value along the way, so cause and effect stay visible. Suggestions from explainable AI point out which parameters drive the outputs, and uncertainty estimates mark where the model is unsure.
