The question is whether these strata, once projectivized, can contain complete subvarieties of positive dimension, which would be entire classes sitting wholly inside the stratum.

The authors construct a globally defined, strictly plurisubharmonic function on the projectivized strata of strictly meromorphic differentials. The existence of such a function rules out positive-dimensional complete subvarieties, giving a proof rooted in flat geometry rather than algebraic methods. Beyond that result, the construction supplies a concrete analytic tool for studying the global geometry of these strata.
arxiv-2511-07202:
Praveen Kumar Donta, Alfreds Lapkovskis, Enzo Mingozzi, and Schahram Dustdar design self-healing for the distributed computing continuum, the layered world running from tiny IoT sensors through edge nodes to high-performance clusters. Failures there are normal, yet AI workloads still need real-time, coordinated reliability. Their work-in-progress agent, PAIR-Agent, applies active inference, a system in which an agent maintains beliefs about its system and acts to keep them consistent.

The agent performs three operations: it builds a causal fault graph from device logs, identifies faults while tracking certainty and uncertainty using Markov blankets and the free energy principle. Then heals problems autonomously by reconfiguring the system. Continuous monitoring keeps services running under diverse failure conditions, and theoretical validations support the system's reliability.
arxiv-2511-07302:
Benjamin Brindle works on q-analogues of multiple zeta values, number patterns that extend classic constants in number theory. In 2015 Bachmann conjectured that the formal version of these values is spanned by one very specific set. Brindle tests that claim on a controlled part of the space.

For words meeting conditions on zeros and depth, the conjecture is proved true. The proof uses linear relations among the formal values that follow from duality, a symmetry linking different expressions. Brindle also lays out an explicit route toward the full conjecture. Specialists get both a partial theorem and a concrete plan for finishing the job.
arxiv-2511-07502:
Galina Weinstein writes an essay linking two famous divides in how knowledge works. Matrix mechanics builds answers step by step, while wave mechanics lets one recognize a solution as a whole. Though the two quantum theories agree formally, Weinstein reads them as different styles of knowing.

That contrast mirrors the P versus NP question, which separates finding solutions efficiently from checking them efficiently. Weinstein treats the parallel as philosophy, not as a claimed proof of either side. The essay traces the math history behind both divides. Readers interested in foundations get a lens connecting physics, computation, and cognition without overstating what analogy can show.
arxiv-2511-07902:
Mohammad Ali Afshar and Javad Sadeghi track how orbits precess near charged black holes pushed toward extremality. The periapsis shift, the slow rotation of an orbit closest approach, encodes spacetime shape. Stable photon spheres outside the horizon add an Aschenbach-like twist previously spotted in rotating cases.

Across representative charged models, the shift stays well defined as extremality nears and keeps mirroring geometry changes. Solutions admitting stable photon spheres show the interplay most sharply. Precession is observable in principle through stars and pulsars near real black holes, so clean theory for extreme cases prepares interpretation of future measurements.
arxiv-2511-08002:
Wejdan Beida and colleagues implement a DFT plus U plus V method inside the all electron FLAPW code FLEUR. Standard density functional theory struggles with localized electrons, so onsite corrections help, yet interactions between neighboring sites also matter in many solids. Adding an intersite term promises better treatment of charge order, charge transfer, and related effects.

The correction values come from first principles through a constrained random phase method, using two different basis choices. Tests cover graphene, silicon, germanium, and nickel oxide. Results improve selected properties across these bonding types and agree better with experiments, earlier calculations, and the authors own many body reference results.
arxiv-2511-08102:
Shohei Okawa and Yuji Omura use leptonic meson decays to set new bounds on neutrino portal dark matter. In this model a neutral fermion and a scalar couple mainly to neutrinos, opening hidden interactions. Ordinary two body meson decays into a charged lepton and an antineutrino can reveal those particles in two distinct ways.

A new three body decay lets the antineutrino split into the hidden pair, escaping the usual helicity suppression. Loop corrections also shift the decay width up or down without changing the lepton spectrum. Comparing modified branching ratios with pion and kaon data beats existing limits across much of the parameter space.
arxiv-2511-08202:
Jiyuan Lyu gives an exact mean field solution for the Mesa Boltzmann wealth model, a standard agent based example of money exchange. The paper replaces simulation with exact analysis for a model that is usually studied only on a computer. Instead of local trades, the mean field version uses global random matching with synchronous updates.

A master equation for the wealth distribution, solved through probability generating functions, yields the steady state in closed form. Variance, the Gini inequality coefficient, and tail behavior follow directly from that solution. Simulations of the matching agent model agree closely with the formulas, giving an analytical benchmark for checking related simulations.
arxiv-2511-08302:
Arshyn Altybay and Michael Ruzhansky attack the inverse problem of recovering a time dependent potential coefficient inside a one dimensional diffusion equation. Only edge data plus a nonlocal integral measure, reflecting spatial averages, can be used to spot the unknown coefficient. The authors first prove the forward problem is well posed and derive an estimate giving uniqueness and stable dependence on data for the inverse problem.

Three numeric routes are then tested: an integration based scheme, a Newton Raphson iterative solver, and a physics informed neural network. Tests with exact and noisy data show how exact, robust, and lean each method is. The comparison guides practitioners choosing a solver for similar coefficient recovery tasks.
arxiv-2511-08502:
Ruya Karagulle, Cristian-Ioan Vasile, and Necmiye Ozay learn autonomous system behavior from human preferences while keeping formal safety guarantees. Feedback arrives as comparisons, rankings, or demonstrations, and many methods adapt behavior without proving the result stays safe in critical domains. Their approach expresses preferences in weighted signal temporal logic, a language for timed requirements with adjustable importance across goals.

A naive setup creates multi linear constraints in the weights to learn. Structural pruning and a log transform shrink the problem and recast it as a mixed integer linear program, preserving the safety guarantees. Experiments on robotic navigation and real Formula 1 data show the method captures nuanced preferences and complex task objectives.
arxiv-2511-08602:
Tatsuru Kikuchi builds a single framework that joins two ways financial crises spread: across bank networks and across space. The test case is the 2008 crisis, using bilateral exposure data for one hundred fifty-six institutions in twenty-eight countries from 2007 to 2023.

Three findings stand out. First, consolidation backfired: bank counts fell by nearly half while a network fragility measure more than tripled, so tighter links mattered more than fewer banks. Second, contagion crossed the globe with almost no distance decay, unlike technology diffusion, which fades within tens of kilometers. Third, standard difference-in-differences estimates overstate crisis damage by almost three quarters when network structure is ignored. Kikuchi argues risk policy must model both geography and network shape together.
arxiv-2511-08702:
David Sanchez Jr. and three co-authors argue that fair and private machine learning cannot be fully automated, because fairness is a human judgment about context. Privacy tools can quietly worsen group disparities, and fairness fixes often need the very sensitive data that privacy rules lock away.

Their framework, FAIRPLAI, puts people inside the loop in three ways. It draws privacy-fairness frontiers so trade-offs among accuracy, privacy, and group outcomes stay visible. It lets stakeholders pick fairness criteria and operating points interactively. And it adds a differentially private auditing loop where reviewers inspect explanations and edge cases without exposing individual records. On benchmark datasets the approach keeps strong privacy while cutting fairness gaps versus automated baselines.
arxiv-2511-09002:
Hongru Zhao, Jinwen Fu, and Tuan Pham analyze a feedback loop now built into generative AI: models retrained round after round on a mix of real data and their own earlier outputs. Earlier work studied such self-consuming models with uniform human curation; here the human curators have heterogeneous preferences, generalizing that model.

The long-run behavior of the retraining dynamics is worked out across four regimes, with tools that include nonlinear Perron-Frobenius theory. The analysis improves on the earlier results and proves convergence in settings where the standard Banach contraction argument fails outright. Stability and instability results for the dynamics round out the picture. The stakes are practical: as synthetic data floods training pipelines, knowing when the loop settles and when it spirals decides how much curation the process needs.
arxiv-2511-09202:
Itshak Lapidot, Yann Sepulcre, and Tom Trigano present a stochastic version of mean-shift clustering, a classic way to group data points around density peaks. In their version, a randomly chosen sequence of points moves by partial gradient ascent steps. Only some points move at each step, unlike the standard algorithm's full updates.

The authors prove convergence results for the stochastic scheme. On synthetic two-dimensional data from Gaussian mixtures, it beats standard mean-shift in most comparisons against state-of-the-art methods. They also test it on a practical task, clustering speakers from audio. The stochastic twist keeps the method's spirit while improving its performance in these trials.
arxiv-2511-09502:
Jerrin Bright, Yuhao Chen, and John S. Zelek estimate three-dimensional human poses from video using a diffusion model that imagines motion. Most pose systems read each frame's geometry alone, so ambiguous movements confuse them and sequences jitter. Humans instead anticipate how a motion unfolds, and the authors borrow that strategy.

DreamPose3D conditions its denoising on action prompts extracted from the two-dimensional pose sequence, capturing intent. A representation encoder folds kinematic joint relationships into the attention mechanism. A hallucinative decoder, used in training, predicts coherent future pose sequences to resolve ambiguity. The system reports state-of-the-art results on the Human3.6M and MPI-INF-3DHP benchmarks, and stays strong on noisy broadcast baseball footage.
arxiv-2511-09702:
Katie Matton and nine co-authors build the first automatic method for grading phonotrauma severity from images of the vocal folds. Phonotrauma is tissue damage from the forces of voicing, and its severity, running mild to severe, guides treatment choices. Today grading rests on clinician judgment, which is costly and varies in reliability between experts.

Because severity labels are ordered, the authors adopt ordinal regression rather than plain classification. Their novelty is a loss modification that trains on soft labels. Those labels encode the whole distribution of annotator ratings, embracing uncertainty instead of hiding it. The method approaches medical experts' predictive performance while producing well-calibrated uncertainty estimates, they report. Automated grading could enable large-scale phonotrauma studies.
arxiv-2511-09802:
Parinaz Binandeh Dehaghani, Danilo Pena, and A. Pedro Aguiar study how to classify environmental sounds with small, cheap neural networks. The work compares ways of shrinking the data, including a sparse salient region pooling method and two variants of it, against the standard principal component approach. Experiments run on the ESC-50 dataset of environmental recordings.

The Top-K variant of sparse pooling reached accuracy up to about eighty-one percent, well above the plain network baseline near sixty-seven percent. Principal component reduction performed poorly by comparison, near thirty-eight percent. The authors conclude that a carefully tuned sparse pooling strategy gives a robust and efficient option for sound classification when computing resources are tight.
arxiv-2511-10202:
Athanasios L. Konstantinidis, Charis Papadopoulos, and Georgios Velissaris study Hedge Cluster Deletion, a grouped version of the classic cluster deletion problem. In a hedge graph, edges come partitioned into hedges, and the task is to remove the fewest hedges so the remaining graph splits into disjoint cliques. Deleting whole groups at once models settings where edges fail or are removed together.

They show the problem is NP-complete, pin down polynomial cases tied to disjoint three-vertex paths, and prove a strong inapproximability result. The problem is fixed-parameter tractable in the solution size but admits no polynomial kernel under standard assumptions. Positive results include a constant-factor approximation when each triangle is covered by at most two hedges, and a polynomial algorithm when the hedge intersection graph is acyclic.
arxiv-2511-10302:
Karim Nasreddine, Christo Kurisummoottil Thomas, and Walid Saad give semantic communication systems a shared memory, so old concepts can be reused instead of retransmitted. Learned semantic codecs usually freeze their representations, wasting bandwidth when content drifts gradually. Their framework stores semantic concepts in modern Hopfield networks held by both transmitter and receiver, and retrieves matches through soft attention.

Soft retrieval adjusts stored prototype weights smoothly as data evolves, avoiding the constant memory updates that hard quantization schemes suffer. The team optimizes encoder, decoder, and retrieval jointly for a reasoning capacity metric combining reuse rate and compression, and proves a rate-distortion-reuse trade-off. Video simulations saved about fourteen percent of bits on average, and up to seventy percent under gradual change.
arxiv-2511-10502:
Vincenzo Carletti and four co-authors examine a privacy risk in federated learning, a method that trains models across many devices without moving private data to a central server. Attackers who control the server can tamper with the shared model so that the updates clients send back reveal their local data, a strategy called an active gradient inversion attack.

Recent attacks claim to be too stealthy for clients to notice. Carletti's team gives the first broad check of those claims, studying four state-of-the-art attacks and proposing lightweight client-side detectors. Their detectors look for statistically improbable weight patterns and odd loss and gradient behavior. Across many test settings, the detectors caught the attacks reliably, without requiring any change to the training protocol.
arxiv-2511-10602:
Ioana A. Stelea leads a 23-author team reporting the first localized detections of the cold neutral medium in IC10, a small starburst galaxy with only about a quarter of the Sun's metal content. Because conditions there resemble the early universe, its gas offers a window into how interstellar material heated and cooled long ago.

Using the Local Group L-band Survey's sharp radio resolution, the team searched for hydrogen absorption against nine background sources and found it along three sightlines inside the galaxy. The cold gas has spin temperatures of roughly 30 to 55 kelvin and makes up about a fifth to a third of the atomic gas along those paths. Molecular emission appears at the same velocities, showing the cold atomic and molecular gas are well mixed and more tightly coupled than in the Milky Way.
arxiv-2511-10802:
Renan da Silva Souza, Youjiang Xu, and Walter Hofstetter simulate a gas of ultracold fermions living in a square optical lattice and coupled to an optical cavity. In the right regime the system's steady state follows an extended Hubbard model in which the cavity mediates long-range interactions between the atoms.

Using real-space dynamical mean-field theory, they focus on the paramagnetic phases at quarter and half filling. At quarter filling, warming the system can paradoxically drive it from a uniform Fermi liquid into an ordered density wave, because the ordered phase carries more entropy. At half filling they map the competition among Fermi liquid, Mott insulator, and density wave phases, finding a coexistence region and settling which phase wins by comparing energies.
arxiv-2511-11302:
Junqing Cai, Guanghui Wang, and their colleagues pin down the exact degree threshold that forces an antidirected Hamilton cycle in an oriented graph. An antidirected cycle visits every vertex once while never letting two consecutive edges point the same way along the cycle. Degree conditions of Ore type, which sum out-degree and in-degree over non-adjacent pairs, are classic tools for forcing such spanning cycles.

Woodall's classic result forced a directed spanning cycle under a strong degree sum, and a recent result covered oriented graphs at a lower bound. The authors prove the sharp threshold for the antidirected case in large oriented graphs and show the bound cannot be improved.
arxiv-2511-11702:
Lian He and five co-authors introduce TASA, a framework that finds where an embodied agent can act in a three-dimensional scene, given a plain-language instruction. Knowing that a handle affords pulling, in the right place, is what separates a robot that watches from one that helps.

Earlier methods handled single objects or simply lifted flat image predictions into 3D, wasting the geometry inside point clouds and paying high computing costs. TASA works coarse to fine, pairing task-aware two-dimensional detection with geometric refinement in 3D. The combination aims at scene-level affordance segmentation that is both semantically aware and spatially precise enough for real interaction.
arxiv-2511-12102:
Abhisha Garg and five co-authors design a method to estimate terahertz wireless channels for many users at once. Terahertz links can carry huge data rates. Their channels are wide in both space and frequency. They suffer losses from absorption and reflection. They must also be read with low-grade converters to save power.

The team models those effects, then linearizes the quantized signals and applies a Bayesian group-sparse method that learns the channel across subcarriers at once. They also derive a bound on the estimation error to judge performance. Simulations show gains over other sparse methods in error measures for these dual-wideband systems.
arxiv-2511-12502:
Yu Liang and six co-authors propose an online training algorithm for binary spiking neural networks, which promise efficiency on resource-limited hardware. Training such networks usually stores latent weights and processes many time steps, so memory cost is high. That burden blocks training on the small devices where the networks are meant to run.

Their algorithm, BSO, updates weights directly through flip signals raised when the product of momentum and weight passes a threshold, with no latent weights kept. A temporal variant uses gradient information across time steps to adapt that threshold. Theory gives convergence guarantees and regret bounds for both versions, and experiments show stronger optimization than existing training methods.
arxiv-2511-12602:
Ria Shekhawat and four co-authors propose a detector for face morphing attacks. In such an attack a synthetic image blends biometric features from several people. It can fool recognition systems at borders and in security checks. Their approach works from a single image, with no reference photo needed. A teacher-student design carries the method.

A convolutional teacher refines a vision transformer student through knowledge distillation. Low-rank adaptation tunes the student cheaply, cutting computing cost while keeping detection accuracy. Experiments use a morphing dataset built from three public face sets and ten morphing algorithms, and compare against six leading single-image detectors. The authors report better detection performance and efficiency than those baselines.
arxiv-2511-12702:
Safaeid Hossain Arib and four co-authors address counting objects that are partly hidden. Counters for visible objects fail under occlusion, because their image features describe the covering surface instead of the target behind it. Their framework, CountOCC, rebuilds the missing features. It combines spatial context from visible fragments with meaning-based cues from text and image embeddings, filling in feature maps at hidden locations across several scales of the image pyramid.

A second objective keeps attention maps consistent between hidden and unobstructed views of the same scene. To test the idea, the team built occlusion versions of two counting benchmarks. CountOCC cut counting error sharply on both, and also set a new best result on a real-world capture dataset. The gains were large, around half the prior error on one benchmark. The work targets open-world counting, where objects of any kind may be blocked from view.
arxiv-2511-12802:
John M. Mango and Ronald Katende study when one small linear sketch can preserve the extreme singular values of every low-rank matrix. Sketches compress matrices for fast computation, but classical results do not control the extreme singular values. The authors state a conjecture: a sketch with only modestly more rows than the rank should suffice for that stronger preservation task.

On the constructive side, they pair a sparse sketch with a balancing map and show the sketched singular values collapse to a common scale when the input is well conditioned and incoherent. On the negative side, they prove sharper accuracy demands force much larger sketches. Experiments on structured matrix families show balancing improves conditioning and speeds iterative solvers, while coherent or nearly rank-deficient inputs fail as predicted. The paper mixes a conjecture, partial progress, and evidence about its limits.
arxiv-2511-12902:
Jose Pinedo Soto's doctoral thesis, completed at the University of Alberta under Valeri P. Frolov, builds black hole models without singularities. General relativity predicts points of infinite curvature inside black holes like the Schwarzschild and Kerr solutions, where the theory stops making sense. The thesis studies modified gravity theories that keep the event horizon but remove the singularity.

Throughout, the models are held to physical standards: each must reduce to ordinary general relativity in the right limits and keep its curvature quantities well behaved. The collected results argue that regular black holes are viable within modified gravity. Offering a semiclassical picture of black holes that does not need a full quantum theory of gravity to erase the singularity. The thesis runs to one hundred seventy-three pages and speaks to relativists weighing how much of classical black hole theory can survive.
arxiv-2511-13302:
Paul Bratch and 4 co-authors build a formal theory of cyclically ordered graphs, objects that sit between plain graphs and graphs drawn on surfaces. In such a graph, the edges at each vertex carry a cyclic order. The objects appear in topological graph theory, knot theory, and mathematical biology.

The authors set out several ways to present these graphs and show how each view helps build invariants, meaning numbers or polynomials that do not change under allowed moves. They adapt the matching, transition, and Yamada polynomials to this setting. The result gives workers in several fields a shared language and a tested set of tools.
arxiv-2511-13602:
Jungwoo Ho, Sangun Park, and Soyeong Oh propose a training-free estimator for multivariate joint entropy based on partitioned sample spacing. Entropy gauges uncertainty, and spacing methods infer it from gaps between sorted samples. Their method extends the one-dimensional idea by cutting space into local cells and pooling within-cell gap statistics.

Under mild conditions the estimator is strongly consistent, meaning it settles on the true value as data grow. Benchmarks across varied distributions beat nearest-neighbor estimators and rivaled recent flow-based methods, all without training or a fitted density model. It scaled well into moderately high dimensions and stayed robust when data were correlated or skewed, suiting information-theoretic machine learning tasks.
arxiv-2511-13702:
Luyao Niu and Nuoxian Huang present ST-ProC, a semi-supervised framework that identifies travel modes from GPS traces when labels are scarce. Naming whether a trip used walking, cycling, or transit powers urban planning, yet hand labeling traces is costly. Standard semi-supervised methods suffer confirmation bias here, teaching themselves their own early mistakes, and ignore the shape of the data.

ST-ProC joins a graph-prototypical core, which anchors classes and rejects noisy pseudo-labels by a margin rule, with contrastive and teacher-student support losses. Graph smoothing exploits the data manifold to steady learning. In sparse-label tests it beat every baseline by a wide margin, gaining over twenty percent against strong methods such as FixMatch.
arxiv-2511-13802:
Filippo Cenacchi and 3 co-authors screen for dementia passively from short talking-head videos by reading tiny facial movements over time. Most tools lean on speech or scripted interviews, which ties them to clinics and to language. Their method needs no words at all: blink patterns, small mouth and jaw motion, gaze shifts, and subtle head adjustments carry the signal.

Stabilized facial streams are summarized per short window by how motion is shared across channels, which makes each channel's role transparent. A new dataset of three hundred public videos, half self-reported dementia and half controls, benchmarks the approach. Shallow classifiers scored strongly on the standard ranking measures, with gaze instability and mouth dynamics the most telling cues.
arxiv-2511-13902:
Sara Jensen and Mark L. Lewis classify certain finite groups using the degrees of their characters, which are numbers tied to a group's representations. For a group whose largest character degree is d, the group order can be written using a gap value e. Earlier work bounded the group order when e exceeds one, and the extreme case is where the order reaches a specific quartic bound in e.

The authors settle that extreme case when e is a prime, and also when e equals four, nine, or twenty-five. Along the way they uncover a new nonsolvable Camina pair, a special configuration of conjugacy classes. The result narrows exactly which groups can attain the maximal character degree bound.
arxiv-2511-14002:
Chengpeng Li, Farnaz Behrang, August Shi, and one co-author present FlakyGuard, a tool that automatically repairs flaky software tests at industry scale. Flaky tests pass or fail unpredictably and waste developer time. Language models can fix them, but earlier tools starved the model of needed code or flooded it with irrelevant code.

FlakyGuard treats the codebase as a graph and explores it selectively to gather only the most relevant context. On real flaky tests from industrial repositories, it repaired nearly half of the reproducible cases, and developers accepted about half of its fixes. It beat prior methods by at least twenty-two percent in repair success, and every surveyed developer found its root-cause explanations useful.
arxiv-2511-14402:
Nicola Gambino, Richard Garner, and Christina Vasilakopoulou give one common account of several tensor products in category theory. Such products describe how two structured systems combine. Past work treated enriched categories, operads, and related structures as separate cases. Each case had its own definitions and proofs.

The three authors show that all these products come from one construction for double categories of monads. They then extend the product to bimodules, which link such structures. As a main build they form a double category for symmetric multicategories with a matching monoidal structure. The unified view should make future transfers between fields much simpler.
arxiv-2511-14702:
Farheen Ramzan, Yusuf Kiberu, and seven co-authors present a method for outlining heart muscle scars in enhanced MRI scans. Scar maps help doctors judge how much heart tissue is still alive, but uneven contrast and image flaws make the maps hard to draw. Heart tracing signals, or ECGs, offer extra clues, since faulty conduction often points to scarred regions.

Their framework blends ECG information with a standard atlas of heart segments to keep results true to the body. A fusion step weighs the two sources by the time gap between the tests, since they are not taken together. On clinical data the method beat prior approaches by a wide margin.
arxiv-2511-15002:
Fatemeh Lotfi, Hossein Rajoli, and Fatemeh Afghah improve resource management for open radio access networks, the modular design behind next-generation mobile service. A controller layer is meant to shift spectrum and computing resources as demand moves, and reinforcement learning agents are a popular way to run it. Those agents, though, often fail to generalize when conditions change.

The authors strengthen a leading actor-critic method with sharpness-aware training, applied through several cooperating agents. The extra regularization is switched on selectively, driven by how much each agent's learning signal fluctuates, so only agents facing complex conditions pay its cost. The targeted design aims at steadier performance with less wasted training effort.
arxiv-2511-15202:
Yinsheng Wang and three co-authors present SOLID, an approach that synergizes mathematical optimization with large language models for choice making. Optimizers excel at structured constraints, while language models add contextual judgment. SOLID lets the two agents collaborate iteratively through dual prices and deviation penalties. That exchange raises choice quality while keeping modules split and data private.

Under convexity assumptions the approach retains convergence guarantees. Those guarantees also inform prompt design for the language model agent. A stock mix case uses historical prices and financial news as inputs. Results show convergence across scenarios and higher annualized returns than an optimizer only baseline. The case validates the claimed synergy in a concrete financial setting.
arxiv-2511-15302:
Radek Machulka, Václav Michálek, and two co-authors calibrate cameras that count single photons using a glow-in-the-dark style light source. Knowing a camera's quantum efficiency, the share of incoming photons it actually registers, is basic to trusting its measurements. The gold standard uses pairs of photons born together, but that setup is demanding.

The team tests radioluminescent emitters, materials that glow steadily from internal radioactivity, as a simpler calibration light. They compare the glow-based method against the correlated-pair gold standard. They also propose using the emitters to transfer an absolute calibration from a reference camera to others. A cheap, stable transfer standard would ease precision photon counting in optics labs.
arxiv-2511-15602:
Midhuna V Ajith, Peter J Cameron, Mainak Ghosh, and Aparna Lakshmanan S build graphs whose points are the elements of a finite group. In the endomorphism graph, an arrow runs from one element to another when some structure-preserving map of the group to itself sends the first to the second. Dropping the arrows gives a simpler undirected version, and using only reversible maps gives the automorphism graph.

The authors study basic graph properties such as size, planarity, and shortest cycle length. They determine for which kinds of groups these graphs are complete, split into pieces, trees, or two-sided, and they compute the graphs for some special groups. Closing examples show the behavior is not always simple.
arxiv-2511-15802:
C. Weeks, P. Strange, P. Drmota, and J. Quintanilla study quantum advantage in a one-step graph domination game played on cycle graphs. In a domination game, players place pieces so every vertex is covered by a chosen vertex or its neighbor, and quantum strategies can use superposition to coordinate choices. Prior work found upper bounds for small graphs, leaving open how far the advantage extends.

The authors give explicit strategies that reach those bounds for small cycles and generalize them to larger cycles. They test the ideas three ways: numerically, analytically, and on noisy intermediate-scale quantum processors available today. The hardware runs realized the predicted quantum advantages with high accuracy, confirming the theory in practice.
arxiv-2511-16202:
Pei Yang, Ke Zhang, and six co-authors present a collaborative reward model for reinforcement learning from human feedback. A single black-box reward model must balance clashing preference dimensions, such as factuality, helpfulness, and safety. It also cannot explain its scores. Their frame instead fields a team of specialist evaluators. Each gives partial signals for its domain, plus global ranker and similarity evaluators.

A central aggregator fuses those signals at each step. It balances stepwise correctness, agreement among agents, and repetition penalties into one training reward that fits standard pipelines. No extra human notes beyond evaluator training are needed. A new benchmark supports training and assessment of such reward designs.
arxiv-2511-16702:
Molla Basir Ahamed, Rajesh Hossain, and Xiaoyuan Wang estimate the pre-Schwarzian and Schwarzian norms for the Robertson class of analytic functions. The family is defined by a rotated positivity condition on the unit disk. These norms measure how far a function bends from simple Möbius behavior and are basic tools in geometric function theory.

The authors first give an equivalent characterization of a subclass of Robertson functions, then prove distortion and growth theorems for it. From those they obtain the pre-Schwarzian and Schwarzian norms, plus a sharp upper bound for the Schwarzian norm expressed through the second derivative at the origin. Sharpness means the bound cannot be improved in general, completing the quantitative picture for this subclass.
arxiv-2511-17602:
Sushant Mehta guards the integrity of foundation model benchmarks against a subtle contamination problem. Models train more and more on synthetic data, which can quietly encode benchmark knowledge in paraphrased, conceptual form. Today's detectors catch token-level overlap with test sets but miss this semantic-level contamination, where nothing is copied word for word yet the answers are in effect rehearsed. Mehta's hierarchical framework checks four levels: tokens, semantics, reasoning patterns, and performance cliffs, sudden score jumps that betray familiarity.

Controlled experiments on three standard benchmarks, covering knowledge, math, and code, showed semantic contamination slipping past existing methods while the hierarchical approach caught it. That lifts detection quality a lot, about a quarter better on average than the best baselines. The framework is offered as a useful auditing tool for teams deploying synthetic training data with care.
arxiv-2511-18102:
Aditya Chinchure, Sahithya Ravi, Pushkar Shukla, Vered Shwartz, and Leonid Sigal introduce Spotlight, a task for finding and explaining errors in videos made by text-to-video models. Modern generators produce smooth, realistic clips, yet faults still slip in, and they are subtler and more local than before. Standard grading judges a whole video at once, without saying when a fault occurs or what kind it is.

The team generates six hundred videos from two hundred prompts with three leading generators. Then annotates over sixteen hundred faults across six types, from motion and physics to failure to follow the prompt. Faults in prompt adherence and physics prove most common and longest lasting. Spotlight gives model builders a finer diagnostic than a single score.
arxiv-2511-18202:
Hugo A Castillo-Sánchez and five co-authors put forward a new model for blood flow in tiny tubes. Red cells are soft and drift away from the wall, which leaves a thin clear layer with no cells near the edge. Old flow models miss that layer, so their speed and cell counts come out wrong.

The team adds the lift force that pushes soft cells off the wall to a standard balance model. Tests in small tubes then show the clear layer grow over time, as in real blood. Known effects on cell share and flow also match past lab and full scale results. The model offers a fast way to study thick soft particle flows.
arxiv-2511-18302:
Mohan Reddy argues, from a large empirical study, that human intelligence test frameworks do not fit large language models. Reddy assesses nine frontier models with a standard theory of human cognitive abilities and reports a paradox. Models with average to high human style IQ scores score near zero on some binary crystallized knowledge tasks, while judge scores vary widely.

Statistical analyses, including item response modeling and cross vendor judge checks, support Reddy's claim that the mismatch is a category error, applying a biological picture of mind to transformer systems. Reddy proposes building assessments native to machine cognition instead of borrowing human psychometrics.
arxiv-2511-18402:
An V. Q. Huynh, Minh B. Nguyen, Nhan X. V. Nguyen, and Minh Q. Vu study what stays fixed when two local shapes are linked by a rough stretch map. The shapes are germs, small local forms, inside a tame logic based class called an o-minimal structure. The map may stretch lengths, but only within a power bound set by a rate close to one.

The team prove a threshold rate: past it, key traits must match. If one germ has a no shortcut trait for its inner paths, so does the other. The tangent cones share size, and their links share hole structure. As a use, a complex analytic germ linked this way to flat space must be smooth. That gives a stronger form of a known smoothness theorem.
arxiv-2511-18502:
Maciej Maliborski and Tobias C. Sutter trace light paths that cross a spinning black hole from one outer zone to the other. The full Kerr space time, stretched to its math limit, has two outer flat zones linked through horizons and a ring singularity. Most light bends away; some special paths thread the throat.

With impact parameters the pair mark a closed zone, the inner throat, where the radial force has no real roots and light has no turn back point. At most two fixed latitude paths live there. They also mark a banned band of polar angles for paths that reach a far viewer. Paths are solved in closed form and by numeric steps, in matching ways that fix and extend past formulas. Mock images use the paths.
arxiv-2511-19002:
Dominik Gond, Justus Arweiler, Thomas Specht, Hans Hasse, and Fabian Jirasek release CHAOS, a large uniform database of molecular descriptors from quantum chemistry. Sigma profiles, which map how charge spreads on a molecule's surface, guide solvent choice and thermodynamic models. Past libraries were small and mixed in quality, which capped their use.

CHAOS holds sigma profiles for over fifty thousand molecules, all computed by one standard workflow at a set level of theory. Extra observables ride along: gas phase shapes, solvent model data, infrared spectra, heat capacities, entropies, and NMR shielding tensors. One protocol for all entries is the point. Data driven molecular design gains a consistent base.
arxiv-2511-19402:
Zichen Li, Renald Brenner, and Lucas Frérot model what happens to a rough contact when the load pressing two solids together drops. The true contact area helps set friction, and experiments on plastic blocks showed the area keeps a memory of its earlier state after unloading. Which model ingredients reproduce that memory was unclear.

The authors adapt contact theory to fractional viscoelastic materials, which relax over a wide range of timescales. Their models reproduce slow logarithmic aging under steady load. Yet on unloading the memory vanishes: the area acts as if the lower load had always applied. No run shows the decreasing phase seen elsewhere, marking a gap.
arxiv-2511-19502:
Udvas Acharjee and N. Uday Kiran generalize Euler's totient function, a classic count of numbers that share no factor with a given input. Their versions are built from elementary symmetric sums, following work by Toth that used the first and the k-th such sums. The focus here is the second symmetric sum.

For those totient variants the authors derive explicit product formulas, and they comment on how the construction behaves for an arbitrary symmetric sum. A method solves a restricted congruence problem with a greatest common divisor condition on a quadratic form. They show the product forms, counting polynomial zeros over finite fields, and that congruence class are all equivalent.
arxiv-2511-19802:
Guanming Liang proposes a dark matter candidate built from an analogy with superconductivity. In the model, interacting fermions with broken chiral symmetry pair up like Cooper pairs in a superconductor. The condensed pairs form the cold dark matter, while a frustrated version of the same transition leaves a residual tied to dark energy.

The thermal story runs from a hot radiation-like era through a freeze-out that fixes the relic amount, then a second-order transition into the condensate. The present-day condensate is predicted to decay slightly faster than standard cold dark matter. Combined microwave background and large-scale structure data could test that distinctive sign.
arxiv-2511-20002:
Changyue Li, Jiaying Li, Youliang Yuan, Jiaming He, Zhicong Huang, and Pinjia He study a new attack on multimodal language models. Such models are being placed in stateless systems like driving and robotics, where each decision stands alone. The authors ask whether one single crafted perturbation could hijack many separate decisions at once.

Their Semantic-Aware Universal Perturbation acts like a router: it senses the input's meaning and steers it toward attacker-chosen targets. Analysis of the latent space guides their SORT optimization method, and a new dataset with fine-grained semantics supports the tests. Across three representative models, the attack reaches a strong success rate over five targets from a single frame, showing the threat is real in principle.
arxiv-2511-20102:
Shen, Lu, Gui, and colleagues fix a paradox in how language models learn sparse attention. Their 2025 paper introduces SSA, Sparse Sparse Attention. Full attention costs grow quadratically with context length. Sparse attention lets each query see only some tokens. Native sparse methods paradoxically end up less sparse than full ones.

Excluded token pairs receive no gradient updates during training. They never learn to suppress themselves properly. SSA trains sparse and full attention together. Outputs of the two are aligned at every layer. Gradients then flow to every token throughout. Sparsity grows stronger under this bidirectional alignment regime. Benchmarks show top results in both inference modes. Models adapt smoothly to different sparsity budgets at runtime. Sparse training also improved long-context extrapolation unexpectedly. Attention sink over-allocation shrinks under the method. SSA showed the strongest extrapolation of all contenders.
arxiv-2511-20502:
Jové and Mencía measure how fast boundary points rush toward an attracting point. Their 2025 paper studies hyperbolic inner functions on the unit disk. Iterating such a function draws interior points to one Denjoy-Wolff point. Almost every boundary point follows it there under radial extension. The speed of that boundary journey was the open detail.

Explicit bounds now quantify the convergence rate. The angular derivative at the attracting point controls the speed. Results hold almost surely across the boundary circle. The shrinking target method underpins the proofs. Compositions of inner functions and their hitting behavior feed in. Even singular Denjoy-Wolff points are covered by the bounds. Earlier work characterized convergence through infinite sums. Hyperbolic functions always satisfy that summability condition. The rate is pinned between two geometric envelopes. Exponents involve the derivative raised to powers near the step count. Boundary dynamics thus becomes quantitatively predictable.
arxiv-2511-20602:
Jha, Parakh, and Subramaniam review quantum key distribution from proofs to real-world attacks. Their 2025 paper surveys how quantum physics promises unbreakable shared keys. Ideal security proofs assume perfect devices and channels. Practice brings photon tricks, hardware flaws, and noisy links. Bridging that divide is the review's mission.

Protocols sort into classes by their core mechanism. BB84-style schemes rest on the uncertainty principle. Hybrid three-stage designs enable direct secure communication. Continuous-variable frameworks form a third family. Twin-field and device-independent methods get modern chapters too. Three attack families receive in-depth treatment afterward. Photon-number splitting, Trojan-horse, and jamming attacks are dissected. Quantum error correction codes then counter the damage. Advanced codes raise channel fidelity and system robustness markedly. Quantum-augmented networks tie the story to deployment. Experimental breakthroughs punctuate the theoretical survey.
arxiv-2511-20902:
Glener Lanes Pizzolato and colleagues catalogue in 2025 the frauds besieging Pix, the payment system Brazil's central bank launched in November 2020. Pix became the country's most used payment method, moving tens of billions of transfers a year. The team combined a structured review with interviews of banking professionals. Three language models, DeepSeek-V3, GPT-4o, and Gemini 2.5 Pro, helped validate the classification.

The survey consolidated 18 records into 15 scam methodologies. They range from tampered QR codes pasted over charity livestreams to divert donations. The list runs through forged receipts and fake scheduling proofs to the Ghost Hand, malware letting a scammer operate the victim's phone. Physical attacks appear too, including express kidnappings forcing transfers at gunpoint. The pattern over time is a shift from pure social engineering to hybrid schemes mixing manipulation with technical exploitation, amplified by AI. The authors conclude defences must adapt as fast, with adaptive measures and user awareness.
arxiv-2511-21702:
Dong Liu, Yanxuan Yu, and Ben Lengerich prune the most expensive step of language model generation with a geometric guarantee, in 2025. Every generated token requires scoring the full vocabulary, 32,000 to 256,000 candidates, through a huge output layer. CSV-Decode instead computes a small sub-vocabulary per step, using geometric upper bounds to certify which tokens can be safely skipped.

Vocabulary embeddings are clustered offline, and centroid-plus-radius bounds identify omissions that cannot change the result. The method carries dual guarantees: exact top-k certification, or a certified approximation of the full softmax distribution with a chosen error tolerance. A complete system implementation adds sparse matrix kernels, multi-GPU sharding, and CUDA graph optimization. Evaluated across 11 models, CSV-Decode delivered consistent, substantial speedups over full-vocabulary decoding with low fallback rates. Users trade a precisely bounded amount of exactness for speed, with the bound proven rather than hoped for.
arxiv-2511-22002:
Xu, Cheng, Capa Salinas, and a large collaboration of condensed-matter physicists use spectroscopic-imaging scanning tunneling microscopy to map the phase diagram of the kagome superconductor CsV3Sb5 as a function of chemical doping. They deliberately suppress the material's 2×2 charge density wave by substituting atoms at two distinct lattice sites. They then watch how the electronic structure's rotational symmetry behaves as the charge order disappears.

Rotational symmetry breaking, called electronic nematicity, does not vanish with the charge density wave. It persists in short-range nanoscale patches across every sample and a wide doping range, long after all charge order is gone. Because the nematic signal survives, the authors argue it is the intrinsic parent state of the kagome superconductors, the background out of which superconductivity and the exotic low-temperature phases later emerge.
arxiv-2511-22202:
Abedi, Khazali, and Mølmer use quantum optimal control to make Rydberg atom processors do in one pulse what normally takes a circuit of gates. Quantum algorithms are usually compiled into one- and two-qubit operations, but Rydberg platforms naturally support conditional dynamics on several atoms at once. The authors shape single continuous laser pulses that directly implement multi-qubit controlled-phase, controlled-NOT, and controlled-SWAP gates, using the Krotov optimization method to tune intensity, phase, and frequency.

Native multi-qubit gates shorten operation time and reduce decoherence exposure, and the control field itself continuously protects the atoms from environmental noise. The standout number is the controlled-SWAP, or Fredkin, gate: 99.74 percent fidelity in simulation while accounting for spontaneous emission, laser fluctuations, and Doppler dephasing. The authors argue such robust native operations are a practical route to shallower, more reliable circuits on neutral-atom hardware.
arxiv-2511-22402:
Sridhar, Ravi, and Ghosh ask where a language model registers doubt in medical writing. Words such as might, could, and should signal uncertainty, and in clinical text they change how a statement is read. Rather than measuring answer confidence, the team probes internal activations to see how strongly each layer reacts when a certain statement is reworded as hedged.

Their metric, Model Sensitivity to Uncertainty, compares activations across matched statement pairs layer by layer. Sensitivity was low in early layers but rose sharply deeper in the network. In the LLaMA 3.2 model, the score climbed from 2.67 at the first layer to 31.96 by layer 15, and the same pattern appeared across the Qwen variants tested. Models thus build an organised internal representation of uncertainty, which could help make clinical AI easier to interpret and trust.
arxiv-2511-22602:
Busalacchi, Martino, and Rizzo build a theory of polynomial identities for a generalised class of algebras. The setting combines group gradings, sorting algebra elements by a finite group's labels, with an extra W-algebra action. It asks which identities such graded W-algebras satisfy and how fast the count of distinct identities, the codimension sequence, grows. Using the graded multiplier algebra of a finite-dimensional algebra, they develop the machinery of generalised graded identities.

Two structural results anchor the theory: the graded generalised exponent, governing codimension growth, exists and equals the graded exponent. The authors then compute explicitly the generalised identities of the two-by-two upper triangular matrix algebra under its canonical two-element grading, for every graded W-action. They close with examples of varieties whose codimensions grow polynomially, the borderline regime between polynomial and exponential growth that classifies how tame an algebra's identities are.
arxiv-2511-22702:
Toomey and colleagues report on three decades of pulsar observations made newly accessible. Murriyang, the CSIRO Parkes 64-metre radio telescope, has observed pulsars since the 1990s. Its data now sit in CSIRO's Data Access Portal, an archive of nearly two million files from more than 400 pulsar projects, described as leading the global effort in open pulsar data. The authors document the archive's status and the full data lifecycle behind it.

The paper covers acquisition, analysis, reduction, visualisation, preservation, and dissemination of the datasets, explaining how researchers can find and use observations spanning the telescope's modern era. It argues for the value of long-term archives, where old observations gain worth as methods improve and pulsar timing builds value with timespan, and presents new results obtained from archival data. For the pulsar community, the archive turns one observatory's accumulated history into a shared, reusable resource.
arxiv-2511-22802:
Ralston, Tangerman, Veerman, and Wu study how evenly the simplest chaotic sequence spreads out. Rotating a point around a circle by a fixed irrational angle generates a sequence whose evenness its discrepancy measures, a notion due to Pisot and Van Der Corput. They study the Birkhoff sum of the centred fractional part along the orbit, a piecewise-linear function, and define Birkhoff measures from the density of its pre-images. They ask how that density's graph changes with step count.

They prove the support length of the Birkhoff measure is expressible directly in terms of the discrepancy. When the step count is a continued fraction denominator of the angle, the density's graph is approximately an isosceles trapezoid. New, brief proofs of two classical results, Ramshaw's and Kuipers and Niederreiter's, allow efficient computation of both sums and discrepancies. An abstract equidistribution question becomes concrete, computable geometry.
arxiv-2511-23202:
Li and colleagues give a new syndrome-based decoding algorithm for Trombetti-Zhou codes, a 2019 family of maximum rank distance codes used in rank-metric coding for networks and cryptography. The obstacle is structural, since these codes are linear only over a subfield of their field, so the generator and parity-check matrices do not exist. The team defines subfield versions of both using a trace almost dual basis.

With those matrices in hand, decoding splits into two cases based on the error's rank weight relative to the code's minimum distance. Below half the distance minus a half step, the problem converts exactly into decoding a Gabidulin code of one larger dimension, for which fast algorithms already exist. At the boundary value, it reduces to computing the rank of a certain matrix. The authors analyze the complexity of the whole procedure.
arxiv-2512-00002:
Tingyen Wang gauges how much firms in one industry differ from each other. The usual way to fit production models rests on tight preset forms. Those forms can miss how firms act when outcomes are unsure. His framework swaps in a maximum entropy fit, which assumes less, plus a shape-based way to sum up the spread.

Entropy here means the fit uses only what the data support, and no more. The shape tool, called a zonotope, turns the spread of firm traits into a form that can be measured. The work draws on Enterprise Surveys, a large set of firm-level data, so the spread it reports rests on real firms, not stylized ones.
arxiv-2512-00102:
Ahmad Al-Badawi, Faizuddin Ahmed, and İzzet Sakallı study a black hole surrounded by a cloud of strings in a 2025 study. The black hole is of Letelier type, static and spherically symmetric, and it sits inside an electromagnetic universe. Both surroundings can distort its basic properties.

By deriving the event horizon from the lapse function, the authors show how the string cloud and the electromagnetic background each change the horizon radius. The comparison case is the standard Schwarzschild black hole. Such exact solutions help theorists test how exotic environments would alter the simplest black hole picture. Clouds of strings are an exotic ingredient from early-universe and string-inspired models.
arxiv-2512-00402:
Fuzzy dark matter imagines dark matter as ultralight scalar particles with wave-like behavior. Hayato Shimabukuro, Shihang Liu, and Bohua Li probe its imprint on the cosmic twenty-one centimeter signal in 2025. They use the wavelet scattering transform to read the signal.

Quantum pressure in fuzzy dark matter suppresses small-scale structure, delaying star formation and altering the thermal history of intergalactic gas. Those changes should show in the signal from cosmic dawn and the epoch of reionization. Detecting or ruling out such imprints would narrow what dark matter can be, using radio telescopes as particle detectors. The twenty-one centimeter line comes from hydrogen, the universe's most common element.
arxiv-2512-00502:
The CMS Collaboration reports a first observation of electroweak production of a photon with two forward jets in 2025. The measurement uses proton-proton collision data recorded at the Large Hadron Collider during 2016 to 2018. The collisions ran at the collider's standard high energy.

Electroweak production is rarer and cleaner than the strong-force processes that usually accompany photons and jets. Observing it confirms a predicted corner of the Standard Model and sharpens tools for hunting deviations. Forward jets are a signature of the exchange of weak bosons, so this channel tests electroweak theory in a distinctive regime. The data set is large, which the rare electroweak process requires to be seen at all.
arxiv-2512-01502:
Dennis Gross studies how to verify policies learned by quantum reinforcement learning. Such policies use quantum traits to pick actions in sequence. They aim to beat classic policies on some tasks. But quantum hardware adds noise from measures and flaws.

That noise makes a policy's acts less sure. Gross works on formal checks that hold under that noise. A checked policy can be trusted to meet set bounds. Trust matters if quantum agents are to run in labs or plants where a bad act has a real cost. Noise-aware checks also state plainly what they cannot promise, so users know which policy acts stay open to hardware drift over time.
arxiv-2512-01702:
Bei Zhou and co-authors map heart activation fast across many atrial shapes. Maps of electrical activation guide treatment of arrhythmias. Detailed simulations are too slow for clinic use or large cohorts. Each heart's shape differs, which breaks fixed-grid methods.

Their operator-learning frame ignores the specific geometry. It predicts local activation time fields almost at once. One trained model serves diverse left atrial shapes. Near-instant maps could let doctors test ablation plans live, tuned to each patient's own heart shape. Near-instant maps also scale to cohorts, letting trials compare activation patterns across hundreds of patients in the time one simulation once took.
arxiv-2512-02202:
Atomic clocks count the shakes of atoms to keep time. Quantum links between atoms can make those counts sharper than any classic method. Raphael Kaubruegger and Adam Kaufman wrote a 2025 chapter on this linked kind of measure. They show what it can do for optical atomic clocks.

When atoms are linked, a joint measure can beat the noise floor of lone measures. Used in a clock, that means finer timekeeping. Finer clocks aid guidance, earth science, and deep tests of physics. The chapter lays out the core ideas and where they may lead, in the field's most grown-up test bed.
arxiv-2512-02402:
Story generators built on language models often drift from what the user asked, because intent is hard to pin down and controls are coarse. Yunchao Wang and six co-authors present TaleFrame in 2025, an interactive story generation system designed to give users fine-grained control.

The system translates user intent into story outputs more faithfully by clarifying input specifications and exposing detailed levers over the narrative. Creative writing tools live or die by whether the author feels obeyed. TaleFrame's design study shows how much control is enough for generated stories to feel authored rather than merely produced.
arxiv-2512-02502:
Luyao Niu and five co-authors design an app that helps people learn their own neighborhood. The 15-minute city idea holds that daily needs should sit within a short walk or bike ride. Living that way takes more than near shops; people also need fast, reliable facts about nearby places.

AskNearby uses a large language model to answer questions about local services and events. It also builds personalized cognitive map suggestions, tuned to how each person pictures the area. Better local knowledge could help residents actually use what their neighborhood already offers, instead of driving farther by habit. The app fits best in dense towns, where most daily needs sit a short walk from home.
arxiv-2512-02902:
Weiqi Li and four co-authors show that vision language action models generalize better than their failures suggest. Such models drive robots by joining sight, words, and action. They perform strongly in distribution, but degrade sharply under new camera viewpoints and visual changes.

The team traces the brittleness to spatial modeling misalignment, not physical modeling. Their one shot adaptation recalibrates visual representations with lightweight, learnable updates. A tiny fix for spatial alignment could make robot policies far more portable across cameras and rooms, without retraining the whole model. One quick fix that saves a whole rig from scrap is the kind of gain shops dream of when fleets must roll each day.
arxiv-2512-03002:
Proton bunches squeezed to extreme density are a critical step toward future proton driven muon colliders. Compressing a high intensity bunch lengthwise fights the bunch's own space charge, which pushes it apart. The proposed test uses the Integrable Optics Test Accelerator ring at Fermilab.

The experiment would search for the best radio frequency cavity parameters and lattice configurations for compression. Results from a real ring beat pure simulation for such unstable beams. A working compression recipe feeds directly into collider designs that need short, dense proton pulses to make muons. Short dense pops of protons are the feed stock of muon beams. A ring test that finds the best squeeze earns its beam time back in kind.
arxiv-2512-03102:
Early guesses in a crisis shape all later choices. Yiwei Shi, Hongnan Ma, Mengyue Yang, Cunjia Liu, and Weiru Liu study how to fix wrong early estimates in this 2025 work. First reports may rest on thin or biased facts, yet plans build on them fast.

Wrong estimates can cause delays, wasted resources, and even harm. The authors propose a method that uses diffusion models to explore and correct the state estimate. Better correction tools could help emergency teams adjust as real facts arrive. The ideas may also serve other high-stakes fields. The method aims to explore better states rather than defend a flawed first guess.
arxiv-2512-03302:
Some particle decays would break a rule thought to be strict. Arindam Das, Takaaki Nomura, and Kei Yagyu study lepton number violation in this 2025 work. They look at decays of the Higgs and Z bosons into pairs of right-handed neutrinos.

Because these neutrinos are Majorana particles, their own antiparticles, the final state can hold same-sign leptons plus jets. That pattern would show two units of lepton number violation. Seeing it would reshape neutrino physics. The authors map where experiments could look for the signal. Same-sign leptons stand out in detectors, since few standard processes produce them.
arxiv-2512-03402:
Fine-tuning large models cheaply is a major goal in AI. Yixing Xu and co-authors present Dual LoRA in this 2025 work. LoRA adapts a model with low-rank updates, but that low-rank limit can hurt performance.

The authors split updates into magnitude and direction parts. Treating those two aspects separately can sharpen adaptation within the same budget. Better parameter-efficient methods let smaller teams customize big models. That lowers cost and energy use while keeping quality high for specific tasks. Splitting magnitude from direction mirrors how vectors change, giving updates more freedom within a small rank budget.
arxiv-2512-03702:
Near the horizon of a black hole, radiation can become so dense that photons and electron-positron pairs form a trapped shell of fire. She-Sheng Xue studies that extreme environment in a 2025 high-energy astrophysics preprint. The shell's temperature varies from place to place and can exceed the energy equivalent of an electron's mass.

Xue examines a Compton-rocket effect, in which intense radiation pushes electrons hard enough to trigger runaway acceleration. In a simplified one-dimensional model based on a gamma-ray burst engine, matter flowing inward forms the trapped shell, which then cools by emitting ultra-high-energy particles and ordinary radiation. The author calculates how the luminosity of those particles changes over time. The accelerated electrons and protons can go on to produce very-high-energy photons and neutrinos, connecting the model to observations and experiments that hunt such particles.
arxiv-2512-04002:
When a gravitational wave passes a black hole's neighbourhood, the hole deforms slightly, and Love numbers measure how much. Dimitrios Kosmopoulos, Davide Perrone, and Mikhail Solon compute dynamical versions of those numbers in a 2025 theoretical physics preprint. Standard effective field theory treatments demand higher-order calculations that grow punishingly hard.

The authors build a new effective theory around a spherical shell. The behaviour of gravitational perturbations is imported directly from known black hole solutions. The shell's finite size tames short-distance divergences, while its tidal responses are carried by higher-dimensional operators. Applying the machinery to scalar perturbations, they derive Love numbers for Schwarzschild black holes and generic compact bodies to unusually high order in Newton's constant. A surprise emerges: the scalar Love numbers arrange around values of the Riemann zeta function, a pattern the authors conjecture persists to all orders.
arxiv-2512-04302:
Shuyuan Zhang surveys how to give learning agents better step-by-step feedback. The survey appeared on arXiv in 2025. It deals with reinforcement learning, where agents learn by trial and error. Reward scores guide what the agent does next. When scores come rarely or late, learning crawls. When scores are shaped badly, agents learn tricks that game the score.

Rich feedback at each step can speed learning up. It can also steer conduct toward the real goal. But hand-made score rules are hard to get right. That is most true in large, tangled settings. Zhang walks through the main fixes now in use. One path learns scores from watching skilled conduct. One builds score models from human likes and dislikes. One lets agents form their own inner drives to explore. The survey weighs what each path does well and where each can fail.
arxiv-2512-05302:
Mike Krebs, Alan Pan, and Anand Prakash prove two results about discrete fundamental groups of graphs. These are algebraic gadgets that imitate the loop-counting fundamental group of a space, but for a network of vertices and edges. For the version introduced by Matsushita at radius two, a clean combinatorial description exists, and the authors exploit it. Similar theorems were known for a rival notion of discrete fundamental group; this paper settles them for Matsushita's.

First, they prove a Seifert-van Kampen-type theorem: the group of a glued graph can be computed from the pieces, the discrete analogue of topology's workhorse gluing principle. Second, they show any group whatsoever can be realized as this fundamental group of some graph, and their construction doubles as a new proof of the corresponding theorem for the rival notion. The work firms up the foundations of discrete homotopy theory.
arxiv-2512-06002:
Evan Conway and four co-authors give robots a planner that thinks ahead without thinking forever. Robots in partly observable worlds must plan under uncertainty; principled planners are often too slow, or wander. POrTAL, Plan-Orchestrated Tree Assembly for Lookahead, is a lightweight algorithm that fuses two existing planners: the replanning discipline of FF-Replan and the tree search of POMCP.

POrTAL is an anytime algorithm: bounded time in, best plan out. Across tests it generally beat both parent algorithms on the length of the plan actually executed, with the advantage clearest at moderate uncertainty, the regime real robots inhabit. In between, orchestrating a search tree with a strong replanner squeezes wasted steps out of robot behavior. Shorter plans mean less time and energy spent.
arxiv-2512-06102:
Ufuk Çakır, Victor-Alexandru Darvariu, Bruno Lacerda, and Nick Hawes build a wildfire simulator fast enough to teach firefighting to machines. Learning agents need millions of practice fires; existing simulators are too slow. JaxWildfire uses cellular automata for fire spread, implemented in JAX. Graphics processors run vast batches at once.

The result runs six to thirty five times faster than existing software, and because the implementation is differentiable, its parameters can be tuned by gradient based optimization. Agents learn suppression policies inside it. Wildfire management is still largely reactive. Fast simulation enables strategies rehearsed in advance. Tools like this move a field from reaction to planning.
arxiv-2512-06402:
Jose Gaspar and Minoru Osawa ask how the map of industry shifts as trade gets freer, when ideas leak between firms by region. In their model, firms climb a quality ladder by inventing better goods, and the pace of invention in a region depends on how much knowledge spills over from nearby and distant regions. A spread mechanism pulls each region's quality toward the world frontier, so lasting gaps trace back to where researchers and firms sit.

The authors solve the model in closed form, then test what happens as trade opens. When local spillovers rule, freer trade pulls firms and researchers ever tighter into one hub. When spillovers reach across regions, the crowd can thin back out: late movers gain by settling in the smaller region, borrowing the hub's knowledge while dodging its congestion. The balance of spillovers decides whether open trade concentrates or spreads economic life.
arxiv-2512-06902:
Fazle Rabbi and co-authors present BabelCoder, a system that moves working code from one programming language to another using a team of specialized agents. Migration between languages is common as systems age, yet automatic translation has long been error-prone. Language models improved matters, but single-pass attempts still miss clues in the code's structure and context. Earlier tools could also patch mistakes, yet lacked an organized division of labor.

BabelCoder splits the job three ways. One agent drafts the translation, another tests whether it behaves like the original, and a third repairs what the tests catch. The loop keeps the specification, what the code is meant to do, at the center. On four public benchmark sets, the system beat four leading rivals in nearly every comparison. Its average accuracy reached a level the authors present as a strong mark for agent teamwork in software migration.
arxiv-2512-07002:
Abdenacer Makhlouf and Andrés Pérez-Rodríguez study evolution algebras, algebraic systems built to mimic how a population's types reproduce from one generation to the next. Their topic is deformation: what happens when the multiplication rules of such an algebra are wiggled slightly. Some wiggles produce genuinely new algebras, while others are the same algebra in disguise. The authors determine when formal deformations exist and sort them into classes of truly distinct ones.

A second half treats degeneration, the opposite journey, where one algebra arises as a limiting case of another. Diagrams in the style of Hasse map out which algebras can degenerate into which others. The census covers nilpotent evolution algebras, a tractable family where repeated products eventually vanish, up through dimension four.
arxiv-2512-07202:
Xi Geng and Sheng Wang estimate how likely a noisy, memory-laden system is to ever visit a given region. Their system is a stochastic differential equation of hypoelliptic type, where noise enters only some directions and spreads to the rest through the dynamics. Driven by fractional Brownian motion, a random process whose past colors its future. The main result bounds the hitting probability from both sides using a capacity, a size measure for sets built from the geometry the system's controls define.

Groundwork comes first: the solution's finite-dimensional distributions possess smooth densities, shown in the general setting of equations driven by Gaussian rough paths. Then a local upper bound on the joint density is derived in terms of the control distance for the memory-driven case. The hitting estimate generalizes a known result for ordinary elliptic equations to this degenerate, rough world.
arxiv-2512-07402:
Mary Eby and Cathal Cummins add memory to the physics of microplastics riding ocean waves. Plastic particles at the surface do not simply drift with the water as the smallest ones do. Most transport models use only linear drag, quietly discarding the history force. The push a particle feels from the wake of its own past motion, which limits them to the tiniest sizes. The authors implement that history term with a multistep integration scheme, extending the models to larger particles in waves over water of any depth.

Their simulations locate the tipping point precisely: once a certain combination of particle inertia and density ratio passes a threshold. The memory force becomes the leading part of the horizontal drag. That threshold sits about three times lower than classical estimates that ignored history had suggested.
arxiv-2512-07802:
Zhaochong An and fourteen co-authors wrote this 2025 paper on AI video that tells a story. Real stories unfold across many shots, each clip separate yet linked in meaning. Generators often lose the thread between shots, breaking characters and settings.

Their system, OneStory, reframes the job as next-shot generation. It builds each new shot on everything the story has shown so far. A pretrained image-to-video model supplies visual conditioning. Two new modules manage the cross-shot memory that stories need. A frame selection module keeps the most informative frames from earlier shots. An adaptive conditioner compresses those frames by importance into compact context. The team also curates a dataset of multi-shot stories with careful captions. Training strategies are tuned to the next-shot way of working. On diverse, complex scenes, OneStory beats rival methods on narrative coherence.
arxiv-2512-08002:
M P Savelov, a mathematician working in probability and statistics, posted a research paper on arXiv in December 2025. His subject is the testing of random number generators, a basic need in computing and cryptography. He studies statistics that generalize several tests found in standard packages such as the NIST suite and TestU01.

Savelov finds the limit joint distribution of these statistics under a null hypothesis of truly random output. He also treats a simple alternative hypothesis that drifts toward the null one as the sample grows. Alongside the main result, he proves an analogue of the Berry Esseen inequality for these statistics. He also gives conditions under which the statistics become asymptotically independent, which helps testers combine separate checks safely.
arxiv-2512-08102:
Misa Viveiros, Samuel S Taylor, Cody Covington, and Kalman Varga, computational physicists, posted a theoretical study on arXiv in December 2025. Their subject is Coulomb explosion imaging, a method that blasts a molecule apart with a fast ion and rebuilds its structure from the flying fragments. They simulate the process from first principles for pyridazine molecules struck by energetic carbon ions.

Using time dependent density functional theory with moving nuclei, the team varies where the projectile hits and how it crosses the molecular plane. Trajectories that avoid direct hits on atoms gave the most faithful structural reconstructions. Direct impacts dumped large, localized momentum into the molecule and distorted the recovered geometry. In plane paths caused much more ionization than paths crossing at right angles, since they travel deeper through the electron cloud. The findings explain much of the noise seen in real experiments and show where the method reaches its limits.
arxiv-2512-08402:
Ties Hendrik Fikkers, Nithesh Balasubramanian, Joost van Hofslot, and colleagues, physicists in the Netherlands, posted an experimental study on arXiv in December 2025. They report a cold beam of barium hydroxide molecules, made with a cryogenic buffer gas source. BaOH is a prized molecule for testing fundamental symmetries, including the search for the electron electric dipole moment, a measurement that could reveal new physics.

Inside the cold source, barium metal is blasted by a laser while water vapor is seeded into neon buffer gas, and the molecules form there. Shining laser light on the barium atoms at a key transition boosted the molecular flux roughly eleven fold, matching a trick seen in kindred molecules. Under typical conditions the beam drifts at a gentle speed with an intensity comparable to established barium fluoride beams. A bright, slow beam like this is exactly what precision symmetry experiments need as their starting material.
arxiv-2512-08502:
Agnieszka Janiuk, Bozena Czerny, Pulkit Ojha, and colleagues, astrophysicists, posted an invited review on arXiv in December 2025. Their subject is radiation pressure instability in accretion disks, the swirling gas that feeds black holes and neutron stars. The classic disk models date to the nineteen seventies, and almost at once theorists saw that disks shining near their Eddington limit should turn unstable when radiation pressure takes over.

In small galactic black hole systems, that instability appears as heartbeat states: huge, repeating pulses of brightness, and possibly a source of the chaotic patterns in their light curves. Neutron stars add a boundary layer where the flow lands, complicating the picture in useful ways. On the largest scales, the same instability may set the duty cycles of radio loud active galaxies, and drive dramatic changing look events where a nucleus transforms its spectrum.
arxiv-2512-08602:
Alessandro Neri and Paolo Santonastaso extend a way to represent matrix algebras using skew polynomials. Matrix algebras here are built as direct sums of matrix spaces over division rings. In the representation, a distance used in coding theory, called sum rank distance, is captured by a weight on the linked skew polynomials.

That weight depends on degrees and on greatest common right divisors with a defining polynomial. Using the representation, the authors build new families of codes that reach the best possible sum rank distance.
