Carriers can react to enzymes, acid levels, heat, light, or magnetic fields. Their surfaces can wear tags that grip tumour marks, such as folic acid. Loads range from small drugs to genes and even living cells. The team ends with a plan for AI-guided carriers.
europmc-pmc1082902:
Gould asks why tree leaves turn red in this 2004 review. Anthocyanins are the pigments, meaning colour-giving chemicals, behind the red and purple of autumn leaves. They were once seen as a wasteful flourish with no real use. Gould gathers newer work that points the other way, toward many protective jobs for these pigments.

The pigments help leaves cope with drought, strong sunlight, heavy metals in soil, leaf-eating animals, and germs, the review says. They soak up high-energy light, which shields the leaf's food-making parts from harm. They also mop up harmful oxygen-based molecules that can injure cells. Gould argues the pigments can be vital for a plant to survive harsh spots. He frames them as a multi-tool rather than mere decoration.
europmc-pmc11292402:
Yan and colleagues review the flexibility of macrophages in tissue repair in this 2024 paper. Macrophages are immune cells that adapt their behaviour to the tissue around them. Old teaching split them into two forms, M1 and M2. Recent work shows a spectrum of states beyond that split. Signal pathways, gene regulators, and chemical tags on DNA jointly steer which state a cell takes.

The review details the cascades involved, including Toll-like receptors, STAT proteins, nuclear receptors, and microRNAs. Two newer concepts get full treatment: metabolic reprogramming, where cells rewire fuel use, and trained immunity, a lasting memory-like tuning. In repair, macrophages coordinate inflammation, new vessel growth, and matrix rebuilding to restore tissue balance. The authors discuss harnessing this plasticity to speed regeneration. They frame control of these cells as a therapeutic lever.
europmc-pmc11294602:
An, Yu, Liu, Tang, Yang, and Chen review cell death driven by oxygen radicals, and its use against cancer, in this 2024 paper. Reactive oxygen species are reactive oxygen molecules made during normal cell work. In balance they aid signalling and immunity. When production outruns defences, oxidative stress damages fats, proteins, and DNA and can kill the cell.

That death takes several forms, among them ferroptosis, necroptosis, and pyroptosis, each with distinct genetics and chemistry. Forcing it in cancer cells is an emerging treatment approach, the authors say. Five antioxidant proteins are named as key targets: SLC7A11, GCLC, GPX4, TXN, and TXNRD. Blocking them tips cancer cells into lethal stress. The review summarises the mechanisms of each death form and the drug opportunities they open.
europmc-pmc1239902:
Sporns, Tononi, and Kötter proposed mapping all brain connections in 2005. They named that full map the human connectome. No such map existed for the human brain at the time. Other mammals had partial connection collections, but nothing complete.

Knowing the parts and links of a network is key to grasping how it works. A full structural map would ground brain science and medicine. The authors lay out a plan to gather, store, and share the data. Sporns argues the map could explain how brain states arise. It could also reshape the study of thought and behavior.
europmc-pmc12687902:
GBD 2023 Cancer Collaborators estimated world cancer burden with forecasts in 2025. Many countries lack current cancer watch data. Estimates cover 47 cancer types or groupings. Data span 204 countries from 1990 to 2023, with forecasts to 2050.

Cancer registries, death records, and verbal autopsies fed the models. Mortality came from pooled models, and incidence from mortality ratios. Survival modeling produced prevalence and disability estimates. Risk-linked cancer burden was tracked across the same years. GBD 2023 Cancer Collaborators give planners a full global cancer ledger. Forecasts extend the same estimates through the year 2050. Risk-linked burden was tracked for the same years.
europmc-pmc1403802:
Bollback introduced a software tool named SIMMAP in 2006. Biologists use family trees, called phylogenies, to trace how traits change over time. Older tools relied on parsimony, which picks the path with the fewest changes. That shortcut can mislead, since it ignores doubt about timing, past states, and the tree itself.

SIMMAP maps traits with chance built in, a method called stochastic mapping. It samples many likely trees and histories rather than trusting one. Bollback notes that users can study trait links, shifts in form, and change in proteins. The tool turns a single fixed answer into a range of well weighed options.
europmc-pmc1435902:
Many adults struggle to read health leaflets, and clinics need a quick way to spot them. Morris and co-authors tested a one-question screen in 2006. The Single Item Literacy Screener asks how often a person needs help reading health papers. They checked it against a full reading test in 999 adults with diabetes.

About 17 percent had limited reading skill. The one question caught just over half of them, but ruled out the problem well. Most who screened clear, nine in ten, could read fine. Morris suggests the screen helps staff aim deeper checks at those most in need, though it misses some cases.
europmc-pmc1448202:
Drugs of abuse act on brain pumps that clear signaling chemicals after use. Han and Gu compared those pumps in humans and mice in 2006. The pumps handle dopamine, norepinephrine, and serotonin, three key brain signals. Past lab reports of drug strength on them clashed by up to sixty-fold.

Han tested five drugs in one shared setup for a fair match. Cocaine blocked all three pumps at like strength. Methylphenidate hit two pumps hard but the serotonin pump weakly. Human and mouse pumps reacted much the same, within four-fold. The work gives drug studies a cleaner shared baseline.
europmc-pmc1550802:
Old antibiotics, dropped for their toxicity, are back in demand. Falagas and Kasiakou reviewed the safety of polymyxins in 2006. These drugs, found in 1947, kill tough Gram-negative bacteria that shrug off newer drugs. Fear of kidney and nerve damage had shelved them, except for cystic fibrosis care.

Old reports warned of frequent kidney and nerve harm, including blocked muscles. Fresh studies found kidney harm less common and less severe. Nerve effects were usually mild and faded when the drug stopped. No recent cases of breathing stoppage appeared. Falagas credits careful dosing and better intensive care for the safer record.
europmc-pmc1557402:
Some bacteria survive antibiotics by going dormant, not by resistance genes. Shah and co-authors found a way to isolate those persisters in 2006. They guessed the cells would make proteins slowly. Using E. coli that glows in step with growth, they sorted out the dim cells.

Those dim cells tolerated antibiotics that killed their kin. Their gene activity profile matched neither fast-growing nor starved cells. Genes for toxin-antitoxin modules, paired poisons and antidotes, were switched on. Shah concludes persisters form a distinct body state. That state, about one percent of a culture, helps explain why infections return after treatment.
europmc-pmc1564002:
Fish keep growing new eye cells all their lives. Raymond and co-authors mapped the stem cells behind that growth in adult zebrafish in 2006. True stem cells renew themselves, make many cell types, and wake after injury.

Two niches sustain them. One is a ring at the retina's edge, the ciliary marginal zone. The other wraps certain Müller glia, support cells inside the retina. In calm eyes those glia feed only rod cell lines. After injury they can rebuild many neuron types. Raymond likens the edge ring to stem cell niches in the adult mammal brain.
europmc-pmc1852402:
Hellemans, Vandesompele and co-authors described qBase in 2007, free software that turns raw quantitative PCR data into clean results. This lab method counts DNA or RNA copies with great sensitivity, and it had become the standard for measuring gene activity. Instrument software, though, stopped at raw cycle values.

Labs were left to normalize and calibrate results by hand, often using a single reference gene and tangled spreadsheets. qBase automates that processing, handling data from several runs and instruments at once. It supports multiple reference genes for fairer normalization, tracks samples and genes without forced replicate counts, and applies quality checks. The framework aims to give relative quantities that are reproducible across labs, a step the field lacked as throughput kept rising.
europmc-pmc1919402:
Frith argued in 2007 that the human brain holds a specialized set of regions for social life, the so-called social brain. Brain imaging and damage studies support the idea, and the parts are gaining defined roles. The puzzle was what the middle frontal region, always active when people think about minds, actually does.

The amygdala, deep in the temporal lobe, tags faces with emotional value, letting us read fear or trustworthiness. A groove region nearby forecasts where someone's actions will end up. For the medial prefrontal cortex, Frith proposes a role in second-order representation: holding in mind another person's picture of your own mental state, the core move in real communication. Those skills are not social in themselves, he notes, but social complexity has driven them to unusual heights.
europmc-pmc2042002:
Wingert and colleagues studied how the early kidney, the pronephros, gets its segments in zebrafish embryos in 2007. A kidney tubule has distinct proximal and distal sections, near and far parts with different jobs. The fish pronephros has two simple tubules along the trunk. The team tested retinoic acid, a vitamin A signal, and cdx genes, which set body pattern along the axis.

Blocking retinoic acid removed proximal segments and expanded distal ones. Adding the acid did the reverse. Losing cdx function erased distal segments and shifted the whole pronephros backwards. Cdx loss also moved the boundaries of enzymes that make and break down retinoic acid. Removing both cdx and the acid rescued the defects. The cdx genes thus place the acid signal, and so position the kidney.
europmc-pmc2124802:
Cyrus W. Field studied an extremely pure preparation of ricin, the castor bean poison, in 1910. He worked from the method Osborne, Mendel, and Harris published in 1905 for isolating ricin from the bean's coagulable albumin.

Field's question was whether ricin's two known actions are really one. The poison both kills and clumps red blood cells. Tested again after two and a half years, the preparation suggested the two actions are distinct properties. Its behavior under an electric current pointed the same way. Either two substances are present, or one substance carries two working groups, one stable and one easily damaged. Doses across rabbits, guinea pigs, dogs, cats, and goats are tabulated. Readers get a chemist's attempt to take a famous poison apart without losing its dangers on paper.
europmc-pmc2125302:
A. R. Dochez and O. T. Avery of the Rockefeller Institute hospital mapped the carriers of pneumonia in 1915. Three quarters of lobar pneumonia, they report, is caused by specific, highly virulent pneumococcus types. Yet pneumococci of some kind live in the mouths of sixty per cent of healthy people. The resolution is that mouth strains are readily told apart from the parasitic types.

Infection, therefore, is usually caught, not self-generated. The recovered also carry their infecting type for a long while; one table tracks type I still present after ninety days. Across 223 cases the types divide roughly into thirds for types I and II, with III near a tenth and IV near a fifth. Readers get the carrier state established as pneumonia's reservoir, with types as fingerprints.
europmc-pmc2125502:
Carroll G. Bull prosecuted a suspect in 1917: the streptococci then being blamed by some for poliomyelitis. Cultures from the tonsils of thirty-two polio cases went into guinea pigs, dogs, cats, rabbits, and monkeys. In no animal did anything resembling poliomyelitis appear, clinically or under the microscope.

The cocci were far from harmless; they simply caused their own diseases. Streptococci from polio patients did all this no more and no differently than streptococci from other sources. Cocci recovered from the brains and cords of monkeys dead of the filtered virus likewise gave monkeys no paralysis and none of polio's signature tissue changes; Bull classes them as secondary invaders. Monkeys recovered from such streptococcus infections were not protected against the true virus, and their blood did not neutralize it in glass. Readers get a false culprit cleared by exhaustive non-resemblance.
europmc-pmc2125802:
Edward Taylor and Harold L. Amoss followed one family through a poliomyelitis outbreak and reported the case in the Journal of Experimental Medicine in 1917. Four children in the family showed symptoms of the disease in varying degrees. The doctors traced where the infection came from, timed the incubation periods, and tested throat secretions by inoculation to find who carried the virus.

Two children proved to carry the virus in the nasopharynx, the space behind the nose. One was found to be a carrier after recovering from a mild, non-paralytic attack. The other carried the virus about five days before symptoms began, and paralysis followed. The first case in the family died, while the youngest child, treated with immune serum, recovered almost fully. Taylor and Amoss propose that every case of the disease grows out of a carrier.
europmc-pmc2128502:
Theobald Smith and Ralph B. Little showed that feeding colostrum puts protein into a newborn calf's urine for its first days. Their paper appeared in the Journal of Experimental Medicine in 1924. Many calves killed within the first three days showed the condition, and it proved nearly universal in that window.

Fetuses and unfed calves had no protein in their urine, so the colostrum feeding itself is responsible. Varying the amount, delaying the first feeding, or alternating colostrum with milk moved the protein's appearance and quantity in step with the colostrum given. Serum in place of colostrum produced the same effect more weakly. The kidney's leakiness, tested in healthy calves, ends after the third day. Two calves fed colostrum repeatedly still showed protein at six days, which may mean a slight kidney lesion, the authors caution, and needs more proof.
europmc-pmc2128602:
C. H. Andrewes and C. Philip Miller found the rabbit virus of their series turning up in rabbits that had never been near a patient. Their paper is the second on this filterable virus infection of rabbits, in the Journal of Experimental Medicine in 1924. Control series began with blood from apparently normal rabbits, with care taken to guard the stock from known virus sources.

In two, and possibly four, of six such control series, the same virus was recovered. It proved identical in properties and in immune reactions with the virus from the rheumatic fever series and with Rivers and Tillett's Virus III. Treating rabbits with benzene did not appreciably raise their openness to the infection. The unavoidable reading is that the virus is probably a natural parasite of the domestic rabbit, living quietly in normal stock. Its natural course in the animal, the authors grant, is still unknown.
europmc-pmc2131402:
Philip McMaster and Robert Elman wrote part eleven of a series on reaction within living tissues in 1928, turning to the kidney. They stained living kidney tubules with erythrolitmin, a dye that turns blue in alkaline fluid and red in acid. The color inside each cell shows the reaction there, letting them compare the cell's state with the urine being made.

In normal function, cells of the glomerulus and the first tubule part held the dye in its blue, alkaline form, while cells near the tubule's end held it red. A narrow violet zone sat between. When acid urine was being secreted, the shift toward acidity moved high up into the early tubules. The inside reaction of kidney cells thus moves with the urine.
europmc-pmc2131502:
James Gamble and Monroe McIver, with the assistance of Pauline Marsh and Maurice Tolman, measured the acid-base makeup of pancreatic juice and bile in 1928. Both fluids pour into the gut, and their salt content matters for the blood's balance. The pair compared fixed base, chloride, and bicarbonate in the two fluids with the same values in blood plasma.

Pancreatic juice held fixed base at about the plasma level. Chloride ran at a quarter to a half of that value, and bicarbonate made up the rest, so shifts in chloride drive shifts in alkalinity. Fresh liver bile matched plasma in both base and chloride. Gall bladder bile, though, held about double the base, and its chloride had been almost wholly removed.
europmc-pmc2131602:
Nelson Davis and Raymond Shannon, working between New York and the Yellow Fever Laboratory at Bahia, Brazil, reported early yellow fever tests on Brazilian monkeys in 1929. Part three of their South American series asks whether a local monkey, the prego or Cebus macrocephalus, can carry the virus. Yellow fever virus from rhesus monkeys was passed into the Cebus by blood injection and by infected mosquito bites.

The Cebus showed no clinical or tissue signs of yellow fever at all. Yet the virus lived on in it for a time. When susceptible rhesus monkeys were inoculated from the Cebus, by direct blood transfer or by mosquito transmission, they developed the typical symptoms and lesions. A silent carrier host, the result implies, can hide in a local species.
europmc-pmc2174402:
Bonefeld-Jørgensen, Long, Hofmeister and Vinggaard tested four industrial chemicals in 2007 for hormone-disrupting activity in the lab. Bisphenol A and its dimethacrylate form are used in plastics and dental sealants. Two alkylphenols are common surfactants, ingredients that help liquids spread. The team measured effects on the estrogen receptor, the androgen receptor, the aryl hydrocarbon receptor, and on aromatase, an enzyme converting testosterone to estrogen.

All four compounds blocked aromatase and switched the estrogen receptor on while blocking the androgen receptor. Nonylphenol raised aryl hydrocarbon receptor activity and boosted a potent dioxin's action. It also showed the highest relative potency in three of the four assays. Octylphenol both raised and lowered that receptor's activity at different doses. The results show these compounds can disrupt hormones through several pathways at once.
europmc-pmc2235902:
Li and a very large team mapped transcription factor binding across the fruit fly genome in 2008. Transcription factors are proteins that switch genes on by binding DNA near them. The team used whole-genome tiling arrays in blastoderm embryos, the earliest embryo stage. They tracked six maternal and gap factors that set up the head-to-tail body axis, measuring where each binds and how strongly.

The factors bound several thousand regions, with highly overlapping sets but different strengths. Strongly bound regions included all forty-plus known enhancers responding to these factors. They also included several hundred likely new regulatory modules near developmental genes. Most blastoderm microRNAs were among the targets. Thousands of weakly bound regions sat far from active genes and in protein-coding DNA. The authors suspect many are non-functional, and warn that DNA sequence comparison alone poorly identifies true targets.
europmc-pmc2253602:
Guerra and co-workers mapped the global range of Plasmodium falciparum malaria in 2008, the first such evidence-based map in almost forty years. Planners need accurate risk geography to target control spending. The team combined national case reports, medical intelligence and biological exclusion rules based on temperature and dryness limits for the mosquito vectors. They also assembled 4,278 survey estimates of parasite prevalence at unique locations.

In 2007, 2.37 billion people lived in areas with any transmission risk. Almost one billion lived under unstable, extremely low risk, where elimination looks feasible. Nearly all prevalence rates above 50 percent were in Africa, in the band matching the main vector mosquito. Outside Africa, prevalence was mostly under ten percent, with a median below five percent. Large parts of Africa proved more amenable to control than previously appreciated.
europmc-pmc2373902:
Ralser and colleagues found a metabolic switch that protects cells from oxidative stress in 2007. Oxidative stress means damage from reactive oxygen chemicals, and cells reroute their chemistry to fight it. The team started from yeast with a weakened sugar-burning enzyme that oddly resisted a strong oxidant, diamide.

They traced the resistance to rerouted sugar flow. Instead of burning sugar for energy, cells pushed it through the pentose phosphate pathway, a side route that restocks a protective molecule pool called NADPH. The same rerouting held in the worm Caenorhabditis elegans, a small lab animal. They then showed a second sugar enzyme, GAPDH, is switched off by oxidants in normal cells, and that this shutoff triggers the same reroute. So the cell uses enzyme shutoff as a built-in switch to rebalance its chemistry under attack.
europmc-pmc2376102:
Bramhall and colleagues ran a randomised trial in advanced pancreatic cancer in 2002. Patients got gemcitabine, the standard drug, plus either marimastat or a dummy pill. Marimastat blocks enzymes called matrix metalloproteinases, which tumors use to chew through tissue and spread, so the pairing was meant to attack on two fronts.

The trial enrolled 239 patients whose cancer could not be removed by surgery. Survival was identical in both arms: a median of about 165 days, and one-year survival of 18% with marimastat versus 17% without. Tumor shrinkage also matched, at 11% versus 16% in the two groups, and time before the cancer grew was the same. The combination was well tolerated, though 59% of marimastat patients reported some muscle or joint aches. The authors found no evidence to support the pairing.
europmc-pmc2413402:
Dylla and colleagues showed that chemotherapy can leave the most dangerous colon cancer cells behind in 2008. Cancer stem cells are the rare tumor cells that can regrow a whole tumor. In colon cancer they carry a surface pattern called ESA positive, CD44 positive. The team grew such tumors in mice and treated them with two standard drugs.

Tumors left after treatment with cyclophosphamide or irinotecan held a higher share of stem-pattern cells than untreated tumors. Those leftover cells also formed new tumors more readily when transplanted in small numbers. Their tumor-seeding power was undiminished. A detox enzyme, ALDH1, ran high in the stem cells, and blocking its activity mattered: the enzyme directly drove resistance to cyclophosphamide in lab culture. The authors said killing the bulk is not enough if stem cells survive.
europmc-pmc2428102:
Baker reviewed rhythmic brain-muscle coupling in 2007. When a muscle holds a steady contraction, the motor cortex, the brain area commanding movement, pulses at about 20 cycles per second, the beta band. Muscles on the opposite side of the body pulse in step with it, a matching called coherence.

Newer work, Baker argues, changes what these rhythms mean. The cortex may not simply echo the rhythm; it may compute with it, shaping how commands are timed. The loop also runs backward: sensors in muscle send rhythmic feedback to the brain through afferent pathways, the nerves carrying signals inward. The touch-processing cortex next door pulses in the same band, locked to the motor cortex. That lock may let the brain read returning touch signals against the command that caused them, like checking an echo against the shout.
europmc-pmc2486302:
Findlay, Yi, MacCoss, and Swanson catalogued the proteins fruit flies pass to females at mating in 2008. Seminal fluid proteins shape sperm competition and change female behaviour after mating, and they evolve unusually fast. But the full transferred set in the fly Drosophila melanogaster was unknown.

The team labelled males with heavy isotopes, a harmless atomic tag, so any tagged protein found in a mated female must have come from the male. That filter identified 63 proteins never before known to act in reproduction, several of them abundant in the fluid. Dozens of predicted seminal proteins were confirmed as genuinely transferred. The same work uncovered 19 previously unnoted genes in the fly genome. Comparing related species showed the fluid's contents shift between lineages, shaped by positive selection and gene duplication, which the authors link to how new species split apart.
europmc-pmc2564802:
Schiff and a large team of collaborators ran the ATTEST trial in 2008, comparing two biological drugs for rheumatoid arthritis in patients whom methotrexate alone had failed. The drugs work differently: abatacept calms T cell activation, while infliximab blocks an inflammatory messenger. Over 400 patients were randomised, double-blind, to one drug or placebo on top of methotrexate.

At six months both drugs beat placebo on disease activity scores, with abatacept improving the score by 2.53 points against 1.48 for placebo. By one year abatacept edged ahead on response rates, with 72.4 percent reaching the basic improvement mark against 55.8 percent for infliximab. Safety favoured abatacept too. Serious infections struck 1.9 percent of its group, against 8.5 percent on infliximab. Fewer patients quit over side effects.
europmc-pmc2643002:
van Leeuwen and co-authors tested in 2009 what a week of short nights does to the immune system and the heart. Thirteen healthy young men slept only four hours a night for five nights, mimicking a hard working week. Six other men kept eight hours a night as a comparison group. Two full nights of sleep followed for recovery.

After the short nights, a blood marker of inflammation, CRP, had risen well above its starting level. It kept rising even after the recovery weekend. Levels of immune signals called IL-1, IL-6, and IL-17 also climbed, and some cell counts shifted. Heart rate was higher after recovery too. The authors link this pattern of simmering inflammation to the raised heart disease risk seen in poor sleepers.
europmc-pmc2682202:
Bushman and a large team merged in 2009 the results of nine genome-wide hunts for human genes that HIV needs to copy itself. Each hunt had screened most human genes, hoping to find cell factors the virus borrows. Such factors could become drug targets that the virus cannot easily escape by mutating.

Alone, the hunts agreed poorly: any two overlapped by less than 7 percent. Pooling all nine with older literature gave 2,410 candidate genes, nearly a tenth of all human genes, many surely false alarms. The team built a public encyclopedia of the overlaps, letting the best-supported factors rise to the top. From those, they drew maps of the cell systems HIV recruits, from gene reading to transport. The maps point to promising drug targets, shared chokepoints in the virus's supply chain.
europmc-pmc2692002:
Sehlmeyer and colleagues reviewed in 2009 the brain imaging literature on fear conditioning and its unlearning, called extinction. In these experiments a neutral cue is paired with something unpleasant until the cue alone triggers fear; later the cue is shown alone until fear fades. The pair of processes models anxiety disorders and their therapy.

Two reviewers sifted the literature to December 2008 and kept 46 imaging studies in healthy volunteers. Across wildly different designs, one network lit up reliably: the amygdala, the insula, and the front cingulate cortex. Other areas joined or stayed silent depending on design choices, such as how well subjects learned the pairing, the timing of cues, and what the unpleasant stimulus was. Some studies missed even the core network, which the authors trace to these method differences. A shared set of design standards, they argue, would make the field's results add up.
europmc-pmc2701602:
Ayres and Schneider asked in 2009 why sick animals stop eating, and whether that anorexia is a defense rather than a breakdown. Infected fruit flies, like sick people, lose their appetite. Fighting infection is costly, so refusing food seems self-defeating, yet the behavior is found across the animal kingdom, hinting it is kept because it helps.

Working in flies, the authors separate two kinds of protection that anorexia could serve. Resistance means killing the germs outright. Tolerance means enduring them, limiting the damage a given germ load does. Their evidence places diet change mainly on the tolerance side. Its effects can flip sign by infection type. What saves a fly from one germ can doom it with another. Sickness anorexia, they argue, is a tuned strategy, not a symptom to be overridden by forced feeding in every case.
europmc-pmc2725302:
Cho and Strafella asked in 2009 whether brain stimulation of the left frontal lobe changes dopamine in other frontal areas. Dopamine is a brain signal tied to movement, focus, reward, and learning. Its faults matter in Parkinson's disease and in schizophrenia. The stimulation method uses magnetic pulses through the skull and is used as a treatment tool.

Healthy volunteers got stimulation to the left or right frontal site. Then a PET scan tracked a tracer that binds dopamine receptors. Left-sided pulses lowered tracer binding in two areas on the same side, which means more dopamine was released there. Right-sided pulses caused no such change. The effect was thus limited to one side and to specific frontal areas.
europmc-pmc2738502:
Goddard, Roth, Reisen, and Scott tested in 2002 which California mosquito species can transmit West Nile virus, a virus that reached North America in 1999 and spread fast. By September 2002 it had caused over nineteen hundred human cases in the United States. Knowing which local mosquitoes carry it well is essential for surveillance and control.

They challenged ten California species known as virus vectors or major pests. All ten became infected and could transmit at some level. Three Culex species groups were the most efficient vectors, while an Ochlerotatus pest species and one southern Culex form were the least efficient. Mammal-feeding species were weaker vectors. Culex species likely play the primary role in keeping the virus cycling in California.
europmc-pmc2742902:
Armougom, Henry, Vialettes, Raccah, and Raoult measured in 2009 gut bacteria in obese and anorexic patients with a new precise counting tool. Gut communities differ in obesity, with a shifted ratio of two large bacterial groups reported before. The roles of Lactobacillus species and of the methanogen Methanobrevibacter smithii had not been described in that work.

In stool from twenty obese, nine anorexic, and twenty lean people, they confirmed fewer Bacteroidetes in obesity. Lactobacillus counts were significantly higher in obese patients than in lean or anorexic groups, a notable link since these bacteria serve as growth promoters in farm animals. The methanogen was much higher in anorexic patients, perhaps as an adaptation to scarce nutrients.
europmc-pmc2795202:
Ghannoum and colleagues catalogued the fungi that live in healthy human mouths, a community they call the oral mycobiome. Bacteria in the mouth had been mapped before, but its fungi had not. In 2010 the team used DNA sequencing on samples from twenty healthy volunteers.

Across the group they found eighty-five fungal genera and one hundred one species, with each person carrying nine to twenty-three species. Candida appeared in three quarters of the volunteers, followed by Cladosporium in about two thirds. Other finds with disease potential included Aspergillus in about a third of volunteers, plus Fusarium and Cryptococcus. The healthy baseline now lets later work spot fungal shifts tied to illness.
europmc-pmc2837402:
Tie and colleagues traced a three-part control circuit in 2010 that, when broken, lets stomach cancer spread. A tiny RNA called miR-218 is made from the gene of a guidance molecule, Slit3, and it normally represses Robo1, a receptor for Slit signals. In spreading stomach cancers, miR-218 levels fell along with its host gene.

With the repressor gone, Robo1 levels rose, and Robo1 meeting its partner Slit2 switched on the very pathway that drives invasion. Restoring miR-218 in cancer cells shut Robo1 down and blocked invasion and spread in lab tests and in animals. The authors describe the loop as a negative feedback circuit whose failure feeds metastasis, and they float restoring miR-218 as a treatment idea.
europmc-pmc2851702:
Coudeville and colleagues built a statistical model in 2010 linking flu antibody levels to actual protection, so vaccine power could be read off blood tests alone. The standard yardstick, an antibody titer of one to forty, is accepted as halving infection risk, but the full curve beyond that point was unmapped. The team gathered fifteen studies covering nearly six thousand adults and over thirteen hundred flu cases, then fitted a Bayesian model that handles study-to-study variation and rough titer data.

Protection rose steadily and significantly with titer across every model tried. The curve looked the same for influenza A and B strains, and for vaccinated and unvaccinated people alike. The authors offer the relationship as a bridge from lab measurements to expected vaccine efficacy.
europmc-pmc2856202:
Hailer, Garellick, and Kärrholm mined the Swedish Hip Arthroplasty Register in 2010. They compared cemented and uncemented artificial hips across more than one hundred seventy thousand operations from 1992 to 2007. Sweden had long favored cement, then shifted toward uncemented implants over the decade before the study. The team tracked who needed revision surgery and why, adjusting for age, sex, and diagnosis.

Uncemented hips survived worse overall: eighty-five percent remained revision-free at ten years against ninety-four percent for cemented ones. The weakness sat in uncemented sockets, which loosened more, while uncemented stems actually loosened less but broke the thighbone more often in the first two years. The best-selling uncemented cups, notably, matched cemented cups.
europmc-pmc2890402:
Cox and colleagues charted in 2010 how the bacterial community in cystic fibrosis airways changes across a lifetime. Cystic fibrosis thickens airway mucus, inviting chronic infection that slowly destroys lung function. Using a DNA chip that detects many bacterial types at once, they profiled stable patients from infants of nine months to adults of seventy-two years.

Young patients started with varied, fairly even communities that diversified further over time. Older patients, who tended to have worse lung function, carried lopsided communities dominated by a few clustered types, and repeat samples showed diversity draining away with age. Early colonizers differed clearly from the late dominators. The arc suggests treatment windows may differ by age, before a few hardy organisms lock in.
europmc-pmc2894102:
Chen, Hung, Liau, and Huang tested in 2009 whether gold nanoparticles, a model nanomaterial prized for easy size control, harm living animals, and whether size decides the answer. They injected naked gold particles from three to one hundred nanometers wide into mice weekly. The dose and route were the same for every size group, isolating size as the variable.

Particles in the middle range made mice severely ill, with fatigue, appetite loss, fur color change, and bent spines, and most died within three weeks. The smallest and largest sizes caused no sickness at all. Organs of sick mice showed immune cell buildup in the liver, structural damage in the lungs, and breakdown in the spleen, with particles present at the damaged sites. Middle size, not the smallest, was the dangerous zone.
europmc-pmc2914702:
Chun-Zhi Zhang and a large team reported in 2010 that two small RNAs drive stomach cancer growth and radiation resistance by silencing a tumor suppressor. The RNAs, miR-221 and miR-222, were already known growth promoters in other cancers through different targets. Working in the human gastric cancer line SGC7901, the team dialed the pair up and down and watched cell behavior.

Raising the pair made cells grow faster, cycle harder, and resist death signals, the full malignant pattern. Knocking the pair down reversed all of it and raised levels of PTEN, a famous brake on growth signaling, which proved to be their direct target in these cells. Knockdown also left cells more vulnerable to radiation killing. A two-RNA signature may therefore flag aggressive gastric tumors and offer a handle for sensitizing them to therapy.
europmc-pmc2920902:
McConnell and colleagues followed in 2010 nearly twenty-five hundred young Southern California children to test whether traffic pollution at school, not just at home, triggers new asthma. The children entered kindergarten or first grade free of asthma and wheeze, and parents reported any new doctor diagnosis over three years. A dispersion model estimated traffic pollution at each home and school from traffic volume, distance, and weather.

One hundred twenty children developed asthma during follow-up. Risk rose with modeled traffic pollution at the residence, and, in a first for the field, it also rose with pollution at school independently. Regional smog measures did not explain the pattern away. School siting and traffic near schools join home address as asthma policy targets.
europmc-pmc2928802:
LaFayette and colleagues traced how protein kinase C signalling helps the yeast Candida albicans resist antifungal drugs, in work published in 2010. Few useful antifungals exist, and resistant infections threaten people with weak immune defences.

Screening a large library of active compounds, the team found blockers of protein kinase C. Those blockers wiped out azole resistance in a lab yeast mutant and in a clinical Candida isolate. Weakening the kinase made cells highly sensitive to azoles and related drugs that target ergosterol. The pathway acted through a MAP kinase route and linked closely to calcineurin and the chaperone Hsp90.
europmc-pmc2957402:
Heisler and co-authors modelled how growth signals organise the tip of a growing plant shoot in a 2010 study of the weed Arabidopsis. Cells there place a hormone pump protein toward neighbours richest in the hormone auxin, creating feedback that patterns new organs.

Live imaging of the shoot tip's surface layer showed the pump's alignment matching the orientation of inner scaffolding fibres called microtubules. Mechanical signals appear to coordinate both patterns at once, tying physical stress to hormone flow. Computer models built on that coupling reproduced how growth direction and extent are orchestrated in the growing tip.
europmc-pmc2966402:
Zhao and colleagues ran a pilot hunt for blood-borne microRNA markers of early breast cancer in 2010. No gentle blood test then caught the disease early with both high sensitivity and accuracy.

Plasma from twenty women with early cancer and twenty matched healthy women was profiled by array, then checked with a precise counting method. Dozens of small RNAs differed in each ethnic group studied, yet only two differed in both groups. Curve analysis suggested panels could separate patients from controls. The group differences warn that marker panels may need tailoring by ancestry.
europmc-pmc3092602:
Theou and colleagues reviewed in 2011 the trial evidence for exercise as a treatment for frailty in older adults. Frailty brings weakness, slowness, and vulnerability to falls and disability. The team gathered randomized trials that enrolled people described as frail and tested exercise as a stand alone part of treatment. Few trials used a validated definition of frailty to select participants, a weakness they flag.

Even so, exercise improved physical measures and every functional outcome the trials reported, from walking to daily tasks. Programs that worked best looked different from standard senior fitness advice. Multi part training mixing strength, balance, and endurance, run for at least five months, three times a week, in half hour sessions, generally beat other formats. The authors conclude structured exercise deserves a central place in frailty care, while calling for sharper definitions in future trials.
europmc-pmc3123702:
John Dixon and fellow experts issued a position statement on weight-loss surgery for diabetes in a 2011 paper in Diabetic Medicine. A taskforce of the International Diabetes Federation, mixing doctors, surgeons, and public health specialists, reviewed when surgery should join drugs and lifestyle care for obese people with type two diabetes.

Surgery, they conclude, can greatly improve blood sugar control in severely obese patients and offers good value for money. It should be considered when medical care fails to meet targets, especially alongside other major health problems. Care must include full assessment, patient teaching, and long-term follow-up by a team. The statement gives weight thresholds for eligibility and calls on countries to write clear rules and widen fair access.
europmc-pmc3163602:
Susana Sotocinal and colleagues adapted a facial-expression pain scale for laboratory rats in a 2011 paper in Molecular Pain. Most pain research uses rats, yet pain is usually gauged by poking and withdrawal, which miss ongoing spontaneous pain, the kind patients complain of most. The team had earlier shown mouse faces betray pain; here they tuned the coding for rats.

Trained scorers reading rat faces, from ear and eye changes to whisker position, rated pain reliably across three models: paw inflammation, joint inflammation, and belly surgery. Scores rose and fell with the expected time course and dropped with morphine in proportion to dose. Companion software automates the slowest step, finding usable face frames in video. The authors urge wider use of spontaneous pain measures to improve translation to the clinic.
europmc-pmc3194102:
Daria Kuss and Mark Griffiths reviewed the psychology of social networking use and possible addiction in a 2011 paper in a public health journal. Networking sites had exploded into a global habit, and case reports hinted some users lose control, yet scientific study lagged. The review organised the scattered evidence under usage patterns, motives, personality, harms, and addiction itself.

People mainly use the sites to maintain existing offline friendships. Outgoing users seek social gain, shy users seek compensation, and both styles, plus low self-discipline and high self-importance, predict heavier use. Harms include shrinking real-life community activity, weaker school results, and relationship strain, each a possible addiction sign. The authors find the addiction concept plausible but under-proven, and map what research must settle.
europmc-pmc3289602:
Haddow and co-authors traced the family history of Zika virus in a 2012 genetics study. The mosquito carried virus, first found in Africa, causes a fever that can look much like dengue. Earlier work based on a single gene had hinted at separate geographic branches, so the team read the full coding region of five isolates gathered between 1947 and 2010.

Their trees split the virus into two main branches, one African and one Asian. The strain behind the Yap Island outbreak of 2007, and a Cambodian child's case in 2010, most likely came from Southeast Asia. The authors warn that Zika illness is probably often misdiagnosed and missed in official counts.
europmc-pmc3303802:
Bruno and colleagues tested whether tiny parcels shed by stem cells could rescue mice from lethal kidney failure, in a 2012 study. Stem cells from bone marrow were already known to ease kidney injury caused by the cancer drug cisplatin. The team asked whether the small vesicles these cells release, rather than the cells themselves, carry much of that benefit.

A single dose of vesicles improved kidney function and survival, though some damage lingered weeks later. Repeated doses lowered deaths further, and survivors examined after three weeks showed normal looking kidneys and normal function. Lab tests on human kidney cells showed the vesicles switching off cell death genes and switching on protective ones, pointing to a survival signal as the main mechanism.
europmc-pmc3322602:
Lebedev and colleagues introduced a drawing tool for editing the chemical dictionary used in protein structure work, in a 2012 paper. When crystallographers refine a structure, software needs a reference description of every molecule present, giving ideal bond lengths and angles. The CCP4 restraint library holds those descriptions for standard building blocks, common modifications, and drug like molecules.

Adding a new molecule to that library once meant writing its entry by hand in a fiddly format. The new tool, JLigand, lets researchers draw the molecule on screen and generate the entry visually, including the links that join molecules into chains. The paper explains the library's history and format, and how the editor fits the workflow of the main refinement programs. The goal is fewer dictionary errors in published structures.
europmc-pmc3334602:
Zheng and a large team read the full genome of a fungus famous in Chinese medicine, reporting in 2011. The fungus, Cordyceps militaris, invades insect pupae and sprouts from them, and its kind have been prized as remedies for centuries. Relatives serve as insect killing pest controls, but the genes behind the medicine making, the insect attack, and the fungus's sex life were unknown.

Family tree analysis suggests these fungi became insect killers several times independently, converging on similar toolkits. The genome carries no genes for known human fungal poisons, matching its long record of safe use. Oddly, the fungus normally needs a mating partner to fruit, yet can sometimes fruit alone. Gene activity studies showed fruiting switches on particular control proteins and a signaling pathway, while a pathway other fungi rely on stayed quiet.
europmc-pmc3378702:
Lee, Stravitz, and Larson introduced the 2011 revision of the AASLD position paper on acute liver failure, issued by America's national liver-disease association. The update fully replaced the 2005 version, adding two authors. It refreshed expert guidance on causes and diagnosis, on intensive care treatment, and on outlook and transplant decisions.

Because the disease is rare, large trials are impossible and much care rests on expert experience. The introduction highlights practical advances, including blood tests that unmask hidden acetaminophen poisoning and ammonia levels that warn of brain swelling. It also stresses quick checks for viral and autoimmune causes, which are often skipped at first. The paper frames slow, steady gains in intensive care as the main progress.
europmc-pmc3412702:
Ye and colleagues introduced Primer-BLAST in 2012, a free tool that designs DNA primers guaranteed to hit only their intended target. Primers start the copying reaction behind most DNA tests, and a stray match can ruin a result. Checking specificity used to mean hand-sifting pages of search hits, a slow and error-prone chore.

The new tool merges primer design and database checking into a single step. It pairs the classic BLAST search with a full-length alignment method, so it catches targets that older checks miss, even with many mismatches. Users can also test primers they already have, steer primers around splice junctions, and keep them clear of known variant sites. The tool runs on the national biotechnology center's website.
europmc-pmc3444902:
Francis, O'Connor, and Curran introduced a journal series in 2012 built around the Theoretical Domains Framework, a map for behavior-change research. Changing what health workers do is the bottleneck in getting evidence into practice, yet dozens of overlapping behavior theories make choosing one a muddle. The framework distilled well over a hundred explanatory ideas from thirty-three theories into grouped domains.

Early experience looked promising: the editors found well over a hundred papers citing the framework, with a core set using it to probe professionals' behavior directly. Its strengths are broad theory coverage and a knack for surfacing the beliefs that mediate change. The overview also airs the framework's limits and sets up the series that follows.
europmc-pmc3558702:
Amanda Sierra and colleagues reviewed microglial phagocytosis in Frontiers in Cellular Neuroscience in 2013, calling these brain immune cells two-faced, after Janus. Phagocytosis is the process where a cell engulfs and breaks down dead cells, microbes, or debris. Microglia clear spinal cord and myelin debris, amyloid deposits in Alzheimer disease, and extra synapses as the young brain develops.

Clearing dead cells is mostly helpful and calms inflammation, the review explains, but the same act can trigger a burst that releases toxic reactive oxygen species. Calm, unchallenged microglia also swallow dying cells during normal development and adult life, not only in disease. Much remains unknown about which molecules handle each type of cargo. The authors map what is known, stress the double-edged results, and mark the open questions for the field.
europmc-pmc3565702:
Panagiotis Kastritis and Alexandre Bonvin examined protein binding strength in the Journal of the Royal Society Interface in 2013. Proteins meet and grip each other in timed, precise ways that run the cell, and the grip strength, called binding affinity, decides whether a pairing forms at all. Drug designers would love to read that strength off a protein's structure, yet forty years of work have not produced a reliable way to do it.

Buried surface area, the patch hidden when two proteins join, predicts strength for stiff pairings but fails for flexible ones, where disorder and motion add costs that models miss. Most work covers simple two-protein cases, while real cell systems are larger and messier. The authors argue that progress needs biology, chemistry, and physics modeled together. The paper is an honest audit of a long-running problem in drug research.
europmc-pmc3599102:
Sarah Schell and colleagues built a framework for keeping public health programs alive in Implementation Science in 2013. Programs only help while they run, and many fade once start-up funding or champions move on. Writing on sustainability was broad but scattered, with no agreed core parts. Their project combined a literature review, an expert panel, and a concept-mapping exercise that sorted ideas from scientists, funders, and practitioners across fields such as tobacco control and injury prevention.

Eighty-five papers fed the review. Mapping distilled nine domains that decide whether a program can last: political support, stable funding, partnerships, organizational capacity, evaluation, adaptation, communication, proven public health impact, and strategic planning. Ninety-three detailed items fill the domains, and eighty-nine percent of them matched evidence in the literature. The framework gives program leaders a checklist for building staying power in from the start.
europmc-pmc3618002:
Syed Jafri, Runhua Shi, and Glenn Mills tested a simple inflammation score in lung cancer in BMC Cancer in 2013. Body-wide inflammation tracks with cancer growth, wasting, and poor outcomes. Their score, the Advanced Lung Cancer Inflammation Index, multiplies body mass index by blood albumin and divides by the ratio of two white cell types, all routine values. The team checked records of 173 patients with metastatic non-small cell lung cancer diagnosed at one center between 2000 and 2011.

Patients scoring below eighteen, the high-inflammation group, carried more spread sites and worse fitness, and fewer received chemotherapy. Their cancer stayed quiet for a median 2.4 months and they lived a median 3.4 months, against 5.1 and 8.3 months in the low-inflammation group. After adjusting for other factors, the low score still predicted worse survival. A free score from standard labs, the authors argue, can flag patients needing closer attention.
europmc-pmc3621202:
Giulia Cesaroni and colleagues followed over a million Romans to test city air and survival in Environmental Health Perspectives in 2013. European evidence covering both fine particles and nitrogen dioxide was thin. Their cohort enrolled everyone aged thirty or more at the 2001 census who had lived in Rome at least five years. It held 1,265,058 people, tracked for nine years, with pollution estimated at each home address.

Both pollutants tracked with higher death rates from non-accidental causes. Each ten-microgram rise in fine particles came with about four percent higher mortality, and about ten percent higher death from ischemic heart disease, the strongest single link. Lung cancer and other cardiovascular deaths followed. Living near heavy traffic added risk in the same direction. The dose-response ran nearly straight, with little sign of a safe threshold within city levels.
europmc-pmc3632802:
Elizabeth Anderson and Geetha Shivakumar reviewed exercise as a treatment for anxiety in Frontiers in Psychiatry in 2013. Exercise is standard advice for preventing chronic disease. Government reports credit it with cutting death rates by up to thirty percent. People who move regularly also report fewer anxiety symptoms and slower memory decline. Their paper asks what the evidence supports when anxiety itself is the target.

Epidemiological studies link regular activity with a lower burden of anxiety symptoms. That supports a protective effect against developing mental disorders. The review works through the proposed mechanisms, among them stress-system tuning, brain growth factors, and mastery and distraction. It also weighs trial evidence in patients. Practical guidance closes it. Moderate to vigorous exercise for two to two and a half hours a week is the dose range where chronic-disease benefits are established. The authors offer it as a floor for anxiety care too.
europmc-pmc3701702:
Morens and Fauci survey emerging infectious diseases. They treat them as a standing threat to health and stability. SARS, pandemic H1N1 influenza, and similar arrivals caused illness and death plus disruption to travel, trade, and daily life far beyond the directly infected.

Most new human infections spill over from animals. Their estimate puts the share at sixty to eighty percent, with rodents and bats the main sources. Others arise when familiar microbes gain new transmissibility or virulence, as with drug-resistant tuberculosis. The authors trace a long history of emergence driven by ecology and human activity. They argue such diseases form a large, lasting share of all infections.
europmc-pmc3717402:
Annabelle Gourlay, Isolde Birdthistle, Gitau Mburu, Kate Iorpenda, and Alison Wringe published a systematic review in the Journal of the International AIDS Society in 2013. It asked why so few mothers and babies in sub-Saharan Africa get the antiretroviral drugs that can stop HIV passing from mother to child during pregnancy and birth.

The team searched four databases for studies from 2000 to 2012 and kept 44 that met their rules. At the personal level, weak knowledge and low schooling held women back. Stigma and fear of telling partners or family were the most common barriers of all, and partner support could help or hinder. Health system faults, such as staff shortages, poor staff attitudes, and hard-to-reach services, had barely changed in over ten years.
europmc-pmc3751802:
Rochelle Eime, Janet Young, Jack Harvey, Melanie Charity, and Warren Payne published a systematic review in 2013 on sport for children and teenagers. It appeared in the International Journal of Behavioral Nutrition and Physical Activity. Activity guidelines stress physical gains, but say little about mental and social health. The team searched 14 databases for studies since 1990.

From 3,668 publications, 30 studies met their rules. The most common gains were higher self-esteem, better social interaction, and fewer depressive symptoms. Team sports looked better for health than solo activities, likely because of their social side. The authors built a model, Health through Sport, linking participation to psychological and social health domains. They caution that most studies were snapshots in time, so cause and effect cannot be proven.
europmc-pmc3757302:
Andrew Wong and five co-authors wrote a review in Frontiers in Neuroengineering in 2013 on the blood-brain barrier from an engineering point of view. Over a century ago, Paul Ehrlich found that dyes injected into the blood did not enter the brain. Only a few small molecules, such as alcohol and caffeine, cross the barrier freely, and that selectivity blocks treatment of many brain diseases.

The authors rebuild the barrier's structure, function, and transport behavior using physics and engineering ideas. The barrier is not a fixed wall but a dynamic system, with mechanical and chemical signaling between blood vessels and brain tissue. Disease can loosen it, changing what crosses and letting immune cells and pathogens in. The authors argue that new insight into its physics could lead to better treatments.
europmc-pmc3809702:
Collin, McGovern, and Haniffa reviewed in Immunology in 2013 the subsets of human dendritic cells, the sentinels that present antigen and steer immune responses. Work on development shows these cells form their own lineage, separate from monocytes and tissue macrophages.

The review argues that distinct subsets are born different, not just placed differently, and that these built-in differences give each subset a special role in raising immunity. Studies after stem cell transplants, for instance, show the subsets turn over at different rates. It gathers the comparative evidence on where each subset sits, what it senses, and how it activates T cells, aiming to give human immunology a shared framework for telling the subsets apart.
europmc-pmc3828002:
Lv Wang, Claus T. Christophersen, Michael J. Sorich, Jacobus P. Gerber, Manya T. Angley, and Michael A. Conlon report a short stool study in Molecular Autism in 2013. Gut germ changes have been noted in children with autism spectrum disorder. A prior study found one germ group, Sutterella, raised in gut tissue samples from such children.

The team checked stool, a far easier sample to take, for Sutterella and two other germ types linked to gut disease. Sutterella counts were higher in stool from children with autism than in controls. One other type, Ruminococcus torques, ran higher in children who also had gut complaints. The results add stool proof to the tissue findings and support a gut link worth deeper study.
europmc-pmc3840702:
For The Journal of Pathology in 2013, Eva Budinska and co-authors typed colon cancers by gene activity. Colon cancer varies a lot in course and in drug response, and known gene marks explain only part of that spread. The team search gene activity patterns for a finer split.

They pooled gene activity profiles from over a thousand tumors and grouped them without using outcome data. At least five subtypes emerged, named for the gut lining states they echo, from surface-like to tissue-remodeling types. Each type carried its own active gene themes and its own known gene changes. The types also differed in patient outlook, though they were not built from it. A finer map could guide more matched treatment choices.
europmc-pmc3877102:
Kun-Yi Hsin, Samik Ghosh, and Hiroaki Kitano present a drug binding predictor in PLoS One in 2013. Most drugs hit more than one protein, which can help or harm. Network pharmacology needs firm guesses of which proteins a compound will bind across a whole cell network.

Their method blends two machine learning systems with several docking tools, which simulate how a compound fits a protein. One learner re-scores the fits, the other picks the most telling pose. Benchmark tests beat rival methods on reliability. A case study caught both main and off-target proteins of kinase drugs. Paired with network maps, the tool can flag safety risks that stem from a drug's spread of targets, early in design.
europmc-pmc3894902:
Steven J. Franks, Jennifer J. Weber, and Sally N. Aitken review plant responses to climate change in Evolutionary Applications, with the record dated 2014. Plant populations worldwide are shifting traits as conditions warm and dry. The open questions are whether climate drives the shifts, and whether the shifts come from flexibility or from evolution.

Every study that met their bar found flexible or evolved responses, and most found both. Worryingly, where pace was checked, responses often lagged behind climate change. Proof that evolved shifts are adaptive, or caused by current climate, stayed mixed. Life history, generation time, and gene flow all shape the reply speed. The authors urge shared methods and open data so forecasts of plant survival improve.
europmc-pmc3898902:
Kirstin R. Mitchell leads a team of co-authors in a survey report in The Lancet in 2013. Sexual function shapes health and wellbeing, yet policy pays it little mind. The report draws on Britain's third National Survey of Sexual Attitudes and Lifestyles, a large probability survey of adults.

A new validated measure scored function across response problems, relationship context, and self-appraisal of one's sex life. Scores were given to adults with a recent partner. Low function clustered with poor health, unhappiness in relationships, and other strains the team map by age and sex. The study gives Britain a population baseline for a topic often left to clinic samples, and a tool other surveys can reuse.
europmc-pmc3925802:
Karl Friston, Rosalyn Moran, and Anil K. Seth compare two ways of mapping directed influence in brain networks in Current Opinion in Neurobiology in 2013. Brain imaging shows which regions activate together, but researchers also want to know which region drives which. That directed, or effective, connectivity is the subject here, set against simple correlation between regions.

Granger causality infers direction from timing: past activity in one region helps predict another's future. Dynamic causal modelling instead builds a small mechanistic model of how regions influence each other and tests which version best fits the data. The review introduces both, tracks recent advances in each, and weighs their strengths and weaknesses side by side, giving brain-network researchers a guide to choosing between a data-led and a model-led route.
europmc-pmc3965102:
Vivian Law and colleagues release DrugBank 4.0 in Nucleic Acids Research in 2014. DrugBank lists facts about drugs, their actions, and their targets. It has served drug research since 2006. Computer screening of new drug ideas is a common use. Version 4.0 adds depth on how the body handles drugs. That means uptake, spread, breakdown, excretion, and toxicity.

The team added more than 1,200 drug metabolites. Each comes with its structure, name, and activity notes. They added over 1,300 breakdown reactions too. Those name the enzymes that do the work. New number data on structure and activity support prediction work. The release aims at three groups. One studies how foreign chemicals are broken down. One tracks how drugs move through the body. One designs new drugs on the computer.
europmc-pmc4014402:
Masafumi Oizumi, Larissa Albantakis, Giulio Tononi, and Olaf Sporns present version three of a theory of consciousness, in PLoS Computational Biology in 2014. The theory, called integrated information theory, starts from traits of experience itself. Each experience is specific, it forms one whole that cannot be split into free parts, and it has set borders in space and time.

Those traits are turned into rules for the physical systems that could give rise to experience, such as neurons or logic gates. A measure of integrated information then grades how much a whole tells beyond its parts. An experience matches a structure that cannot be reduced further, and the measure gives its quantity. Odd results follow: inactive parts can still hold such a structure, simple systems may be faintly conscious, and some complex systems may lack experience. The paper lays out the updated maths in full.
europmc-pmc4016702:
Eugene Andres Houseman, John Molitor, and Carmen J. Marsit present a way to clean DNA methylation studies of a hidden snag, in Bioinformatics in 2014. Blood samples hold a mix of cell types, each with its own tag pattern. Small shifts in the mix can look like true tag changes.

Known fixes lean on reference data from pure cell types, which can be costly to gather. For tissues such as placenta or tumours, the right cell types may not even be known. The new method works with no reference set at all. It infers the mix effect from the study data itself and adds a resampling step for sound error bars. In test runs and real data sets it matched or beat reference-based fixes. It could even adjust for fine cell differences reference sets miss. The tool ships free for the R language.
europmc-pmc4021402:
Xiang-hua Liu and twelve co-authors uncover a role for a long RNA in stomach cancer, in Molecular Cancer in 2014. The RNA, called HOTAIR, does not build a protein, yet high levels of it had been tied to cancer spread. Its role in stomach cancer was largely unknown.

In seventy-eight paired tissue samples, tumour tissue held more HOTAIR than matched healthy tissue. High levels went with larger tumours, later stage, wider spread, and shorter survival. Raising HOTAIR in stomach cancer cells sped their growth, movement, and invasion. Cutting it slowed growth and invasion and stalled cell division, in dishes and in mice. The team found HOTAIR acts as a sponge for a small RNA that normally holds back a growth gene called HER2. Soaking up that small RNA frees HER2. The pair rose together in advanced cancers.
europmc-pmc4029002:
Germán L. Rosano and Eduardo A. Ceccarelli review how to make proteins in the bacterium E. coli, in Frontiers in Microbiology in 2014. The bacterium is the most popular factory for recombinant proteins, proteins built from a pasted-in gene. Labs prize it for its speed, low cost, and deep tool kit.

In practice, much can go wrong: hosts grow poorly, the protein clumps into useless lumps, or no protein appears at all. The review walks through the full pipeline, from gene carriers and engineered strains to growing conditions. Fresh advances in each step are set out, with tips to coax out active, soluble protein in high yield. Strain tweaks and feed plans that ease common failure points get close attention. The authors present the field as fast-moving, with steady gains in yield and quality for research and industry use alike.
europmc-pmc4050302:
The German National Cohort Consortium lays out the design of Germany's largest health study, in the European Journal of Epidemiology in 2014. Chronic diseases drive most deaths in the country, yet their causes and early stages need study at a scale no single institute can reach.

Eighteen regional centres will draw a random sample of the adult population. The plan enrols two hundred thousand people, half women and half men, aged from twenty to sixty-nine. Baseline visits combine long interviews, questionnaires, medical exams, and stored samples. A fifth of members get a deeper exam round. Thirty thousand will also have whole-body magnetic resonance imaging at five centres. Everyone is invited back after four to five years, with questionnaires and record linkage in between. The study is built to run twenty-five to thirty years.
europmc-pmc4055302:
Nida Iqbal and Naveed Iqbal review imatinib, the drug that opened the era of targeted cancer therapy, in Chemotherapy Research and Practice in 2014. Many cancers run on overactive tyrosine kinase enzymes. Imatinib blocks a chosen few of them rather than poisoning all dividing cells.

Its targets are the fusion kinase behind chronic myeloid leukaemia and two related kinases that drive other tumours. Approved in 2001, it turned a fatal leukaemia into a manageable condition and worked the same change in a rare gut tumour. Benefits extend to other cancers carrying its target faults, and even to a graft-versus-host disease driven by one target. The review covers the drug's pharmacology and its record across these uses. It frames imatinib as proof that matching a drug to a cancer's exact molecular fault can transform outcomes, the template later targeted drugs follow.
europmc-pmc4063702:
Karolina Skorupskaite, Jyothis T. George, and Richard A. Anderson reviewed the kisspeptin pathway, a brain signal chain that sets the release of sex hormones in train. Their review came out in Human Reproduction Update in 2014. The find of kisspeptin had changed views of how the brain runs puberty and the power to have children.

Kisspeptin drives the release of GnRH. That hormone in turn makes the glands send out the signals that drive sex hormone output. The team sets out how kisspeptin works with two partner signals and how cues from the body and from food intake feed in. They cover its roles in puberty, in feedback loops, and in adult life in both sexes. Drugs that tune this chain could treat faults in hormone timing.
europmc-pmc4124702:
Jyoti Tanwar, Shrayanee Das, Zeeshan Fatima, and Saif Hameed reviewed the spread of germs that shrug off many drugs at once. Their review came out in Interdisciplinary Perspectives on Infectious Diseases in 2014. Germs of all kinds, from bacteria to fungi and beyond, have built high levels of such strength.

When the standard cure fails, the sick stay sick for longer. Care costs more, and the risk of death grows. Strength of this kind grows in the wild on its own. But wrong use of drugs, poor hygiene, unsafe food work, and weak steps to stop spread in wards all speed it up and help it spread. Such germs earn the name super bugs. The team calls for new drugs, for work to grasp how such strength works, and for drives to teach right use.
europmc-pmc4138502:
Francesc Baixauli, Carlos López-Otín, and Maria Mittelbrunn argued that exosomes and autophagy work as a coordinated team to keep cells fit. Their perspective appeared in Frontiers in Immunology in 2014. Stresses such as oxidation, inflammation, and clumped proteins threaten the cell's internal balance and contribute to ageing.

Autophagy digests damaged proteins and organelles inside the cell. Exosomes instead expel unwanted proteins and RNAs in tiny parcels. The authors discuss evidence that secretion of harmful material, coordinated with the digestion pathway, is essential for keeping protein and RNA order inside. They also overview what happens when parcel contents spread to other cells, in health and disease, where the same system can carry damage outward.
europmc-pmc4180002:
David J. Johns, Paul Aveyard, and two co-authors compared weight loss programs in the Journal of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics in 2014. Programs that combine diet advice, exercise, and behaviour support are widely offered. Yet it was unclear whether the mix beats diet or exercise alone in head-to-head trials.

Pooling eight trials with 1,022 adults, the review found no clear edge for combined programs over diet alone in the first six months. By twelve months, though, the combined programs had pulled ahead, with about 1.7 kilograms more weight lost. Against exercise-only programs, the combined approach won clearly at both time points. The results back combined programs for lasting change, while showing that diet alone does most of the early work.
europmc-pmc4234002:
Janice L. Atkins, S. Goya Wannamethee, and four co-authors followed older British men for the joint risk of muscle loss and obesity in the Journal of the American Geriatrics Society in 2014. Ageing strips muscle while belly fat often grows, and each alone raises death risk. Their combination, sarcopenic obesity, might be worse still.

The British Regional Heart Study tracked 4,252 men aged 60 to 79 for an average of 11.3 years, sorting them by waist size and arm muscle measure. Men who were sarcopenic or obese each died at higher rates than the fittest group, and sarcopenic obese men carried the highest all-cause risk of all. For cardiovascular death, the sarcopenic and obese groups stood out, but the combined group did not. The authors back efforts that fight fat gain and muscle loss together.
europmc-pmc4271702:
Amandeep Sawana, Mobolaji Adeolu, and Radhey S Gupta propose splitting a large bacterial genus into two. Their study appeared in Frontiers in Genetics in 2014. Burkholderia holds dangerous pathogens, plant pests, and harmless soil species, yet few firm markers separated its groups.

The team compared the full protein sets of dozens of sequenced species and built family trees from shared proteins. Two deep branches stood out again and again, and they found dozens of small sequence markers that mark one branch or the other. They propose keeping the name Burkholderia for the branch with the pathogens and naming the soil branch Paraburkholderia. The split gives labs clear, testable lines for naming new species.
europmc-pmc4383202:
Xiang Wan, Wenqian Wang, Jiming Liu, and Tiejun Tong tackled a common statistics headache in BMC Medical Research Methodology in 2014. Meta-analyses pool the means and standard deviations of many trials, but some trials report only the median, the range, or the quartiles instead. Analysts must estimate the missing values before pooling. The widely used older method for the standard deviation, the authors show, has serious limits and always performs poorly in practice.

Their new method folds sample size into the estimate. Across simulations for three common reporting patterns, it greatly improved accuracy, giving nearly unbiased standard deviations for normal data and only slight bias for skewed data. With the middle-quartile range also available, it still performed very well. The paper closes by comparing the estimators across all patterns, giving analysts a clear pick for each case.
europmc-pmc4400102:
Beatriz Vicoso and Doris Bachtrog surveyed sex chromosomes across flies, in PLoS Biology in 2015. Many animals determine sex with unlike X and Y chromosomes, and flies were thought to share one conserved set. Yet similar-looking chromosome sets can hide real change. The team analyzed whole genomes of 37 fly species from 22 families, comparing which chromosome carries the sex-determining role and how gene activity is balanced between the sexes.

They found over a dozen different sex chromosome setups. The small dot chromosome serves as the sex chromosome again and again, likely the ancestral state. Other species replaced it, folded up to three elements into the sex pair, or flipped to a ZW system where females are the unlike sex. Dosage compensation, boosting the single male X, evolved several times independently. Flies offer a rich natural laboratory for sex chromosome change.
europmc-pmc4460802:
Norman Farb and eight co-authors reviewed interoception, the sense of signals from inside the body, in Frontiers in Psychology in 2015. Heartbeat, breath, gut feelings, and other inner signals shape a person's sense of self, drive, and well-being. Despite that importance, the sense remains poorly understood, studied separately by brain science, medicine, and contemplative traditions.

The authors offer a broader classification of inner sensing processes. They also offer a unifying model from predictive coding. In it, the brain constantly compares expected body signals with felt ones, and the tension between them guides feeling and action. Misreading body signals, they argue, may sit at the heart of many emotional and body-based disorders. Practices such as meditation and body-focused therapy train attention to those signals and may ease that mismatch. The review names the open questions a shared framework must answer.
europmc-pmc4463002:
Frauke Kracke, Igor Vassilev, and Jens Krömer reviewed how microbes trade electrons with electrodes in Frontiers in Microbiology in 2015. Bioelectrochemical systems use that trade to make electricity, clean wastewater, repair polluted sites, or produce valuable chemicals. The microbe is the working catalyst, so its metabolism decides how well any of these systems perform.

Many of them can pass electrons to solid surfaces or carrier molecules, but few have been studied deeply. Flow from an electrode into a cell, needed for making products from electricity, is understood worst of all. The review compares electron transport chains in metal-breathing bacteria, in microbes that build acetate, and in standard production organisms. It stresses the often ignored link between electron balance and energy saving, and draws design rules for improving these systems.
europmc-pmc4480902:
Heidi Dvinge and Robert Bradley found widespread intron retention across cancers in Genome Medicine in 2015. When a gene's RNA is processed, the spacer pieces called introns are normally cut out. Mutations in the splicing machinery are common in tumors and warp that cutting. The team asked how common one warp, intron retention, is across cancer as a whole.

Comparing hundreds of matched tumor and normal samples from many cancer types, they found retained introns far more often in tumors. That held for both optional and standard introns. It held even in cancers with no splicing mutations. Breast cancer was the lone exception, showing retention in normal tissue instead. Each cancer type favored its own introns, though a small shared set, rich in splicing and export genes, recurred broadly. Retention levels also tracked with certain driver mutations in leukemia. The authors argue this overlooked pattern reshapes most cancer transcriptomes.
europmc-pmc4503802:
Hyojin Park, Robin A. A. Ince, Philippe G. Schyns, Gregor Thut, and Joachim Gross wrote a 2015 Current Biology study on how the brain tracks speech. People can follow speech even in poor sound, and the brain seems to use forecasts of what comes next. Slow brain waves in hearing areas lock onto the rhythm of speech, and the lock grows stronger when speech is clear.

Using magnetoencephalography, a method that tracks brain fields, the group watched 22 listeners during steady speech. Signals from frontal and motor areas set the phase of the slow waves in hearing cortex. That push was stronger for clear speech than for scrambled speech, and stronger on the left side. The stronger the push, the tighter the link between speech and hearing cortex.
europmc-pmc4518302:
Shan Cong leads an eleven-author team giving a cheap material a skill once limited to gold and silver, in Nature Communications in 2015. Raman spectroscopy reads the light a molecule scatters to name it, and rough noble-metal surfaces swell that signal hugely. Semiconductor bases would widen the method's use, but their signals have stayed weak.

The team used tungsten oxide wires shaped like sea urchins, in a form short of oxygen. Missing oxygen atoms on the surface, called vacancies, strengthened the grip between base and molecule and boosted the signal further. Their base detected amounts as low as one ten-millionth of a mole per liter, with a top boost rivaling noble metals. The result ranks among the best reported for semiconductors.
europmc-pmc4637302:
