Caltech held Prudential Life policies for lab staff. When Prudential changed its form, Caltech got stock as compensation. The stock was later sold for cash.

GAO held that NASA may not keep the sale cash. The cash was not a repayment to NASA. No law lets NASA credit it to its own funds. NASA must put the cash in the Treasury as miscellaneous receipts. GAO also faulted the wait to deposit it. Staff had told Caltech to hold the cash in a money market fund. That broke the prompt deposit rule.
gao-gaoreports-b-310502:
Bottled water for field crews is cleared, with terms, in this GAO decision, B-310502, dated February 4, 2008. The Army Corps of Engineers runs work sites in its Savannah District. Some far sites have no safe water at hand. Law and Corps rules call for safe water for staff at work. A pay officer asked if funds could buy bottled water for those crews.

GAO raised no bar to the buy. The Corps may pick the best way to get safe water to a site. Jugs and coolers are one path. Bottled water is a fair path too. The Corps must first judge, site by site, that bottles are the best fit.
gao-gaoreports-b-310902:
Ceres Environmental Services, Inc. lost its protest. GAO decided B-310902 on March 3, 2008. The Army Corps of Engineers sought a firm to build a drain canal. The canal is the last leg of a flood plan for southeast Louisiana. The Corps used talks-based bids, not sealed bids. Ceres said sealed bids were the right path for build work of this kind.

GAO denied the protest. The Corps judged that speed of build was key here. That need made non-price points count in the pick. Sealed bids weigh price with scant room for such points. A rush need can back the talks path.
gao-gaoreports-b-311002:
LEADS Corporation lost its protest; the GAO decision is B-311002, dated March 26, 2008. The Patent and Trademark Office sought program aid services. The order went to Enterprise Information Services, Inc. LEADS held the past deal for the work. Its quote scored high on know-how and shift plans. The winner's quote scored low on those points and cost less in price.

GAO denied the protest. The agency weighed the score gap against the price gap. It found the high marks did not earn the high price. That trade call was fair on the facts. A past holder's edge in know-how can be outweighed by cost.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-202:
Homeland Security, GAO-05-202 of February 23, 2005, reviews the spend plan for a vast border check system. The US-VISIT program tracks set foreign guests as they enter and leave the United States. It holds facts and body marks, such as finger scans, on each guest. Congress told the department to send its spend plan for GAO review first.

GAO tests the plan next to each rule Congress set for it. It adds notes on how the build is run day to day. Some gains stand, the title grants. Many hard tests still wait, from data flow to cost control across the program's long life.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-702:
A blueprint for the Pentagon's back office has consumed years and money, GAO-05-702 reports on July 22, 2005. After almost 4 years and about $318 million, the defense department still lacks a working business enterprise architecture to guide its system buys. The governing board set up in 2001 holds too little power. No program plan sets measurable goals, tasks, or dates. No one has mapped the staff skills the work needs.

Draft products are patchy, at odds with each other, and unapproved. A law-set deadline lands in September 2005. GAO repeats its standing advice and scores the department against each past recommendation.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-802:
The national archives' digital records project is tracked in GAO-05-802, released July 15, 2005. Work began in 2001 to build a system for electronic records. Two design contracts were let in August 2004. One design was to be picked in August 2005. Congress told GAO to report on cost, schedule, and performance. GAO also checked status on its past recommendations.

GAO found the program is meeting its cost, schedule, and performance aims so far. All major milestones were met on or ahead of time. Three big deliverables met the set standards. Risks were named, though no single schedule ties all related agency work together. One past recommendation is fully done. Others are partly done. New security flaws were found, including the lack of a tested disaster recovery plan.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-102:
Truck crash data quality is graded in GAO-06-102, a report dated November 18, 2005. Big trucks are 3 percent of registered vehicles. They were in 11 percent of fatal crashes in 2003. States gather crash data and send it to a federal safety agency. That data must be complete, timely, accurate, and consistent to be useful. GAO asked what is known about its quality and what states do to lift it.

Headings state the pattern. States still have data quality problems, but they pursue many fix efforts. Meeting the standards remains a challenge. Faults often start at the scene, where officers misread criteria on report forms. Processing backlogs add more. The federal agency's grant program has supported state work with real gains. Its data quality map spurred states to improve, GAO found. But the map's limits curb its further use.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-202:
Livestock price reporting and the trust it needs are reviewed in GAO-06-202. The report is dated December 9, 2005. Ranchers earned $63 billion in gross income in 2004. They lean on the Agriculture Department's daily, weekly, and monthly market news to price cattle, hogs, and lamb. Packers use the same averages to pay many growers under contract. A 1999 law forced packers to report far more of their deals. GAO judged the department's quality checks as Congress debated renewing that law.

The department took real steps to guard report quality, GAO found. Yet its reporters left some packer deals out of the reports they built. That habit clouds how open the reports are. GAO urged the department to make the reports clearer and to audit packer data more closely. It also weighed how two department arms share the job of guarding competition. The department broadly agreed and said work on the advice had begun.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-402:
Once a drug is on sale, watching for harm is a second, vital job. GAO's March 31, 2006 report, GAO-06-402, reviews the Food and Drug Administration's postmarket drug safety work. High-profile cases in 2004 raised doubt about the agency's skill. In some cases, staff inside the agency disagreed on how to act.

GAO describes the agency's structure and process for safety choices. It grades how well that process works. It also checks steps the agency is taking to improve. Case studies cover four drugs: Arava, Baycol, Bextra, and Propulsid. GAO called for improvement in decision making and oversight. Readers see how disputes can slow safety action.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-502:
Tobacco settlement money flows to states each year, and this report tracks where it went. GAO's April 11, 2006 report, GAO-06-502, is the fifth and final in a yearly series. In 1998, four large tobacco companies signed a Master Settlement Agreement. They agreed to pay 46 states each year, without end. The payments repay states for past tobacco-related health care costs. A 2002 farm law requires these yearly GAO reports through fiscal year 2006.

GAO surveyed all 46 states. It reports payments received in fiscal year 2005 and expected in fiscal year 2006. It shows how states split the funds among program types. Changes from prior years are included.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-802:
Joint war training is the subject of GAO-06-802, which GAO issued on August 11, 2006. The Defense Department built its Training Transformation Program so forces arrive in theater ready to fight jointly. The centerpiece is the Joint National Training Capability, a web of linked ranges and simulations. It accounts for 84 percent of the $2 billion the department plans to invest by 2011. GAO checked whether the effort is improving joint training.

GAO found that the department does not know how far the initiative has improved joint training. It had not yet assessed the program's impact. GAO's review of five enhanced training events found some signs of potential gains. But the first department assessment was still pending. GAO urged management actions to prove the value of the investment. Training claims, GAO implied, need evidence like any other program.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1102:
Patent backlogs will not shrink on hiring alone, GAO finds in report GAO-07-1102, dated September 4, 2007. More, and more complex, patent bids have stretched the time the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office takes to work them. A growing pile of unexamined bids waits.

GAO traced 5 years of hiring. It asked how the office sets its yearly hiring aims, and how those aims link to the pile. It weighed how far new hires are offset by staff who leave, and why they leave. It checked if efforts to keep staff match why staff stay. GAO polled 1,420 examiners, with an 80 percent reply rate.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-202:
The federal long-term care insurance program sells coverage to federal workers and retirees. GAO compared its design with private rivals in GAO-07-202, dated December 29, 2006. Long-term care spending ran about $193 billion in 2004 and is set to rise. This is the second of two reports the 2000 law required. GAO studied the program's profit setup and its marketing. It also updated the picture on claims.

The program pays its manager under a set profit formula, GAO found. Three yearly payments stand apart from program costs. Two rest on premiums and one on program assets. Some of those profits are guaranteed, unlike in private plans. Marketing hit a snag: the program lacked home addresses for nearly all active workers. It had to rely on less direct outreach. Claims also ran below forecasts. The program had paid 44 percent of the expected claim dollars per enrollee.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-102:
Federal support for electricity is cataloged in GAO report GAO-08-102 (October 26, 2007). Electricity comes mostly from coal, other fossil fuels, and nuclear power, with hydropower and renewables behind. The federal government aids the sector in many ways. It funds research, grants tax breaks, and runs other support programs.

GAO estimates that research funds for the sector came to $11.5 billion from fiscal year 2002 through fiscal year 2007. That sum grew 35 percent across the period. Nuclear programs took the largest share, at $6.2 billion. The report sorts support by fuel type and by kind. It gives Congress a single tally of what the government spends to back power production.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-402:
Nanotechnology risk research reporting is examined in GAO report GAO-08-402, released March 31, 2008. The National Nanotechnology Initiative links 25 federal agencies that fund work at the scale of a nanometer. GAO checked how five agencies reported their fiscal year 2006 research on environmental, health, and safety risks.

The initiative said agencies spent $37.7 million on such risk research in fiscal year 2006, 3 percent of the $1.3 billion total for nanotechnology. GAO found that 22 of 119 projects counted as risk research were not truly aimed at measuring risk; many used nanotechnology to clean up hazards instead. Weak reporting rules and a lack of guidance caused the mix-up. GAO recommended clearer guidance from the Office of Science and Technology Policy, which generally agreed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-502:
Defense base facilities come up in GAO report GAO-08-502, issued April 24, 2008. The Defense Department runs about 577,000 structures worldwide, valued at about $712 billion. It plans to spend over $55 billion in fiscal year 2008 to support these facilities and run its bases.

A sustainment model used since 2003 gives a steady way to estimate yearly upkeep needs, but two of its inputs are shaky. Services have not verified property records as rules require, and an outside study found only 13 of 45 cost factors sound. Services also missed department funding goals for upkeep, citing tight funds and higher priorities. The Army, Navy, and Air Force each report repair backlogs over $50 billion. GAO recommended fixing the model inputs and the deferred work. The department generally agreed.
gibbs-elementary-statistical-mechanics-1:
Elementary Principles in Statistical Mechanics, from 1902, was the one book J. Willard Gibbs shaped as a whole. In it he founds statistical mechanics, the study of how vast groups of particles act. Rather than track each particle, Gibbs studies whole ensembles of possible systems. From those ensembles he derives the behavior of heat and energy.

The canonical distribution, his central tool, states how energy spreads among a system's states. Entropy gains a clear statistical meaning in his hands. The book's math is dense, yet its plan is clean. Physicists treat it as a founding text. It gave physics its statistical soul, as one summary puts it.
gorky-lower-depths-1902:
The Lower Depths, Maxim Gorky's play of 1902, reached English in Jenny Covan's translation of 1922. The scene is a night lodging house in a Russian city, run by a hard landlord and his wife. Thieves, ruined nobles, sick women, and a former actor fill its bunks and argue through the night.

An old pilgrim named Luka comforts each lodger with kind, useful lies. When he vanishes, hope collapses and the actor hangs himself offstage. The Moscow Art Theatre made the play a triumph under Stanislavsky in 1902. Gorky asks whether truth or mercy serves the desperate better. The question, never settled, keeps the play alive.
govdocs-archive_org-ProjectSCANATECIARDP:
Project SCANATE was an early CIA effort to test remote viewing, the claimed ability to describe distant places using only the mind. The declassified file preserves the agency's own paperwork on that research, approved for public release in 2003.

Inside are the records of a program that treated psychic perception as a possible tool for gathering intelligence during the Cold War. The papers show officials taking the idea seriously enough to fund and file formal studies of it. For readers, the file is direct evidence of how far intelligence agencies were willing to go in the 1970s.

Filed under the CIA's own name, a second copy of the Project SCANATE document holds the agency's early study of remote viewing. The research centered on Ingo Swann at SRI, who reported that he could view far-off locations without leaving the room.

The papers record how the agency set up and judged those tests, and they were approved for release in 2003. Keeping this duplicate matters because releases can differ in small ways, and researchers compare copies line by line. Together with its twin file, it documents the first step in the government's long remote-viewing program.
govdocs-archive_org-ks_-_cia_vault_8_201:
On November 9, 2017, WikiLeaks published Vault 8, source code and technical analysis from the CIA's Hive project. The release belonged to the long Vault 7 series of CIA hacking documents that WikiLeaks issued through 2017. It was the eighth installment in that series.

Hive was the agency's system for controlling implanted malware on target computers while hiding the CIA's hand in the operation. Vault 8 went past description to the code itself, together with analysis meant for technically minded readers. It is kept complete for researchers of cyber history and of the leak era, when secret tools became public documents.
govdocs-archive_org-ting_environment_201: WikiLeaks released the CIA's Vault 8 material on HIVE, a piece of agency hacking infrastructure. The HIVE operating environment papers describe the environment in which that system ran. Vault releases show the tools behind public headlines about state hacking. Technical readers can study how the environment was organized in 2012. The release is held as a United States government document taken from the archive's holdings.
guy-mannering-or-the-astrologer-volume-0:
Sir Walter Scott's Guy Mannering, volume two, resumes the novel at chapter thirty-two with Gilbert Glossin in possession of Ellangowan. Glossin, the low-born lawyer who engineered the Bertram ruin, finds the county cold to him. Gentry exclude him from their clubs, and common people refuse him the name of Ellangowan. The shooting of young Charles Hazlewood draws his anxious exertions.

The second volume carries the exposure: the lost heir Harry Bertram returns from India, and the smuggler Dirk Hatteraick's confession nears. Meg Merrilies, the gypsy prophetess, drives the reckoning she foretold at Harry's birth. Dominie Sampson, Colonel Mannering, and Julia's romance fill the social frame. Glossin's guilt ripens toward the doom the first volume promised. Scott's second novel ends as romance and justice in one knot. This hosted volume completes the tale from its midpoint, the astrology of the opening fulfilled in gypsy vengeance.
hale-modest-enquiry-witchcraft-1702:
John Hale was pastor at Beverly, near Salem, and at first he backed the witch trials of 1692. A Modest Enquiry into the Nature of Witchcraft, printed at Boston in 1702, is his second look at that hard year. He wrote it after doubt had time to grow.

Hale asks what witchcraft is, how a guilty person can be proved, and how the innocent can be kept safe. He casts doubt on spectral proof, claims based on visions only the accusers could see. Scripture and hard experience guide his argument on both sides. The book is the first clear critique of Salem from a man inside it.
harold-the-last-of-the-saxon-kings-volum:
Book Two of Lytton's Harold is titled Lanfranc the Scholar, and the hero of its early pages is the Norman churchman who would one day be Archbishop of Canterbury. Its first chapter dwells, though, on Saxon appetites: four meals a day, from earl to ceorl, were not thought too lavish an reading of the daily bread. Happy times, the narrator sighs, for the ceorl, yet never sweet is the food of servitude.

Drink, the vice of the warlike nations of the North, is traced to the example of the Danes. Around the feasting, Lytton weaves the scholar Lanfranc's rise at the Norman court and the tightening web between England and Normandy. The part is more chronicle than romance in stretches. It shows Lytton's method at full stretch: history first, with the tale carried along on a strong current of learning.
hastings-dictionary-bible-vol4-1902:
Volume Four of Hastings's Dictionary of the Bible, published in 1902, completes the main alphabet, from Pleroma to Zuzim. James Hastings had driven the huge project for a decade. The final alphabetical volume was long awaited by subscribers.

Long articles on prophecy, the Psalms, Rome, sacrifice, and the Temple anchor this volume. Writers sum up the scholarship of the 1890s on the Bible's history and teaching. The set's balance of faith and learning made it a fixture in seminaries. Readers today use it to see how the best scholars of 1900 understood the scriptures. Sets were sold volume by volume to ministers across the English-speaking world.
hilbert-foundations-geometry-townsend-19:
David Hilbert rebuilt geometry on strict axioms in The Foundations of Geometry, Englished by E. J. Townsend in 1902. The text here is the second edition of Hilbert's German work. He starts from undefined terms and a short list of axioms. Every theorem must follow from those axioms alone, with no help from pictures.

Hilbert tests his axioms for consistency and for freedom from hidden overlap. He shows which theorems fall if a given axiom is dropped. The rigor of the method set a new standard for all mathematics. Teachers call the book the axiomatic method's manifesto. Readers need patience, and gain precision. Its influence spread to every exact science.
history-of-friedrich-ii-of-prussia-volum:
Thomas Carlyle's History of Friedrich the Second, in twenty-one volumes, reaches its second here, containing Book Two, Of Brandenburg and the Hohenzollerns, from 928 to 1417. Carlyle warns that Brandenburg before the Hohenzollerns has little history worth remembering, though much has been written. Henry the Fowler and the town of Brannibor open the story.

He traces Saxon emperors, margraves, and the empire's loose German politics, with Richard of Cornwall buying gleams of authority in the Rhenish provinces before quitting Germany in 1263. Pytheas of Marseilles, sailing past two thousand years before, gets the book's first backward glance. This deep background prepares the elector family from whom Prussia, and finally Frederick, will come.
history-of-the-revolt-of-the-netherlands:
The second book of Friedrich Schiller's History of the Revolt of the Netherlands centres on Cardinal Granvella, born Anthony Perenot at Besançon in 1516. Perenot's father, a blacksmith's son, rose by merit to serve Margaret of Savoy and then Charles the Fifth, becoming privy counsellor and keeper of the king's seal.

Schiller shows how the son inherited his father's honours, influence and political knowledge, and how, as Archbishop of Malines and minister in the Netherlands, he became the target of his contemporaries' hatred. The book follows Granvella's career through the councils and intrigues that made him the symbol of Spanish rule. Readers will find Schiller's portrait both hostile to its subject's policies and fair to his formidable ability.
hobson-imperialism-1902:
John Atkinson Hobson was a British journalist and economist who reported from South Africa before writing Imperialism: A Study in 1902. He asked why rich nations were racing to seize colonies across Africa and Asia. His answer pointed home, to the flow of money itself.

Hobson argues that the rich save more than they can spend at home, a fault he calls underconsumption. Surplus capital then hunts for profit abroad, and flags and armies follow the investments. Lenin read the book closely and named it as a source for his own theory of imperialism. Hobson wrote with direct sight of the South African war and its costs.
homo-sum-volume-02:
Volume 2 of Homo Sum, by Georg Ebers, stays through one night watch beside a sick old hermit. Ebers shows Paulus sitting motionless by Stephanus, holding back even a cough so the light sleep will not break. A senator's potion has done its work, and past midnight the old man wakes with his deepest worry ready to speak in this volume.

Chapter V gives Stephanus a long, honest confession about his son Hermas. He admits that love, not duty alone, kept the boy beside him on the Holy Mountain. Hermas's mother fled with a lover and never asked for the child. The father hoped desert life would spare his son the world's sorrow. Now the young man has come back from Alexandria unable to laugh, and the old plan looks like a kind mistake.
in-the-blue-pike-volume-02:
Volume 2 of In the Blue Pike, by Georg Ebers, gives the rope dancer Kuni a task worth more than applause. Ebers writes that she has been nursing a sick mother and her babies, working with all her strength for strangers. The man who promised the woman a cart ride to her home village of Schweinfurt has quietly withdrawn his help in this volume.

Chapter IV explains his reason without cruelty. He keeps himself and his family alive by trained poodles performing in taverns, under village lindens, and at fairs, where children clap heartily and often pay nothing. Feeding a mother and twins is more than his tricks can carry. Kuni, herself near the roadside's edge, takes the burden up. Finding someone needier than herself lifts her out of her own despair, and service becomes the one success left to a failing performer.
iraq-wmd-nie-2002:
In October 2002 the American intelligence agencies issued a National Intelligence Estimate on Iraq's weapons programs. Congress had demanded the summary judgment before voting on whether to allow war against Saddam Hussein. The declassified excerpts released to the public stated the agencies' key claims in strong terms.

The estimate said with high confidence that Iraq held chemical and biological weapons and was rebuilding its nuclear program. After the 2003 invasion, search teams found no such stockpiles and no active nuclear effort. Reviews later found that weak evidence had been stated as near certainty and that doubts inside the agencies were buried. The episode became a standard case of intelligence failure, since the estimate had served as the public basis for war.
jacobs-lady-of-the-barge-1902:
W. W. Jacobs mixed sea tales and dark tales in The Lady of the Barge and Others, his set from 1902. Most tales are brisk and wry. Sailors spin yarns, con men scheme, and small folk meet odd turns of luck in port towns.

One tale towers past the rest. In it, a paw plucked from a mummy grants three wishes, and each wish turns to grief. That tale is now the most famed short fright tale in the tongue. It taught hosts of scribes how dread can grow from one small, plain choice. Jacobs, a clerk turned scribe, had a keen ear for dock side talk. That ear makes both the jokes and the dread feel true to life.
jesuit-relations-thwaites-vol-02:
Acadia in 1612 to 1614 is the ground of Volume 2, printed in 1896. Thwaites placed these reports second in his vast edition of the Jesuit Relations. The French missions on the Atlantic shore were still small and weak.

English raids, bitter winters, and thin supplies test the priests at every turn. Their letters home mix faith, fear, and plain facts about the land. They note Mi'kmaq customs, trade goods, and the mood of each camp. Step by step, the volume preserves the first French foothold in North America. Few records of those years are as close or as frank.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aaron-of-york-f:
Aaron of York was a Jewish financier and chief rabbi of England, born in York before 1190. He died after 1253. He was probably the son of Josce of York, the leading figure in the York massacre of 1190. In 1237 he was made presbyter, or chief rabbi, of the Jews of England.

Aaron told Matthew Paris he had paid the king no less than 30,000 marks in silver and 200 in gold in all. In 1250 he was fined 14,000 marks of silver and ten of gold on a charge of falsifying a deed. A number of Hebrew deeds from his dealings still exist, one wholly in his own hand.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abdima-b-hamdur: Abdima ben Hamdure was an amora of the third century. The entry is short, and its one claim is a matter of identity. He is most likely, it says, the same man as Mar Bar Hamdure. That man was a disciple of Samuel, the Babylonian master. Four Talmudic passages are cited in support of the link, from Shabbat, Yoma, Sukkah, and Menaḥot. No ruling, saying, birthplace, or date of Abdima ben Hamdure is given in this notice beyond that match of names.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abner-of-burgos:
Abner of Burgos, later Alfonso of Valladolid, was born in 1270 and died in 1348 or a little later. Trained in Bible, Talmud, philosophy, and astrology, he qualified as a physician at twenty-five. At about sixty he converted to Christianity.

Contemporaries held that gain, not belief, drove his conversion. He won a sacristan post at Valladolid. In his Epistle on Fate he blamed the planets for his choice and denied free will. He then wrote many works against Judaism. In 1336 he pressed charges that led to a royal ban on an old prayer formula.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abraham-ben-ben:
Polish Talmudist Abraham ben Benjamin Aaron died at Brest, Lithuania, in 1642. He served as rabbi at Tarnopol in 1636 and in other Polish towns. That year Brest, then Poland's largest Jewish community, called him to its rabbinate, and he stayed there until his death.

Leading rabbis such as Joel Sirkes, Meir Kohen-Zedek, and Rabbi Heschel of Cracow treated him with the greatest respect in their writings. His responsa survive inside their works. He also left notes on the Tur Orah Hayyim, added to his father's book. His father, Benjamin Aaron, who died in 1620, wrote the responsa collection Masat Binyamin.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abraham-ha-levi: Abraham ha-Levi was a tosafist who is not yet fully identified. A Piske Tosafot quote names an Abraham ha-Levi known in no other way. He was probably one of the many German or French tosafists named Abraham, with ha-Levi dropped for ease. He may be Abraham ben Baruch, brother of Meir of Rothenburg. That man flourished about 1225-93 and wrote a work still in manuscript. The entry leaves the puzzle open, resting on Zunz's study of the sources.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abraham-of-troy:
Abraham of Troyes headed the community of Troyes, France, about the middle of the twelfth century. He was a contemporary of Rabbenu Tam. The sway he held at Troyes gave rise to a curious legal incident, told in some detail.

Eleazar ha-Nadib, sued by Abraham, refused to face the rabbinical court at Troyes. Backed by Isaac ben Samuel of Dampierre, he got his case sent to another court. Eleazar's son later did the same and won backing from Judah Sire Leon of Paris. In a linked case, kin of Simson of Troyes also feared the local court's bent and objected to trial there.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abumai-702: Abumai was Gaon in Sura from 811 to 819. He was a brother of Rabbi Mordecai. He seems to have been the father of Cohen-Ẓedeḳ. That son also became Gaon of Sura. He won fame for his many calls on ritual and court questions. The hosted text is very short. It gives the office, the years, and the two family links. It points the reader to the entry on the Geonim for more, and it adds no facts about Abumai's own acts or works.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-adibe-jacob-802: Jacob Adibe was a Jew cast out from Portugal in 1496. He lived at Azamor, in the province of Duccala, Morocco. In 1512 that town's ruler had bowed to Portugal, then broke faith. King Manuel sent a fleet under his nephew Don Jaime, duke of Bragança. A day of hard fight gave no clear win. At dawn Adibe came to the duke with news. The city had been left empty. He asked cover for his family and his fellow Jews, and got it.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-agobard-902:
Agobard was archbishop of Lyons, born in 779. He died on June 6, 840. He ranks as a chief foe of Judaism in the ninth century. Jews of Lyons lived in a set quarter at the foot of Fourvière hill. King Louis the Debonair gave them a court shield, a master of the Jews named Eberard. That grant roused Agobard's wrath.

He set his case in four letters to the king, court priests, and bishops. He told the faithful to shun trade and meals with Jews. He charged that Jews boasted of court favor and fine gifts. He charged them with building new synagogues against law. Last, he charged them with stealing Christian children for sale as slaves. His push failed. In 834 he lost his post and fled to Italy.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ahot-ketannah-t:
Ahot Ketannah, "The Little Sister," is a ritual poem of eight stanzas. Its title comes from a verse in the Song of Songs. The stanzas carry the acrostic of Abraham Hazan. In the Sephardic ritual it is sung before the New-year's evening prayer. Its refrain asks that the year end with her woes. The last stanza changes the line to a hope for blessings.

Abraham Hazan was a cantor born in Salonica in 1533. He probably composed the melody as well as the words. The tune is in the hypo-dorian mode. The entry compares it with airs from the Greek islands of the same age. Italian Jews altered its coloring, it says. Dutch, English, and West Indian Sephardim kept older traits of the tune.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aldabi-meir-ibn:
Meir ibn Aldabi was a writer of the fourteenth century. He was a son of Isaac Aldabi, called the Pious. He was also a grandson of Asher ben Jehiel, and he traced descent from the exiles of Jerusalem. His name is fixed by an acrostic poem in his chief book, where its letters spell Aldabi.

In 1360 he wrote "Shebile Emunah," the Paths of Faith. It is a wide treatise on philosophy, science, and theology. Its ten chapters run from the being of God to the world to come. They cover creation, the spheres and stars, the body and its health, the soul, reward and punishment, and Israel's redemption. The book stayed a favorite with the educated for centuries, in many editions. Later study showed it to be a gathering from older writers, chiefly Gerson of Arles.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-america-the-dis:
Discovery of America is tied to Jews at more than one point. Star books by Jewish hands helped Columbus sail. One tool for reading the stars was a Jewish find. Levi ben Gerson first set out the Jacob's Staff. Abraham Zacuto fit that tool to sea use. His tables served Columbus on the voyage. Once, the entry says, they saved the whole crew.

Luis de Santangel took a chief part on land. He was a Marano close to King Ferdinand. He won Queen Isabella to the plan. He then lent the cash to fit out the ships. Columbus sent his first full report to Santangel. That letter was dated Feb. 15, 1493.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-amittai-1402: Amittai was the father of the prophet Jonah. Two verses name him as Jonah's father. Rabbinic sources place him in the tribe of Zebulon. They say he lived at Zarephath. One tale makes his wife the widow of that town. That widow fed the prophet Elijah in a famine. The child Elijah raised from death was Jonah. That chain rests on later tradition, the entry shows.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-andreas-1502:
Andreas is the hero of a medieval legend about a Jewish pope. The entry draws the tale from an old Spanish document found among penitential prayers. In the story, Andreas was a Jew who became a Christian and rose, step by step, to cardinal and then pope.

When a slander against the Jews threatened an outbreak, the pope spoke for them and calmed the crowd. Grateful Jewish leaders came to thank him. He gave them a penitential prayer he had written in Hebrew and asked that all communities adopt it. The entry treats the tale as one version of a Jewish pope story told widely in the Middle Ages.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aram-rehob-ii-s: Aram-Rehob was a district of Syria whose chief city was Rehob, or Beth-Rehob. It stood alongside Aram-Zobah as a foe of David, as Second Samuel, chapter 10, verses 6 to 8, shows. Numbers, chapter 13, verse 21, and Judges, chapter 18, verse 28, place a Beth-Rehob in the Lebanon region near Dan. The entry is only a few lines long. Its one modern note is Moore's guess, in his commentary on Judges, that Beth-Rehob may be Paneas.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-arnstein-fanny-:
Fanny Vogele von Arnstein led society in Vienna from a base of wealth, reading, and wide kindness. Born in Berlin on September 29, 1757, she died near Vienna on June 8, 1818. Her father was Daniel Itzig, the rich banker who headed Berlin's Jewish community. His house drew the Mendelssohn circle, and Fanny grew up among the women of the Jewish salon period, such as Henriette Herz and Rahel.

Marriage to the banker Nathan Adam von Arnstein carried that Berlin salon style to Vienna. Her mansion and her villas at Schonbrunn and Baden filled daily with guests of every rank. Her charity was constant, above all after the disasters of 1809. She raised 7,000 florins among her fellow Jews for a hospital at Baden, and in 1813 she sent supplies to Rahel's relief work at Prague.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ascoli-jacob-be:
Jacob ben Abraham Rofe Ascoli was an Italian physician and liturgical poet of the second half of the fifteenth century. He lived at Camerino, perhaps at Ascoli. Two of his Reshuts, opening poems for the Nishmat prayer, are printed in the Mahzor Romania. One serves the Day of Atonement, praising the God who shows every living being the road back to him.

The second serves the Feast of Tabernacles. It asks the Redeemer to spread a tabernacle of peace over the people chosen among all peoples. Signing these poems, Ascoli added a word matching a verse of Psalm 119: Let thy mercies also come unto me, O Lord. The entry rests on Landshuth and Zunz, and gives no dates, no family, and no other works.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ashre-ha-am-200:
Ashre ha-Am is Psalm 89 verse 16, placed before the Ashre prayer on the Day of Memorial, the New Year, right after the sounding of the shofar. In Ashkenazic congregations it carries a fine melody of medieval origin. The tune stands in the fourth, Hypophrygian, mode of Gregorian plain song. It ranges from the fourth degree below the middle note to the fifth above it.

That melody has become one of the representative themes of the penitential season. It is heard ahead of time in the Selihot that come before it. It returns in the Shema that closes the Day of Atonement. The entry praises its closing fall of a fourth onto the final note, a cadence it calls characteristically Oriental and common in older medieval chants.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aub-hirsch-2102:
Hirsch Aub was a rabbi and Talmudist. He was born in 1796 in Baiersdorf, a small town near Erlangen, and died at Munich in 1876. He studied in Prague and won a name as a Talmudist. In 1827 he was chosen chief rabbi of Munich. He held that post for forty-nine years.

His flock held both Orthodox and Reform Jews. His love of peace held the two camps together, and it earned him the name ba'al sholom, peacemaker. In 1848 he worked for Jewish emancipation. Three Bavarian kings esteemed him, and Ludwig II. gave him the Cross of St. Michael at seventy.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bacharach-micha: Michael Bacharach was a dayyan, a judge in a rabbinical court, in Prague. He held that office in the second half of the eighteenth century. The entry is one of the shortest in its run. It gives that office, that city, and that period, and then stops. What remains is a list of the reference books in which his name can be found.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-baldness-2402:
Baldness, among the Hebrews, drew a sharper reproach than among the classical nations. The entry notes that Hebrews prized long, well-oiled hair. "Bald head" served as an insult in II Kings ii. 23. Yet baldness cannot have been rare: Egyptian paintings often show old Semite chiefs as bald, and Leviticus speaks of baldness on the crown and in front. Names meaning "bald" were common.

Most Bible passages on the subject, though, treat shaving the head as a sign of mourning. Making baldness for the dead is barred in Deuteronomy, and priests are barred from it in Leviticus. The entry lists many texts where shaving marked grief before the exile. It also traces the long temple-locks of the Ashkenazim to the ban on cutting the corners of the head, and compares the customs of Philistines, Moabites, Tyrians, and Egyptians.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-barasch-julius-:
Julius Barasch, Rumanian author and physician, was born at Brody in 1815 and died at Bucharest on March 31, 1863. Married against his wish at sixteen, he lost his fortune and went to Germany to study medicine. He took his degree at Berlin in 1841. After posts as quarantine physician and chief state physician, he settled in Bucharest. There he became professor of natural science and founded the first children's hospital in the city.

Barasch wrote on Ḥasidism in Poland and on Jewish religious philosophy while still a student. In Rumania he created a scientific vocabulary for the language and wrote popular works on hygiene, botany, and zoology. He founded "Isis," Rumania's first scientific journal, and gave free Sunday talks on hygiene. In 1852 he opened a modern school for Jewish children. He also founded the country's first Jewish newspaper and wrote on Jewish emancipation in Rumania.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-basch-abraham-2: Abraham Basch was a German poet and teacher born at Posen on July 17, 1800, who died at Berlin on Sept. 24, 1841. He could expound the Talmud at age twelve and later studied German, French, and Latin at Prenzlau. He moved to Berlin in 1817 and lived poorly by copying Hebrew manuscripts and writing verse. In 1825 he traveled in South Germany and met Goethe. Back in Berlin he taught Hebrew at Weyl's seminary, but its failure left him in poverty again.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-becher-2702: Becher is a name borne by two men in the Bible lists, and the short entry keeps them apart. The first is a son of Benjamin, named in Genesis and in First Chronicles. He does not appear in two other family lists, in Numbers and in a later chapter of Chronicles. The second is a son of Ephraim. From him the family of the Bachrites takes its name, as the book of Numbers states in its twenty-sixth chapter.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-belfast-2802:
Belfast is the chief town of County Antrim, in Ulster, Ireland. Its Jewish community of some 400 or 500 souls was new when the entry was written. One man who arrived in 1851 founded it. A synagogue opened in 1870, and two ministers are named in turn.

Russian Jews settling there in later years brought new needs. A board of guardians arose in 1893, a women's benevolent society in 1896, and a Hebrew national school in 1898. The entry ends by noting that Sir Otto Jaffe was mayor of Belfast in 1899. Two ministers, named Chotzner and Myers, filled the pulpit post of that synagogue one after the other.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-benash-benjamin: Benjamin Benash, also called Benush, was a cabalist of the early eighteenth century. He was the son of Judah Löb Cohen of Krotoschin, in Prussia. His book Shem-Ṭob Ḳaṭan drew extracts said to come from Isaac Luria and Moses Naḥmanides. It gave prayers and formulas for the practical use of the Cabala. One prayer claimed to make a traveler invisible to robbers, and another aimed at putting out a fire. A second book, Amtaḥat Binyamin, followed the same line.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-benloew-louis-3:
Louis Benloew, a French scholar of language, was born at Erfurt on Nov. 15, 1818, and died at Dijon in February 1900. He studied at Berlin, Leipsic, and Göttingen, then moved to France in 1841 to teach modern tongues. He became a librarian at the Sorbonne and a professor at Dijon.

As dean at Dijon he held high rank until his pension in 1882, and he wore the Legion of Honor. His long book list covers the shared roots of tongues, rhythm, number names, and the laws of history. He also edited Sophocles and wrote on Latin accent with a partner.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bermann-adolf-p: Adolf Bermann, a Hungarian writer who used the pen name Kobor Tamas, was born at Presburg in 1867. After law study he took a post at the Hungarian Credit Bank. His brother-in-law, the ballad writer Joseph Kiss, spurred his early gift for fine writing. In time he won wide fame in Hungarian letters. His novels and tales of love all satirize the social order of his day, the entry says, and they are read very widely. No titles or dates for the works themselves are given.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bloch-rosine-34: Rosine Bloch was a French singer. She was born in Paris in 1844. Her father was a merchant. She had a magnificent mezzo-soprano voice. At the Conservatoire she won first prizes in 1865. They covered both singing and opera. She debuted at the Paris Opera as Azucena. That role is in "Il Trovatore." She created Chloris in 1867 and Claribel in 1873. In 1880 she sang Amneris in "Aïda" with success. She stayed fifteen years at the Opera.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bonastruc-desma:
Bonastruc Desmaestre, also called Astruc Maestre, was a Spanish controversialist at the disputation at Tortosa in 1413-14. He was a leading citizen of Gerona. In 1411 town lawyers pled his case before the queen dowager of Aragon.

They said danger to Jews on the roads made a royal summons hard to obey. Pope Benedict XIII then had Gerona send learned men to Tortosa. Bonastruc went as a delegate with Todros and Ferrer. He disputed with Geronimo de Santa Fe on three days in February. His frank speech once angered the pope, and his fellow delegates reproached him for it. A circular report on the dispute went back to Gerona, though probably not from his pen.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-boule-plural-an: Boule, a Greek word, means a council. Here it stands for a court of justice, or Sanhedrin, and also for the seat of a senate. Josephus uses it in that sense, the entry notes. Talmudic sources name twenty-four boulés in the south of Judea. Those bodies passed out of existence, one source says, because the sanctity of the oath was widely disregarded. The entry points readers to the articles on the Sanhedrin and on the Prosbul for more.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-budushchnost-th: Budushchnost, meaning The Future, was a Russo-Jewish weekly founded in 1900 and edited by S. O. Gruzenberg. Like Voskhod, it gave solid coverage of Jewish history, social life, and institutions. The two papers differed in direction. Voskhod favored assimilation, while Budushchnost leaned toward Zionism. Most leading Zionist writers of Russia wrote for it. The paper also issued a sbornik, or literary annual, as a supplement. The entry is brief and gives no circulation or closing date for the weekly.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cahun-david-leo:
David Leon Cahun was a French Orientalist and writer born June 23, 1841, at Haguenau, in Alsace. His family had planned a military career for him, but family affairs forced a change. He turned to geography and history and began publishing travel pieces in 1863. A long journey from 1864 took him through Egypt, Nubia, and Asia Minor.

Back in France he wrote for political papers and served as a war correspondent, then as a volunteer officer in 1870. A post at the Bibliothèque Mazarine followed in 1875. His historical novels retold Phoenician voyages, the Crusades, and Norman invasions with close detail. Later travels reached Syria, Iceland, and Mesopotamia. From 1890 he lectured at the Sorbonne on the history and geography of Asia. He died at Paris in 1900.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-caslari-abraham:
Abraham ben David Caslari, a physician at Besalu, in Catalonia, worked in the first half of the fourteenth century. Contemporaries counted him among the most skilful physicians of his time. He taught Moses Narboni of Perpignan. In 1323 Kalonymus ben Kalonymus addressed a moral treatise to him and nine other notables.

Caslari wrote on fevers in works that survive in manuscript. One treatise, finished in November 1326, served friends as a handbook. A second, from 1349, treats pestilential fevers, in the year the Black Death struck Provence, Catalonia, and Aragon. He also wrote rules for bleeding and a work on support in sickness. A Latin rendering of Razi's Antidotarium is ascribed to him. One book on foods, by Isaac Israeli, was wrongly put under his name.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cherei-4302: Cherei is a small town in the government of Mohilev, in Russia. In 1898 it held about 3,000 people, of whom 1,300 were Jews. Trade and handicrafts were the chief Jewish work. Of 298 artisans, most owned shops, and shoemaking and tailoring led the trades. About 61 Jews worked as journeymen. A few families farmed, gardened, or kept dairies. The town had 20 ḥadarim with 120 scholars. Jewish children entered the town school only for a fee, while others studied free.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-choir-1602:
Singers set apart from the congregation for divine service form the subject here, traced from the Temple onward. The Bible's first choir was organized by the Levites, with musicians beside them. Two priests with silver trumpets gave the signal to begin. Samuel and David are said to have divided the Levites into twenty-four orders for set days of duty.

Rules fill much of the entry. Singers and players could not swap posts. Levites trained for five years before service. Later sections follow the choir into synagogue life and record complaints about singers who stretched out endings or split words badly. Named writers and works close the long survey.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-congress-of-jew:
Congress of Jewish Women was one of the denominational congresses of the World's Parliament of Religions. It met at the Columbian Exposition in Chicago in 1893. The entry calls it the first delegate body of Jewish women ever called together. Ninety-three delegates came from 29 cities of the United States.

Hannah G. Solomon chaired the congress, with Sadie American as secretary and a committee of 25 Chicago women. Sessions ran Sept. 4-7. Papers set out Jewish women's work and thought in charity and religion. The final session voted to form a lasting body, the National Council of Jewish Women. A souvenir volume of traditional Jewish melodies, edited by two cantors, marked the event.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cotton-4702: Cotton never appears as an English word in the Authorized Version, the entry argues. Yet the thing itself is named in Esther, in the hangings of the king's palace garden. The Hebrew word there, karpas, should likely be read as cotton or cotton muslin. It is a loan-word from Persian, from a Sanskrit term. The plant was grown and used for cloth in ancient India. Alexander's eastern conquests first taught the Greeks its fabrics. Its culture then spread across the whole East.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-darius-i-4902:
Darius the First was king of Persia from 521 to 485 before the common era. He was a son of Hystaspes, governor of Parthia. A Magian usurper had seized the throne and wed Cyrus' daughter. Darius and six noble friends struck back. In October of 521 they killed the usurper in a Median city, and Darius took the crown. Revolts at once shook the empire. Babylon rose under a man calling himself Nebuchadnezzar the Third.

For the Jews, Darius proved a just ruler. When officials questioned the Temple work at Jerusalem, he searched the records. Cyrus had ordered the house built, so the cost came from Syrian tribute. He ordered a daily offering for the kingdom and his sons. On March 10, 515, in his sixth year, the Temple stood complete.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-davis-miriam-is: Miriam Isabel Davis was an English painter born in London. After touring the galleries of Venice, Florence, and Rome, she studied art in earnest at the Bloomsbury School of Art. Her career began in 1882 with an exhibit at the Society of Lady Artists. In 1887 the Royal Academy hung her picture "New Music," and in 1889 she showed at the Paris Salon. The entry lists her paintings year by year through 1892. From 1895 she turned to portrait painting. She helped found the Society of Women Painters.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-derek-erez-rabb:
Derek Ereẓ Rabbah is one of the small treatises of the Talmud, a book of conduct and morals. Printed editions group it with two other works, the Small Derek Ereẓ and the Section on Peace. The entry warns that the names mislead: the large and small books are separate works, not long and short versions of one text.

The book has eleven sections. It opens with rules on forbidden marriages, plus moral sayings about marriage. One section sorts twenty-four classes of people, twelve bad and twelve good, each with a Bible verse. Other sections give rules for scholars and their pupils, drawn from Bible events. Later sections treat humility, table manners, and the duties of guests and hosts.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-din-from-dun-to:
Din is a Hebrew word of law with five linked senses: argument, judgment, the rules behind them, justice, and punishment. It is generally used of proceedings in a court. Rabbi Simon ben Gamaliel counted din among the three things on which the world stands, with truth and peace. A judge who gives true judgment is ranked with a partner in creation.

The first lesson of the Great Synagogue was to be slow in din, not to decide before a case is fully weighed. Yet the rabbis also damned the opposite fault, holding a decision back without cause. They praised the person who gives up part of his right for the sake of peace. The entry then separates money cases from criminal and capital ones.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-drachman-bernar:
Bernard Drachman was an American educator and rabbi born in New York city on June 27, 1861. He came from a rabbinical family and graduated from Columbia College in 1882. Study in Europe followed, at Breslau and Heidelberg. He took his doctorate at Heidelberg in 1884.

Ordained at Breslau in 1885, Drachman led pulpits at Newark and then in New York. He helped Sabato Morais found the Jewish Theological Seminary in 1886. He taught Bible, Hebrew grammar, and Jewish philosophy there. In 1902 he moved to the new Seminary of America as instructor. His books treat Hebrew grammar, and he translated Hirsch's Nineteen Letters.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ebed-melech-540:
Ebed-melech was a Cushite officer at the court of King Zedekiah. He spoke up for the prophet Jeremiah. Cast into a pit by the princes, Jeremiah faced death there. The king sent Ebed-melech with thirty men to haul him out. Some scholars read the number as three.

For that rescue, Jeremiah promised Ebed-melech safety when the city fell. Legend then takes over the story. One tale has him sleep sixty-six years under a tree, while his figs stayed fresh. Another count places him among nine men who entered paradise alive. Rabbinic writers argued over who he really was, some reading his name as the king's servant.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-education-13302:
Education, for the Jews, meant the moral and religious training of children. From the start of their history it counted as a chief aim of life. God, in Genesis, singles out Abraham to command his household in God's way. Feasts and ceremonies were built to teach lessons to the young.

Deuteronomy orders the Law's words kept before children's eyes day by day. Every seventh year the whole people, children included, gathered to hear the Law read. Public reading of the Pentateuch grew from that command. The long entry then follows Jewish schooling through the ages. It ends with trade training run by charities like the Alliance Israélite Universelle.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-eliezer-ben-far: Eliezer ben Faruh was a Jewish mathematician of early note. Muslim writers say he first set up the Jewish calendar. Al-Biruni names him in a book on the dating systems of old nations. Scholars link him to a famed Jewish star expert of like name. That man's name comes down in many garbled forms. The entry thinks he was Persian by birth. It also warns of a mix-up in the sources. He may be confused with Eliezer ben Hyrcanus or with Eleazar ben Arak.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-elmira-5702: Elmira is a city in the state of New York. Jews first settled there about the year 1851. In 1860 twelve families formed a congregation. They called it Children of Israel as their name. In 1886 a new synagogue was dedicated in town. By the count given, some sixty families belong to it. Russian Jews came after 1881 and formed two Orthodox flocks. The town's Jewish count is put at about 1,200 souls. Lodges and aid groups serve the flock there. A reformatory in town holds 180 Jewish inmates, the entry adds.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ephraim-maksha-: Ephraim Maksha'ah, called the Objector, was a scholar of the second century and a pupil of R. Meir. The entry says he is known only for a few sayings in his teacher's name. One saying explains why Obadiah was sent with bad news to the Edomites. Obadiah himself was an Edomite who had turned to Judaism. His mission fits a proverb about the woods supplying wood for the hatchet. The entry cites Sanhedrin 39a for the saying.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-eulenburg-alber:
Albert Eulenburg was a German nerve specialist born in Berlin on August 10, 1840, son of a Berlin physician. He took his doctorate in 1861 and worked at Greifswald's university hospital. As an army surgeon he served in the campaigns of 1866 and 1870-71, winning the Iron Cross for noncombatants. In 1890 he became assistant professor at Berlin.

His standing rests on editing as much as practice. He edited the Realencyklopadie der Gesammten Heilkunde, a standard medical reference that grew to twenty-seven volumes by its third edition. His own books cover drug injection by needle, nervous diseases, and water-based electric baths. With Paul Guttmann he wrote on the sympathetic nervous system, a work that won the Astley-Cooper prize in London.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-fettmilch-vince:
Vincent Fettmilch led the Frankfort guilds against the Jews in 1612 and drove their expulsion in 1614. He was hanged in 1616. A Calvinist among Lutheran rulers, he sought revenge on the city fathers through the Jews, the entry says. Turned down for a hospital clerk post in 1595, he became a soldier, then a gingerbread baker. His boldness won the mob for four years.

On August 22, 1614 his crowd stormed the Jewish quarter. About 2,000 Jews fought back bravely, but they were beaten and driven out, 1,380 leaving in all. Looting and burning caused 176,919 florins in damage. The emperor at last ordered arrests. Fettmilch was caught, hanged, and quartered on March 10, 1616, and his house was razed.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-frankenberg-abr:
Abraham von Frankenberg was a German mystic of the seventeenth century. He was a nobleman and the most influential man in the district of Oels in Silesia. He was a disciple of Jacob Böhme and a friend of Manasseh ben Israel. The two men wrote to each other. Frankenberg told him that the true light will come from the Jews.

Their time, he said, is not far distant. A Latin saying of his runs that the Hebrews have the fountains, the Greeks the rivulets, and the Latins the swamps. Manasseh sent him a portrait of himself as a token of friendship. It bore a wanderer and a torch, and a verse from Psalm 119.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-frohman-charles:
Charles Frohman, an American theater manager born at Sandusky, Ohio, about 1858, began as an advance agent for minstrel troupes. A tour to the Pacific coast ended in failure, and he made his way back east as best he could. In New York he took road rights to plays, with little success at first.

In 1895 he helped form a theater trust with partners who held houses across the country. The group began with thirty-seven theaters and pressed weaker rivals hard. Stars and managers rose against him in 1898, but the revolt faded. By the end he owned or leased five theaters in New York and three in London.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-gomperz-theodor:
Theodor Gomperz was an Austrian philologist. He was born at Brünn on March 29, 1832. His family story opens the entry. His great-grandfather spoke for Bohemia's Jews in 1745 when expulsion loomed. Theodor entered Vienna University in 1849. He studied classical philology and philosophy there. He translated the works of John Stuart Mill into German.

He rose through Vienna's ranks to full professor of classical philology in 1873. Academies at Vienna and St. Petersburg admitted him. In 1901 the emperor placed him in the House of Lords. His books treat Greek writers, Herodotus, Plato, and Theophrastus. His main work, "Griechische Denker," began in 1893. It aims at a full picture of ancient Greek thought.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-grape-14702:
The grape entry starts with Hebrew words for the fruit. One term covers ripe grapes off the cluster. Another covers grapes in clusters. Further words name sour grapes, wild grapes, fallen grapes, and raisins. Two small words spark a rabbinic debate. R. Judah and R. Jose differ on which means the skin and which the seed.

A second half reads grapes as symbols. Micah despairs that no good man can be found, like grapes after vintage. Ezekiel's proverb says the fathers ate sour grapes and the children's teeth ache. A Talmud saying compares marrying a daughter to a scholar with mixing vine grapes with vine grapes. R. Aibu even held that Eve's forbidden fruit was the grape.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-grun-maurice-69:
Maurice Grün was a Russian painter born at Reval in 1870. He studied art at Munich and Geneva. In 1890 he went to Paris. There Jules Lefèbre and Benjamin Constant taught him. He won the Academy medal and several honorable mentions.

At twenty-four he became principal of the School of Arts at Bahia, Brazil. In 1896 he returned to Europe and settled again in Paris. In 1898 he moved to London, where he has lived since. The entry names eight of his paintings. It also calls him well known as a portrait painter.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-halhul-7102: Halhul was a city in the hill country of Judah, named in the list of that tribe's towns at Joshua xv. 58. It stood about four miles north of Hebron. A Jewish tradition told by Hottinger makes it the burial-place of Gad, David's seer. The entry identifies it with the modern Ḥalḥul. That is the whole of the short article: a Bible list entry, a distance, a tradition about Gad's grave, and a modern name.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hanina-hananiah: Hanina (Hananiah) II was an amora of the fifth century. He studied in Palestine under Mani II. He rose to discuss halakic questions with his master as a fellow student. He became religious head of Sepphoris, cited as Hanina of Sepphoris. Then Mani also fled persecution at Tiberias for Sepphoris. Hanina resigned the leadership to him. The Rabbis praised that act as nearly without parallel. As persecution spread, he emigrated to Babylonia. There Ashi often sought information from him. His family came too. His daughter married the son of Rabina.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hasdai-hisdai-a: Abu al-Fadl ben Joseph Hasdai was a Jewish convert to Islam who lived at Saragossa in the later eleventh century. A medical writer praised him in grand terms, even calling him a descendant of the prophet Moses. That same source credits him with skill as a poet and a speaker. He was also trained in logic and medicine. Math and the study of the stars are named among his fields. The entry is short and rests on that one Arabic source and a modern note.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hayyon-gedaliah: Gedaliah Hayyon was a Turkish rabbi born at Constantinople in the later seventeenth century. He studied under Alfandari the Younger. He settled in Jerusalem and later traveled as an unpaid messenger for the city of Hebron. Then he went back to Jerusalem. The entry says he was not known as a scholar in the usual sense. He studied the Cabala instead and won a name for rare piety. A namesake scholar of an earlier time may have been his forebear.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hazkarat-nesham:
Hazkarat Neshamot is the memorial service for the dead in the German ritual. It is held after the readings on set days of the year. Those days are the last day of Passover, the second of Pentecost, Shemini Azeret, and the Day of Atonement. Each mourner recites a prayer for a parent's soul and vows alms in that name.

The article prints the core prayers in full. One asks God to bind the soul up in the bundle of life. Another, for martyrs, asks God to recall holy communities that died for His name. The history is traced from old sources. Sephardic practice, with its Hashkabah prayer, is set beside the German form.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-heim-michael-75: Michael Heim, born on Aug. 18, 1852, at Jakosic in Slavonia, was an Austrian jurist. He read law at the University of Vienna from 1871 to 1875. He served as assistant state attorney at Essegg, then as district judge at Brod. In 1898 he was named attorney-general. The entry notes that this was a rare honor for a Jew in Austria. On Aug. 24, 1903, he became first president of the royal tribunal at Mitrovicz. No writings or family facts are given.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hillel-of-erfur: Hillel of Erfurt was a Talmudic authority who lived at Erfurt in the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries. He was a pupil of Meïr ben Baruch Faleri and a contemporary of Shalom of Neustadt. One scholar identifies him with a Hiller named chief rabbi of Thuringia in a document of 1416. The entry recounts his broken vow to end his life in Palestine. Rabbis at Vienna canceled it, fearing loss to Erfurt's school. His divorce bills were later praised as models for spelling names.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hoffer-leopold-:
Leopold Hoffer, born in Budapest in 1842, was a journalist and chess editor. He moved to France about 1866 and began playing chess in Paris. In 1870 he settled in London, where he lived from then on. He grew widely known as a chess writer.

Hoffer helped organize major world tournaments in England, notably Hastings in 1895. From 1879 to 1888 he co-edited a chess monthly with Zukertort, then ran it alone. He also edited chess for two London papers for some years. The entry calls him a leading analyst. He helped found chess groups in Pest and in Britain.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hoshea-god-is-s:
Hoshea was the last of the nineteen kings of Israel and a son of Elah. He took the throne by conspiracy, killing Pekah, and reigned nine years. Assyria reduced him to a tribute-paying vassal. When he stopped the payments and turned to Egypt for help, the Assyrian king seized and jailed him.

Samaria held out through a siege of three years, then fell, and its people went into exile. Two critical sections weigh Assyrian records against the Bible account. They date his rule from 733 to 724 and doubt parts of the Bible chronology. Egypt's promises, one view says, misled him into revolt.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ibn-malkah-juda:
Judah ben Nissim ibn Malkah was a Spanish philosopher of the middle of the fourteenth century, working in Spain or in Africa. He thought as a Neoplatonist. His main work, in Arabic, has three parts. The first introduces the Sefer Yezirah through talks between the author and his soul and between pupil and master.

The second part comments on the Sefer Yezirah itself. The third comments on Pirke Rabbi Eliezer and was finished on February 8, 1365. Ten added chapters treat how man wins perfect bliss. His view of the active intellect matches that of Ibn Gabirol, though no proof shows he knew the Fons Vitae. A key work of his and a prayer commentary are lost.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-indemnity-8102:
Indemnity is the repayment owed to a surety who has been forced to pay his principal's debt. Rabbinic law grants the right, but the surety must prove payment by witnesses; producing the joint bond alone is not enough unless the creditor's receipt is attached. The right against the debtor's land, sold or charged after the bond, passes only if the bond is formally assigned to him.

If the principal dies first, the surety must show the debt was not already paid. If the surety pays a debt the principal had already settled, he has no remedy. A surety who sees the debtor wasting his estate may ask the court for security even before the debt falls due.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-isaac-ben-morde: Isaac ben Mordecai Gershon was a Talmudist of the fifteenth century. He wrote "Shelom Ester," a commentary on the scroll of Esther, printed at Constantinople in the fifteenth century. Steinschneider also assigned three more commentaries to him, on Canticles, on the Pentateuch, and on Esther. The entry corrects that grouping: the first two of those works belong to Isaac Gershon, the press-corrector of Venice. Fuenn, it adds, wrongly treated the two men as one person.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-israelit-des-ne: Der Israelit des Neunzehnten Jahrhunderts was a German periodical of the first half of the nineteenth century. It began as a monthly at Meiningen, running from October, 1839, to October, 1841. Enlarged, it came out weekly at Herzfeld from 1842 to June, 1848; at Frankfort in 1845 it served as the organ of the Reformverein. Mendel Hess edited it, with S. Holdheim joining for its last months. The paper was noted for advanced theology and sharp attacks on Orthodoxy.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jacob-b-eleazar:
Jacob b. Eleazar was a Spanish grammarian of the first third of the thirteenth century. Older scholars put him a century too early, the entry corrects. He was probably born at Toledo, where he used the famed Bible Codex Hilleli. He later went to southern France and wrote one work there at the request of two brothers, Samuel and Ezra.

His chief work, the "Kitab al-Kamil," or "Sefer ha-Shalem," was written in Arabic and is long lost. It joined a grammar and a lexicon, and its name, the Complete Book, was earned, Tanhum Yerushalmi said. Abraham Maimonides cited it, and David Kimhi quotes Jacob's views in about twenty articles of his book of roots. As late as the fourteenth century it was still quoted freely. Complete copies were once reported in Egypt; only fragments may survive, at St. Petersburg.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jahvist-usually:
Jahvist, usually marked with the letter J, is the name modern Bible critics give to a supposed early writer behind parts of the Pentateuch. Critics spot his work where the name Yhwh is used for God, unlike writers who prefer Elohim. The entry says his material was later joined with a kindred source called E.

Passages credited to J include the creation and fall story in Genesis, part of the Flood account, tales of Abraham and Lot, and much of the Joseph story where Judah stands out. The entry classes J with the prophetic school and sets out his teaching and likely time, while noting that scholars differ on exact limits.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-joel-8702:
Joel is the name at the head of the second book of the Minor Prophets, whose heading calls him Joel son of Pethuel. No firm record of the man survives. His book gives no clear picture of him, though readers can tell he was a Judean who lived at Jerusalem in his working days. Some guess from his words that he was a Levite, but the entry calls that a stretch of fancy.

The name means that God is God, and it was a common one. The entry lists twelve more Joels from the Bible, among them Samuel's first-born son, whose bribe-taking as a judge helped push the people to demand a king. A chief of Issachar, a mighty man of David, and a post-exile overseer also bear the name.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-josephs-michael: Michael Josephs, also known as Myer Konigsberg, was an English Hebraist and communal worker born in Königsberg on October 8, 1763. He died in London on February 9, 1849. He left home at thirteen for Berlin, where he met Moses Mendelssohn. In 1781 he went to London and worked in trade while keeping his love of Hebrew letters. In 1818 he helped found the Jews' Free School and taught and examined there himself. As a Hebraist he outdid all his English peers, the entry says.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-judah-ben-lakis: Judah ben Lakish was a tanna of the second century whose name appears only in the Tosefta and the Mekilta. One ruling of his lets a corpse be carried on the Sabbath to save it from a fire. Another holds that a judge who has heard both sides and formed a view may not refuse to judge. A few of his haggadic lines survive. One says Israel had two arks, one holding the broken tablets and one the book of the Torah.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kaposi-hayyim-9:
Ḥayyim Kaposi served as a dayyan, a judge, in Egypt about 1600. He later became known as the "Ba'al ha-Nes," the master of the miracle. The entry tells how he went blind. Suspected of taking bribes, he called on Heaven before the whole congregation. He swore that his sight would return if he was guiltless. As the story is told, his sight came back at once.

Azulai, the entry says, saw Ḥayyim's signatures from both periods. His grave in Cairo is still held in honor. His writings include a commentary on three early law collections. His responsa survive inside the books of other rabbis. Some of them are still in manuscript.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kefar-salama-ca: Kefar-Salama is the place where Nicanor attacked Judas Maccabeus and failed. The fight is told in First Maccabees and in Josephus. The entry says the true site is not sure. Several modern places between Jaffa and Jerusalem have been put forward for it. One guess makes it the Carva Salim named near Ramleh before the Crusades. Another makes it the Kefar Shalem of the Talmud. Neubauer, though, takes that Talmud place to be Salim, where John was baptizing.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-khurilkar-josep: Joseph Daniel Khurilkar was a Bene-Israel soldier in the Anglo-Indian army. The short entry gives his rank as bahadur subahdar. He joined the Sixteenth Regiment of Bengal Native Infantry. He rose step by step through the ranks. He was made jemidar on July 14, 1856. He became subahdar on Jan. 1, 1858, and subahdar major on Jan. 1, 1872. He held the Indian Mutiny medal of 1857. He also held the star of the Order of British India, second class.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kraus-leopold-g: Leopold Gottlieb Kraus, an Austrian physician born at Kolin in Bohemia on Dec. 22, 1824, died in 1901. He studied at Prague, made neurology his special field, and took his degree in 1847. Practice followed at Leipnik and Vienna. His books run from a therapy pocketbook dated 1863 to a work on hygiene dated 1878. They include a dictionary of state medicine issued from 1872 to 1878. His brother Bernard wrote for early Vienna medical journals, the entry adds.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lampon-greek-96: Lampon, an enemy of the Jews who lived at Alexandria in the first century, is named by Philo as a ring leader in the outbreak of the year 38. Governor Flaccus made no move to check that riot under Caligula. Philo names Isidorus and Lampon together as the drivers of the trouble. Both men were later put to death under Claudius. Trial papers in Berlin and Gizeh papyri preserve parts of the case at Rome. The Gizeh text breaks off as the emperor orders the two men led away to death.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lecce-9702: Lecce, a town of southern Italy, held a noted Jewish settlement in the Neapolitan kingdom before the expulsion. Traces reach back to Norman times. Jews there dyed cloth, raised cattle, and lent money until lending was banned in 1471. Badges and bans on land and high callings applied, yet the law shielded them. When the count died in 1463, a mob sacked the ghetto and killed Jews. The king ordered the Jews recalled in 1464. A worse fire attack came on March 21, 1495. Expulsion from the kingdom in 1540 ended the story.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-levi-b-sisi-sis:
Levi bar Sisi was a Palestinian scholar of the late second and early third centuries. He learned under the patriarch Judah I and helped him compile the Mishnah. His rulings, called baraitot, were later gathered in a set known as "Kiddushin de-Be Lewi." Judah spoke of him as an equal.

The entry tells one sharp tale. Judah sent Levi to Simonias as an all-round leader: lecturer, judge, scribe, and teacher in one. Put to the test there, Levi froze and left hard questions unanswered. Called back, he answered each one with ease. His courage, he explained, had failed him before the crowd. The entry also notes that the Gemara seldom gives him the title Rabbi.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-levy-michel-990:
Michel Lévy, a French publisher, was born at Pfalzburg on Dec. 20, 1821. He died in Paris on May 6, 1875. In 1836 he settled in Paris. With his brothers Calman and Nathan he went into publishing. Their firm soon ranked among the top houses in France.

The Lévy list held the core of modern French letters. It printed both Dumas, George Sand, Balzac, Vigny, Lamartine, and Hugo. It also printed Guizot, Renan, and Michelet, and foreign names like Heine and Thackeray. The firm ran famed series for drama and modern books. After Michel's death his brother Calman ran it, and then Calman's three sons.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lion-henri-juli: Henri Julius Lion was a Dutch journalist born on March 23, 1806, at Elberfeld, and he died on Oct. 19, 1869. He served first in the Prussian army and then in the Dutch army. In 1834 he went to India and was discharged as an officer in 1841 at his own request. He then worked in business and used his knowledge of Indian affairs in writing. He founded the Bataviaasch Handelsblad and led Indian journalism. He also pushed for a committee on a railway in Java.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-luzzatti-luigi-:
Luigi Luzzatti, an Italian statesman and economist, is profiled at length in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born at Venice on March 11, 1841, he studied law at Padua and took his degree in 1863. He was lecturing on economics in Venice by age twenty. In 1867 he became a professor at Padua and a government commissioner for the Paris Exposition.

The article follows his long parliamentary career and his economic reforms. He brought the ideas of Schultze-Delitzsch to Italy and backed cooperative associations across the country. He also pushed postal and school savings banks for working people. Luzzatti served as minister of the treasury in two periods during the 1890s. Governments trusted him with delicate trade talks, including the 1902 commercial treaty with France. The entry presents a Jewish economist who helped build modern Italy's finances.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-margolioth-the-:
Margolioth, a Polish family of Talmudic scholars, is traced in a long 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry. Ten contributors worked on the article. The family claims descent from Rashi on one side and from the Shor and Edels families on the other. The first known Margolioth, Samuel, was a judge at Posen about 1550.

The article follows the line through Cracow and Przemysl. Mendel Margolioth, rabbi at Przemysl, had eight sons, all distinguished Talmudists. From that stock came generations of scholars the entry profiles one by one. The most renowned of one branch was Ephraim Solomon of Brody, who died in 1828. Though never a rabbi, his works were accepted as authoritative in the rabbinical world. Other profiles reach a preacher of Kalisch who ended his life in Palestine. The entry admits that many Margolioths cannot be placed in the tree with certainty.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mauthner-ludwig:
Ludwig Mauthner, an Austrian eye specialist, is profiled in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906 by Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman. Born in Prague on April 13, 1840, he took his medical degree at Vienna in 1861, became a lecturer in ophthalmology there in 1864, and in 1869 won a professorship at Innsbruck. He gave that chair up in 1877 and returned to Vienna, where full professorial rank came only in 1894, months before his death on October 20 of that year.

His reputation rests on a shelf of textbooks written across thirty years. The entry lists works on the ophthalmoscope, on the optical errors of the eye, on sympathetic eye diseases, on glaucoma, and repeatedly on the eye muscles and their paralysis. Vienna University honored him after death with a monument in its arcade, erected in 1899.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-melchizedek-kin:
Melchizedek, "king of righteousness," was the priest-king of Salem who blessed Abraham. Isidore Singer and Kaufmann Kohler treat him in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. In Genesis he brings out bread and wine, blesses Abram, and receives tithes. Psalm 110 calls the winning ruler a priest for ever. It adds, "after the order of Melchizedek."

The article defends the tale as old Jerusalem lore, not a late invention. Zedek was an old name of the city. Its first king joined crown and priesthood, like other kings of old, making him a natural type for the psalmist. Later lore then magnified him. Alexandrian Jews prized him as a monotheist before Abraham, and outside Israel, which helped in courting proselytes. Rabbinic and Christian sources set him beside Elijah and the Messiahs, calling him one "without father, without mother, without descent." Philo made him the Logos itself. The entry traces that whole afterlife.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-meron-or-miron-:
Meron, or Miron, is a Galilean hill town. It sits three miles northwest of Safed. Joseph Jacobs and M. Seligsohn survey it from Talmud to pilgrimage in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The rabbis pair it constantly with Giscala. Its ascent was so narrow two men could not walk abreast. Priests lived there. Its people once came to blows with Giscala's people.
