They tracked DNA shifts in triticale lines after the cross. Rearranged and lost stretches showed up in the new plants. The results back the idea that doubling can trim as well as add. That helps explain why plant genomes do not just grow without end after each round of doubling.
plos-pone-0001502:
Tige Rustad and colleagues published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on how the TB germ answers low oxygen. Low oxygen zones in the body had long been tied to the latent, quiet phase of TB. Past work mapped the germ's first reply to low oxygen. The team tracked the longer, lasting reply that follows.

Their data show the germ settles into a steady state tuned to low oxygen. That state may be what lets TB hide for years in a host. Drugs that work on active germs may miss this quiet state. Naming its genes gives drug teams targets for the latent phase.
plos-pone-0001602:
Huan Chen and co-authors published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on a peroxide sensor in a hardy germ. Most germs sense peroxide, a toxic byproduct, with a protein that uses two sulfur atoms as the switch. The germ studied here shrugs off radiation and dryness that kill most kin. Its sensor was found to bear just one such sulfur atom.

Despite the lean build, the sensor still spots peroxide and switches on defense genes. A one atom switch breaks the standard design for this sensor family. The finding may help explain the germ's famed grit. It widens the known range of how cells sense harm.
plos-pone-0001702:
Simone Rossi, Alberto De Capua, Patrizio Pasqualetti, and their co-authors tested whether smells can move the motor system in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Watching actions or hearing action sounds is known to activate the viewer's own motor system across senses. Smell is the oldest sense, and it can steer behavior, yet its link to movement was untested.

Using transcranial magnetic stimulation, which probes motor excitability through the skull, the team measured cross-modal effects of odors on the motor system. They report distinct olfactory effects, per the paper's title. The full text gives the odors used, the stimulation results, and how effects differed by smell type. Results like these widen the picture of how the senses jointly prepare the body to act.
plos-pone-0001802:
Heather Powell, Joanne Smart, Lisa G. Wood, and their co-authors tested a symptom questionnaire in asthma patients in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. The Common Cold Questionnaire, or CCQ, is used to tell who has a viral infection and who does not. Its usefulness in people with acute asthma was unknown, though colds are a top trigger of asthma attacks.

The team assessed whether the CCQ can detect viral infection and monitor recovery during virus-induced asthma exacerbations. The full text gives the patient results, the virus tests, and how well questionnaire scores matched them. A cheap questionnaire that reliably flags viral attacks could steer asthma care and research without waiting for lab results.
plos-pone-0001902:
Sampson Kyere and co-authors probed the shape of a small viral protein part in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The part, called p12, sits inside the Gag building blocks of a mouse leukemia virus. It plays key roles as the virus is built, copies its genes, and slips its DNA into the host cell.

Using nuclear magnetic resonance, a method that maps atomic shape, the team studied p12 joined to its next-door part in Gag. They report that p12 has no fixed fold in that construct; it stays loose and unstructured. A loose part can still be vital, since loose regions often serve as flexible links or binding pads.
plos-pone-0002002:
Zilal Kattan and co-authors studied a DNA repair protein that also shapes breast cancer growth, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The protein, DDB2, helps fix DNA damage by nucleotide excision repair. It also plays roles in normal cells, such as gene control and cell cycle timing. Loss of DDB2 had been tied to a higher risk of tumors.

The team tested what DDB2 does inside breast cancer cells as they grow. If a repair protein also brakes or spurs growth, its loss could drive cancer by two paths at once. Work of this kind refines which tumors might react to drugs that target DNA repair.
plos-pone-0002102:
Thomas Jensen and co-authors split the roles of two forms of an energy enzyme in mouse muscle, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The enzyme, AMPK, is a promising drug target for metabolic disorders, in part because it promotes glucose uptake in skeletal muscle without insulin. It comes in two catalytic forms, alpha one and alpha two, and the alpha two form was clearly required for some uptakes.

As the title states, alpha one activation is required for glucose uptake driven by twitch contraction, but not for uptake driven by hydrogen peroxide. Two forms, two triggers: the split refines which form a drug should hit.
plos-pone-0002202:
Puspha Sinnayah, Erin Jobst, Joseph Rathner, and co-authors asked how cannabis-like drugs drive hunger, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Cannabinoids, the active parts of marijuana, stir appetite, while drugs that block their main receptor, CB1, suppress appetite and aid weight loss. How these effects run through the brain's feeding circuits was unclear.

The team tested whether the melanocortin system, a known appetite control circuit, carries the feeding effect. They report that cannabinoid-driven feeding works independently of that system. The result redraws part of the hunger map and hints that appetite drugs may need to aim at more than one circuit at once.
plos-pone-0002302:
Shanthi Muttukrishna, Sangeeta Suri, Nigel Groome, and co-authors measured growth factors and oxygen inside the early pregnancy sac, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. In the first trimester, a steep oxygen gradient runs between the mother's circulation and the tissues of the gestational sac. That gradient helps steer how the placenta's trophoblast cells behave.

The team asked whether the oxygen level inside the sac shapes the making of TGF beta proteins, signals that control cell growth. They measured both in early human pregnancies. Knowing how oxygen tunes placental signals bears on healthy placenta growth and on problems like miscarriage and pre-eclampsia that begin in these weeks.
plos-pone-0002402:
Work from Burgevin and fellow authors appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline credits Anne Burgevin, Loredana Saveanu, Yohan Kim, and others. Its subject is a Detailed Analysis of the Murine TAP Transporter Substrate Specificity. The transporter linked to antigen processing (TAP) supplies cytosolic peptides into the endoplasmic reticulum for binding to major histocompatibility complex (MHC) class I molecules.

Its specificity therefore influences the repertoire of peptides presented by MHC molecules. Readers get the background first, then the path the team took and the care they took with it. That makes the article a clear record of one research question, the path taken to test it, and the limits the authors faced.
plos-pone-0002502:
In 2008, Loarie and colleagues published a study in the journal PLOS ONE. The byline credits Scott R. Loarie, Benjamin E. Carter, Katharine Hayhoe, and others. Its subject is climate Change and the Future of California's Endemic Flora. The flora of California, a global biodiversity hotspot, includes 2387 endemic plant taxa.

With anticipated climate change, we project that up to 66% will experience >80% reductions in range size within a century. Key terms are set out in context, so a reader new to the field can still follow the work. The result is a compact record of the work, of use to readers who study the same problem or teach it to others.
plos-pone-0002602:
A research team led by Saayman reported its work in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline credits Sheena Saayman, Samantha Barichievy, Alexio Capovilla, and others. Its subject is the Efficacy of Generating Three Independent Anti-HIV-1 siRNAs from a Single U6 RNA Pol III-Expressed Long Hairpin RNA. RNA Interference (RNAi) effectors have been used to inhibit rogue RNAs in mammalian cells.

However, rapidly evolving sequences such as the human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV-1) require multiple targeting approaches to prevent the emergence of escape variants. Readers get the background first, then the path the team took and the care they took with it. As a record, it keeps the focus on facts and method, and lets readers judge the claims for themselves.
plos-pone-0002702:
Hoang Hoa Long led a team whose work appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was native bacterial endophytes promote host growth in a Species-Specific manner; phytohormone manipulations do not result in common growth responses. Authorship is credited in the record to Hoang Hoa Long and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

The abstract begins from a clear premise. All plants in nature harbor a diverse community of endophytic bacteria which can positively affect host plant growth. Its abstract frames the work for later readers, who can judge the full text against the aims stated at the start.
plos-pone-0002802:
Aron J. Fazekas led a team whose work appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was multiple multilocus DNA barcodes from the plastid genome discriminate plant species equally well. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Aron J. Fazekas, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract begins from a clear premise. A universal barcode system for land plants would be a valuable resource, with potential utility in fields as diverse as ecology, floristics. Anyone studying the topic can use the article to see how the authors framed the problem at the time of publication.
plos-pone-0002902:
Perayot Pamonsinlapatham, Réda Hadj-Slimane, Françoise Raynaud and co-authors built a peptide tool against Ras signaling in 2008. RasGAP normally switches Ras off, but it also helps Ras and can block cell death through its SH3 domain. That second role does not depend on its switching job.

The team used a peptide aptamer, a short crafted protein piece, aimed at the RasGAP SH3 domain. In PLOS ONE they report it blocked a RasGAP link to Aurora and drove tumor cell death without using caspases, the usual death enzymes. Cancer researchers get a fresh angle on a well-known pathway.
plos-pone-0003002:
Jung Kyoon Choi, Sohyun Hwang and Young-Joon Kim studied chromatin silencing and stress response in yeast in 2008. Cells balance variety against fidelity by controlling random molecular noise. Epigenetic silencing, switching genes off via chromatin state, plays a critical role when environments change.

The team shows incomplete silencing increases random noise in gene expression in yeast. That noise can be a feature, letting a uniform population hedge bets under stress. Published in PLOS ONE, the study frames silencing as both a stabilizer and a source of useful diversity in genomic responses. Full methods, data, and references appear in the complete article for readers who want more detail.
plos-pone-0003102:
Krishnaraj Rajalingam, Manu Sharma, Christine Lohmann and co-authors studied apoptosis resistance in Chlamydia-infected cells in 2008. Chlamydia are bacteria that live inside host cells and cause a variety of human diseases. Infected cells are protected against many different triggers of apoptosis, planned cell death.

That resistance is thought to be an important immune escape mechanism letting the bacteria persist. Mcl-1 is a key regulator of that resistance, the title reports. Published in PLOS ONE, blocking Mcl-1 might let infected cells die on schedule, a possible treatment angle. Full methods, data, and references appear in the complete article for readers who want more detail.
plos-pone-0003202:
Olyana N. Grod, Amber E. Budden, Tom Tregenza and colleagues survey peer reviewers in ecology and evolution in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Referee traits and their effects on peer review matter because the integrity of the system depends on fair evaluation of merit. In 2006 the team conducted an online survey of 1,334 ecologists and evolutionary biologists.

They report systematic variation in reviewer practice according to country and gender. Readers get data on a process usually hidden behind closed editorial doors. Evidence on reviewer differences can inform fairer review policies, even if it cannot settle every bias claim.
plos-pone-0003302:
Samuel Huber, Jörg Schrader, Gerhard Fritz and colleagues study a kinase needed for regulatory T cell conversion in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. CD4+CD25+ regulatory T cells are important mediators of immune tolerance. A subset can be generated in the periphery by TGF-beta dependent conversion of conventional CD4+CD25- T cells into induced regulatory T cells. In chronic viral infection or malignancy, such induced cells matter greatly.

The title reports that p38 MAP kinase signaling is required for conversion into induced Treg. Readers learn of a specific signaling step behind tolerance formation. Blocking or boosting that step could shift immune balance in autoimmunity or cancer.
plos-pone-0003402:
Karoliina Harkonmäki and co-authors asked how far genes shape early retirement in this 2008 study. They followed about 24,000 Finnish twins for thirty years. Records showed which twins left work early due to disability. Common causes included depression and other major illnesses.

Comparing twin pairs let the team split genetic effects from life experience. Genes did carry part of the risk of disability retirement. The share differed by the medical cause behind the retirement. The findings inform debates on work ability, welfare, and fair support for sick workers. Twin studies remain one of the few ways to split those two forces apart.
plos-pone-0003502:
Nicholas P. Holmes, Charles Spence, and Peter C. Hansen scanned brains during tool use in this 2008 study. Holding a tool merges touch at the hand with sights far away. The brain must link those split sources into one event. They tested attention shifts while people felt vibrations through a simple tool.

Brain imaging showed how attention networks handle that split. Tool use changed which locations drew multisensory attention. The results map part of the neural choreography of tool skill. Such skill sits near the root of human technology. Tools extend the body in the mind as well as in the hand.
plos-pone-0003602:
Kelly B. Wyatt and co-authors studied a mammal die-off on Christmas Island in this 2008 paper. Christmas Island sits in the Indian Ocean. Its native mammals vanished in a historical extinction event. Novel infectious disease can drive declines and even extinction in some animal groups.

For mammals, well-corroborated disease extinctions were still lacking. The team's evidence correlated the island losses with introduced infectious disease. Arriving pathogens, not just habitat loss, may erase a fauna. The case strengthens disease as an extinction force. Island species are most at risk, since they evolved with few germs around.
plos-pone-0003702:
Xiaosi Gu, Xun Liu, Kevin G. Guise, and colleagues published this psychology study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Alexithymia is a trait marked by trouble knowing, handling, or describing one's own feelings. Brain scans have tied it to weaker activity in a region that helps control thought. The authors tested healthy adults.

They compared people high and low in the alexithymic trait on voluntary control tasks. The study probes how a blind spot for one's own emotions relates to steering attention on purpose. It links a personality trait to the mechanics of mental control in everyday life.
plos-pone-0003802:
J. R. Managbanag, Tarynn M. Witten, Danail Bonchev, and colleagues published this aging study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Finding genes that modulate longevity is a major goal of aging research. Such genes could become targets for treatment as well as keys to basic biology. The authors took a network approach.

They applied shortest-path analysis to gene networks, tracing the shortest routes between known aging-related genes. Genes lying on those paths became candidates for affecting lifespan. The network approach offers a new compass for aging research beyond one-gene-at-a-time hunts. The method can be reused for other traits tied to long life.
plos-pone-0003902:
Bindi Thomas, John D. Holland, and Edward O. Minot tracked an elephant by satellite for five years. Their 2008 PLOS ONE article follows an African elephant cow, Loxodonta africana. Tracking ran from September 2003 to August 2008. The cow ranged across Sabi Sand Reserve and Kruger National Park.

GPS records showed her daily movements over the whole period. She was confirmed as part of a group of seven elephants. Long tracks like this reveal how elephants use land across seasons. Park managers can use such maps to plan fences, water, and safe corridors. The article came out in PLOS ONE, an open journal for science and health research.
plos-pone-0004002:
Liliana R. Vitorino, Gabriele Margos, Edward J. Feil, and co-authors mapped a Lyme disease relative's geography in 2008. Borrelia lusitaniae is a tick-borne spirochete of the Old World. It occurs mainly around the Mediterranean Basin. Lizards of the Lacertidae family serve as its reservoir hosts.

Their PLOS ONE article used multilocus sequence typing to sort strains. Fine-scale patterns emerged in where each strain type lives. Host lizards likely shape that patchy distribution. Knowing strain geography helps predict where human exposure may occur. The work appeared in PLOS ONE, with its methods and data open for all to see.
plos-pone-0004102:
Andrew Hollands, Ramy K. Aziz, Rita Kansal, and co-authors studied a natural mutation in strep bacteria in 2008. Group A streptococcus causes diseases from sore throat to severe invasion. Studies noted high SpeB output tracks with less invasive disease. What SpeB does during infection stayed unclear, though.

Their PLOS ONE article uses a clinical strain lacking SpeB expression. A natural mutation in the ropB gene suppressed SpeB in that strain. The same change reduced systemic virulence of M1T1 strep. The result helps untangle a long-standing pattern in strep epidemiology. The full report sits in PLOS ONE, free to read with all its data shown.
plos-pone-0004202:
Camille Martinand-Mari and colleagues published this developmental study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Programmed cell death is one of the clearest signs of how flexible living systems are. It usually sits upstream of major patterning events, such as the shaping of fingers in vertebrates or the facets of the fly eye.

The authors studied non-proliferative epithelia, sheets of cells that no longer divide. They asked how the sheet's topology controls who lives and who dies. Topology here means the pattern of cells and their neighbours. Their work shows that in a quiet tissue, geometry itself can be a fate decision.
plos-pone-0004302:
Shahin Zangenehpour, Asif Ghazanfar, and David Lewkowicz published this primate development study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Knowing a trait's evolutionary origin means knowing how development and ancestry interact. Human infants undergo perceptual narrowing in their first year, losing some ability to match sights and sounds across species.

The team studied infant vervet monkeys, testing heterochrony, shifts in developmental timing, and cross-species intersensory matching. Comparing monkey infants with human infants shows whether narrowing is a human quirk or a primate pattern. Such comparisons anchor big claims about human development in evidence. Monkeys and humans share much early development, so the test is a fair one.
plos-pone-0004402:
Anorexia nervosa is far more often studied in women than in men. Anu Raevuori, Hans Hoek, Ezra Susser, and co-authors measured it in Finnish men. Their 2009 PLOS ONE paper screened male twins born from 1975 to 1979. The men came from the FinnTwin16 birth cohorts. In all, 2,122 men answered a screening questionnaire on lifetime eating disorders.

Men who screened positive, plus their co-twins, got closer study. Eighteen men screened positive in the first pass. Twin data let the authors check shared genes and upbringing. The study gives rare nationwide numbers for male anorexia. It shows the illness in men is uncommon but real. Those figures help correct a strong gender gap in eating-disorder research.
plos-pone-0004502:
Sugar signals and the plant hormone auxin work together to shape roots, show Bhuwaneshwar Mishra, Manjul Singh, Priyanka Aggrawal, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. The plant is Arabidopsis thaliana, a small weed used as a model in labs worldwide. Root growth is highly plastic: roots reshape themselves to match soil conditions.

Sugar signaling was already known to affect roots, and to interact with several plant hormones. Auxin is the hormone that most directly steers root growth and branching. The team studied how glucose and auxin signaling interact in seedlings. Their results help explain how a plant balances its food supply against its growth plan. That balance decides how well crops forage for water and nutrients underground.
plos-pone-0004602:
A hormone best known for fat can tip a small songbird toward raising a second family in one year, show Mare Lohmus and Mats Bjorklund in PLOS ONE in 2009. Organisms face trade-offs in their life-history strategies, such as single or multiple broods within a year. In passerine birds that can breed more than once, the chance of laying a second clutch depends on several factors.

The hormone is leptin, a signal of body fat stores. In a field experiment, the team tested its effect on the breeding decision. If a fat signal persuades a bird that times are good, it should breed again. Showing a hormone steering a whole life-history choice in wild birds links physiology to evolution in a direct way.
plos-pone-0004702:
Anton Moll and colleagues found a way to read single gene versions from standard chip data, in PLOS ONE in 2009. One gene can make several message versions by cutting and joining parts in unlike ways. Each version can do a distinct job in the cell, so lumping them hides real change.

Common gene chips measure a gene as a whole with sets of small probes. The team used the probe layout to split signal by version. That lets old chip data yield finer results without new lab work. Doctors and researchers can spot version shifts tied to disease.
plos-pone-0004802:
Han Si and colleagues showed that human and mouse kidneys show gender and species specific gene expression after injury, in PLOS ONE in 2009. End stage renal disease incidence is approximately fifty percent higher in men than women. To understand the molecular basis of this disparity, the team examined sex specific expression patterns in control, and Diseased kidney samples from both species using transcript profiling.

Patterns differed by sex and did not fully match between species. That cautions against direct transfer of mouse findings to patients. Sex aware analysis is needed in kidney research. The data provide a reference for such work.
plos-pone-0004902:
Mireille St-Onge and colleagues studied impact of anti inflammatory agents on gene output in stimulated human neutrophils, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Adenosine, prostaglandin E2, or increased cyclic AMP each elicit potent anti inflammatory events in neutrophils, inhibiting phagocytosis, superoxide production, adhesion, and cytokine release. Endogenous resolution pathways were unraveled by profiling how these agents reprogram gene output during active swelling.

Resolution is active gene switching, not passive fading. Endogenous molecules orchestrate the switch. Pro resolution drugs could mimic these programs. Chronic swelling might reflect failed resolution. The study gives researchers concrete leads that later work can verify and extend. The team also set out clear next steps for work in this field. More tests with more samples will help show how strong the effect is.
plos-pone-0005002:
Preventive drugs can stop Pneumocystis pneumonia before it starts. Yet it remains the most common serious infection in people with HIV. James Heffelfinger and colleagues asked why prevention fails. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. They studied nonadherence to primary prophylaxis. The data came from United States surveillance records for 2000 to 2004.

The team identified factors linked to skipping the preventive drugs. Those factors point to gaps in care. Patients at highest risk are not always reached. The findings guide efforts to keep at-risk patients on treatment. Closing those gaps could prevent many cases of a dangerous but preventable disease.
plos-pone-0005102:
Wildfire depends on climate, vegetation and people. Climate change will redraw its map. Meg Krawchuk and colleagues modeled that future in PLOS ONE in 2009. They built a global pyrogeography, a geography of fire. Current fire distribution was their starting point. Future climate scenarios drove the forecast.

The model shows where fires burn now. It also shows where they will burn in a warmer world. Fire zones shift and grow in many regions. Some regions may see less fire instead. Planners gain a map of tomorrow's fire country. Land management can prepare for the shift. The study was a first step, as the authors frame it. Later work can refine the forecast.
plos-pone-0005202:
Stress can damage plant DNA, and plants answer with repair systems that include gene swapping. Some reports claimed that stressed plants pass a heightened repair state to their offspring. Pecinka and colleagues tested that claim in Arabidopsis, the standard lab plant, in PLOS ONE in 2009.

Their title gives the verdict: transgenerational stress memory is not a general response in this species. Offspring did not broadly inherit the stressed state of their parents. Careful negative findings like this one prune ideas that sound appealing but do not hold up across conditions.
plos-pone-0005302:
Lung cancer risk grows with age and smoking, and family history and gene variants add to it. Young and colleagues built a susceptibility model combining those factors, reported in PLOS ONE in 2009. Their study compared healthy smokers with lung cancer cases.

Genetic markers tied to the disease joined age and family history in the model. A combined score can sort smokers into risk groups better than smoking history alone. That sorting could focus screening and quitting support on the smokers who need it most. No one test can say who will get lung cancer, but a score that joins age. Kin, and genes can at least pull the highest-risk group out of a large crowd.
plos-pone-0005402:
Calmodulin is a calcium sensor found in all cells, and it grips a huge range of target proteins. One target is calcineurin A, a phosphatase involved in immune and brain signaling. Majava and Kursula solved structures of their complex in PLOS ONE in 2009.

The complex showed domain swapping, where partners exchange matching sections. It also appeared in different oligomeric states, groupings of different sizes. Flexible recognition like this helps explain how one small sensor can manage so many different partners. Grip by swap is a strange trick, yet it may let this sensor hold a target in a firm clamp. And such clamps are just what drug teams seek when they build a blocker.
plos-pone-0005502:
Bernhard Egger and co-authors weighed a dispute over tiny worms in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Acoels are small, simple marine worms with no gut cavity. They were long classed as flatworms, but no clear shared traits unite the flatworm groups.

Gene-based family trees point another way, hinting that acoels split off very early from other animals. The authors reviewed the traits and the gene evidence side by side. Where acoels belong matters because, as early branches, they can show what the first animals with two sides looked like. The dispute also shows how new gene tools can upset long-settled groupings in the animal family tree.
plos-pone-0005602:
Helen Ayles and co-authors measured tuberculosis and HIV in two Zambian communities in a 2009 PLOS ONE study. Global targets call for tuberculosis rates to fall by half over a set period. Few surveys had actually counted cases in countries hit hard by both diseases.

The team screened whole communities for tuberculosis, HIV, and breathing symptoms. Real counts show how much disease clinics miss and where HIV fuels tuberculosis. Surveys like this tell control programs whether their plans stand a chance of meeting the targets. Community counts are costly to run, which is why so few exist despite the need for them.
plos-pone-0005702:
Karin Knieke and colleagues tracked how a brake molecule on T cells also shapes where those cells travel, in a 2009 study. The molecule, CD152 or CTLA-4, is known mostly for damping T cell action. Migration matters too: T cells must reach lymph organs and sites of attack to do their job.

The team tested movement both in lab dishes and in living animals. They found CD152 guides how antigen-experienced T cells move. That dual role, brake and guide, changes how doctors might use drugs that target CTLA-4. Such drugs are now central in cancer care, so the detail counts.
plos-pone-0005802:
Peter DeScioli and Robert Kurzban proposed in 2009 that human friendship evolved, in part, as a way to line up allies. Friends are not just pleasant company; they are people who might take your side. The alliance hypothesis says the mind builds support groups ahead of possible conflicts.

That view predicts quirks in how people rank, keep, and drop friends. Closeness should track how useful an ally would be, and how likely they are to choose you over rivals. The paper lays out the logic and its tests. It reframes friendship as strategy as well as warmth, without denying either.
plos-pone-0005902:
David Vader and co-authors measured in 2009 how stretching a collagen gel lines its fibers up. Collagen is the main scaffold protein in animal tissues and in lab-grown tissue models. Its versatility comes partly from its ability to remodel under force.

Strain induced alignment in the gels, turning a random mesh into ordered fibers. Aligned collagen can steer cell growth, as in tendons and healing wounds. Tissue engineers need that control to build replacements that bear load correctly. The study quantifies how much strain gives how much order, a practical recipe.
plos-pone-0006002:
Stress can push a gamble up or down, and not the same way for everyone. Nichole Lighthall, Mara Mather and Marissa Gorlick tested stress and risk in 2009 using a balloon game, where players pump a virtual balloon for money and risk popping it. Their PLOS ONE study compares men and women after an acute stress.

The title states the result: stress widened the sex gap in risk seeking on the task. A difference that grows under pressure matters wherever hard choices are made under strain. The work adds a clear lab finding to the debate on sex, stress and choice, and it warns against treating stressed decision-makers as one uniform group.
plos-pone-0006102:
Attention requires the brain to quiet its idle mode while it works. Dardo Tomasi, Nora Volkow, Ruiliang Wang and colleagues linked that quieting to dopamine pumps in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper measures dopamine transporters in the striatum, the proteins that clear dopamine away, and compares their levels with deactivation of the default mode network during visuospatial attention tasks.

Higher transporter levels tracked stronger quieting of the idle network, the title reports. The link gives dopamine a concrete part in focus: clearing the signal helps the brain leave rest mode. Findings of this kind inform work on attention disorders, where both dopamine drugs and network quieting are already in play.
plos-pone-0006202:
Proteins that hold sister chromosomes together were first known as chromosome glue. Cheri Schaaf and colleagues show that these cohesion proteins also steer genes in the fruit fly, in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. They focus on two gene groups: Enhancer of split and the invected-engrailed group.

Cohesion proteins favour active genes, yet how they control gene activity was unknown. The study maps their effects on the two fly gene groups in detail. Gene control emerges as a second job for the chromosome glue. That dual role may help explain disorders where cohesion fails. It also links chromosome handling to everyday gene switching.
plos-pone-0006302:
A protein that drives cell growth can be flipped to drive cell death by removing one tag. David Butler and colleagues studied Id2, a regulator of cell division, in muscle precursor cells in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Id2 normally promotes proliferation, and its front end carries a site where an enzyme adds a phosphate tag.

Without that phosphate, Id2 became growth suppressive and pushed dividing myoblasts toward programmed death. One small chemical tag thus decides the protein's whole effect. The switch matters for muscle development and repair. It may also matter in cancers where Id2 runs high.
plos-pone-0006402:
In April 2009, a novel swine-origin influenza virus emerged in patients from Mexico and the United States. Carl Kingsford, Niranjan Nagarajan, and Steven Salzberg compared its genome with earlier isolates in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Within a very short time the H1N1 strain spread across the world.

The new virus resembles previous influenza isolates in key respects, per the title. Resemblance to known strains informs vaccine strain choices and risk judgements. Rapid genomic comparison was a hallmark of the 2009 pandemic response. The paper shows bioinformatics keeping pace with an unfolding outbreak.
plos-pone-0006502:
Lei Zhang, Yu-Fang Pei, Jian Li, and colleagues improved genome-wide study methods in PLOS ONE in 2009. Genome-wide association studies were becoming more popular for finding disease genes. To improve statistical power, researchers can combine data from families and from unrelated samples. Each design has strengths, but mixing them is tricky.

The authors present univariate and multivariate scans that use both kinds of data together. Methods that squeeze more power from existing data find more real signals. They also cut the need for ever larger samples. The paper is a tools contribution for geneticists planning association studies.
plos-pone-0006602:
Brankica Mravinac and co-authors mapped chemical marks at the center of the human X chromosome in PLOS ONE in 2009. Centromeres are the parts of chromosomes that guide their split in cell division. The X centromere is made of long arrays of a repeat DNA called alpha satellite. Histones are the proteins that wrap DNA, and they carry chemical marks that change by place.

The team charted histone marks across the X centromere region in fine detail. Those marks help define where the centromere works when a cell divides. If they are wrong, chromosomes can split in the wrong way. The map is a base map for work on chromosome stability and disease.
plos-pone-0006702:
Ilya Golovaty and colleagues surveyed trachoma risk in an Ethiopian district in PLOS ONE in 2009. Trachoma is an eye infection that can lead to blindness. The study took place in Ankober, Ethiopia, during July of 2007. It was a cross-sectional, community-based survey. More than five hundred children aged one to nine took part.

The children came from over two hundred households. Examiners checked each child for active trachoma. The team also recorded water access, latrine facilities, and other risk factors. Linking home conditions to infection shows where prevention can bite. Clean water and sanitation are known levers against trachoma. Local numbers like these help health workers aim those levers well.
plos-pone-0006802:
Robert I. McDonald and colleagues weighed land costs of American energy policy in PLOS ONE in 2009. Climate concern pushed the United States to consider cap-and-trade. New energy development needs land, sometimes lots of it. The authors illustrated land-use impacts on natural habitat. Different policies create very different energy mixes.

They estimated total new land area needed under each path. Energy sprawl means development spreading across wide habitat. Energy efficiency shrinks the footprint by cutting demand. Comparing footprints shows climate policy is also habitat policy. The analysis helps lawmakers see the land price of each option before choosing.
plos-pone-0006902:
Seiki Haraguchi and Akira Nakagawara simplified genetic screening of a cancer model mouse in PLOS ONE in 2009. The TH-MYCN mouse is the most widely used model of neuroblastoma. A human MYCN oncogene is targeted to developing nerve cells. A rat promoter drives its expression. Breeding and checking these mice is routine but slow work.

Homozygous transgenic mice, carrying the gene on both chromosomes, are especially important. The authors' simple PCR method speeds genotype analysis. Faster genotyping means colonies can be managed with fewer wasted animals. Reliable models of childhood cancer depend on such practical improvements. The method serves any laboratory maintaining this neuroblastoma line.
plos-pone-0007002:
Mark Welch, Sridhar Govindarajan, Jon Ness, and colleagues studied synthetic gene design in PLOS ONE in 2009. Many protein drugs and research tools are made in foreign host cells. Synthetic genes are increasingly the starting point for that production. Their sequence is easier to obtain than the physical gene itself.

Working in E. coli, the team varied design choices in synthetic genes. They measured which parameters control how strongly the genes express. Clear design rules help engineers get more protein from each construct. That lowers costs for medicines, reagents, and molecular tools built in bacteria.
plos-pone-0007102:
Aaron DeWard, Kellie Leali, Richard West, and colleagues studied a blood disorder in mice in PLOS ONE in 2009. Myelodysplastic syndrome, or MDS, makes bone marrow produce blood poorly. Loss of part of chromosome 5 is common in the disease. One candidate guardian gene there builds a formin protein, mDia1.

Mice lacking mDia1 show an MDS-like illness. Removing a second gene, RhoB, made that illness worse. The double loss sharpens the picture of how 5q genes protect marrow. It also gives researchers a stronger mouse model for testing MDS treatments. Together, the two losses give readers a clearer genetic account of the syndrome.
plos-pone-0007202:
Helena Hernández, Olga V. Makarova, Evgeny M. Makarov, and colleagues studied the human spliceosome in PLOS ONE in 2009. The spliceosome joins gene pieces called exons together, often in alternative arrangements. Its U1 particle is essential and contains RNA plus ten proteins in humans.

The authors examine different forms of one protein, U1-70k. They show how these isoforms control how the U1 particle changes during splicing. Their work adds useful detail to a basic process that shapes most human proteins, and errors in that process underlie many human diseases today.
plos-pone-0007302:
Seth Owusu-Agyei, Daniel Ansong, Kwaku Asante, and colleagues ran a randomized malaria vaccine trial in Ghanaian children in 2009. The RTS,S vaccine was a leading malaria candidate. In endemic African countries it would be delivered through the World Health Organization immunization program for young children.

The authors test two vaccine formulations with different schedules. The trial serves as an age de-escalation and schedule selection step. They assess safety and immune responses in Ghanaian children. Their PLOS ONE results helped choose schedules for larger trials of this first malaria vaccine candidate.
plos-pone-0007402:
Nicola Canessa, Matteo Motterlini, Cinzia Di Dio, and colleagues scanned brains while people judged others' regret in 2009. Earlier studies showed understanding others' basic emotions uses a resonant mechanism. The observer's brain reactivates areas linked to those same experiences, allowing shared feeling without direct experience of the event itself.

The authors ask whether that mechanism extends to regret, a complex social emotion. They use functional MRI during regret judgments. Their PLOS ONE study investigates how the brain understands regret felt by another person. The answer informs theories of empathy, which matter for social behavior and its disorders.
plos-pone-0007502:
Vijaya Ramachandran and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on pancreatic cancer and a growth signal called adrenomedullin. Pancreatic tumors produce large amounts of this signal. It stimulates the cancer cells, raising growth and spread. The team examined the receptor that receives the signal, ADMR. They looked at tumor cells and at the supporting cells around the tumor as well.

ADMR proved to mediate the signal's effects on both fronts. Cancer cells respond through it, and so do cells of the tumor's microenvironment. Blocking that one doorway could therefore starve the tumor's whole growth network. Pancreatic cancer badly needs new points of attack. A shared receptor on tumor and support tissue is an efficient one. The study gives drug developers a defined target to test.
plos-pone-0007602:
David Katz and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on involving men in HIV testing during pregnancy. When male partners join antenatal counseling and testing, uptake of steps that protect babies rises. Yet men rarely attend. Working in a resource-limited setting, the team asked men directly for their views. The goal was practical: find methods that would actually bring fathers in.

Men's answers pointed to concrete barriers and workable invitations. Clinics learned what times, messages, and formats men would accept. That kind of listening turns a known good idea into an achievable one. Mother-to-child transmission can be cut sharply when both parents engage. The study treats men as partners in prevention rather than as obstacles. Its lessons apply wherever antenatal programs struggle to reach fathers.
plos-pone-0007702:
Avelin Aghokeng and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It examines HIV testing in Cameroon, where wider access to treatment depends on correct diagnosis. The country carries both major forms of the virus, group M and group O.

The team checked the HIV tests and testing plans then in use. They found that some infections, in particular group O, were missed or misread. A wrong result can deny a patient treatment or give false reassurance. The authors argue that better test choices are key to fair access to HIV care in Cameroon.
plos-pone-0007802:
Rui-Wu Wang and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It examines the partnership between fig trees and fig wasps. Wasps pollinate the figs, but they also lay eggs in the flowers. Their larvae gall and eat some of the seeds.

The tree gains because wasp offspring carry its pollen away. It loses if wasps take too many seeds. The authors show that wasp competition and high temperatures curb wasp virulence. That restraint keeps the exchange from tipping over. The work explains how this famous mutualism stays stable over time.
plos-pone-0007902:
Maria Cerezo and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It checks the stability of mitochondrial DNA in a slow-moving leukemia. Chronic lymphocytic leukemia builds up lymphocytes in blood, marrow and lymph tissue. Earlier findings suggested mitochondrial DNA might play an important role in the disease.

Mitochondrial DNA often mutates in other cancers, so change was expected. The team analyzed its control region in patients. Against expectation, they found high stability in this leukemia. A stable mitochondrial genome is itself a clue. It suggests this cancer's energy machinery follows different rules from many tumors.
plos-pone-0008002:
Rachana Agarwal and colleagues studied a cell glue protein lost in stomach cancer, in PLOS ONE in 2009. The protein, claudin-11, helps seal the tight joins between cells. Sealed joins keep tissue in order; loose joins let cells wander.

In gastric cancer cells, the gene for this protein was silenced, and the cells pushed into new territory more readily. Loss of glue thus doubles as loss of a leash. The finding suggests that restoring the protein, or the paths it guards, might restrain this cancer's spread. Such silencing is common in tumors that learn to break free of their tissue.
plos-pone-0008102:
Peter McCormick and colleagues traced a stuck-on immune receptor in a rare disease in PLOS ONE in 2009. WHIM syndrome leaves people prone to warts and infections. Its cause is a cut tail on the receptor CXCR4, which guides immune cells around the body.

A healthy receptor calls in two proteins that shut it off and pull it inside the cell. The cut receptor failed to call them, so it stayed loud on the surface. That stuck signal explains much of the cells' odd behavior in WHIM, and names the shutoff crew as a treatment clue.
plos-pone-0008202:
Simone Wüst and colleagues tested a new steroid-like drug in mice in a PLOS ONE study from 2009. The drug targets the glucocorticoid receptor, a switch for inflammation. Classic steroids help many disorders but cause harsh side effects. A dissociating ligand aims to keep the benefit while avoiding the harm. That split rests on two modes of receptor action.

The team challenged that hope in a mouse model of multiple sclerosis. They measured both healing effects and adverse effects of the ligand. The results test whether benefit and harm can truly be separated. The answer matters for safer anti-inflammatory drugs.
plos-pone-0008302:
Uwe Jerke and colleagues studied a transcription factor in blood cells in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Stat proteins carry signals from outside the cell to its genes. They cross into the nucleus through the nuclear pore complex. That complex acts as a selective filter for protein import. When monocytes mature, Stat1 must reach the nucleus to work.

The team found the protein nucleolin helps move Stat1 into the nucleus. This translocation happened upon monocyte differentiation. A dedicated carrier for a key signal protein is notable. It adds detail to how immune cells switch on their mature programs.
plos-pone-0008402:
Natalia V. Strunnikova and colleagues studied an inherited eye disease in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Choroideremia is a progressive X-linked disorder that destroys the retina. Mutations in the CHM gene cause it, disabling a protein called REP-1. REP-1 escorts Rab proteins through a chemical step called prenylation. Without that step, certain Rabs are under-prenylated and transport inside cells falters.

The team studied fibroblasts and monocytes from choroideremia patients. Loss of REP-1 function affected intracellular transport in those cells. Tracing that defect explains how the mutation blinds patients. It may also reveal treatment points.
plos-pone-0008502:
Ozlem Equils and co-authors build a computer model of preterm labor in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Preterm labor threatens babies born too early. Enough lab and animal data now exist to model the womb muscle in labor. The muscle, called the myometrium, contracts to deliver a baby. The model lets the team test disease paths in silico, meaning in a computer.

They simulate treatment with progesterone, a hormone that can calm the womb. They also simulate a Cox2 inhibitor, a drug that blocks inflammation signals. The model predicts how each drug might delay labor. Such trials in a computer can guide real clinical studies.
plos-pone-0008602:
Norbert Babai and co-authors study calcium channels in lab cells in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. L-type calcium currents are influenced by chloride levels outside cells. But the sites where anions act had not been identified. The team express CaV1.2 channels in HEK293 cells. Those channels are the main L-type form in heart and brain. Replacing external chloride strongly inhibits the channel currents in their tests.

They map anion-sensitive regions of the CaV1.2 channel. Those regions explain how chloride tunes channel activity. Calcium channels control heartbeat, hormone release, and nerve signals. Knowing their anion sites may matter for drugs that target them.
plos-pone-0008702:
Eiron Cudaback, William Marrs, Thomas Moeller, and colleagues asked how receptor counts shape a drug effect. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study used astrocytoma cells, a kind of brain tumor. Cannabis compounds can push such tumor cells to die. Two docking sites, CB1 and CB2, catch those compounds. Which site does the work was unsettled.

The researchers built tumor cell lines with set amounts of each receptor. They then dosed the cells and watched for self-destruction, called apoptosis. The balance of CB1 and CB2 decided how strong the killing was. Tumor tests may need receptor counts before cannabis-based treatment makes sense.
plos-pone-0008802:
Irene Lurkin, Robert Stoehr, Carolyn Hurst, and colleagues built a fast mutation test for cancer care. Their assay study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Some advanced colorectal cancers resist drugs aimed at a growth receptor. Resistance follows mutations in genes like KRAS, BRAF, and PIK3CA. Testing each mutation separately wastes tissue and time. Clinics needed one combined check.

Their two multiplex assays read twenty-two mutation sites at once. Four genes are covered in the same workflow. Validation showed the combined test catches the key changes reliably. Faster genotyping helps oncologists skip drugs that cannot work for a patient.
plos-pone-0008902:
Catherine Hyams, Jerry Tam, Jeremy Brown, and colleagues tested whether HIV weakens a germ-tagging defense. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Streptococcus pneumoniae causes pneumonia and meningitis, often in HIV patients. The complement system tags germs so immune cells can grab them. Tags called C3b and iC3b are central to that marking. The team suspected HIV patients might tag pneumococcus poorly, perhaps through low antibody levels.

Tagging on the germ proved just as strong in HIV-positive samples. The hypothesis failed its direct test. Pneumonia risk in HIV must come from other breaks in defense. A clean negative result redirects research to likelier causes.
plos-pone-0009002:
Anup Sharma and co-authors linked one altered protein to the clutter found in several brain diseases, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Diseases like Alzheimer's and Parkinson's share some features despite their differences. Clumps called inclusions build up in nerve cells, synapses fail early, and certain neurons die. Few molecules had been tied to all of those shared features.

The team found a phosphorus-tagged form of the protein Elk-1 inside the inclusions. This form appears toxic and turns up across multiple neurodegenerative diseases. One molecule linking clumps and neuron loss gives researchers a common thread. Following it could reveal shared drug targets for diseases usually studied apart.
plos-pone-0009102:
Martijn Weisfelt and co-authors charted meningitis cases in patients with alcohol problems, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Heavy drinking leaves people open to infections, above all pneumonia of the lungs. Meningitis, infection of the membranes around the brain and cord, is another threat. The cases studied were caught outside hospitals, in daily life.

The team set these patients' cases beside those of adults who did not drink heavily. Symptoms, germs, and outcomes differed between the two groups. The drinking group often arrived sicker and fared worse in the end. A clear chart of these patterns helps doctors spot the disease early in this group.
plos-pone-0009302:
Rex Jung and co-authors published this lupus brain study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Lupus is an autoimmune disease that attacks many organs. Some patients develop central nervous system involvement, classed as neuropsychiatric lupus. That form can bring seizures, psychosis, and thinking problems, and it is hard to measure.

The team used brain imaging to compare patients with this neuropsychiatric form. They measured the thickness of the cortex and the volume of deep gray matter. Both were reduced in these patients. Objective brain measures like these could help doctors recognize and track a disease that otherwise hides behind varied symptoms.
plos-pone-0009402:
Feng Ding and co-authors published this mouse development study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Babies with Prader-Willi syndrome feed poorly at first. Later, the same children develop an uncontrolled appetite and obesity. The switch suggests the brain's appetite center, the hypothalamus, is set wrongly from birth.

The team modeled early deprivation in newborn mice. They profiled gene activity in the hypothalamus as the pups developed. The profiles show how early hardship rewrites appetite genes over time. That record may explain how a feeding problem in infancy becomes overeating later in life.
plos-pone-0009502:
Elham Schokraie and co-authors cataloged the proteins of a tardigrade in PLOS ONE in 2010. Tardigrades are tiny animals that can dry out fully and revive later. The species studied, Milnesium tardigradum, is a common model for that feat. No one had yet listed its full set of proteins. The team used large scale protein analysis to build that list.

The catalog shows which proteins the animal makes in its normal, hydrated state. It gives a base line for studies of the dried state. Comparing the two states should reveal the tools of extreme survival. Such tools could one day inspire ways to protect cells and tissues from drying.
plos-pone-0009602:
Li Ye and co-authors studied immune failure in hepatitis C patients who use heroin in PLOS ONE in 2010. A liver rich cell group, CD56 positive T cells, helps fight viruses. Interferon gamma is one of their main weapons. Its response depends on a signal from interleukin-12. The team compared these cells in heroin users with and without hepatitis C.

SOCS-3 and PIAS-3, two proteins that brake immune signals, were raised in the patients' cells. With the brakes up, the interferon gamma response to interleukin-12 was blunted. The study maps a specific failure in a group at high risk. Releasing those brakes could be a way to restore antiviral defense.
plos-pone-0009702:
Tuberculosis and HIV often strike the same patients, yet many TB patients never get an HIV test. Animut Ayenew and colleagues asked what predicts testing among TB patients in northwest Ethiopia. Their case-control study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Testing matters because care for one infection affects the other.

The team compared patients who took an HIV test with those who did not. Differences between the groups pointed to traits and settings linked with testing. Knowing who gets missed helps health workers close the gap. Closing it matters because treating both infections together saves lives.
plos-pone-0009802:
Dario I Carrasco and colleagues ask, in a 2010 PLOS ONE article, whether muscle fibers help drive nerve ending damage in a mouse form of motor neuron disease. In these SOD1 G93A mice, a faulty protein is made in many cells, and nerve endings die back early.

The team swapped leg muscles between normal mice and the diseased strain, then checked nerve-muscle junctions two months later. Diseased muscle did not harm nerves in normal mice, and healthy muscle did not save nerves in diseased mice. Damage, they conclude, does not need the faulty protein in muscle alone. Nerve endings, nerve fibers, and their Schwann support cells together may be enough.
plos-pone-0009902:
A gene that digests tissue scaffolding is itself controlled differently by each DNA variant. Veronika Souslova and colleagues traced that allele-specific control in a 2010 PLOS ONE study. The gene makes matrix metalloproteinase-3, an enzyme tied to arthritis and healing.

Allele-specific regulation means one copy of a gene behaves differently from its twin copy. The control came from NF-kappa-B, a transcription factor that switches genes on during inflammation. Small DNA differences changed how strongly that factor acted. Such details explain why the same gene can raise risk in one person and not another.
plos-pone-0010002:
The authors were Feng Wang, Ruixue Zhang, Xiaomeng Wu, and others. Their 2010 study looked at gene control. It asked how low oxygen switches on the erythropoietin gene. That gene makes a hormone that tells the body to build more red blood cells. In the liver cell line they used, a factor called HIF-2 alpha drives most of that switch.

The team tested helper proteins called coactivators, including p300, CBP, and the p160 family. They asked whether these helpers boost the gene's response when oxygen falls and cells need more red blood cells. Knowing the full cast of helpers can guide drugs for anemia and other low-oxygen states.
plos-pone-0010102:
Michele A Gaston leads a 2010 PLOS ONE study of the critically endangered Houston toad and its breeding ponds. Frogs that breed in groups may do worse when too few gather, a pattern called an Allee effect. More suitable ponds could, in theory, spread callers too thin.

The team related yearly chorus size, the number of calling males at a pond, to signs of successful breeding. Ponds with breeding evidence had clearly larger choruses, and chorus size alone best predicted success. Calling counts by themselves, they warn, are a poor sign of a stable population. Wetland plans for such species should guard against thinning out breeding gatherings.
plos-pone-0010202:
Piwen Wang, Susanne Henning, and David Heber warned about a lab test flaw in 2010. Green tea compounds, called polyphenols, can slow cancer cell growth in dishes. One compound, EGCG, is the most studied of them. Published studies, though, report a wide range of doses needed to halve cell growth in culture.

The team showed that two common assays, MTT and MTS, have limits with these compounds. The tests themselves can distort the readings for green tea polyphenols. Their PLOS ONE warning helps explain the scattered results and pushes labs to check tea findings with other methods.
plos-pone-0010302:
Karen L Posey is first author on a 2010 PLOS ONE study of a gene-silencing treatment for two bone growth disorders. Faults in a cartilage protein, COMP, make the protein pile up inside cartilage cells, killing them and stunting growth. Mice lacking COMP entirely grow nearly normally, hinting that lowering it could help.

The team tested small RNA pieces designed to cut COMP messages. One piece slashed the message sharply, and its effect lasted up to ten weeks. Treated cells showed less internal stress and less pile-up of other cartilage proteins dragged in with COMP. The work is a proof of principle for a therapy based on lowering COMP.
plos-pone-0010402:
J. Marcus Schartau, Ronald Kröger and Bodil Sjögreen studied a fish eye that retunes itself twice a day, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The cichlid fish Aequidens pulcher lives where light changes fast at dawn and dusk. Its lens changes optical power at those times to match. At dusk, the outer lens gains focusing strength. The team asked what chemical signal sets off that change.

Dopamine, a common brain and eye messenger, proved able to trigger the shift. Adding it reproduced the dusk change in lens optics. A daily chemical clock in the eye thus fine-tunes vision. That is a neat solution for animals active in dim, changing light. The study connects a familiar messenger to a precise optical trick.
plos-pone-0010502:
Sandra Knapp described four new vining nightshade species from tropical American mountains in PLOS ONE in 2010. The genus Solanum holds about fifteen hundred species, including potato and tomato relatives. Its greatest diversity lies in the New World tropics. Knapp focused on the Dulcamaroid group, mostly climbing species. Field and herbarium work revealed four species new to science.

Each new species got a formal description, name, and placement in the group. Mountain habitats in the tropics are rich and threatened, so cataloguing them is urgent. New species descriptions are the bedrock on which ecology and conservation stand. Knapp is a leading authority on this genus. Her paper adds four vines to the known tree of life.
plos-pone-0010602:
Muammar Kabir and colleagues measured heart and breathing rhythms in sleep apnea, in PLOS ONE in 2010. In healthy sleep, heartbeat and breathing fall into brief stretches of lockstep. People with obstructive sleep apnea stop breathing many times each night.

Overnight recordings showed weaker lockstep in apnea patients than in healthy sleepers. The two rhythms drifted apart more often and for longer. The authors measured that loss carefully with a phase-coupling score. A simple score like this could one day help grade apnea severity from a standard overnight sleep study.
plos-pone-0010702:
Linda Björkhem-Bergman and colleagues pooled studies on statin use during bacterial infection, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Statins are best known for lowering cholesterol. Several single studies had hinted that patients already taking statins survived severe infections more often, possibly because the drugs also calm inflammation.

The review combined results from many hospitals and patient groups. Taken together, statin treatment was linked with lower death rates during infection. The studies were not trials, so sicker or healthier patients may have skewed the pool. Still, the signal was strong enough to justify proper trials of a cheap, widely stocked drug.
plos-pone-0010802:
Michaela Norum and colleagues studied skin building in fruit fly larvae, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Fly skin cells lay down a layered outer shell, the cuticle, on their outward face. Building it takes heavy, one-way shipping of materials to that face. The shipping route runs through membrane carriers sorted by a system called COPII.

When COPII shipping faltered, cells lost their sense of which face was outward. Cuticle layers came out thin and disordered. Shipping and polarity thus hold each other up in a loop. The loop is a general lesson in how surface tissues in any animal keep their inside-outside order while growing.
plos-pone-0010902:
Aaron Marley and Mark von Zastrow published this cell study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Changes in the DISC1 gene are strongly tied to schizophrenia and other major mental illnesses, yet what the protein actually does inside cells was murky. The authors found it working at the primary cilium, a tiny antenna-like structure that most cells carry.

A tagged version of the protein gathered near the cilium's base in mouse cells and rat brain neurons. When the team dialed the protein down, far fewer cells grew a cilium at all. They also showed that certain dopamine receptors, the D1, D2, and D5 types, concentrate on the cilium's surface, while their D3 and D4 cousins stay off it. Marley and von Zastrow link a psychiatric risk gene to the cell's antenna, where dopamine signals may be received.
plos-pone-0011002:
Michael Boettcher, Frank Kischkel and Jörg Hoheisel published this cancer epigenetics study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Cancers that survive chemotherapy are a leading cause of treatment failure, and abnormal DNA methylation, chemical silencing tags on genes, is increasingly blamed for helping tumors resist drugs. The authors profiled those tags in breast and ovarian cancer cell lines with differing resistance to doxorubicin.

They measured methylation at hundreds of sites around the start regions of twenty-eight genes already linked to drug resistance or tumor progression. Comparing sensitive and resistant lines at that resolution reveals which silencing patterns travel with resistance. Boettcher and colleagues treat methylation as a readable record of how tumors adapt to chemotherapy. Such profiles could one day warn doctors that a cancer is learning to resist before scans show it growing again.
plos-pone-0011102:
Jaeger, Pickford, Sun and colleagues published cell research in PLOS ONE in 2010. Their subject was the protein whose cutting leads to the amyloid plaques seen in Alzheimer disease. They asked how a complex built around Beclin 1, a protein tied to cell cleanup, controls that cutting.

The team found that this cleanup complex does shape how the precursor protein is processed. That links the cell's waste removal system to the buildup seen in dementia. Boosting cleanup could become one route to clearing toxic material in the brain. The study gives that idea a concrete mechanism to test.
plos-pone-0011202:
Smet, Van Nieuwerburgh, Vandekerckhove and colleagues read drug resistance plasmids in full for PLOS ONE in 2010. Hospital strains of a common gut germ carry rings of DNA that confer resistance to key antibiotics. The team sequenced plasmids carrying a strong resistance gene from patients' germ samples.

Reading the plasmids end to end showed where jumping genes had inserted over time. Those inserts explain how resistance builds up step by step on a mobile element. Tracking that march helps hospitals and health agencies slow resistance spread. It also supports wiser use of antibiotics worldwide.
plos-pone-0011302:
Liu, Navarro and Mauvais-Jarvis studied hormone excess in female mice for PLOS ONE in 2010. Too much androgen, a hormone class best known as male hormones, occurs in some women's disorders. The team asked what that excess does to the insulin making beta cells of the pancreas.

Excess androgen produced oxidative stress across the body in the mice. It also predisposed their beta cells to fail over time. That chain links a hormonal fault to diabetes risk through cell damage. The finding informs women's health care where hormone balance and blood sugar intersect.
plos-pone-0011402:
Keith Ballingall and co-authors studied immune genes in domestic sheep in 2010 and found a pattern that crosses species lines. The genes in question help the immune system display germ fragments to patrolling cells, and variety in them helps flocks survive new diseases. Some variants in sheep turned out to be older than sheep themselves as a species.

Those shared variants, kept across species by natural selection, are called trans-species polymorphism. Their survival implies the variants were so useful that evolution retained them while species split apart. For sheep breeding, the finding counsels care: breeding purely for production could discard ancient immune variety that flocks may need in a future outbreak. For evolution, it shows selection can preserve useful immune options far longer than a single species lasts.
plos-pone-0011502:
Corey Frucht and co-authors searched in 2010 for what switches on cell growth in the bird inner ear. Birds, unlike mammals, can regrow damaged hearing cells, and the basilar papilla is the tissue where that regrowth happens. The team treated the tissue with forskolin, a chemical that provokes growth, and read which genes and microRNAs changed as cells began to divide.

They identified microRNA-181a as a mediator of the growth response, a small RNA that helps carry the signal from treatment to division. Naming the middleman matters, because a defined molecule can be tested, blocked, and perhaps one day borrowed. Mammals cannot regrow hearing cells, and every step of the bird pathway that is mapped is a candidate step to restart in human ears. The study is basic science with a clear long-term hope behind it.
plos-pone-0011602:
Yasuhito Shirai and co-authors studied an enzyme that helps brain cells build connections, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The enzyme, called DGK beta, is common in brain areas tied to thought and memory, including the cortex and hippocampus. It converts one fatty signal molecule into another, but its exact job in neurons was unclear.

The team showed that DGK beta is needed for neurons to grow spines, the tiny knobs where nerve cells receive signals. Without it, spine formation falters. Since spines underpin learning, the result links a single enzyme to the physical basis of mental function and suggests a new angle on disorders of thinking.
plos-pone-0011702:
Sarah To and co-authors studied layered controls on a family of gene switches, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The CP2 family of transcription factors turns genes on across many tissues. One member, CRTR-1, is unusual because it appears only at specific places and times, and removing it disrupts the maturation of the organ it serves.

The team showed that CRTR-1 and a chemical tag called sumoylation both modulate the family's activity. Two different modifiers tuning the same switches gives cells finer control over gene programmes. Such layered management is likely a general feature of development, not a quirk of one family.
plos-pone-0011802:
Jennifer Hsu and co-authors studied meal-time excitement in mice that lack a serotonin receptor, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Animals can tune their daily clocks to food times, growing active just before a meal is due. That meal-anticipation behaviour helps survival, but the molecules and brain paths behind it were not fully known.

Mice with no serotonin 2C receptor showed stronger meal anticipation, tied to more activity in brain paths outside the hypothalamus. The find shows the circuits of hunger reach far past the usual brain spots. It may also help explain appetite troubles tied to serotonin signals.
plos-pone-0011902:
Delira Robbins and co-workers studied in 2010 whether a plant-based supplement could help prevent skin cancer. The supplement, Protandim, blends five medicinal plants and is known to raise the body's own antioxidant enzymes. The team focused on events inside cells as skin tumors form, including the movement of the guardian protein p53 into mitochondria.

Tracking that movement and the resulting cell death offers a concrete check on claims of cancer prevention. Supplements are often sold on antioxidant language alone, so mechanistic evidence matters. If boosting internal defenses also pushes damaged skin cells to die on cue, that is a stronger and more testable basis for prevention than marketing suggests.
plos-pone-0012002:
You Jin Hong, Paul Marjoram, and Darryl Shibata proposed in 2010 reading a tumor's family history from chemical marks on its DNA. Watching a human tumor grow over time is impractical, so its history must be inferred from the variation among its cells today. The more differences on average, the longer the tumor has been growing and branching.

Methylation patterns, chemical tags that shift as cells divide, serve as the record they used to infer tumor ancestry. Reconstructing that ancestry shows whether a cancer spread early or late and how its parts relate. Such histories could eventually help judge which parts of a tumor carry the dangerous lineages.
plos-pone-0012102:
Wieke Altorf-van der Kuil, Mariëlle Engberink, Elizabeth Brink, and colleagues reviewed the research on protein in the diet and blood pressure for PLOS ONE in 2010. High blood pressure is common worldwide and is a major cause of heart disease and stroke. Diet is one of the few levers people can adjust daily, and protein intake had drawn growing interest as a possible part of that lever.

A review pulls all the published studies together and weighs them as a whole, instead of trusting any single trial. The authors gathered that full record on dietary protein and blood pressure. Reviews of this kind shape the advice doctors and health agencies give, because they show where the evidence is firm and where it is still thin.
plos-pone-0012202:
Tai-Ho Hung, Szu-Fu Chen, Meng-Jen Li, and co-authors tested vitamin C and E on placenta cells for PLOS ONE in 2010. Giving both vitamins in pregnancy had been linked to harm in some trials. The women in those trials faced a dangerous blood pressure condition. Harms included low birth weight and early birth, and no one knew why. The placenta's surface cells face cycles of low and returning oxygen. Those cycles look much like the ones in that condition.

Under those oxygen swings, the vitamins changed cell death and self-recycling. The effects differed from those under steady oxygen. In short, context flips the vitamins from help to harm. The work warns against trusting supplements in pregnancy just because they are familiar. It also points at the mechanism behind the reported harms.
plos-pone-0012302:
Alexander Lorestani, Lilach Sheiner, Kevin Yang, and co-authors disabled a division protein in the Toxoplasma parasite, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The protein, MORN1, is kept across the whole parasite group that includes malaria, and it sits in several structures tied to cell division. Toxoplasma divides by an internal budding process simpler than most, making it a good place to dissect the protein's job.

Without MORN1, the parasites kept starting divisions they could not finish properly: the base of the new cells assembled badly, the internal organelle failed to split, and final separation failed. A protein this central to division in a group of major parasites is a plausible drug target, provided human cells lack its twin role.
plos-pone-0012402:
Michelle Hildebrandt, Ritsuko Komaki, Zhongxing Liao and colleagues hunted gene clues to radiation harm in lung cancer care, in a 2010 PLOS ONE study. Radiation and chemo-radiation cure some non-small cell lung cancers, but they often inflame the food pipe and lungs. Doctors cannot yet tell in advance which patients will suffer the worst side effects.

The team linked variants in inflammation genes to higher risk of esophagitis and pneumonitis after treatment. If confirmed, a gene test before therapy could flag fragile patients for gentler plans or closer watching. It is a step toward cancer care fitted to the patient, not just to the tumor.
plos-pone-0012502:
Ifedayo Adetifa, Martin Ota, Brigitte Walther and colleagues tracked a TB blood test during treatment, in a 2010 PLOS ONE study of newly diagnosed patients. The test, an interferon gamma release assay, measures immune memory of TB germs. If its signal fades predictably as drugs work, clinics could use it to monitor therapy and compare new regimens.

The team measured how fast the signal decayed once anti-tuberculosis therapy began. The decay pattern was slower and messier than a simple cure meter would need. Their caution saves programs from over-trusting one number and points to what a true treatment-monitoring biomarker must still prove.
plos-pone-0012602:
Das, Ghosh, Manna and co-authors tested whether taurine can shield the liver from arsenic harm. Arsenic poisons the liver in part by draining glutathione, a key defence against chemical stress. Taurine, a compound found in many tissues, helps cells make more glutathione, but its exact protective route was unclear.

Their 2010 rat and cell work traces taurine's effect through a chain involving the proteins PKC delta and JNK. Blocking that chain kept liver cells from dying by the self-destruct route called apoptosis. The findings matter where arsenic in water remains a daily health threat.
plos-pone-0012702:
Hatakeyama, Cheng, Wirth and co-authors traced how head and neck cancers escape a targeted drug. Cetuximab blocks the EGFR growth receptor, yet tumours often learn to resist it over time. Their 2010 study proposed that long blockade makes the cancer raise levels of the receptor's own trigger molecules.

One such trigger, HB-EGF, turned out to be raised by a small RNA called miR-212 falling away. Restoring that balance could revive the drug's power. The chain they outline gives doctors a marker for resistance and a possible way around it.
plos-pone-0335002:
Calista Ogechukwu Dozie-Nwakile and colleagues used a 2023 national survey in Lesotho to study smoking among three hundred and twenty six people with tuberculosis. Smoking worsens tuberculosis outcomes, and both burdens run high in poorer countries. Weighted survey models weighed sex, media exposure, alcohol use, stigma, mental health, and household traits against smoking status and daily versus occasional smoking.

About one quarter of patients smoked, most of them daily. Being male raised odds enormously, and alcohol use and no media exposure also raised odds clearly. Daily smoking showed the same pattern even more strongly. TB programmes in Lesotho should bundle quit help with alcohol care, and use media reach as a health channel.
plos-pone-0337902:
Sasichakorn Wongsaichia and co authors surveyed just over six hundred shoppers in Thailand about green fashion made with buyers help. In joint design, shoppers share ideas early, so goods fit what people truly want. The survey asked whether that joint work changed how useful green fashion felt, how ready people were to adopt it, and how well brands seemed to perform.

Feeling part of the design raised both the felt benefits of green fashion and readiness to adopt it, and those steps in turn lifted brand performance. The chain matters for firms in growing markets. Inviting buyers in does more than improve a product. It builds trust and attachment that make a green brand look stronger and sell on more than price alone.
plos-pone-0340602:
Ismail Marouani and co-authors modelled what it would cost to make green fuel gas for heavy industry by splitting water with clean power. Their system pairs solar panels and wind turbines with an electrolyser, batteries, and storage tanks, sized by computer to meet hourly demand. They compared the same setup with and without government support for building it.

Without help, the gas came out costly; with strong building subsidies, the price per kilogram fell by nearly half and the carbon cost dropped sharply too. Battery storage only made sense once its price fell a lot. Their results suggest that early public money, not just cheaper gear, is what can get clean hydrogen into factories soon.
plos-pone-0342702:
Maria-Angeles Fuentes-Expósito and colleagues spent a year testing a phone app that helps breast cancer survivors track side effects and symptoms from home. Sixty-one survivors in a European project installed the Xemio app, logged how they felt, and later rated the experience, while the team compared app reports against standard quality-of-life questionnaires.

Forty-nine women used the app actively. Engagement started very high, with nearly everyone participating in the first three months, then faded to about a third by the last quarter, a familiar pattern for health apps. Usability scored in the excellent range, and most users said they would recommend it. The app also captured finer symptom detail than the questionnaires, especially for joint problems. The authors call it feasible and welcome, with adherence the challenge to solve.
plos-pone-0343902:
Comkrit Lomloy and co-workers search for drug pairs that work better together against the most common form of lung cancer. Single drugs often stop working as tumors resist them, but testing every pair in the lab is impossible. Their 2026 paper builds a computer method that spreads each drug pair's effects across a network of interacting molecules in a lung cancer cell line.

Grouping hundreds of pairs by shared effect patterns surfaced clusters rich in pairs that amplify each other. One shared pattern drove the boost in most of those clusters. That pattern centers on three linked growth pathways inside the cell. Naming the shared route gives drug hunters testable ideas for why certain pairs help each other and which pairs to try next.
plos-pone-0345902:
Michelle Hirsch and colleagues interviewed younger and older adults about what curiosity means to them and how it feels, a basic question curiosity science has skipped. Definitions used by researchers may not match everyday understanding, and aging shifts emotions and goals in ways that could reshape curiosity. Both age groups described curiosity as joyful exploration.

Younger adults more often tied curiosity to a feeling of deprivation, to thrill seeking, and to being central to what makes us human.
