pmc-12859102:
Dawit Andualem Asrate, Fekerte Berhanu Tadle, and Yordanos Derseh Mihretie even out the airflow in industrial multi-tray dryers by optimizing fan placement, in a two thousand twenty-five food engineering paper. Uneven airflow leaves some trays under-dried and others scorched.

The framework couples computational fluid dynamics with sequential linear programming over a twenty-five-run experimental design for a thirty-two-tray dryer. A regression model linked fan positions to a uniformity index with strong fit. Trust-region methods collapsed the optimization from six hundred sixty-one iterations to as few as eight. The optimal layout reached seventy-six point five percent uniformity with minimal prediction error. The authors offer the approach for thermal process optimization broadly.
pmc-12872902:
Alessandro El Motassime and others put out a 2026 review of robotic knee swap surgery. Robots help surgeons place man-made knee parts exactly. Most systems plan from medical scans taken beforehand. Newer systems work without those scans. The review asks whether scans are truly needed.

Imageless systems matched scanned systems on how well parts lined up. Patient results and how pleased they were also matched. Skipping scans cuts cost and radiation dose. Surgery room flow became simpler too. Surgeons faced a fair learning curve with the new method. The authors see imageless robots as a real option. Hospitals can choose based on means and training.
pmc-13122002:
Abdellatif Bouayad, writing alone, reviews autoantibodies in Still's disease in a 2026 minireview. Still's disease is a rare, severe whole-body inflammatory disorder with spiking fevers, rash, and joint inflammation. Some patients make antibodies that neutralize IL-1RA, a natural brake on inflammation, but why they arise is unclear.

The review weighs host factors, such as certain immune gene types, and changes to the brake protein itself, including excess phosphate tagging. Detection is hard because lab assays vary, so combining methods is advised. For now, Bouayad argues, these antibodies are best read as a sign of immune dysregulation, meaning a misregulated immune system, rather than a proven direct driver.
pmc-13138902:
Steffi Kar Kei Yuen leads a large multicentre team following kidney stone patients for a year after a new suction technique, in a study published in two thousand twenty-six. A flexible suction sheath navigates the urinary tract, clearing stone dust during laser surgery. Early results were favorable.

Adults across eleven centers in nine countries underwent the procedure for kidney and ureter stones, including in abnormal anatomy. One-year imaging checked the upper urinary tract's anatomical outcomes; thirty-day scans measured stone-free rates. Long-term safety was the primary question, since suction pressures act on delicate tissue. Prospective multicentre data of this size are rare in endourology. The results inform whether the technique graduates from novelty to standard equipment.
pmc-13139602:
Raiane Ferreira Monteiro and colleagues combined quantum calculations with machine learning in 2026 to explain how sulfur poisons tiny metal catalysts. Clusters of just thirteen atoms, arranged as icosahedra, can outperform bulk metals in catalysis, but sulfur contamination shuts them down. The team studied clusters from thirty different transition metals. They measured where sulfur prefers to bind, the energy involved, and how bonding distorts the cluster's structure and electronics.

Vibrational checks confirmed true energy minima, and the physics-informed learning model drew on those descriptors. For most metals, the metal-sulfur bond itself mainly set the adsorption energy. Knowing which clusters resist poisoning, and why, guides catalyst design for processes where sulfur is unavoidable, such as fuel processing. Interpretable models matter here because a black box cannot teach chemists the underlying rule.
pmc-13146302:
Pol Camps-Renom and others told of a randomized trial in 2026. The HOPE trial studied blood pressure after stroke thrombectomy. Taking out a clot can restore brain blood flow. Strong pressure cuts after that had shown no benefit. The trial tailored pressure targets to reopening success. Hundreds of patients whose reopening worked were assigned by lot. Plan targets varied from standard rules of care clearly. Treatment lasted three days after the operation. Drugs raised or lowered pressure as needed. Function at three months was the main outcome.

The abstract presents the full trial design and group. The targets were based on final vessel reopening grade. Blinded judges weighed the daily-life outcomes later. Such trials test whether exact pressure care helps healing. Results will inform post-thrombectomy ward plans in every place.
pmc-13157302:
Bowen and five co-authors report leukemia showing first in the skin, in work from twenty twenty-six. Leukemia cutis is the spread of leukemic blasts into the skin. It usually appears in patients who already know they have leukemia, not as the first sign.

Their patient was a woman aged seventy-eight with advanced lung cancer treated earlier with chemotherapy and immunotherapy. Skin findings led to a new diagnosis of acute myeloid leukemia. The pattern fit therapy related disease, a known late risk of prior cytotoxic drugs. The case reminds teams to biopsy odd skin lesions in cancer survivors rather than assume spread of the first cancer.
pmc-13179202:
Jorge Antonio Gonzaga Santos, Leiliane Oliveira dos Santos, and colleagues test whether charred sewage sludge can lock away heavy metals in a 2026 soil science study. The setting is a tropical clay soil contaminated with several metals at once. Biochar made from sewage sludge offers a double service: disposing of a waste and amending a poisoned soil, provided the metals stay immobilized rather than washing out.

Pyrolysis temperature turns out to govern how well the biochar holds the metals, a relationship the authors assess with several variables at once. Choosing the right charring temperature decides whether the remedy works or merely moves the pollution.
pmc-13195902:
Laura Klempp and others surveyed medical PhD students in Germany in 2026. The survey asked who gets authorship credit. It also asked who merits that credit. World Vancouver rules define fair authorship. The study covered North Rhine-Westphalia students. That state has nine medical schools.

Knowing the rules was limited. Practice often fell short of guidance. Gender-related gaps also showed. Adviser gender pairing shaped felt practice. Students said rule spread was uneven. The authors call for stronger school frameworks. Regular teaching on credit ethics is needed. Clearer duty in supervision is also urged.
pmc-13196002:
Richard Mills and colleagues published a 2026 study of walking in idiopathic normal pressure hydrocephalus. In that condition, fluid builds up in the brain and walking becomes slow and unsteady. Standard timed walk tests may miss joint-level detail, so the team used full three-dimensional motion capture.

They compared 23 patients with 18 healthy adults of like age. Patients walked much slower, with shorter steps and wider steps. Joint tracking showed less motion at the pelvis, hip, knee, and ankle at key points in each step. A math model sorted patients from controls with high accuracy. The gait pattern could help doctors spot the condition in a more exact way.
pmc-13197202:
Valeria Hirschler wrote a 2026 letter to the editor on Mauriac syndrome, a growth delay tied to long-term insulin shortage in diabetes. She responds to a case where an automated insulin delivery system, a pump guided by a sensor, aided a young patient over two and a half years.

Writing from Latin America, she notes that growth delay from poor insulin supply stays common there. Test strips, sensors, and pumps are scarce in public clinics, and many patients miss visits or doses. The reported patient, by contrast, kept all visits and stuck with care. She asks how much gain came from the device versus family effort and close staff support. Most likely, she argues, all parts worked together.
pmc-13197302:
Miguel López and colleagues present a 2026 model of the word fluency task. In that task, a person names as many words as they can in a class, such as clothing. Word lists reveal how the mind stores and finds words, shifting between tight clusters and new groups.

Their model treats each list as a walk across a word network, with added nodes for sudden jumps. New scoring tools check not just fit but how real the word links look. On 677 clothing lists, their BIGRAM-CN model made the most lifelike lists. It avoided overfitting, meaning it did not just memorize training lists. The tools can compare groups and thinking profiles.
pmc-13198502:
Camila Suguiura Evangelista and colleagues checked mold toxins in dried tea herbs in a 2026 study. Mycotoxins are poisons made by molds that can taint plant goods. Dry herbs for tea are rarely screened, so the team validated a broad test and surveyed market samples.

Their method tracked fifteen toxins and related products at once. It passed accuracy and repeatability checks at three dose levels. Of ninety-one samples across thirty-three herb types, about a quarter held at least one toxin. Zearalenone appeared most often, then a fumonisin and two other toxins at low rates. Diet risk math for the two main toxins stayed far below daily safety limits. Tea drinkers face no clear concern from these herbs, they conclude.
pmc-13200002:
Qixin Wang and ten colleagues build a platform that predicts, from a single blood sample, how broadly a person's antibodies can neutralize many virus variants at once. For constantly evolving viruses, testing neutralization variant by variant is slow. Their system measures antibody binding across many receptor proteins simultaneously and layers in broader immune profiling.

Validated on the original SARS-CoV-2 spike and highly diverged Omicron sublineages, the platform found immune signatures predicting broad neutralization, differing between vaccine-only and hybrid immunity. Broad responses turned out to be woven through multi-type antibody networks rather than single markers. The authors propose the approach for rapidly gauging protection against newly emerged variants.
pmc-13201802:
Diabetic wounds often stall in inflammation, and a 2026 study led by Pengfei Wen describes a flexible device that senses the wound and treats it in a loop. The research article presents a dual-channel electrocatalytic system built around a palladium catalyst, microneedle arrays, and paired electrodes for nitric oxide sensing and hydrogen delivery.

Nitric oxide levels at the wound guide the system, which then produces hydrogen treatment on demand before sensing again. According to the authors, this single-cycle rhythm clears harmful reactive species, calms inflammation, and supports tissue regeneration. They report faster diabetic wound healing with good biocompatibility, pointing toward adaptive, feedback-controlled wound care.
pmc-13201902:
Most colorectal cancers resist immunotherapy, and a 2026 study by Limian Ling identifies a mitochondrial protein that may help unlock a response. The research article investigates PLSCR3, a protein of the inner mitochondrial membrane, and what happens to tumor immunity when it is missing.

Screening cancer cohort data singled out PLSCR3, and experiments in human and mouse tumor cells showed its loss damaged mitochondria. Leaked mitochondrial DNA then switched on the cGAS-STING immune alarm pathway, raising interferon signals and helping natural killer cells kill tumor cells. Mouse experiments extended the work to anti-PD-1 treatment, suggesting PLSCR3 as a possible target for resistant tumors.
pmc-13203502:
The red pigment in tomatoes may protect fatty livers by cleaning up damaged mitochondria, and a 2026 study by Ze Xu tests that mechanism. The research article examines lycopene in mice with diet-induced fatty liver disease and in cultured liver cells exposed to fat and a mitophagy blocker.

Mice fed a high-fat diet for twelve weeks while receiving lycopene gained less weight and showed less liver fat, injury, and enzyme leakage. Lycopene restored energy levels in liver cells and switched on the PINK1 and Parkin cleanup pathway for worn mitochondria. Blocking that pathway in cells partly undid the benefit, tying the protection to mitophagy activation and reduced cell death.
pmc-13204802:
Rhea Sharma and Daniel Shain argued in two thousand twenty-six that a shorter repeat stretch in the androgen receptor gene may itself help cause polycystic ovarian syndrome. Many patients show classic symptoms while their blood hormone levels stay normal, which standard explanations miss. A shorter repeat makes the receptor more active without more hormone being present.

Stronger receptor activity in the brain could disturb hormone signals from the pituitary gland, upsetting egg development and monthly cycles. The authors suggest drugs that quiet the receptor directly as a more precise treatment. Doctors get a genetic explanation for puzzling cases and a new direction for therapy research.
pmc-13212402:
Axelle Hoge and co-authors, reporting in 2026, look for eating patterns tied separately to liver and muscle insulin resistance. Whole-body resistance is a known step toward type 2 diabetes, yet different tissues may respond to diet in different ways.

The analysis covered 700 adults with overweight or obesity screened for a larger study, using food questionnaires and metabolic tests. One pattern stood out, rich in red and processed meat and cream, but low in fruit, vegetables, and tea. That pattern linked more strongly to liver resistance than to muscle resistance. The authors argue diabetes research should treat tissue-specific resistance as distinct outcomes.
pmc-13214702:
Umberto Cornelli, Giovanni Belcaro, and Claudio Casella test in 2026 whether a chitosan supplement, made from crayfish shells, can trap microplastics in the gut and lower the amount circulating in human blood. Tiny plastic particles now show up in everyone's blood, and no removal method existed.

Eleven healthy adults took the supplement for fifteen days while ten matched peers took a placebo. Blood plastic levels fell by about a quarter in the treated group and did not budge in controls. Mid-sized particles dropped most, and reductions spanned the main plastic types. The pilot is small and short, yet it offers the first human evidence that gut trapping might cut internal plastic burden.
pmc-13215202:
Yan Xu and colleagues build in 2026 a cryptographic key system that hides its own secret and self-destructs its evidence when attacked. Conventional detectors watch a device from outside, a vantage attackers can sometimes fool.

Their platform uses spin-orbit torque devices, which flip magnetic states with electric current, as both unclonable fingerprints and true random number sources. At rest the hardware holds only random numbers, concealing any extractable key. Forcing the key out irreversibly destroys those numbers, and a comparator circuit flags the attempt so the owner can revoke the key. Generation, concealment, and attack detection merge into one physical device, rooting protection in hardware rather than software vigilance.
pmc-13216102:
Taylor E. Arnold and co-authors present a 2026 case series on broken bones in children and teenagers injured at organized rodeos. Rodeo trauma is high-energy, and the authors asked how often these fractures resist the usual closed realignment.

At one paediatric trauma centre, records from 2017 to 2023 yielded 41 injured young riders, of whom 18 had extremity fractures. Thirteen fractures needed surgery, and five of those first failed closed reduction and required open surgery to realign the bone. The stubborn patterns included thigh bone, elbow, and forearm injuries. The authors caution that the series has no comparison group, so rates should be read as descriptive.
pmc-13218102:
Ave Voit and a large Estonian team set out the EE-PRS trial in a 2026 protocol, testing whether genetic risk scores can steer preventive statin treatment. Atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease remains a leading cause of preventable death, and polygenic risk scores can flag people whose inherited risk is high long before symptoms appear. Scores like these are still absent from routine primary care, so a pragmatic trial is needed.

The open-label trial will randomize 2,700 adults with a high genetic risk score for coronary artery disease: women aged 55 to 80 and men aged 45 to 80. Half receive preventive rosuvastatin at 20 milligrams daily, and half continue with standard care. Over five years, the primary outcome is time to a first major cardiovascular event. That combined measure covers heart disease, stroke, blocked limb arteries, vessel-reopening procedures, and cardiovascular death. Event data will come from national health registries, keeping the design close to everyday care.
pmc-13219102:
Umida Khojakulova and co-authors map eight decades of research on handgrip strength in a 2026 bibliometric analysis of the Scopus database. Grip strength sounds like a niche measure, yet clinicians treat it as a window on muscle health, frailty, and ageing. The team wanted the field's shape: who publishes, where, and on what.

The search, run in April 2026 with no date limits, captured 12,221 publications stretching back to 1944, with output peaking in 2025 and rising steadily on regression analysis. Authors in 128 countries contributed, led by the United States, Brazil, and China, and the journal Nutrients carried the most papers. The most productive institution was the University of São Paulo. The most-cited work centered on diagnosing and treating sarcopenia, the loss of muscle, which the authors read as proof of grip strength's central place in musculoskeletal medicine. Six retracted papers were catalogued by the reasons given in their retraction notices.
pmc-13219402:
Hiroshi Ureshino and colleagues report extended follow-up of the DAVLEC trial, which tested low-dose dasatinib for chronic myeloid leukemia in older patients, in a 2026 letter. Tyrosine kinase inhibitors transformed the leukemia's outlook, but patients over seventy carry heart disease and other medicines, making full-dose treatment risky. The trial gave twenty milligrams daily as first treatment and reports outcomes over years.

Forty-eight patients from the trial, median age seventy-eight, were followed for a median of sixty-eight months. Five-year rates of major molecular response reached 89.3 percent, and more than half achieved the deepest response category. Over half reached major response while staying at or below the twenty-milligram dose. Responding early predicted deeper responses, while male sex predicted shallower ones, and patients starting with more natural killer cells fared better. They present the data as support for dose-optimized treatment in the older group.
pmc-13219902:
Nazli Karami and colleagues test adding dexmedetomidine to a nerve block for thigh fracture surgery in a 2026 trial. The fascia iliaca block numbs the hip and thigh, and anesthesiologists hoped a dose of the drug mixed into the anesthetic would stretch the pain relief into the first day. Seventy patients aged twenty to seventy-five having fracture surgery under spinal anesthesia enrolled.

Half received bupivacaine and half the drug plus fifty micrograms of dexmedetomidine, assigned by block randomization with neither patients nor assessors aware. It took hold fast in both groups, but pain relief lasted longer with it, a mean of 11.4 hours against 9.3 hours. Fewer patients in the dexmedetomidine group needed painkillers in twelve hours. Pain scores at time points, including recovery and two hours, did not differ, so the gain showed up as duration rather than depth. The authors support the mixture for analgesia in surgery.
pmc-13220902:
Kena Zhou and colleagues present a 2026 analysis of IL18, a gene they link to acute pancreatitis from two directions at once. The team searched for core genes of the disease, which inflames the pancreas and still lacks targeted treatment. IL18 emerged as the standout marker for diagnosis and outlook.

Combining bioinformatics, machine learning, mouse models, and genetic data, the authors found IL18 expression rose sharply in pancreatitis cases. High levels tracked with suppressed immune responses, yet genetic analysis suggested higher IL18 may lower disease risk. That tension frames IL18 as both a warning signal and a possible protective factor, a puzzle needing care in any future therapy.
pmc-13221502:
C. Vanden Bulcke and colleagues probe unmet needs in Belgian HIV care using patient questionnaires and brain screening, in a 2026 clinic study. At Ghent University Hospital, 836 of 1,473 people with HIV completed surveys on health, sleep, support, stigma, and substance use. Cognitive screening followed guideline questions and two standard tests.

Satisfaction with physical and mental health ran high, yet nearly half reported major sleep disturbance. Regular substance use appeared in about one in five respondents. Forty-four percent reported cognitive complaints, and formal testing found impairment in many of those screened. Sleep, mood, social support, and cognition together predicted quality of life, arguing for integrated follow-up care.
pmc-13222002:
Zhao Mei and colleagues evaluate a pharmacist-led stewardship program in a large Chinese hospital over seven and a half years, in a 2026 time-series analysis. The program sorted 29 departments into a grid and applied four supporting pillars from July 2020. Researchers tracked antibiotic use density, costs, patient outcomes, and links between use and resistant organisms.

Antibiotic use density dropped by about a quarter right after launch, and key drug classes fell sharply. Hospital stays shortened and overall mortality halved across the period. The statistical link between use and resistance detection weakened for several major resistant organisms, though it strengthened for one. Causality cannot be proven from observation, the authors note.
pmc-13222402:
Yan Yuan and co-authors build iCRCexp, a combined database of gene expression profiles for colorectal cancer, in a 2026 resource paper. No single archive of transcriptome data for this cancer existed. The team gathered datasets from major public sources through 2022, ran them through one pipeline, and mined published work for cancer-linked genes and drugs.

The database holds over eighteen thousand tissue samples from 231 studies, plus thousands of listed genes and drugs with rich study details. Built-in tools cover differing expression, correlation, and survival checks, plus drug predictions from connection scores. Results are shown as networks inside the database, giving colorectal research teams a single starting point for expression questions.
pmc-13222602:
Qiuyu Zhu and co-authors review immunotherapy for colorectal cancer from mechanisms through nursing care, in a 2026 full review. Checkpoint blockers and oncolytic viruses headline the treatment advances. The review separates patients by tumor subtype, since mismatch-repair status strongly predicts who benefits from immune treatment.

Sections cover biomarker screening, judging efficacy, resistance routes, and ways around resistance. New targets and sharper markers for precision selection get attention as well. Immune side effects need special handling, so the authors present a named nursing model for whole-course management. Clinicians and nurses both get a reference for matching therapy to the individual tumor.
pmc-13223702:
Mengke Li and co-authors whip structured bigels into foams meant to replace natural cream, in a 2026 food materials study. Bigels blend a beeswax and soybean oil gel with a gelatin water gel. Varying the oil gel share changed texture, structure, and melting behavior, and the foams were judged physically and by taste panel.

The forty percent blend performed best, expanding nearly as much as commercial cream and winning the highest sensory acceptance. More oil gel softened the foam, with hardness bottoming at seventy percent. Spectroscopy showed the two phases interact physically rather than chemically. Heat analysis tracked lower melting points as oil content rose. Such foams could cut cost and stretch supply in desserts and toppings.
pmc-13223802:
Tomonari Oki and co-authors show how growth speed helped unmask a benign lung lesion that looked like cancer, in a 2026 case report. A 72-year-old woman with a treated colon cancer history carried a small, irregular lung nodule watched for three years. It grew only about a third of a millimeter every six months, yet suspicion of cancer or spread led to surgery.

The removed lesion proved to be a ciliated muconodular papillary tumor, a rare benign growth rich in mucus. Measuring its volume doubling time retrospectively gave over twenty-five hundred days, far slower than the roughly four hundred forty days typical of the invasive cancer it mimicked. Slow volumetrics, the authors argue, can steer clinicians toward benign explanations before surgery.
pmc-13224502:
Louis Kreitmann and a large intensive-care collaboration examine a 2026 analysis of whether negative-pressure isolation rooms protect ventilated COVID-19 patients from a fungal lung complication. The mould Aspergillus can invade the lungs of severely ill patients, with deadly results. Earlier work blamed host and treatment factors, while the role of room air pressure stayed untested.

Data came from 1,233 mechanically ventilated patients treated during the first pandemic wave in France, Belgium, and Switzerland. Probable invasive fungal infection occurred in two percent of patients in negative-pressure rooms, compared with a higher rate in neutral-pressure rooms. No clear difference appeared for weaker diagnostic categories, so the authors treat the protective signal as specific but preliminary.
pmc-13227602:
Vaughan C Turekian writes a 2026 essay on how AI is reshaping science itself, and what that means for international cooperation. Discovery increasingly runs through joined platforms that bind data, models, computing, and machines into single systems, with protein-structure prediction as the showcase example. A United States programme to build one shared AI research system shows the direction of travel.

Access to those platforms is becoming governed by national policy regimes that may never converge. Turekian argues that science diplomacy must therefore shift its job: less about encouraging exchange, more about structuring participation across separated systems. Joined regional hubs, which he calls technopoles for science, are emerging across universities and industry alike, including drug research.
pmc-13230302:
Ruby Olivia Nagano Crocker and Gyorgy Fazekas introduce in 2026 an updated public dataset linking film music, sound features, and felt emotion. FME-24 covers two hundred seventy-five film scores from the past two decades, mixing experimental and mainstream works. Ninety-eight listeners rated how pleasant and how intense the music felt moment by moment.

Each scored moment pairs a two-second sound clip description with dozens of measured audio features. They cover tone color, rhythm, roughness, and harmony shifts, alongside familiarity ratings and written emotion notes. Full audio cannot be shared for licensing reasons, so codes and exact timings let others rebuild the set. Uses span music research, psychology, and training artificial intelligence systems that read emotion in sound.
pmc-13230502:
Nakamura and colleagues ask whether the cancer drug cisplatin makes chicks feel sick, using nausea-like behaviour rather than vomiting. Cisplatin causes strong nausea and vomiting in people and in several mammals. Those responses are a standard lab model for studying sickness, but birds had not been checked in this way.

Injecting cisplatin into the body cavity of domestic chicks brought on nausea-like responses, yet no vomiting followed. That split is useful: it lets researchers study the feeling of nausea apart from the act of throwing up. It also matters for farm welfare, since sickness in poultry is real but hard to read from behaviour alone.
pmc-13233502:
Jing He, Xianxi Liu, and Qing Yang published a 2026 cost-effectiveness analysis of a two-drug combination for mantle cell lymphoma that has returned or stopped responding to treatment. The SYMPATICO trial had shown that adding venetoclax to ibrutinib delays disease progression. The authors modeled costs and health gains over 35 years for the health systems of China and the United States.

In both countries, the combination cost far more per quality-adjusted life year than accepted willingness-to-pay thresholds. Sensitivity analyses found no realistic chance of cost-effectiveness at current prices. Deep price cuts changed the picture, especially for venetoclax in China. The authors conclude that price negotiation, not clinical doubt, is the barrier to adopting the regimen.
pmc-13233802:
Pavla Bartošová-Sojková and colleagues published a 2026 study of Smolstatin1, a protease-blocking protein from Sphaerospora molnari, a myxozoan parasite of fish. Protease blockers help them survive inside hosts by disarming digestive enzymes. The team examined where this stefin-family protein sits in its body, when it is produced, and what happens when it is switched off.

Smolstatin1 production rose during spore formation, and the protein appeared inside cells and on the outer surface. It blocked cysteine proteases from both host and parasite, mainly cathepsin L. Silencing its gene slowed its movement and changed its cell shape. Crystal studies showed the protein locks together as an unusual domain-swapped pair. The authors conclude the blocker is needed for normal growth.
pmc-13234102:
Bernhard Wiechens and colleagues published a 2026 laboratory study of clear orthodontic aligners, comparing heat-formed trays with directly 3D-printed ones. How hard an aligner pushes, and how fast that push fades, shapes tooth movement. A printed model jaw with a mounted front tooth simulated a quarter-millimeter bodily shift, while a multi-axis sensor recorded forces for three aligner designs, including two edge trims on the printed versions.

Heat-formed aligners pushed hardest along the direction of movement. The printed aligner with a scalloped, garlanded edge pushed most gently and controllably in both movement directions, and vertical forces nearly vanished compared with the heat-formed trays. Printed aligners also relaxed their force quickly within the first hour. The authors say trim design gives orthodontists a dial for force, pending longer observation.
pmc-13235202:
Ming-Da Zhang and Kai-Wen Pan proposed in 2026 a knowledge-guided computer method for outlining brain tumours in magnetic resonance scans. Standard deep learning relies mostly on image features and struggles where tumour borders look ambiguous. Their framework adds three kinds of medical knowledge to the image data. Contrast patterns between scan types, written anatomical descriptions, and geometric shape constraints all feed the model.

Fusion happens at two levels, adjusting the weight of each knowledge source for each tiny volume element and each scan. Output layers were built to respect the nested structure of tumour regions. On a standard 2020 benchmark, the method scored higher than the best comparison approach and stayed stable across repeated validation. Removing the shape or meaning knowledge lowered performance notably in ablation tests. The authors see potential for clinical use after further validation.
pmc-13235902:
Wen-Chao Zhang and co-authors tracked in 2026 how a white blood cell type changes over time in intensive care patients after heart attack. Earlier studies disagreed on whether eosinophil counts help or harm prognosis in this setting. Nearly fifteen hundred critically ill patients came from a large public intensive care database. A trajectory method grouped patients by the pattern of their counts during admission.

Three patterns emerged, ranging from stable low counts to a medium level rising quickly. Both rising patterns carried clearly lower twenty-eight-day death risk than the stable low pattern. The fastest rising group also showed lower one-year mortality in the adjusted analysis. Kidney injury partly carried the link between count pattern and short-term death in mediation tests. The authors propose the count trajectory as a simple marker for risk sorting after heart attack.
pmc-13236902:
Meenakshi K and Suresh Sankaranarayanan built a computer vision system in 2026 that spots diseases on cashew leaves. Their design joins two efficient image networks, then hands the extracted features to boosted decision-tree classifiers tuned by an automated search method. The test set covered anthracnose, gummosis, leaf miner damage, red rust, and healthy leaves.

The combined model classified the leaf images with accuracy between 90 and 93 percent, depending on the classifier. Each decision also came quickly, in well under a second, which matters for tools farmers might run on modest hardware. The authors argue that pairing light neural networks with boosting gives accuracy without heavy computation. Farm advisers could use such a system for earlier, cheaper disease checks.
pmc-13237102:
Heba Seyam, Sameh H. Ismail, and Heba M. Hamama tested nanocomposites of chitosan mixed with propolis, the resin bees collect, against deformed wing virus in honey bee cells in 2026. The virus is among the most dangerous threats to bees. Propolis came from two sources, described as Caucasian and Egyptian, and the team measured the mixtures' chemistry, cell toxicity, and effect on virus load in cultured cells from bee heads.

The Caucasian propolis composite carried more phenols and flavonoids and a larger surface area, though it was also harsher on the cultured cells. It cut the virus load more than the Egyptian composite and more than raw propolis. The authors recommend the Caucasian blend as a feed supplement candidate for easing virus pressure in hives.
pmc-13238502:
Jacob Rong Bentsen and team reported a nationwide case series in 2026 on testosterone-lowering drugs given to men with intellectual disabilities and problematic sexual behavior. Such drugs are used in severe cases, yet their use in this group was poorly tracked. A survey of specialist clinics found five male patients who had received the treatment.

Four of the five showed reduced harmful behavior while treated, and three relapsed after the drug stopped. Side effects included bone thinning, high blood pressure, depression, and suppressed sexual development. Checks and access differed between regions. The authors conclude the drugs can work in selected patients, but only with careful checks and ethical oversight. The very small numbers underline how rare this treatment remains.
pmc-13238902:
Thomas Lemberger and Kevin M. Ryan wrote a 2026 editorial about making scientific publication smoother and less bruising. Publishing, they note, crowns years of work yet often delivers rejection and frustration, sometimes because authors simply pick the wrong journal. Their short piece gathers suggestions and initiatives meant to ease the path from manuscript to print.

Choosing the right home comes first: journals differ in scope, audience, and appetite for novelty versus clinical relevance. The editorial then walks through the choice between subscription, open access, and hybrid outlets, noting that open access makes work free to read from day one and can raise visibility and citations. The authors write as journal insiders hoping to cut wasted rounds of submission.
pmc-13239202:
Benjamin Kinnear and colleagues argued in a 2026 perspective, written after a national consensus conference, that competency-based medical education should be treated as a training philosophy, not a fixed checklist. Emergency medicine is their home field, and the piece reacts to conference debate about competency-based training and certification. A philosophy, unlike a recipe, is expected to look different in different places.

Three consequences follow in their reasoning. Programs must balance faithful use against the flexibility local contexts demand. The philosophy itself will keep evolving over time. The profession keeps the agency to steer that evolution, or to choose another philosophy if this one fails its promises. The authors urge emergency medicine to reframe assessment through this lens. Training to a standard, they suggest, is a stance before it is a system.
pmc-13239602:
Gosse and colleagues sound an alarm on adolescent mental health in sub-Saharan Africa. About one in five teenagers in the region lives with a mental health disorder, by their account. Yet the need stays near the bottom of health priorities, squeezed by stigma, thin funding, weak facilities, and a severe shortage of trained mental health workers across the region.

The authors call that neglect unignorable and demand urgent action. Untreated illness in the teenage years shadows schooling, work, and adult health for decades, so delay compounds the cost. Their commentary marshals the burden figures to argue that governments and funders can no longer treat youth mental health as a luxury item.
pmc-13241502:
Myriel Staack and co-authors describe a 2026 taxonomy study of three bacterial strains from northern Germany. The strains came from water at three separate sites, including a chalk quarry area, a Baltic estuary, and an island shore. All belong to a bacterial family known for acorn-shaped cells.

The isolates formed pale pink colonies and reproduced by budding from one pole. They shared a preferred growth temperature yet differed in their preferred acidity. Genome sizes varied considerably across the three strains. Combined evidence from family trees, body features, and growth traits supported naming two new genera. The authors propose three new species, with type strains deposited in public collections for other researchers.
pmc-13241702:
Ashkanani and colleagues in Kuwait built a flowchart to rescue junior clinicians from AV-block ECG confusion. The algorithm splits first on whether beats arrive grouped, then checks QRS and P-wave patterns. Forty junior doctors and medical students were randomized to test it. Half received a one-hour teaching session; half did not.

Trained participants diagnosed the block types more accurately on standardized tracings. The method proved reliable and practical in their hands. Distinguishing Wenckebach from the dangerous Mobitz II pattern anchors the design. Ashkanani offers the chart for emergency and ward use by less experienced readers.
pmc-13242202:
Gui Li and co-authors present a 2026 evidence summary on nursing care for low blood oxygen around the time of surgery. This complication is common and dangerous, driven by anesthesia, surgical trauma, and position changes. The team searched guidelines, reviews, trials, and consensus documents using a structured evidence pyramid approach.

Twenty sources met the quality bar, yielding dozens of evidence statements. Topics run from first assessment and oxygen targets through high-risk patient screening and operating room ventilation choices. Non-invasive breathing support, high-flow nasal oxygen, recovery room care, positioning, and drug measures also feature. The authors offer the synthesis as a standardized reference, while reminding clinicians to adapt it to each patient and setting.
pmc-13242402:
Nikolova and de Wit in Groningen asked whether how workers see work predicts whether they truly leave it. Dutch LISS panel survey data from the Netherlands split job, career, and calling outlooks. Models controlled for personality, pay-linked traits, and job satisfaction. Quit aims, on-the-job search behavior, and actual exits were tracked.

Career-minded workers showed the strongest quit intentions and active searching. Feeling blocked for promotion sharpened that restlessness further. Calling-minded workers barely searched or intended to quit at all. Actual job exits one and two years later followed outlooks only weakly.
pmc-13242802:
Wenjuan Cao and a large team publish a 2026 response to a letter about their trial protocol on virtual reality for children dental pain. The trial tests whether virtual reality immersion sedates and relieves pain in children with acute tooth pulp inflammation. Commentators raised design questions about screening, blinding, and measurement.

The authors accept that their motion sickness screening was too loose and promise a mandatory familiarization session with standardized reaction records. Recent painkiller use is now defined as within twenty-four hours. They explain that children and operators cannot be blinded to a visible headset, so only outcome assessors are blinded, scoring recordings without watching procedures. Anxiety measurement at key painful moments is also addressed in the reply.
pmc-13243102:
Jiaoniu Duan and two co-authors set out a 2026 opinion piece on denosumab, a bone drug, as a possible treatment for osteoarthritis. The joint disease affects more than 600 million people, yet no approved drug can slow or change its course. Care still starts late, eases pain for a time, and often ends in joint replacement.

The authors trace how the drug blocks RANKL, a signal that drives bone breakdown and joint inflammation in lab work. They weigh early signs from hand and knee studies and ask who should get the drug and at what dose. They also ask how stopping treatment should be handled. Their plan for future trials gives clinicians a clear map of the proof that is still missing.
pmc-13243202:
Guisi Xie and colleagues compare one cage versus two cages in a 2026 spine surgery study. The operation fuses worn lumbar vertebrae through small cuts with the help of a camera. Surgeons can place a single support cage or a pair of cages between the bones.

The team reviewed 103 patients treated from 2021 to 2023 and matched them into groups of 51 and 17. Two-cage surgery took longer and lost more blood, yet cages sank into bone far less often afterward. Fusion rates and pain scores were close in both groups at one and two years. The study helps surgeons weigh a shorter operation against firmer early support.
pmc-13244102:
Ply Chichareon and a large team update a classic score that foretells if a balloon fix will work for a narrowed heart valve. Their study is from two thousand twenty-six.

The old score reads the valve's shape and parts. New heart guides urge the use of more facts when one picks who gets the balloon fix: a set of body and life facts, plus two shape facts. The team built the old score anew with those facts joined in. They then matched the new score's calls to the old one's, in a large group of cases. The aim is a truer tool for picking who gains from the fix.
pmc-13244302:
Mo Wang and a national expert group summarize 2024 Chinese guidance on bone and mineral problems in children with kidney disease in 2026. Failing kidneys disturb mineral balance, bone growth, and blood vessel health in children. No child-specific guidance existed before, so care borrowed adult rules that ignore growth.

The guideline answers key questions on testing, diet, and drug care for these children. It weighs how growing bodies differ from adults and which newer drugs have been checked in children. Experts from kidney, nutrition, and pharmacy fields shaped the advice together. The goal is care fitted to each child's stage and needs, rather than scaled-down adult care.
pmc-13244502:
Bhensri Naemiratch and co-authors evaluated a dialogue-based method for involving communities in the fight against drug-resistant germs. Their cross-country study appeared in Global Health Action in 2026. The Responsive Dialogues framework, built as a Wellcome Trust toolkit, runs in three phases: groundwork, community conversations, and sharing what was learned. Malawi and Thailand both adopted it, bending it to local politics and culture.

Four lessons crossed both sites. Adaptation was the engagement itself, built on trust and flexibility. Rank distorted who spoke, and tactics like rotating leadership and agreed ground rules only partly leveled the floor. Structural barriers, from transport to institutional caution, shadowed both programs. Malawi's tight alignment with policymakers carried local insights furthest into antibiotic rules. The authors offer the comparison as a field guide: participatory methods travel, but only when rebuilt locally, never photocopied.
pmc-13245802:
Aljughaiman, Tabash, and Issa traced how volatility shocks jump between carbon markets and emerging European stock markets, in this 2026 PLOS One finance study. Using a quantile-based vector autoregression, which separates calm, normal. Extreme market states, they measured spillovers from the European Union emissions trading system to the Czech, Slovak, Greek, Hungarian, and Polish equity markets.

Transmission was lopsided: shocks from the carbon market hit equities much harder in bullish, high-volatility conditions. Overall connectedness ballooned to roughly eighty-eight percent there, against bearish or moderate states near thirty percent. Greece, Poland, and Hungary were the most exposed markets, while Slovakia stayed least affected in every regime. The authors pitch Slovak equities as a low-beta hedge ingredient and warn fund managers that diversification thins exactly when volatility converges.
pmc-13246702:
Jiao Liu and co-authors recheck a pain drug in breast cancer surgery in a 2026 secondary analysis. Pain after modified radical mastectomy troubles many patients in the first day. Whether a lidocaine drip eases that pain under two common anesthesia styles was the question.

One hundred patients were split into four groups by anesthesia gas or vein drug, with or without lidocaine. Pain scores across the first day ran clearly lower in both lidocaine groups, at rest and in motion. Blood markers of inflammation also settled lower after surgery with lidocaine. Drug use, side effects, and satisfaction stayed alike across groups. The drip thus helped pain without extra cost in harms.
pmc-13247302:
Aldaithan and co-authors report a child's difficult lung disease in this 2026 Case Reports in Pulmonology article. Idiopathic pulmonary hemosiderosis causes repeated bleeding into the lungs, producing anemia and hazy lung scans, and it is often diagnosed late because early signs mimic common illnesses. Their patient, a young girl, suffered recurrent episodes of low oxygen and severe anemia needing intensive care and transfusions.

Steroids controlled her disease only while doses stayed high, and she relapsed on every taper despite added hydroxychloroquine and azathioprine. Doctors then gave rituximab, an antibody that depletes B cells, as a steroid-sparing move. She improved markedly and stayed in durable remission. The authors support rituximab's emerging role in stubborn cases, while calling for larger studies of long-term safety in children.
pmc-13249402:
Chi-Hsun Chen and co-authors pinpoint a single protein change that lets a childhood virus grow in vaccine factory cells in 2026 work. Coxsackievirus A10 causes hand, foot, and mouth disease and resists growth in Vero cells, the workhorse of vaccine making. One adapted strain, though, grew well.

Full particles of the adapted strain raised strong immunity in mice, while empty shells did not. Mixed with another enterovirus bulk, it drew good neutralizing responses to both. Comparing strains found five protein differences, and single-change clones tested each. One change in the VP1 protein governed cell entry by altering attachment. The strain could anchor a combined vaccine made in Vero cells.
pmc-13249802:
Xu and colleagues compared severe and milder sinus disease at the molecular level, in a 2026 study. Thirty-eight patients with chronic rhinosinusitis and nasal polyps were split by how completely their sinuses had clouded on scans. Tissue from the polyps and brushings from the sinus lining were examined for structure and for inflammatory gene activity, with ten healthy volunteers as a comparison.

The severe group showed thicker membranes, swollen mucus glands, and a mixed crowd of inflammatory cells. Their genes told a double story: the expected allergy-style signals plus a second, neutrophil-style program switched on together. The authors suggest severe disease is biologically distinct, which may explain why standard treatments so often fail it.
pmc-13251702:
Simon Bylund and colleagues report a 2026 marker analysis from a pilot trial of rituximab in treatment-resistant schizophrenia. About a third of patients never reach remission on standard antipsychotics, and evidence hints that immune activity drives illness in a subset. Rituximab, an antibody that depletes B cells, was given as a single infusion to nineteen severely ill patients, nine with schizophrenia and ten with obsessive-compulsive disorder.

Six of the schizophrenia patients improved markedly within twelve weeks, with large drops in symptom scores and clear gains in daily functioning. Blood taken before treatment separated responders from non-responders: responders started with higher levels of two genes, TBX21 and RORC, which steer helper T cell types tied to immune attack. A score combining the two genes showed the strongest link to outcome. The authors suggest immune profiling could show who benefits from immune therapy.
pmc-13252702:
Xiongwen Yang and Chuan Xu argue for new ethics rules around chatbots in health care in this 2026 viewpoint. Large language models now sit inside everyday clinical communication, and the authors say the real risks grow during routine use, not in lab tests.

They frame the issue as adoption-phase ethics across three fronts. Trust depends on institutions and relationships, not accuracy alone. Responsibility blurs when model-written text steers decisions. And people differ in their power to question or benefit from model output, raising equity concerns. The authors call for constant system-level oversight, clear accountability, and role-aware rollout.
pmc-13253002:
Jordan Rasmussen and colleagues describe a rare artery detour in this 2026 case report and review. A 56-year-old man with worsening right leg weakness and falls was found to have two benign brain tumours and a tangle of abnormal vessels.

Detailed vessel imaging revealed the surprise. The artery that normally feeds the brain's covering from the jaw area instead sprang from the basilar artery, deep at the brain's base. It then followed its usual route. Embryonic links between those systems explain how such a route can persist. Surgeons removed the vessel tangle and both tumours. The authors say this is the first documented case of this variant feeding both a tumour and a vessel tangle.
pmc-13253102:
Jia Huang and colleagues build an automated tool for counting osteoclasts in cell culture in a 2026 methods paper. Osteoclasts are the cells that break down bone, and counting them under the microscope is a standard but slow way to study bone loss. Existing automated options demand programming skill most laboratories lack.

Their software uses the YOLOv8 image segmentation model, trained on a dataset annotated by bone specialists, to outline and count osteoclasts and measure the area they cover. It processes each image in under a second and immediately produces a visualized report. On mouse bone marrow derived osteoclasts the model reached a mean average precision of 95.3 percent, a strong accuracy score for this kind of task. The program runs offline as a standalone application needing no coding from the user. The authors intend it to free researchers from tedious manual counting in bone biology experiments.
pmc-13253602:
Hou-Ping Sytwu and colleagues chart a gene's role in motor neuron disease in Taiwan in this 2026 study. Faults in the FUS gene cause a minority of ALS cases, the fatal disease that wastes movement-controlling nerve cells, and the local pattern of those faults was unmapped.

Sequencing the gene in 650 unrelated Taiwanese patients found eight distinct harmful variants in eleven index patients and five relatives. One variant recurred in four families, and shared DNA markers around it pointed to a single common ancestor, a founder mutation. Patients with FUS faults fell ill far younger than other patients, averaging about 40, and more often began with speech and swallowing muscles.
pmc-13253902:
Muhammad Faisal and co-authors compare four classic fluid flow setups in a 2026 modeling study. They use the Buongiorno model for nanofluids, fluids carrying tiny particles, flowing over a heated flat surface. The four setups cover flow over a still plate, a moving plate, a stagnation point, and a stretching sheet.

Equations were solved with the Keller-Box method, and wall friction, heat transfer, and mass transfer were compared. Stretching-sheet flow gave the strongest heat transfer gain. Stagnation-point flow gave the largest share of wall friction, at 41 percent, while Blasius flow over a still plate was weakest for momentum transfer.
pmc-13254902:
Yue Zhang and colleagues invent a probe that reads the acidity inside single RNA granules in a 2026 study. These droplet-like condensates, including processing bodies and stress granules, warehouse messenger RNA when cells are stressed, yet their inner chemistry has been nearly impossible to measure. The new ratiometric probe can be targeted to granules and reports pH granule by granule.

Mapping revealed that granules are not uniform: their outer rim runs more alkaline while the side nearer the nucleus runs more acidic. Under oxygen stress, salt stress, or drugs that halt protein production, granules acidified and cellular translation fell in step, making granule pH a sensitive live marker of protein-making activity. Two natural compounds, myrtenol and oridonin, reversed peroxide-driven acidification, restored translation, and delayed cellular aging in the team's tests. The authors propose screening anti-aging drugs by watching granule pH recover.
pmc-13255202:
Xueling Qiu and co-authors test laughing gas for rehab pain in a 2026 randomized trial. Ankle fracture surgery is often followed by painful rehabilitation training. One hundred patients with strong pain during rehab were assigned to breathe either 65 percent nitrous oxide or pure oxygen, with neither side knowing which.

Pain scores were clearly lower with nitrous oxide at both check times, with median gaps of 3.0 and 2.0 points. Patients and therapists in the gas group reported higher satisfaction, and acceptance differed clearly too. Anxiety scores did not differ, and no severe side effects appeared in either group.
pmc-13255702:
Tlacaélel De la Cruz-Torres and co-authors report a 2026 meat science study comparing dry-aged beef from Raramuri Criollo cattle with a Hereford-Angus cross. The Criollo breed survives harsh Mexican desert conditions, yet its beef is barely documented and often dismissed as tough. Dry ageing is known to tenderize meat, so the team tracked quality over thirty days.

Ageing improved quality measures most during the first fifteen days. Crossbred beef tenderized faster early on, while Criollo beef improved more gradually and steadily. By day thirty, the Criollo meat reached lower shear force, meaning greater tenderness, than the crossbred meat. It also held its color better in storage. The authors argue that Criollo beef ages well and that raising the breed suits sustainable production in dry regions.
pmc-13256502:
Yusaku Arima and co-authors wrote a 2026 feasibility study of heart rehabilitation done at home with a smartwatch and a game-like phone app. Patients had acute coronary syndrome, a sudden cut in blood flow to the heart, and had a stent procedure before discharge. The Shin-po Kei app gave points when patients walked for thirty minutes or more inside their target heart rate range, three to five days a week or more.

Sixteen patients at two Japanese sites took part, with a mean age of 62 years and 94 percent men. App use averaged 59.9 percent of days, and half met the target exercise rate. Peak oxygen use rose from 18.4 to 21.1, and exercise felt less of a hassle. No harm linked to the app was found, though the authors say the reward rules need refining.
pmc-13257202:
Vivian Ya-Wen Cheng leads a 2026 randomized trial of augmented reality aromatherapy teaching for early dementia care. Behavioral symptoms distress patients and caregivers, and drug-free options often fail to hold attention. A twelve-session program blended scent education with interactive digital overlays.

Compared with routine care, the program cut the frequency and severity of behavioral symptoms by a larger margin. Caregiver distress also fell more in the program group. Pain, insomnia, well-being, and life satisfaction each improved significantly. The authors present the approach as clinically relevant for long-term care homes. Engagement, often the weak point of non-drug care, may benefit from the interactive format. Larger trials will show whether gains last and whether staffing costs stay reasonable in daily practice.
pmc-13257302:
Jerome Lian and colleagues test cannabinoid combinations in mice fed a Western diet in a 2026 liver study. Fatty liver tied to metabolic dysfunction still lacks good drug options. The endocannabinoid system, which helps govern energy balance, offers a tractable target.

Two weeks of combined treatment lowered body weight and improved blood sugar control in the mice. Liver weight fell, enzyme profiles improved, and tissue sections showed less fat and injury. The authors read the pattern as an acute benefit under diet-driven metabolic stress. Mechanisms remain to be mapped, and longer treatment may behave differently. Hepatology researchers get a reason to keep probing this signaling system. Any human relevance is unproven, so the work belongs at the preclinical stage for now.
pmc-13258302:
Florian Descamps and colleagues designed new drug-like molecules aimed at the angiotensin II type 1 receptor. That receptor helps drive blood pressure and kidney disease, and blocking it is a proven treatment strategy. Their 2026 chemistry paper builds a family of imidazole-based candidates.

Each compound was tested for how well it displaced labeled angiotensin from type 1 versus type 2 receptors. Adding a sulfonamide group boosted grip on the target, while bulky or ester-bearing versions fared worse. Computer docking into the receptor's known structure explained the ranking. The best molecule matched the grip of losartan, the classic drug in this class.
pmc-13258402:
Andrés Alarcón and co-authors review piperine, the sharp-tasting alkaloid that gives black pepper its bite. Beyond flavor, piperine rewrites gene activity without changing DNA itself, which interests cancer and chronic disease researchers. Their 2026 review gathers the molecular evidence for those effects.

Piperine dials down enzymes that methylate DNA and strip acetyl tags from histones, and it reshuffles microRNA networks. It can also clamp onto folded DNA structures in a cancer gene's promoter, quieting it. Low doses protect cells from oxidation, while higher ones stress tumor cells into dying. Poor solubility and thin animal data still block clinical use.
pmc-13258502:
Dorota Zierkiewicz and colleagues review preparation programs before colorectal cancer surgery in a 2026 narrative article. These programs combine exercise, nutrition support, and behavior coaching to build strength before an operation. The authors searched five databases for trials published between twenty fifteen and twenty twenty five.

Twenty three studies met their criteria, most of them randomized trials. Programs usually improved walking distance and fitness before surgery, with good attendance and few safety problems. Effects on complications and hospital stay were mixed overall. Benefits looked clearest for older, frail, or undernourished patients. Surgical teams can use the summary to target preparation where it helps most.
pmc-13258902:
Raynier Zambrano-Villacres and coauthors set out a nutrition first framework for patients on modern weight loss drugs in a 2026 review. Gut hormone drugs produce large weight loss, yet nausea, low intake, and muscle loss limit real world success. Direct nutrition trials in this drug group remain scarce.

Practical guidance covers protein priority, meal structure, fluids, and fiber handling. Symptom targeted steps address the common stomach complaints during dose increases. Resistance training support aims to protect muscle during rapid loss. Maintenance planning prepares patients for life after dose reduction or stopping. Clinics gain a structured dietetic companion to drug based obesity care.
pmc-13259302:
Gang Lu and colleagues map microplastics below ground in mulched bamboo forests in a 2026 field study. Sites spanned suburban and exurban zones with no, short, or long mulching history. Plastic counts were taken from soil, roots, rhizomes, and edible shoots.

Suburban forests carried more plastic overall, peaking under long mulching. Long mulching raised counts in every plant and soil compartment. Root zones near the surface held about triple the plastic in one suburban comparison. Most particles were tiny fragments from common packaging polymers. Overall load rated moderate, yet ecological risk scored high. Shoot safety deserves monitoring even though shoots themselves showed no strong buildup.
pmc-13260302:
Pollyanna Pinto Maia and co-authors present a 2026 computational chemistry study predicting how the two mirror-image forms of levobunolol separate. Levobunolol is a beta-blocker drug used in eye drops for glaucoma. Its two enantiomers, mirror-image molecules, behave differently, and only one is therapeutically active. The team modeled how each form binds inside ring-shaped sugar selectors called cyclodextrins, using quantum and semi-empirical calculations in gas and water.

The active S form consistently formed more stable complexes than the R form with both selectors tested. With the best selector, a sulfated cyclodextrin, binding free energy was far stronger for the S form, giving a large energy gap that signals exceptional selectivity. The analysis credits a more compact network of hydrogen bonds and better shape fit. The authors predict the S form will migrate more slowly in separation runs.
pmc-13260402:
Wenhui Yu and colleagues pooled in 2026 trial evidence on non-drug measures meant to lift quality of life after intensive care. Survivors often leave the unit with lasting physical and mental problems. Their network meta-analysis gathered 19 randomized trials with 2,654 patients and compared twelve approaches, from ICU diaries to exercise programs.

No approach proved clearly better than the rest, since every comparison's margin of error crossed zero. Ranking scores still placed the ICU diary, a written record kept for the patient, among the most promising options. A care bundle known as ABCDE ranked highest for the physical and mental summary scores. The authors warn that rankings show relative promise, not proven benefit. They call for larger, better trials with longer follow-up.
pmc-13260502:
Armia Ahmadi-Hadad leads a 2026 systematic review of artificial intelligence in mitral regurgitation, a common heart valve disease in which blood leaks backward through the mitral valve. Diagnosis and timing of treatment are hampered by observer disagreement. The reviewers searched three databases on May 9, 2025, for studies applying AI to this disease using imaging, ECG, or clinical data, and extracted model designs and performance figures.

Eleven studies with 80,915 patients were included. Six used echocardiographic imaging, two used electrocardiography, two used clinical data, and one used chest X-rays. Reported accuracy scores, measured as AUC, ranged from 0.74 to 0.94, with imaging models using color Doppler or 3D valve geometry performing best. Few studies validated models externally or reported clinically usable thresholds. ECG models scaled easily but were less sensitive, the authors note.
pmc-13260602:
Mei Xue and co-authors built in 2026 a prediction chart for later development problems in newborns with jaundice from excess bilirubin. Most such babies recover fully, yet some suffer quiet harm that shows up months later. Their study followed 234 full-term newborns and checked development at one year of age.

Thirty infants, about one in eight, showed developmental impairment at follow-up. Higher inflammation marker levels, a higher bilirubin-to-albumin ratio, and higher levels of a nerve injury protein each raised the risk. Stronger early behavior scores on a newborn examination lowered it. The combined chart sorted babies by risk with fair accuracy and matched observed outcomes well. The authors propose it for picking out high-risk infants for closer follow-up and early support.
pmc-13261302:
Gabriel Schmitt da Cruz and co-authors present a 2026 rapid review of teledentistry for homebound older adults and those in care homes. Teledentistry gives dental checks and advice from afar. The review asked what is in use and whether it could fit primary healthcare settings.

The team searched 10 sources in October 2024 without language or date limits. Sixteen studies were covered, covering 15 programs in the United States, Japan, Australia, and Chile, among others. Nine took place at home and seven in long-term care homes, with 4 to 252 people and a mean duration of 6.7 months per program. None ran inside primary healthcare. Uses covered checks, treatment planning, referral, teaching, and bringing back oral function. Most models were asynchronous, meaning not live. Findings suggest help with spotting oral problems, gum swelling, swallowing, and patients were pleased. Tech barriers and low digital skill were challenges.
pmc-13262102:
Xinyi Gao and co-authors build computer models to predict kidney transplant outcomes in a 2026 journal article. Their patients received kidneys from deceased donors, and grafts, the transplanted organs, often fail within years. The team wanted risk scores using routine clinical data, first before surgery and then with data from the first year after it.

They studied 940 adult recipients, all followed for more than five years. The pre-transplant model, called KAPTOR-pre, scored 0.813 on a standard accuracy curve. Adding first-year lab results, tissue findings, and other measures lifted the fuller model to 0.904. Both beat an older donor index in the team's own tests, but outside hospitals must still check them.
pmc-13263302:
Julia Cauvila dos Santos and co-authors report a 2026 journal article testing a short Zika virus fragment as a target for antibody blood tests. Zika is a mosquito-borne virus that can harm unborn babies. The fragment, called PEP03, comes from the virus capsid, the protein shell around its genes.

The team built enzyme-linked tests, which use color changes to detect antibodies, around this fragment. For IgG antibodies, the test separated Zika cases from controls well, with an accuracy score of about zero point nine two. Crucially, sera from dengue patients showed no detectable cross-reaction, and chikungunya sera reacted only minimally. Tests for IgM antibodies, which signal recent infection, performed poorly on specificity.
pmc-13263702:
Reem Shihab and co-authors present a 2026 case report with a literature review on a dangerous diabetes crisis in a teenager. A previously healthy 14-year-old girl arrived with new-onset severe diabetic ketoacidosis, where the body burns fat and floods the blood with acid. Her blood also showed low potassium and unusually high sodium.

Standard treatment did not stop her heavy urine output, and her sodium kept climbing. Urine tests pointed to arginine vasopressin resistance, a state where the kidneys ignore the hormone that conserves water, triggered by her low potassium. Aggressive potassium replacement, carefully tuned fluids, and a hormone-copying drug called desmopressin normalized her chemistry. She recovered fully.
pmc-13264002:
Lei Huang and colleagues model how brain death wounds the heart that transplant teams hope to save. Donor hearts often weaken after brain death for reasons tied to inflammation. Their 2026 mouse study pairs ultrasound monitoring with tissue chemistry across two phases.

Every brain-dead mouse developed depressed pumping within an hour, while controls stayed normal. Their heart tissue overexpressed the NLRP3 inflammasome parts and a trio of inflammatory messengers. An upstream sensor stayed flat, while a protective regulator trended upward. Blocking the NLRP3 pathway, the authors propose, might preserve donor hearts for the recipients waiting on them.
pmc-13264102:
David C Garrett and Lihong V Wang demonstrate a swallowable light source for deep photoacoustic imaging in a 2026 study. Photoacoustic imaging reads sound waves created when tissue absorbs light pulses, giving optical contrast at depths ultrasound can reach. Light sent from outside the body fades quickly, which caps depth at a few centimeters and blocks views of the gut interior.

Their compact device sits inside the target area and is powered wirelessly by low-frequency ultrasound sent through tissue. That power drives a small laser diode whose pulses create the signals to be read. Imaging through a thick laboratory phantom showed the concept works at clinically relevant depth. The approach could open gut imaging that surface light cannot reach.
pmc-13264202:
Xiaoyan Cai and colleagues compare delirium prevention strategies around bone surgery in older adults in a 2026 network meta-analysis. Postoperative delirium, a sudden confused state after surgery, harms recovery and independence. Seventy-nine randomized trials covered over sixteen thousand patients aged sixty and above. Bayesian methods ranked many interventions against each other, even when trials had not tested them head to head.

The sedative dexmedetomidine carried the most consistent evidence for lowering delirium risk versus placebo. Several other drugs, including ketamine and rivastigmine, showed promise but with more varied results across studies. Evidence for pain and anesthesia technique choices was thinner. Certainty grading accompanies the rankings, helping surgical teams weigh likely benefit against the strength of proof.
pmc-13264302:
Li-E Wu and colleagues report two children with Kawasaki disease that resisted standard treatment in a 2026 case report and review. Kawasaki disease inflames blood vessels in young children and can damage heart arteries. Both children kept fevers despite antibody infusion and steroids. One also failed an additional immune drug. Levels of the inflammatory signal interleukin-6 climbed in each case before a targeted antibody was tried.

Fever broke within a day of tocilizumab, which blocks that signal. Heart artery widening normalized or shrank during follow-up extending to three years in one child. A rash after a later dose was the notable reaction in the first case. Fourteen published cases are summarized to place the experience in context.
pmc-13264402:
Tao Qiu and colleagues report nine-year follow-up of a modified headgear-activator appliance for a teenager with complex jaw and airway problems in a 2026 case report. The patient combined a receding lower jaw pattern, narrow upper and lower arches, lip incompetence and chronic mouth breathing with enlarged tonsils and adenoids. Treatment began at an early growth stage, aiming for vertical control, jaw advancement and arch widening before fixed braces finished alignment without removing teeth.

Measurements at the end of active treatment showed the jaw angle relationship improving while vertical proportions stayed stable. Back teeth crossbite resolved and arches became harmonious ovals. Lip seal and a straight profile were achieved without airway surgery. Long soft tissue adaptation argues for extended follow-up in growth-guided treatment.
pmc-13265002:
Ing-Tiat Tiunn and co-authors published a 2026 survey study of loneliness among older adults living in the community in Taiwan. Loneliness harms health in later life, and clinics need short tools to spot it. The team compared a full 20-item scale, a three-item short form, and a single direct question.

Among 186 adults aged 65 and over recruited at community centers in southern Taiwan, loneliness rates ran from 18 to 27 percent depending on the tool. Higher depression scores linked to loneliness in every model. Social network size, living alone or with others, anxiety, and self-rated health also played a part. The short form and single question sorted people nearly as well as the long scale. The authors back brief tools for community screening, with the long scale for fuller assessment.
pmc-13265202:
Jin Lu and the team build a gene signature from ageing support tissue to forecast liver cancer results, in a 2026 study. Liver cancer survival varies widely between patients. Senescence, an aged state, in tumour support cells complicates prediction. Data came from several public genomic and protein data banks.

Single-cell analysis showed support cells carried the strongest senescence signals. Machine learning selected six genes for the signature. Risk groups differed in survival, mutation patterns, immune checkpoints, and drug answers. Checks across gene, protein, and spatial datasets supported the signature. Computer screening also found small compounds that may bind one signature gene.
pmc-13265402:
Qin-Mei Lin and co-authors wrote a 2026 study building a risk model for clots tied to PICC lines, long catheters threaded from the arm, in cancer patients receiving radiotherapy. They reviewed 335 patients at one center who had the line placed from 2023 to 2024, and checked them with ultrasound for clots in the vein.

Seventy patients, 20.89 percent, had a clot, and most, about 93 percent, had no symptoms. Analysis tied clots to the cancer diagnosis type and total radiation dose. pmc-13266202:

pmc-13266802:

pmc-13267202:

pmc-13267302:

pmc-13267502:

pmc-13267702:

pmc-13268602:

pmc-13269902:

pmc-13271102:

pmc-13271602:

pmc-13272202:

pmc-13272602:

pmc-13273902:

pmc-13274502:
Lars Helander, Anne Silviken, and Trond Heir present a 2026 journal article on mental health among the Sámi, the Indigenous people of northern Norway. Most Sámi groups showed slightly higher psychological distress than non-Sámi neighbors on a standard ten-item checklist. Sámi-speaking women were the exception, scoring no higher. Changes over the eight years were small, though men with Sámi heritage inched upward. pmc-13274702:
Xun Yang, Liangdong Zhu, and Ruijie Ren present a 2026 exploratory study on two ultrasound measures of the breathing muscle in patients hospitalized with a flare of chronic lung disease. The diaphragm's thickening fraction shows how hard it contracts, while excursion shows how far it moves. After accounting for standard clinical signs, that difference lost significance. Among mask-treated patients, excursion was clearly higher in those who responded well. pmc-13275502:

pmc-13275702:

pmc-13275902:

pmc-13276002:

pmc-13276402:

pmc-13276502:

pmc-13277402:

pmc-13278802:

pmc-13278902:

pmc-13279202:

pmc-13279502:

pmc-13279702:

pmc-13281302:

pmc-13281802:

pmc-13282302:

pmc-13282802:

pmc-13283302:

pmc-13283402:

pmc-13284502:

pmc-13285102:

pmc-13285302:

pmc-13285502:

pmc-13285602:

pmc-13285702:

pmc-13286302:

pmc-13286702:

pmc-13286802:

pmc-13287102:

pmc-13287202:

pmc-13287302:

pmc-13287402:
