pmc-13287702:
Hanan Abdelmawgoud Atia and co-authors tested a gout drug, febuxostat, in 2026 as a shield against testis damage caused by a common cancer drug in rats. Fifty male rats were split into a healthy group, a group given only the cancer drug, and three groups given the cancer drug plus rising daily doses of the shield drug.

Higher doses steadily restored hormone balance and antioxidant defences in testis tissue. A cell-death pathway driven by inflammation eased, while a self-cleaning pathway recovered. Tissue slides matched the chemical gains. The authors propose the gout drug as a candidate to protect male fertility during chemotherapy, pending human evidence.
pmc-13288102:
Juan Carvajal-Garcia and Houra Merrikh study clashes between DNA copying and gene reading in bacteria, in 2026 work. Both processes run on the same DNA strand at once, and head-on meetings stall the copying machine. Stalled forks can break DNA and form harmful RNA-DNA loops. The team ran an unbiased genetic screen in Bacillus subtilis to find factors cells need to survive deadly clashes.

The screen flagged three hits, including two partner proteins called AddA and AddB. Follow-up tests showed the pair's unwinding activity matters, while its DNA-cutting activity does not. When a clash hits, the new DNA strands fold back into a reversed fork shape. AddAB unwinds that shape so the strands can rejoin their parents. The result is a whole fork again, ready to restart copying once the clash clears. The model explains a long-missing step in conflict repair.
pmc-13288902:
Hawa Sophia Bouzidi, Xavier De Lamballerie, and Franck Touret review dengue care in 2026. Dengue has four distinct virus types. No vaccine protects against all four well. No drug has wide approval yet. Some antibodies can even worsen the disease.

Live weakened vaccines have reached late trials. Lab-made antibodies now hit shared virus targets. New designs aim to cut the risk of harm. Some drug plans attack the virus head-on. Others target the human host instead. Strong lab results have been slow to reach clinics. The authors call for joint work across all three paths.
pmc-13289202:
Btissame Zouini and colleagues study pain sensitivity in children with ADHD in 2026. The work is a case-control study. It deals with central sensitization. That state means a heightened response to pain. Past work hints at a link with ADHD.

The set held 37 children with ADHD. It also held 29 children without it. Mean ages were near 12 and 13 years. Each child rated pain at the moment and across the prior week. A survey also went to one parent of each child. ADHD children scored far higher on sensitivity. They also hurt more now and that week. Parents of ADHD children scored high as well. Scores ran in families across the set.
pmc-13289302:
Lisa Wein headed a 2026 prospective two-arm study, called PRIA, on hard-to-treat side effects from cancer immune drugs. When steroids fail or cannot be stopped, doctors need a second option that calms immune harm without wiping out tumor control. The study compared extracorporeal photopheresis, a blood light treatment, with standard immune-suppressing drugs.

Each arm held 23 patients, covering 12 kinds of immune side effects across six tumor types and many body systems. Care ran for six cycles over 12 weeks, with checks on symptoms, quality of life, steroid dose, and tumor response. The blood treatment group needed far less steroid by week 12 and reported better quality of life scores. Response rates looked slightly higher too, though that gap was not statistically firm.
pmc-13289402:
Asantewaa Jones led a 2026 scoping review on physical activity and heart disease among African-born adults living in the United States. The team mapped what kinds of activity this group reports and how activity links to cardiovascular risk. Searches covered four databases for work published from 1990 to 2024 under standard scoping guidance.

From 258 records found, 17 papers passed full-text review for synthesis. The share meeting activity guidelines varied widely across studies, but inactivity was the broad pattern overall. Among active adults, walking stood out as the most common form reported in qualitative work. Gaps remain in device-based measures and in linking daily activity types to heart risk markers for this population.
pmc-13290102:
Ni Zhang and colleagues ask in 2026 which kinds of social media support actually move Chinese college students toward exercise. Many students get too little leisure-time physical activity, and support shared online is one possible lever, framed here through the theory of planned behavior.

The team surveyed students at one university in East China in 2022 and analyzed 310 valid replies with structural equation modeling. Companionship support showed the strongest positive link to exercise intention, both directly and through attitudes, and self-esteem support helped through attitudes as well. Informational support, by contrast, was tied to weaker intention through attitudes, suggesting that low-credibility content can backfire. Norms and perceived control did not carry the effects.
pmc-13292002:
Mariko Inoue and colleagues move a carbon dioxide conversion from batch pots to a continuous reactor in 2026. The reaction hydrogenates bicarbonate, made from captured carbon dioxide, into formate. Formate serves as a hydrogen carrier and industrial feedstock. A ruthenium catalyst works across three phases at once: gas, oil, and water. The team ran the mix in a stirred tank under fifty bar of hydrogen.

A viewing cell helped tune stirring so the three phases actually met. A kinetic model that includes the reverse reaction predicted how yield grows with residence time. That prediction let the team pick flow settings for high formate output. An antioxidant additive curbed the oxygen contamination that plagues flow systems. Catalyst recycling and phase separation were built into the same loop. The authors present the setup as a scalable frame for carbon utilization chemistry.
pmc-13292202:
Angela Medvedeva and colleagues ask which molecular descriptors explain peptide blood toxicity, in a 2026 analysis. Antimicrobial peptides can kill germs yet also burst red blood cells, a side effect called hemolysis. Models predict that toxicity well, but the reasons inside the models stay murky. The team compared sequence-derived descriptors with structure-based ones for interpretability. A trimmed descriptor set kept the predictions nearly intact.

Toxicity clustered with greasy patches on the peptide, striped polarity patterns, and exposed surface area. Certain two-letter sequence motifs also marked the dangerous peptides. Safer peptides tended to clump together more and placed polarizable building blocks early. Broader molecular descriptors added signals from repeating electronic patterns and local charge patches. The authors argue that representation choice is itself a source of insight. Their rules of thumb can guide design of germ-fighting peptides that spare blood. That balance is the field's central hurdle.
pmc-13292302:
Weina Zhang and co-authors follow a 2026 mouse study tracing where kidney cysts begin in nephronophthisis type 1, the commonest genetic cause of childhood kidney failure. They used mice lacking the Nphp1 gene, balanced by sex, at 8, 12, and 24 weeks of age. Cyst counts, serial tissue sections, segment markers, and 3D reconstruction mapped the process.

Cyst numbers jumped between 8 and 12 weeks, then held steady through 24 weeks, and cyst size barely changed. Tracing showed the cysts grew out of the distal convoluted tubule, which swelled in segments while staying connected to normal-looking neighbors. Cysts sat singly or in bead-like strings. Human cyst cells from patients matched the same origin. The authors say the work pins down the starting point of cyst formation in this disease.
pmc-13293402:
Debra L. Wohl and colleagues compare, in a 2026 study, mouth bacteria in Old Order Amish and non-Amish adults. The Amish live apart to keep a faith-based way of life, and their mouth microbes had not been described before.

Plaque and saliva from 14 Amish and 13 non-Amish people were read by gene sequencing, alongside surveys on dental habits. Amish participants visited dentists less and used fluoride less, yet brushed just as often. Variety of mouth species differed clearly between groups, and samples grouped by lifestyle factors. The same five main bacterial phyla dominated both groups, with one group lower in Amish mouths.
pmc-13293602:
Mohamed Ebraheem and co-authors review, in a 2026 paper, methods that explain how deep learning models judge voice and speech in health care. Voice markers promise cheap screening, yet black-box models raise trust and safety concerns for clinics.

The review followed standard steps across six databases for studies from January 2015 to February 2025 that explained model choices on voice data. Bias risk was checked with a prediction-focused tool. The team mapped which explanation methods are used, what clinical insights they gave, and how well they fit real users. Design advice for future voice tools closes the work, though study detail is limited here.
pmc-13294202:
Lihong Ye and colleagues lay out a protocol for switching off a chosen gene only in the lungs of mice, published in 2026. Such lung-specific knockout models help researchers trace how single genes drive lung disease. Their method starts with mice engineered so a target gene is flanked by marker sequences, then delivers the cutting signal through the airway rather than by breeding.

A virus carrying the Cre enzyme is sprayed into the trachea as a fine mist, so the gene is disabled in lung tissue while the rest of the body stays normal. The protocol also covers clearing whole lungs afterward, a process that makes tissue transparent for imaging. Steps are given in detail, from building the engineered mice to the nebulization and clearing procedures. The authors present the approach as a precise tool for studying lung disease mechanisms and testing future treatments.
pmc-13294902:
Victor Lorejan Pinto, Rafael A. L. Chioquetti, and Silvia H. P. Serrano build a titanium dioxide nanotube electrode that senses a common dye pollutant, in a 2026 electrochemistry study. Methylene blue colors factory waste water and resists natural breakdown, so cheap detection matters. The team grew neat nanotube arrays on titanium sheets, then ran current through them in a phosphate bath.

That step doped the tubes with a more conductive form of titanium and dressed the surface with phosphate. In acid, the dressed surface drew in the charged dye and piled it up for reading. Voltage scans showed how the pace of the reaction shifts with scan speed. The paired doping and coating sharpened the signal and kept readings steady, a model for tuned sensors.
pmc-13295002:
Yanhong Kang and colleagues map trial evidence on drug-free complementary therapies for knee osteoarthritis in a 2026 scoping review. The worn knee joint causes pain and disability for many adults, and hands-on or movement based options are widely used. Trials vary greatly in approach, comparison, and outcomes measured.

Searches of four databases for trials from 2016 to early 2026 gathered 53 randomised studies. Approaches ranged from acupuncture and manual therapy to exercise, mind-body programmes, and physical agents. Pain and physical function were measured most often, while quality of life and adherence appeared less consistently. The map shows a broad but uneven evidence base needing steadier designs.
pmc-13295102:
Ethan P Dudley, Brennen O Hunt, and Robert Valeris-Chacin test nose swabs for cattle immunity in a 2026 study. Mycoplasma bovis helps drive bovine respiratory disease, a costly feedlot problem. No checked test existed for measuring local antibodies at the nose surface where defences first meet the germ.

Stored swab washes came from 100 feedlot steers, half positive for the germ's DNA and half negative. A multi-target enzyme test was judged against DNA status and against a statistical model that estimates hidden antibody status. Two targets together reached high accuracy under the model, with strong agreement between operators. The approach offers a gentle way to track mucosal immunity in herds.
pmc-13295902:
Zeinab El Mawla and colleagues study, in 2026, a brain scan measure for predicting recovery after cardiac arrest. The grey-to-white matter ratio on early head scans reflects brain swelling, but hand measurement varies between readers and centres.

Records for 120 comatose patients with restored circulation were reviewed, using scans taken within a day. Higher ratios in every brain area tracked with better recovery at six months. An automated whole-brain measure performed best and predicted poor outcome on its own. The authors argue automation could make this early judgement more consistent across hospitals.
pmc-13296002:
Katerina Chavatza and colleagues ask, in 2026, whether keeping steroids during maintenance care prevents serious flare-ups in ANCA-associated vasculitis, a disease attacking small blood vessels. Records from three Greek centres covered 171 patients followed for a median of over seven years.

Steroid dose showed no link to lower risk of major relapse, while the drug rituximab did cut that risk. Higher steroid exposure instead tracked with more organ damage building up and more hospital admissions. Disease activity at diagnosis also raised relapse risk. The authors say the findings should inform long-term steroid decisions.
pmc-13296302:
Dana Patenaude, David McNaughton, and Rebecca DeLaMare report a 2026 study of video-based communication support for young children. The children were preschoolers with neurodevelopmental disabilities who watched a shared video alongside typically developing peers. Tappable hotspots on the video offered vocabulary the children could select to communicate.

All three children in the study used symbolic communication more often once the video displays were in place. Two showed very large gains and one showed a moderate gain. Peer interaction matters here, because shared activities give children reasons and chances to communicate. The authors suggest later work with less researcher help, plus checks on whether vocabulary itself grows through the activity.
pmc-13296802:
Monika Stefanska and co-authors profile, in 2026, immune cells inside mouse hearts during autoimmune myocarditis, an inflammation that can scar the heart into failure. Gene reading of over forty-six thousand heart cell nuclei at four time points mapped eighteen cell kinds and their chatter.

Resident macrophages dominated healthy hearts but collapsed when inflammation hit. Recruited macrophages flooded in, took over seventy percent of the group and stayed dominant into late remodelling, driving fiery signals and talking heavily with resting fibroblasts. Talks between cells peaked early, dipped, then rose again during repair. The authors pinpoint the macrophage handover as a driver worth targeting.
pmc-13297102:
Csaba Csutak and colleagues test whether CT texture can flag stroke patients likely to bleed after clot-busting treatment in a 2026 study. Bleeding into the brain is the feared complication of thrombolysis, and ordinary scans predict it poorly. Fifty treated patients from one centre were split by whether bleeding followed within a day.

Two texture measures of the infarcted area differed strongly between the groups. Their scores separated bleeders from non-bleeders with high accuracy in this small dataset. Such numbers could one day feed bleeding-risk models used before treatment. The authors label the work exploratory, citing the small sample, single centre, and lack of outside validation.
pmc-13297202:
Diren Beyoğlu and Jeffrey R. Idle review the two-way conversation between gut and lung microbes in a 2026 article. Gut bacteria ferment fibre into short-chain fatty acids and other products that travel to the lungs. Those molecules calm lung inflammation and support immune balance there.

Traffic also runs the other way, with lung microbes and their products able to disturb the gut. The review walks through asthma, chronic obstructive disease, cystic fibrosis, lung cancer, COVID-19, pneumonia, and tuberculosis. Diet, smoking, and vaping shape both microbial communities at once. The authors conclude that gut health forms a real part of lung health and disease.
pmc-13297302:
William García-Rodríguez and colleagues build graphene electrodes with a carbon dioxide laser for sensing histidine in fake sweat, in a 2026 study. Histidine is an amino acid whose levels in sweat can hint at health states. The electrodes were scribed onto plastic film, and planned test grids tuned laser speed, power, and line width.

The finished electrodes beat standard carbon electrodes in current tests, giving a far higher peak signal. They then sensed histidine in lab-made sweat with no added labels, with readings rising in a straight line across the tested range. Cheap, throwaway sensors of this kind could one day sit in wearables that track body chemistry during daily life.
pmc-13297402:
Yuan Shu and colleagues knit four fabrics modelled on bird feathers to keep older wearers comfortable outdoors, in a 2026 study. Feathers resist water, hold warmth, and let air pass, and each feather zone does so in its own way. The team copied down feathers, feather vanes, hooklets, and fluffy filaments into four knitted structures, then tested warmth, water resistance, airflow, and moisture handling.

Each structure led on a different measure. The first kept heat best, the second shed water and breathed best, and the fourth moved moisture vapour best. The third scored most balanced across all measures. Since older bodies heat and sweat unevenly by zone, the authors propose placing each fabric where its strength fits best.
pmc-13297502:
Daniela Taurino and a large team review whether a strong first drug regimen still lets lymphoma patients gather their own stem cells for transplant, in a 2026 single-centre study. The patients had aggressive B-cell lymphomas with high-risk traits, where standard results are often poor. The regimen, a dose-adjusted mix called R-DA-EPOCH, doubles as a platform for collecting stem cells from the blood.

Most patients gathered enough stem cells for the purpose. Transplant went ahead in over half the group, the grafts settled in predictably, and no death was tied to the transplant itself. The findings support the regimen as a workable first step for high-risk patients headed toward transplant.
pmc-13298302:
Qianqian Gao, Hongjie Pan, Yinglin Liu, and Naixi Chen simulate bank resolution choices when liquidity and credit risks interact, in a 2026 agent-based study. Their network holds banks, depositors, firms, and a central bank, letting plans play out over time. Resolution options included selling assets, expanding liabilities, granting debt relief, and extending debt maturities.

Selling assets helped at mid-level depreciation yet hurt when losses grew severe. Debt relief clearly made the whole system steadier, while extension helped only under certain liquidity settings and extension limits. Pairing debt relief with asset sales produced a positive synergy. The authors offer the results as guidance for joined, adaptive regulation.
pmc-13298502:
Doctors who treat brain aneurysms from inside the blood vessel often pick unlike plans for the same case. Sanjana R Salwi and her team show that spread in a 2026 survey. From June to September 2024, 108 doctors took case tales and named the fix they would choose.

Picks split hard by field of training. For burst cases, the scan group chose stent-aided coiling more than the brain and nerve groups did. Time in training, before or after flow tools came in, did not shift how often new tools were picked. Match scores were low, from 0.07 to 0.31 by type. The team call for work on why training steers these calls.
pmc-13298702:
Jakub Kwiatek and colleagues present a digitally planned implant case combining bone grafting and immediate restoration, in a 2026 case report. A patient needed ridge reconstruction plus implant therapy. Digital planning guided harvest of a bone cylinder from the same surgical site and its repositioning for augmentation, avoiding a second donor site.

A provisional crown shaped the soft tissue, and its profile was copied into a pre-designed final crown, streamlining delivery. Two years later, examinations showed stable hard and soft tissues without marginal bone loss or gum recession. The authors claim fewer stages and lower morbidity, while asking for larger prospective studies with cost analysis.
pmc-13299202:
Ndabereye Aubin Ndizeye and Makhutsisa Charlotte Mokoatle survey healthcare workers' trust in protective equipment during the COVID-19 years, in a 2026 study at a Johannesburg tertiary hospital. A structured survey took past accounts covering 2020 to 2022. Shortages forced reuse, while changing guidance bred confusion and falling confidence among staff.

Only a modest share believed the gear worked to prevent infection, and positive views tracked lower infection rates. Perception gaps across racial and occupational groups suggested risk communication missed some workers. The authors urge ongoing hands-on training for all staff groups, plus steady, fair supply tracked at ward level in poorer settings.
pmc-13299302:
Fatigue sits at the center of the symptom web for older people living with both hypertension and diabetes, find Xin Deng and co-authors in a 2026 network analysis. They surveyed 766 patients aged sixty and older in northern Xinjiang, China, mapping how their symptoms cluster and connect.

Fatigue was the most common complaint at 73.5% and also the most burdensome, ahead of dry mouth, pain, and dizziness. Symptoms grouped into three clusters spanning circulation and metabolism, endocrine and nerve effects, and general physical problems. Network statistics confirmed fatigue as the core node. The authors urge community nurses to screen for fatigue routinely and manage symptoms by cluster.
pmc-13299402:
Meryem Cansu Şahin, Ebru Başkaya, and Mihaela Tinca Udriștioiu compare workplace mobbing, gender role attitudes, and job satisfaction among radiation workers in Türkiye and Romania, in a 2026 cross-cultural study. Nearly two hundred healthcare staff completed three standard scales. Mobbing, meaning repeated hostile treatment at work, counts as a psychosocial hazard in radiology departments.

Job satisfaction fell as mobbing scores rose in both countries. Gender role attitudes linked to satisfaction and to mobbing only within the Romanian group, which shows culture shaping the pattern. The authors call for context-specific strategies tackling mobbing, gender perceptions, and work organisation to protect staff well-being.
pmc-13300002:
O Ventosa Blazquez and a large team map scar and slow-conduction zones in patients with dangerous ventricular rhythms after valve surgery, in a 2026 retrospective study. Seventeen ablation patients had heart scans defining scar and electrical mapping defining deceleration zones, then the two maps were compared segment by segment against valve positions.

Nearly every deceleration zone sat inside or beside scan-defined scar, mostly scar unrelated to heart attack. Zones clustered frequently around valve rings or prostheses, and most patients carried at least one such peri-valvular zone. The authors argue peri-valvular fibrosis forms an important rhythm substrate here, and mapping-guided ablation aimed there deserves larger prospective testing.
pmc-13300202:
Lycopene, the red pigment in tomatoes, gets a broad health audit in a 2026 review by Saleh A. Almatroodi and two colleagues. Drawing on cell and animal studies, the authors survey how the carotenoid acts on oxidative stress and inflammation, and where it might help across organ systems.

Reported benefits span protection for kidneys, liver, heart, and brain, plus roles against arthritis, obesity, and several cancers. The review also covers pairings with other compounds and nano-sized formulations meant to raise absorption. Poor water solubility and low uptake remain the main barriers, and the authors call for firmer dosing, safety, and interaction data from trials.
pmc-13300802:
Piotr Wróbel and co-authors run a randomized trial of socket preservation after tooth extraction in a 2026 dental study. Filling the empty socket with bone substitute aims to hold the ridge's shape for later implant work. Forty healthy patients were split into four groups by jaw site and material, receiving either human donor bone material or a bovine derived product, each sealed under a collagen membrane.

Imaging at one week and six months showed no significant difference between the materials in preserving ridge height or width. Both groups gained radiographic bone density over the healing period, with the bovine product ending significantly denser. Biopsies taken when implants were placed at six months went for microscopic analysis of the new bone. The authors conclude the materials tie on shape preservation, while the quality of the bone formed may still differ by material.
pmc-13300902:
Tianbo Kang and co-authors propose a mask refinement method for measuring tiny regular shapes under the microscope in a 2026 paper. Spheres, pores, and tubes in micro scenes are small, faint, and ragged edged, so ordinary segmentation outlines are too crude for precision measurement. Their framework starts with a segmentation pass boosted by adaptive super-resolution, then iterates, blending pixel evidence with the known geometry of the target to polish the outline toward a clean, continuous boundary.

On a sphere and tube assembly dataset, the method produced lower geometric errors on samples that could be fitted and raised the fitting success rate substantially. Removing either the dynamic super-resolution or the iterative refinement hurt performance, which the ablations read as proof both parts carry weight. The authors argue that baking geometric consistency into mask cleanup is the practical route to trustworthy micro measurement for assembly and quality control.
pmc-13301002:
Injecting treatment straight into a tumor can spark immune attack there and beyond, Vincent T Ma and colleagues survey in a 2026 review of intratumoral therapy for advanced melanoma. The field began with talimogene laherparepvec, a modified herpes virus that became the first oncolytic therapy approved for a solid tumor.

Newer viruses carry extra genetic tweaks, from fusogenic proteins to immune-stimulating payloads, aiming at stronger local killing and wider immune priming. Trials since 2010, alone and with checkpoint inhibitors, show better response rates and some lasting remissions even after checkpoint failure. Image-guided injection into deep lesions and use before surgery mark the newest directions, the authors note.
pmc-13301402:
T So and co-authors report stacking pulsed field energy on radiofrequency for ventricular tachycardia in a 2026 single center study. Eighteen patients treated between mid 2023 and late 2025 were split by whether operators added pulsed field deliveries, through a five spline catheter, after heat based work. Safety events and freedom from the rhythm over follow-up were the yardsticks.

Procedure and imaging times matched between the seven combined and eleven radiofrequency only cases. No pulsed field harm appeared: no blood breakdown, no clots, no coronary spasm, and no catheter injuries across a median of twenty-one applications per patient. The one heart block occurred in the radiofrequency group. Freedom from tachycardia at two years trended better with the combination, about eighty-six versus thirty-four percent, without reaching significance, though major cardiovascular events were fewer. The authors call the pairing safe and promising, with numbers too small for verdicts.
pmc-13302702:
A Saglietto and a multicentre team train, in a 2026 study, machine learning models to predict rhythm recurrence after pulsed field ablation for atrial fibrillation. Ablation slots are limited, so choosing patients most likely to benefit matters. Routine demographic, clinical, and ultrasound data from nineteen centres fed five candidate models.

The cohort held 1,688 patients, of whom about eighty-one percent stayed free of recurrence over roughly a year. A random forest performed best among the tested models, reaching moderate discrimination on unseen patients. Time between diagnosis and ablation was the single strongest predictor of recurrence, ahead of body mass index and upper-chamber size. The authors support model-guided selection to personalise who gets offered the procedure.
pmc-13302902:
Severe infection, autoimmunity, and inflammation mark whose thinking fades after long COVID, Iulia Elena Diaconu and colleagues track in a 2026 two-year study. Patients with neurological long COVID symptoms were split by baseline cognitive score, then matched on age, sex, and prior neurological illness, leaving fifty-four per group. Labs, vitamin levels, and brain imaging accompanied them over twenty-four months.

Among initially sharper patients, severe COVID, autoimmune disease, and a high neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio predicted decline. In the already-impaired group, diabetes joined autoimmunity and the same inflammation ratio, with stronger odds. Vitamin D levels tracked cognitive scores in both groups. The authors flag these factors as targets for early intervention trials.
pmc-13303202:
Signet ring cells in a stomach biopsy pointed at the wrong cancer, Amalia A. Sofianidi and colleagues warn in a 2026 case report. A fifty-two-year-old woman with metastatic lobular breast carcinoma, controlled since 2022 on hormone therapy and ribociclib, developed stomach pain and rising tumor markers. Biopsies showed diffuse adenocarcinoma with signet ring shapes and were first read as a new primary gastric cancer.

Expert review flipped the verdict: breast markers GATA3 and TRPS1 were positive, gut marker CDX2 negative, and E-cadherin lost, matching her breast tumor. Weekly paclitaxel followed. In lobular breast cancer patients, the authors insist, gastric signet ring findings demand a lineage panel before surgery is planned.
pmc-13303702:
Seong-Joon Kim, Sang-Jin Lee, and Sung-Deuk Choi report a 2026 field study of airborne volatile chemicals in small neighborhoods beside industrial complexes in Ulsan, South Korea. Such compounds are widely emitted and can harm health, yet tiny residential pockets near plants are rarely monitored.

Passive samplers at seven sites measured 59 compounds, with xylenes, toluene, and ethylbenzene most common. Levels rose near solvent-heavy industry, and pattern checks pointed to local sources within a few kilometers rather than distant drift. Only naphthalene passed a short-term non-cancer risk limit, while long-term risks stayed within accepted bounds.
pmc-13304402:
Yanyun Ru and colleagues build a computer method for tracking cracks in brittle solids in a 2026 engineering study. Sudden cracking threatens structures, and standard tools struggle to follow cracks that split and turn under fast loads.

Their peridynamics approach pairs a mesh-free solid model with an energy integral to compute crack-tip stress measures. Tests covered single and mixed crack types under still, slow, and fast loading, plus plates with holes that bend crack paths. Peak stress values under fast loads topped the still-load values, and crack branching was captured cleanly. Matches with theory and standard models confirmed accuracy.
pmc-13304702:
Tilek Kuanyshbekov and co-authors study membranes blending graphene oxide with a plant-based polymer in a 2026 materials report. Changing polymer share may tune strength, electric behavior, and moisture sensing in the same sheet.

Tests with infrared light, X-rays, microscopy, pulling, and electric meters tracked structure as polymer content rose. Layer gaps widened while crystal grains shrank, and sheets grew more even as polymer wrapped the flakes. Strength climbed a great deal, while dry electric resistance also rose. Wet air lowered resistance in a reversible way through water-assisted charge flow, suiting humidity sensors.
pmc-13305402:
Addisu Simachew Asgai leads a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis of bowel obstruction surgery outcomes in Ethiopia. Blocked bowel is a common surgical emergency, and results in low-resource hospitals vary widely between reports.

Twenty-one studies with 5,429 patients entered the pooled analysis. About one patient in four suffered a poor outcome, meaning complications or death in hospital, though rates swung widely by study. Arriving a day or more after symptoms began, staying over a week, and having bowel cut and rejoined each raised poor outcome odds. Earlier arrival and stronger ward care are urged.
pmc-13305502:
PingBo Zhang and DaWei Zhao share a 2026 case of breast cancer arising in both breasts at once with sharply different types. Paired cancers are uncommon, and mismatched biology between sides makes treatment planning genuinely hard.

A 51-year-old woman after menopause found a painless left breast lump, and scans flagged several spots on both sides needing checks. Both breasts were removed, and lab work proved two separate cancers: a triple-negative type with gland features on the right, and a mucus-rich hormone-linked type on the left. Tailored chemo and hormone care followed, and she stayed disease-free past thirty months.
pmc-13306002:
Larisa E. Botte reviewed methods for pulling fungal toxins out of complex samples in a 2026 survey of old and new techniques. Such toxins threaten food safety yet may also serve as farm pest controls, so clean separation matters for both aims.

Classic liquid extraction, cartridge cleanup and column methods suffer from weak selectivity, many steps and heavy solvent use in the authors' account. Newer ideas include designed crystals, pressurised fluid extraction, smart porous membranes and artificial intelligence guided by physical models. The review urges standard reporting so data can train prediction tools, moving isolation toward precise, greener practice.
pmc-13306102:
Faiza I. A. Abdella tested betanin, a natural pigment, on enzymes tied to obesity and diabetes in a 2026 lab and computer study. Red blood cells from humans were exposed to the compound to track sugar use and pathway switching.

Betanin slowed digestive enzymes more as dose rose, with half-blocking levels of 48.8 and 31.9 µg/mL for fat and starch enzymes in reported figures. Computer fits suggested tighter binding than two standard drugs used for comparison. The compound also switched on the energy sensor AMPK at low levels, supporting further checks as a metabolic aid.
pmc-13306502:
Riccardo Gaetano Cirrone reviewed how cheap light based water sensors are checked for truth in a 2026 scope review. Such tools could widen lake and stream watch, most of all for town led work, yet proof of truth is rare.

Forty studies were read for how they showed sense skill, truth, fine grain and repeat runs next to lab tools. Most gave sense limits, while full truth checks stayed thin and mixed across the set. The team gives a plan to make checks firm, so cheap tools can earn trust next to bench gear in the field.
pmc-13307602:
Giulia Russo and co-authors review in 2026 how to judge cat welfare in animal assisted services, where cats now join therapy, learning, and support work. A first broad search found no study that dealt squarely with welfare checks for cats in that setting, so they searched again by topic.

The wider search sorted known checks into health, behaviour, and body measures such as stress signals. No single check can capture welfare alone, so the authors favour a combined protocol that draws on all three fields. Vets, handlers, and researchers could use that mix to watch cats during sessions and to pull a cat out when strain shows.
pmc-13308302:
Lukas Trzebiatowski and co-authors review twenty-five years of studies in 2026 on how events during calving itself shape calf sickness and death on dairy farms. Four factor groups were covered: calving management, birth monitoring, induced birth, and difficult birth. Problems around birth echo through the calf's first weeks.

Every factor group influenced deaths immediately after birth in the gathered literature. Management quality and difficult birth also affected survival up to weaning. Good monitoring and preventing difficult births improved the calf's uptake of antibody-rich first milk. Morbidity fell when calving was managed properly across the board. The authors aim the synthesis at farmers who want healthier calves and at public reassurance. Birth is a short window with long consequences, and their review shows where attention pays off.
pmc-13308702:
Zheng Liu and co-authors recount in 2026 a rare case of bowel telescoping in an adult, caused by a lone Peutz-Jeghers polyp that mimicked colon cancer. The patient, a man aged 30 years, had a year of on and off belly pain and sickness, with no skin pigment marks and no family tale of polyps.

Direct checks during surgery found the true site in the end of the small bowel, which spared a needless colon cut. Gene reads found fresh changes in POLE and EXO1, and no change in the classic syndrome gene.
pmc-13309002:
Łukasz Lamch and colleagues build in 2026 a family of two-headed magnetic surfactants, soap-like compounds whose partner ions contain iron and answer to magnets. Three chain lengths were made and checked with several spectral methods. Heat traits, surface activity, and magnet response were set against simpler one-headed magnetic surfactants.

Cooling speed decided whether the compounds sat in uniform or layered phases, sometimes both side by side. pmc-13309202:
Brian Yu Chieh Cheng and co-authors report in 2026 neuroinvasive eastern equine encephalitis, a rare grave mosquito borne brain disease, in a healthy woman aged 56 years in Ontario. She came to urgent care in late July with four days of fever, headache, nausea, and vomiting, a week after mosquito bites at a lake.

Spinal fluid showed a white cell surge with high protein, and early scans could not split germ, herpes, or mosquito causes apart. Age over 50 years raises the risk of brain spread, and warm season growth may widen the map for this virus.
pmc-13309502:
Maha Kabil and co-authors introduce a virus that kills drug-resistant staph germs in a 2026 study of wound infection. The germ, MRSA, resists standard drugs and often infects chronic and surgical wounds. Viruses that infect bacteria, called phages, offer a targeted option when drugs fail.

Its gene map showed no genes for dormancy, harm, or drug resistance. In infected mice, cream with the phage cut germ counts and sped wound closing, matching a phage-plus-drug mix. The authors propose it as a wound treatment candidate.
pmc-13309602:
Cornelia Westerberg and co-authors engineer small binding proteins that block an immune signal in a 2026 study. The authors offer collagen tails as a general way to triple other binders.
pmc-13309902:
Karim Lakhdar and co-authors present a 2026 case of seizures as the first sign of high pressure inside the skull. The patient, a 41-year-old woman, had two weeks of severe headache before full-body seizures began. Her eye exam and brain scan pointed away from the usual seizure causes.

Eye checks showed swollen optic discs on both sides, and imaging showed an empty sella, a flattened pituitary space tied to raised skull pressure. A spinal tap measured pressure at 32 cm H2O with normal fluid makeup, matching idiopathic intracranial hypertension in the report. Hormone tests found one low pituitary signal. Two pressure-lowering drugs brought fast relief, pressure normalized, and seizures did not return.
pmc-13310102:
Seunghye Jang and colleagues tackle a materials flaw in 2026 that limits sodium-rich Prussian Blue, a cheap and promising sodium-ion battery cathode. The team instead drove out crystal water at room temperature by bubbling nitrogen through the synthesis mixture.

Sodium-ion batteries appeal because sodium is abundant and inexpensive compared with lithium. A gentler dehydration step could lift cathode stability without extra processing cost. The authors frame surface chemistry, not bulk composition, as the decisive lever for quality.
pmc-13310502:
Wu-lan Ao and co-authors review non-invasive brain stimulation for chronic insomnia in a 2026 article. Long-term insomnia dulls daytime function and raises mental and heart-metabolic risks. Talking therapy and drugs help many, yet access gaps, partial response, relapse, and side effects leave others searching.

Four stimulation routes are weighed: magnetic pulses, weak direct current, alternating current, and ear vagus nerve stimulation. Studies suggest gains in felt sleep quality and some measured sleep traits, but results vary widely by target, dose, schedule, and patient type. The authors argue for tailoring stimulation to patient profiles rather than one fixed recipe, a shift they call precision neuromodulation.
pmc-13310602:
Food Safety Commission of Japan presents a 2026 risk assessment of oxolinic acid, an antimicrobial used in crops and animals. Safe intake levels rest on how the chemical moves through bodies and where its harms begin.

Evidence spans fate in animals, humans, and plants, residues in crops and livestock foods, and toxicity tests from short-term to cancer and two-generation breeding studies. Main harms centered on slowed weight gain, testis and ovary changes in rats, and excitatory nerve signs. No fertility harm, birth defects, or meaningful gene damage appeared. The authors derive safe levels from the lowest no-harm dose found.
pmc-13310702:
Ji Li and co-authors report a 2026 case study and review on stomach surgery for adults with Prader-Willi syndrome and very severe obesity. The syndrome drives constant hunger, low energy use, and hard behavior issues, so weight loss care is complex. The team judged safety and weight change after sleeve surgery in this group.

One man aged 24 years had the operation after full team review, and his early recovery was smooth. Past studies show only modest weight loss, plus lasting needs for food checks, behavior support, and close follow up. The authors advise against routine use and urge careful case choice, with drug and breathing aids as added options.
pmc-13311202:
Huihui Sun and co-authors build a light edge model to spot wildlife and cut junk camera trap photos in a 2026 study. Remote cameras fire on wind and heat shifts, flooding scholars with empty frames and draining power. A single field ready model that filters fakes and names animals could run on the device itself.

Their WS-YOLO design adds wave based feature pulls, joint space and channel focus, and a loss that stresses hard border cases. Tests on four wildlife sets gave strong accuracy scores, led by tiger and park infrared sets. Running on a small Jetson board proved real time, low power field use.
pmc-13311302:
Md Fuad Al Fidah and co-authors examine a 2026 surveillance study of malnutrition in Bangladeshi teens who came to care with diarrhea. Growth faltering in the teen years can shape adult health.

Records covered 1597 patients aged 10 to 19 seen at a Dhaka hospital from 2012 to 2023. Stunting affected 29.6 percent and thinness 24.3 percent across the years in this group. Stunting fell from 40.8 percent in 2012 to 25.7 percent in 2023, while thinness edged up. Older age raised stunting odds, while a mother's schooling past primary level and richer households lowered them. Girls were less often thin.
pmc-13311702:
Ruben Mijnster and co-authors present the NISONE trial protocol in a 2026 article. The trial tests personal N-of-1 studies for people who quit statins over muscle symptoms, to sort true drug effects from nocebo effects.

The trial will enroll 249 patients with artery disease or inherited high cholesterol who stopped two or more statins. Two thirds get the personal study path: four blinded six-week rounds of statin or dummy pills, with symptoms logged in an app, then a feedback round. The rest get usual care. The goal is to restart statins safely where fear, not the drug, caused the symptoms.
pmc-13312002:
Yoseph M Habte and co-authors report the 2026 case of Chilaiditi sign found by chance in a healthy young woman during routine pre-travel screening. The sign, bowel looped between liver and diaphragm, can mimic a surgical emergency.

The 28-year-old had no symptoms, a normal exam, and normal labs. Her chest X-ray showed a gas-filled colon loop with fold markings under the right diaphragm and no free air. With the classic picture and no complaints, no further tests or treatment were done. The authors stress matching the image to the patient before rushing to procedures for what is often a harmless variant.
pmc-13313002:
Martin Milata and colleagues validate, in a 2026 multicenter study, a bedside sleep questionnaire against wrist actigraphy in hospital patients, and ask whether either can warn of delirium. Poor sleep is a known delirium risk, but general wards need a cheap way to spot it, and the Richards-Campbell questionnaire's agreement with objective recording was untested in this setting.

Across seven Czech institutions, 133 patients contributed 424 nights of paired questionnaire answers and MotionWatch recordings. Patients rated their sleep moderately good even when the recorder showed it badly broken. Only the questionnaire's sleep-depth item lined up meaningfully with the device, and the total score tracked objective sleep weakly. Subjective ratings did not predict delirium at all, while low measured sleep efficiency did, marking the wearable, not the form, as the useful risk signal.
pmc-13313202:
Weronika Pawlik leads a 2026 study that hunted through human RNAs for tracts of CAG repeats, the DNA pattern that grows too long in some brain diseases. Such tracts sit in many RNAs and have lengthened over evolution, and they may aid nerve cell work when kept at normal size.

One round RNA was traced in the cell fluid and in protein-making fractions, and was found in skin cells, blood, and cerebellum. Most striking, the team found a round RNA that carries a mutation, which may matter for how that ataxia unfolds.
pmc-13313302:
Zhongqin Huang reviews, in a 2026 article, the long-running question of whether gallbladder removal raises colorectal cancer risk. Huang argues the answer runs through gut microbes and a bile acid sensor called FXR. Gallbladder surgery is among the world's most common operations. Population patterns keep recurring. Cancers favor the proximal colon, risk runs higher in women, and incidence peaks five to fifteen years after surgery.

The mechanistic story centers on changed bile flow reshaping the gut community. Some protective bacteria shrink and others expand. Bile acid mixtures shift in ways that suppress FXR signaling. One 2025 study showed this suppression loosening FXR's restraint on a growth pathway and promoting tumors. An FXR-activating drug prevented the effect in animals, though toxicity limits its use in people. Huang proposes personal risk scoring from demographics, microbial signatures, and metabolic markers. That scoring would pair with gut-restricted drugs, probiotics, and Mediterranean-style eating.
pmc-13313802:
Haitham Elaadli and seven colleagues measure exposure to Chlamydia abortus, a bacterium that causes abortion in sheep and can pass to humans, in northern Egypt. They tested 196 sheep and 242 women with a history of abortion at an Alexandria hospital using antibody assays.

About twelve percent of sheep carried antibodies, with breed, governorate, breeding system, pregnancy status, and abortion history all shaping risk. The authors present the first human seroprevalence data for the region and a One Health warning about occupational exposure around lambing.
pmc-13314002:

pmc-13314202:
Hao Xie and a large team review MTA2, a gene-control protein, across diseases in a 2026 paper. MTA2 sits at the core of the Mi-2 chromatin remodeling complex and shapes gene activity through epigenetic control and many signal paths.

The authors weigh MTA2 as a sign for diagnosis and as a drug target, and they survey plans to block its control network. They close with the push for sharp, specific blockers of MTA2, which could turn a broad control protein into a precise point of care.
pmc-13314502:
Dongdong Zhang and co-workers report a 2026 case of an autoimmune brain and cord disorder with two rare twists. The disease, GFAP astrocytopathy, stems from antibodies against a cell protein and usually shows as brain and cord inflammation, often with clear brain scan changes.

Spinal fluid held high pressure, extra cells, raised protein, and a share of 10 percent eosinophils on cell study, as stated in the report, a rare find in this disease. pmc-13315002:
Zong-Xia Yu and co-workers build the chromosome-level genome of a medicinal mint kin from high land, in a study put out in 2026. Mosla chinensis is a prized herb with few gene resources for sharp breeding.

Repeats fill much of the genome, and a species own duplication event stands out. pmc-13315502:

pmc-13315802:

pmc-13315902:

pmc-13316202:

pmc-13316302:

pmc-13317202:

pmc-13317702:

Magnetic resonance measurements showed faster lithium ion movement, and titration tests showed quicker reaction kinetics. pmc-13318702:

pmc-13318902:

pmc-13319302:

pmc-13320502:

pmc-13320602:

pmc-13320702:

pmc-13321002:

Later steps check that resistance is real, test whether it spills over to other drugs, and run a measured cell killing assay. pmc-13321302:

pmc-13322502:

pmc-13323302:

pmc-13323502:

Support from the institution and professional development shaped how far those gains went, and interviews added context on daily classroom use. The authors frame AI adoption as a belief-shaping change, not only a technical one.
pmc-13323802:

pmc-13325902:

pmc-13326302:
Ephrem Kedir, Temesgen Teklu Alemayehu, and Mihiretu Tesfamriam Goshu present a study from twenty twenty-six on cesarean births at a hospital in southern Ethiopia. Just over two thirds had first stage surgery. Harm rates ran near a quarter for mothers and near a third for babies. Second stage surgery carried far higher odds of harm for both mother and baby. The team urges strong readiness for surgical snags and fast baby revival in late cases.
pmc-13327102:

Blood thinners were started and later scans showed no bleeding, showing how wide imaging can link separate events to one source.
pmc-13327402:

Variation among brands ran from 20.8 percent for carbamazepine liquid up to 1604.4 percent for clonazepam 0.5 mg tablets, and median brand prices sat above the generic prices throughout. Wide gaps like these can push poorer patients to skip doses, so the authors press for wider use of the cheap scheme.
pmc-13327802:
Yuichi Kato and co-authors test knee-watching cameras as a movement alarm during prostate radiotherapy in a 2026 study. Movement of at least 4 mm showed up in 357 sessions, 14.1 percent of the total, grew more common late in sessions, and often hinted at a full bladder or urge to urinate. Bladder volume predicted both average shift and the share of large shifts. One patient's motion eased after a spoken prompt, showing the value of live detection for keeping dose on target.
pmc-13327902:
