pmc-13328402:
Luca Jokic and co-authors test overlooked light colors on basil photosynthesis in a 2026 study. Growers long assumed green light feeds plants poorly, based on old action spectra, and most trials still use just three standard wavelengths. The team measured fluorescence and gas exchange in basil under extra colors at strengths up to 5000 units on their irradiance scale.

Colors inside the supposed green gap gave the highest carbon dioxide uptake rates, ahead of deep blue and reddish light, a surprise against textbook ranking. Topping white light with shorter wavelengths worked best at a 25 percent share in the blends tried. Fine color tuning could raise yields in indoor farms, the authors suggest.
pmc-13328902:
Bushu Harna, Dinesh Sandal, and Shivali Arya review salvage hip replacement after failed thigh bone nails in a 2026 study. Nails are often used for breaks between the hip and shaft, but screws can cut out, slip back, or break, and bones may fail to heal. The group studied 59 patients who later had hip replacement.

Surgeons used either partial or full hip replacement, chosen for each patient. Removing old hardware and filling bone gaps made surgery hard. Problems after surgery included dislocation, deep vein clots, and new breaks near the implant. Average hip function at 24 months reached a Harris Hip Score of 79.2 in the reported follow-up. Careful choice and technique matter, the authors conclude.
pmc-13329502:
Jianguang Li and a large team test a plant tannin feed for broiler chickens in a 2026 trial. Tannic acids from Chinese gallnuts were added to feed as limits on antibiotic growth promoters grow. In total, 224 one-day-old male Ross 308 chicks were housed in 28 cages for a 35-day trial with four diets.

Diets were plain feed, plain feed plus one of two antibiotics, or plain feed plus the gallnut product. The gallnut diet improved feed conversion in early growth phases compared with plain feed in the reported results. Gut lining height rose and surface thickness fell, hinting at better uptake. Gut microbe diversity did not shift. The authors present the additive as a useful feed option.
pmc-13330802:
Daniel Schwarte and colleagues report two tin compounds and an unusual decay path in a 2026 crystal study. A 1 to 3 mix of isopropyltin iodide with pyridine N-oxide formed a previously unknown complex. Left in solvent over long storage, part of it broke down into a mixed tin(IV) and tin(II) salt, claimed as the first of its kind.

Both compounds are ionic, the authors report. Each holds an octahedral tin cation with three base molecules in a facial layout and two iodine atoms side by side. Balance comes from a lone iodide in the first salt and from a tri-iodide tin(II) anion in the second. That anion links into chains through weak tetrel bonds.
pmc-13331902:
Dragoș-Cătălin Vovea and Vasile Chiș built a 2026 machine learning model that predicts how long organic dye molecules keep glowing after excitation, a property called fluorescence lifetime. Measuring it in the lab is slow, so a fast estimate could speed screening for imaging probes, sensors, and light-based devices.

They trained tree-based models on molecule and solvent data from the Deep4Chem database, encoding structure with computed descriptors and fingerprints plus features for how molecule and solvent interact. LightGBM performed best, reaching a mean error of 0.8324 ns and an R² of 0.7523 under cluster-split cross-checks, with the weakest accuracy at very short and very long lifetimes where data are sparse. Checks against quantum calculations and fresh experiments supported the trends, and importance analysis pointed to quantum yield and molecular shape as leading drivers.
pmc-13332002:
Yasunori Matsuzaki and colleagues spent a decade testing virus shells meant to carry genes across the blood-brain barrier, and report the head-to-head results in marmosets in 2026. Gene delivery into the whole brain could help many brain diseases, but most engineered adeno-associated virus capsids were proven only in mice.

Using one shared protocol, the team gave eleven capsid variants, mostly derived from AAV9, plus plain AAV9 by vein injection and measured reporter glow across the whole brain. Most celebrated variants, including ones from their own screening, did no clearly better than AAV9 in the primates. One, VCAP-102, stood out with far stronger brain-wide expression, more vector copies in the cortex, and most marked cells being neurons. The authors offer the comparison as a benchmark and VCAP-102 as a leading candidate for whole-brain gene therapy.
pmc-13332402:
Patrick J Lao and a large team used three kinds of brain scan in a 2026 study to test whether inflammation sits between amyloid, tau, and tissue loss in Alzheimer's disease. Microglia, the brain's resident immune cells, can turn chronically hostile, and the team measured their density with a dedicated PET tracer.

The study covered 46 people, 21 thinking normally and 25 impaired, all scanned for amyloid, tau, microglia, and grey matter volume across 13 regions. In impaired participants, high microglia density overlapped with tau in 10 regions. That is more than with amyloid in 8 or shrinkage in 4. Statistical paths showed inflammation carrying part of tau's link to tissue loss. In people without amyloid, tau-linked damage still ran through inflammation. The authors suggest glial cells as a treatment target against tau-driven decline.
pmc-13333302:
Yu Liang and colleagues compare 2026 anti-CD20 therapies with steroids in IgA kidney disease with minimal change disease. In this combined disease, the efficacy of anti-CD20 antibodies and the profile of nephrin antibodies remain poorly understood. The retrospective cohort compared anti-CD20 antibodies, or combined short-course low-dose steroids, against full-dose prolonged steroids, and measured nephrin-antibody rate. Forty-five adult patients with the combined disease were studied.

Total remission rates for nephrotic syndrome were comparable between the antibody group and the steroid group. Notably, the antibody group achieved a longer relapse-free period after complete remission, a median of about thirty months versus about seventeen months. The antibody group also had significantly fewer total adverse events and return hospital stays. Nephrin antibodies in blood were detected in about thirty-one percent of patients tested.
pmc-13333402:
Magali de Sauvage and Jeffrey Patterson-Fortin describe a rare chemotherapy side effect in a 2026 case report: a painful vulvar reaction after a single cycle of treatment for rectal cancer. Mouth sores are a familiar cost of fluoropyrimidine drugs, but vulvar involvement is almost unheard of.

The 53-year-old woman had stage IIA rectal adenocarcinoma and was receiving modified FOLFOX-6 before surgery when the acute mucocutaneous reaction appeared. A low-strength steroid cream failed and pain grew, so care stepped up to a high-strength steroid cream, topical lidocaine, and vaginal estradiol. Timing and appearance pointed to a drug reaction, possibly a fixed drug eruption. The team then dropped the 5-fluorouracil bolus from later cycles while keeping the rest of the plan, and she finished all planned rounds with no return of the reaction. The authors say the tweak preserved treatment strength while preventing a repeat.
pmc-13334402:
Diwakar Suresh and colleagues test 2026 whether aiming at AATF rewires the tumor surroundings and curbs liver cancer through MIR100HG-TGF-beta signals. Liver cancer, a leading cause of cancer death, has a dynamic and varied tumor surroundings driving progression and treatment resistance. The team earlier showed that cell-death-blocking gene factor AATF drives blood vessel growth in liver cancer, yet its role in the surroundings remained unstudied. A mouse model implanted human liver cancer cells into the liver.

Liver switching off was achieved by tail vein injection of adeno-associated virus 8 carrying mouse siAATF or siControl. Tissue, chemical, and molecular studies plus whole-genome gene readouts mapped to mouse and human genomes studied tumor and surroundings parts apart. Switching off AATF in the surroundings clearly reduced tumor growth versus controls and disrupted inflammation, immune response, blood vessel growth, and outer matrix reshaping.
pmc-13335402:
Nur Aziemah Mohd Fauzi and co-authors checked the quality of health literacy questionnaires used with Asian schoolchildren in a 2026 full review. Many instruments exist, but weak measurement properties can make their scores meaningless.

Using PRISMA guidance, the team searched three sources for studies from 2013 to 2023 involving children aged 6 to 18 that graded measurement quality. Ten studies made the cut and were judged with the COSMIN checklist. Across 90 checklist items, only 25 rated very good, concentrated in structural validity, while internal consistency drew the most inadequate ratings and reliability the most doubtful ones. The patchy record tells schools and researchers to choose tools with care and to demand better proof before trusting scores.
pmc-13336002:
Katarzyna Kuncewicz and colleagues present 2026 AI-designed cyclic peptides enabling controllable modulation of the CD28 immune checkpoint. Immune checkpoint treatments have transformed immune therapy but remain dominated by bio agents characterized by long receptor hold and limited drug control. Although multiple classes of immune-tuning drugs exist, synthetic types capable of directly targeting outside-cell immune checkpoint protein-protein contact points while enabling controllable immune modulation remain less explored.

The authors report an AI-guided strategy for discovering cyclic peptide blockers of the helper receptor CD28. The lead peptide, CIP-3, binds the CD28 outside-cell domain with tight binding and breaks CD28-ligand interactions. In primary human immune systems, CIP-3 blocks CD28-dependent T-cell firing without built-in agonist activity and exhibits rapid drug switch-off, enabling dose control of immune signals. In a T-cell transfer model of chronic colitis, CIP-3 confers dose-based defense.
pmc-13336102:
Michael Haug and co-authors unveiled the MyoRobot 3.0, a 2026 biomechatronics platform that measures single muscle fibers while watching them. Older rigs assumed a fiber keeps its shape during stretch, an assumption this device was built to test.

The system couples automated force measurement with a motorized optical setup that tracks the same fiber segment as it elongates. Stretching fibers to 40 percent strain thinned their diameter by about 13 to 15 percent, cutting cross-sectional area by roughly 27 percent and making uncorrected stress values systematically too low. Slow continuous stretch recordings revealed calcium-dependent stiffening that rapid step protocols missed entirely. The platform gives muscle physiologists a way to pair exact structure with function in one experiment.
pmc-13336702:
Peng Liu and co-authors build a brain-mimicking gel for traumatic brain injury in a 2026 study. Low oxygen and inflammation drive much of the damage that follows the first impact. A danger signal called S100A8 fuels harmful talk between neurons and microglia, the brain's immune cells. Their gel, HPC@Gel, carries altered hemoglobin particles plus curcumin-based carbon dots.

In cell models the gel lowered S100A8 and calmed the neuron-microglia crosstalk; adding S100A8 back partly undid the benefit. In rats with a cortical injury, the gel eased low oxygen, cut inflammation, and supported nerve regrowth. Treated animals recovered better movement and thinking. Aiming at oxygen and immune signals together offers a fuller repair strategy.
pmc-13336802:
Take Hirooka, Zhaolin Liu, Ivan P Parkin, and Guanjie He review carbon cathodes for zinc-ion hybrid supercapacitors in a 2026 article. These water-based devices promise safe, cheap storage that blends battery-like energy with capacitor-like power and long life. The cathode largely sets performance, and porous carbons lead the field.

The review sorts recent cathode families, from activated and template-made carbons to framework-derived and biomass-derived ones. It weighs how pore shape, surface chemistry, and conductivity shape zinc storage. Added atoms and hybrid mixes get critical attention as routes to higher output. Gaps remain in pore control and in understanding how storage really works. The survey charts design rules for cheaper, safer grid and portable storage.
pmc-13337002:
Yu-E. Wang and co-authors build a self-fueling nanoplatform against colon cancer in a 2026 study. Their hollow manganese dioxide particles carry a lactate-burning enzyme and a light-sensitive dye, coated to home to tumor cells bearing CD44. Tumors hoard lactate, so burning it both starves them and reshapes their surroundings.

The enzyme turns lactate into pyruvate and hydrogen peroxide, which react with the carrier to release oxygen. Acid speeds the carrier's breakdown, freeing dye and manganese ions. Near-infrared light then drives dye-based heat and radical therapy while manganese sparks more radicals. The loop feeds itself, easing low oxygen as it attacks. Strong tumor suppression in animals supports metabolism-first cancer therapy.
pmc-13337402:
Haider H. Motlak, Mahmoud Elshal, and Marwa S. Serrya test a liver shield against a common drug's toxicity in a 2026 rat study. Methotrexate fights cancer and calms immunity, but dose-linked liver damage limits its use. The team induced injury with one injection and gave the NLRP3 blocker dapansutrile by mouth for seven days.

Methotrexate alone spiked liver enzymes, scarred tissue under the microscope, drained antioxidants, and fired inflammatory pathways that end in a fiery cell death called pyroptosis. It also stalled the liver's recycling system. Dapansutrile at both tested doses eased nearly every measure, damping oxidation, cytokines, and cell death while restoring recycling balance. The results nominate inflammasome blocking as a companion strategy for methotrexate users.
pmc-13337602:
Heinrich and co-authors grade PET scans for tumors that cause tumor-induced osteomalacia. These small phosphaturic tumors waste phosphate and soften bone. The study held 20 patients with suspected disease at one center. Scans targeted somatostatin receptors on tumor cells. Lab marks and clinical exams were tracked at follow-up visits.

Tumors were found in 12 patients, or 60 percent of the group. Those tumors were removed and confirmed by immunohistochemistry. Phosphate handling marks ran lower when tumors were found. FGF23 rise did not split the two groups clearly. Total lesion uptake tied inversely to phosphate recovery marks.
pmc-13337702:
Yun Zheng heads a 2026 search for better blood markers of rheumatoid arthritis. Lasting joint inflammation in this autoimmune disease slowly damages joints, and current markers lack accuracy. The team combined large gene datasets with single-cell data to find stronger candidates.

Machine learning and expression checks pointed to three genes: CD74, PGLYRP1, and TXN. Further work mapped their pathways, immune setting, and possible drug binding, using docking and motion simulations. Single-cell data showed which cell groups carried the signals. Tests on clinical samples with PCR, blotting, and tissue staining confirmed the pattern, supporting the three genes as candidate markers for diagnosis and study.
pmc-13337802:
Lynn A. Cialdella-Kam and co-authors evaluate a phone app for new Navy recruits in a 2026 study. Future Sailors in the Delayed Entry Program must build fitness and knowledge before basic training. The CoachMePlus app delivered general training, nutrition, and exercise modules with recruiter tracking.

A total of 92 recruits aged 18 to 28 enrolled, logging in about twice daily on average. Weight and body fat were checked monthly, and food logs were reviewed by a dietitian. Most recruits, 92.4 percent in the reported count, finished basic training. Knowledge of training and nutrition improved during the program, supporting app-guided preparation before service begins.
pmc-13340202:
Chapter 11 of a reference work on fish lesions, published in 2026, covers the respiratory system. Wes Baumgartner leads a large author team describing how gills work and how they change in disease. Beyond moving oxygen and carbon dioxide, gills also clear nitrogen waste, balance salts, and guard against harmful agents in the water.

Readers learn how gill cells such as mucous and chloride cells adjust to shifts in gases, temperature, pH, and pollutants. Crucian carp show how gills can remodel when oxygen falls, while pollution can shrink the exchange surface through extra pavement cells and mucus. For pathologists, these responses help separate normal adaptation from damage.
pmc-13341502:
Pairing a black seed compound with standard chemotherapy rewires death pathways in colon cancer cells, in a 2026 study by Natalia Kurowska and colleagues. RKO cells received thymoquinone, 5-fluorouracil, or both for 24 hours before genome-wide expression profiling.

The combination reshaped networks for apoptosis, stress response, and proliferation without classic synergy in the math sense. Genes such as FAS and CYLD tied into stronger death signaling, while BIRC3 and EIF2AK3 marked adaptive, resistance-leaning responses. Validation by PCR and protein blotting backed the array data. Thymoquinone looks less like a direct killer and more like a context-dependent tuner of drug response.
pmc-13341602:
Why reinforcement learning struggles outside simulations is organized by Amar Ahmad and coauthors in their 2026 tutorial survey. Systems that beat humans at games still falter in the real world, and the authors blame four statistical limits rather than engineering gaps.

The four are sample inefficiency, nonstationarity as environments shift, partial observability that breaks the Markov assumption, and dimensionality that explodes exploration needs. Known lower bounds from theory are reviewed for each, plus mitigations like model-based methods, robust formulations, memory architectures, and hierarchies. Safety, explainability, and multi-agent issues are flagged as related but distinct concerns for deployment.
pmc-13343402:
Marta Goglia and co-authors open volume two of a research collection on proctology and colorectal surgery with a 2026 editorial. Colorectal care is shifting fast. Robotic and keyhole methods, dye-guided surgery, enhanced recovery paths, and precision cancer plans are all spreading. The editors frame the gathered studies within that change.

The studies span checks before surgery, new tools in the operating room, recovery care, cancer prediction, and hard cases. One highlighted study uses MRI markers in rectal cancer to flag aggressive features and tailor treatment tiers. Aging patients, frailty, and new tools such as immunotherapy and artificial intelligence raise complexity throughout. The editors cast modern colorectal care as personal, team-based, and guided by biology.
pmc-13344202:
Anna Marie Pacheco Young and colleagues tested perinatal quality drives in 2026 for reducing caesarean gaps in the United States. Racial and ethnic gaps exist in caesarean rates and reasons, prompting quality drives targeting drivers of inequity. Few studies had assessed whether those drives actually narrow gaps.

The look back cohort took in 3,629 first time mothers with full term, live born, singleton pregnancies in vertex position. They delivered at a large academic tertiary centre from October 2019 through December 2022. Caesarean rates and reasons before and after perinatal quality drives, aimed at more vaginal births and fairer care, were weighed. The study tests whether quality improvement can close equity gaps in childbirth.
pmc-13345802:
Ricardo Ortiz-Lozada and Pablo Salinas argue, in a 2026 commentary, that better stents alone will not fix coronary intervention outcomes in diabetes. Diabetes now fills nearly 40 percent of all stent procedures, and patients keep facing higher rates of heart death, heart attack, and repeat treatment than others despite steady device gains.

Diffuse disease, small vessels, and diabetes-specific vessel changes, including endothelial cells turning mesenchymal, keep arteries primed for failure across every platform, from coated stents to drug balloons. Trial history shows each new design's edge fading against this biology. The authors urge unified care: best drug therapy and healthy habits wrapped around any device, rather than chasing innovation in hardware alone.
pmc-13347802:
Kamilla R. Snyman, Jacques R. Snyman, and Angelique Coetzee compare iron products for treating low iron, in a prescribing review published in 2026. Iron drives oxygen carriage, DNA building, and energy flow, yet excess harms tissue. Shortage is the most common mineral lack, touching about 20 percent of people worldwide by the cited estimate.

Anaemia shares tied to iron lack are given for young children and women, noting that low iron without anaemia is even more common in clinic visits. The review weighs how well each iron complex works and how well patients tolerate it, aiming for patient-centred choices rather than habit picks when doctors write iron prescriptions.
pmc-13348402:
Muritala Issa Bale and colleagues report a draft genome for a drug-resistant staph strain from a caesarean wound in Nigeria, in an announcement from 2026. Strain MB02 was swabbed in July 2024 from a 32-year-old woman at a teaching hospital in Ogbomoso, grown on selective agar. Confirmed by stain and enzyme tests before sequencing, with disk tests showing wide drug resistance.

Surgical wounds after caesarean birth give skin staph an easy entry, and resistant strains can drive deep infection, wound opening, and body-wide spread in the risk picture given. The public draft supports tracking of resistance and harm genes for stewardship and outbreak watch in maternity care.
pmc-13349002:
Simon Londono and co-authors told in 2026 of an aortic dissection spotted at the bedside with suprasternal notch ultrasound in a 73-year-old man. Early spotting is vital since dissection can be elusive. Yet this ultrasound view remains little used in emergency departments.

The man, with hypertension, high cholesterol, smoking past, and a known aortic aneurysm, came in with two hours of severe left chest pain plus leg pain, numbness, and weakness. Checks found an odd slow pulse and an absent leg pulse, while a standard ultrasound view showed a dilated aortic root. The suprasternal view, done by an intern, clearly showed an intimal flap. CT confirmed a Stanford type A dissection needing urgent surgical transfer.
pmc-13349202:
Noor Eweis and co-authors told in 2026 of cytomegalovirus-driven haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis in a prior healthy 33-year-old woman. This is a life-threatening syndrome of excess immune firing and cytokine storm. Secondary HLH most often follows malignancy, autoimmunity, or infection. Acute cytomegalovirus rarely causes it in immune-competent adults.

She came in with three weeks of high fever and flank pain after treatment for a presumed urinary infection, with symptoms persisting despite antibiotics. Checks found liver inflammation, low blood counts, and an enlarged spleen. Testing confirmed acute cytomegalovirus infection, though at low viral levels. She met HLH diagnostic criteria with a high score and responded to treatment. The case urges clinicians to weigh HLH even when the trigger virus seems modest.
pmc-13349402:
Toshihiko Matsuo and colleagues piloted in 2026 whole-exome sequencing of preserved eye tumour samples from retinoblastoma and choroidal melanoma, the two major intraocular cancers. These tumours are extremely rare, small, and hard to biopsy, yet genomic analysis could guide understanding and treatment.

DNA was extracted from tumour areas in 105 thin sections from seven enucleated eyes with each cancer type, after excluding one sample per group for low sequencing output. Quality-controlled reads were aligned to the reference genome and analysed for pathway enrichment. The pilot shows that archival eye samples can yield usable exomes, opening a route to genomic study of cancers that are otherwise nearly inaccessible to molecular research.
pmc-13350002:
Roberto Carmagnani Pestana and Douglas Dias e Silva commented in 2026 on inherited variants in the ETV1 gene as possible outcome markers in gastrointestinal stromal tumours. Imatinib improved the outlook for advanced disease, yet response length still varies widely between patients.

Usual risk guides, tumour size, site, division rate, and KIT or PDGFRA changes, leave that variation partly unexplained. ETV1 is a growth factor switch central to these tumours, kept stable by active KIT and found even in KIT-negative cases. If a person's ETV1 variants forecast behaviour, they could refine risk estimates and follow-up intensity alongside existing measures.
pmc-13350802:
Yuxin He and Jian'an Wang wrote a 2026 editorial on electrosurgical leaflet modification during catheter aortic valve replacement. A feared complication is the new valve's frame or the old leaflet blocking a coronary artery, a risk growing as younger patients and repeat procedures become common.

Cutting or piercing the leaflet with electric tools keeps blood flowing to the heart without leaving a permanent stent scaffold. Nearly all evidence so far comes from North American and European registries. The editorial introduces the first systematic Asia-Pacific registry evaluation of these techniques, a step toward knowing whether results travel across populations and practice settings.
pmc-13351402:
Matheus Salera Gordim and colleagues wrote a 2026 letter reporting psychotropic medicine use among surgical patients checked before anaesthesia at a Brazilian university hospital. Records covered adults seen through 2024 at the Onofre Lopes University Hospital clinic.

Mental health drug use is rising worldwide, and these medicines can interact with anaesthetics in how the body handles and responds to both. Yet current figures for surgical patients are scarce. By counting actual use in clinic records, the authors give anaesthetists a realistic picture of how often such interactions must be planned for, guiding safer drug choices on the day of surgery.
pmc-13351702:
Zi-Yi Huang leads a 2026 gene study of support cells in the bone marrow of children with B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukaemia. Leukaemia is shaped by the marrow niche, yet how stromal cells change at the RNA level is poorly defined. Arrays from the GSE101425 dataset covered stromal cells at diagnosis, in remission, at relapse, and from healthy donors.

Analysis found 78 genes with changed levels in leukaemia-linked stromal cells. A four-gene set, including DKK1, separated groups well within the dataset. Pathway tools and public single-cell data added context for the signal. Blood tests were used only as an early check of wider expression, and the authors frame the set as a partner to blast-based tests.
pmc-13351902:
Leilei Wu and colleagues test osalmid against lung adenocarcinoma in a 2026 lab and translational study. The drug blocks RRM2, a protein whose excess is linked to tumour growth and drug resistance. Patient data first compared survival by RRM2 level, then cell and animal tests explored single and combined treatments.

Patients with high RRM2 had poorer survival, with a P value below 0.001. Osalmid was tested alone and with two third-generation EGFR drugs, osimertinib and alflutinib, and a combination index measured joint effect. Gene screens and protein tests linked RRM2 to guards against ferroptosis, a form of cell death. Tissue staining for a lipid damage marker checked effects inside tumours.
pmc-13352402:
Patrick G. Kelly and co-authors test how reliable fNIRS brain data are during a reasoning task in 2026. The portable, motion-tolerant method suits developmental and natural settings, but its stability for tracking people over time needs proof. Seventy-three young adults did a relational reasoning task while activation and connectivity were recorded.

Activation in side frontal and parietal areas matched earlier scanner studies in strength. Gains in signal and precision mostly levelled off beyond about 7 minutes of data. Stability was very low for one task contrast yet extremely high for connectivity measures. Grouping channels into anatomical regions helped some checks. Findings support connectivity as a steady marker for repeat studies.
pmc-13354802:
Ana Katic and others discovered a second job for the Legionella tool RidL, in 2026. Legionella pneumophila sends tools that steer host cells to support germ living, and RidL was known to block backward moving through its N-end domain. Its C-end domain, however, had no assigned function.

That domain binds straight to Drp1, the power fission GTPase, and related large GTPases, promoting power breaks. In lab tests, RidL reduced Drp1 enzyme action while driving breaks. The discovery shows how one germ protein can hijack two host systems, and it reveals a new angle on how Legionella reshapes host cell biology.
pmc-13355202:
Felice Crocetto and co-authors compared blood hormone and prostate test results in 2026 between 40 cancer-free African migrant men in Italy and 47 white controls. Men of African roots face higher prostate cancer rates, yet hormone patterns in this group were little studied. The team measured PSA forms and sex hormones in both groups.

Total PSA and testosterone were much the same in both groups. But the migrant men had higher estradiol, a lower hormone ratio, and lower values on two PSA-based risk scores. The authors suggest hormone balance shapes how prostate tests should be read in this group, which matters for fair early detection.
pmc-13355602:
Jean-Michel Halimi and Laurent Fauchier replied in 2026 to a letter questioning renal-risk guessing from high-feeling C-reactive protein in chronic kidney disease. The authors agreed that death was a competing event, explaining that the TriNetX platform's limited tools prevented a Fine-Gray study. They also acknowledged that the single-value split was debatable and that their results were exploratory, with some measurement quirks traced to query configuration. The reply models transparent handling of methodological limits in real-world data research.
pmc-13355802:
Omri Cohen and co-authors set kept gainst drawn vena cava nets in folks with vein clots. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-six. Such nets catch clots when blood drugs can not run, and heads urge their draw once drugs can run. More than one thousand folks from a world list were read past day ninety by net state and drug state.

Kept nets bore more clot back-hits, most as deep vein clots, and more deaths. Draw tied to far low back-hit risk. Big bleeds were rare, and net harms tied tween packs past checks. The team back set watch and on-time draw.
pmc-13356602:
Meng-Kan Chen and Chih-Cheng Wu replied in 2026 to a letter on causal interpretation in their haemodialysis blood pressure study. pmc-13357602:
Meshcheryakov and co-authors describe two swimming filaments from a salt-loving microbe, Haloarcula marismortui. Many archaea swim with rotating helical threads called archaella, about ten nanometers wide. Both filaments here carry an extra outer sheath, a trait not seen before in archaea.

The two sheaths differ at a basic level. In one type, the outer part flips 180 degrees and pairs up, likely stiffening the thread. The other type shows no flip or pairing, and moves in a distinct way. The stiffer type also bears more negative surface charge, which may help in very salty water.
pmc-13358502:
Jianxin Cai and co-authors report a 2026 study on blood signs of inflammation around lung cancer surgery. They followed 368 patients who had surgery to cure their cancer between 2022 and 2024. Blood counts and markers like C-reactive protein were checked before surgery and on the first day after. By tying these shifts to survival and the return of cancer, the study aims to sharpen risk checks that use cheap, routine blood tests.
pmc-13358602:
Tongxin Li and co-authors present a 2026 study on predicting who will respond to immune therapy for throat cancer. A scan-based forecast could spare poor responders harsh treatment that will not help, and push likely responders toward it sooner.
pmc-13359002:
Zein Kattih and co-authors review 25 years of lung transplants for sarcoidosis in a 2026 paper. Sarcoidosis can scar the lungs beyond repair, leaving transplant as the last option. Most patients had the most advanced stage of lung scarring, and nearly nine in ten also had high pressure in the lung arteries. The authors compare outcomes across three eras to see whether results improved as methods modernized. Long records like this help centers counsel patients on what transplant can realistically offer.
pmc-13359502:
Maciej Gawęcki and co-authors scan the backs of eyes in a 2026 study of central serous chorioretinopathy. In this condition, fluid leaks under the retina and blurs central vision. They studied 50 eyes with the disease and 56 healthy eyes matched for age and sex. The choroid was thicker at every one of 24 measured points in diseased eyes, by more than a third at the center and even more toward the edges. Wide maps of the choroid may sharpen diagnosis and tracking.
pmc-13360002:
The journal Cells published a 2026 correction to a 2022 paper by Yair Romero and co-authors on lung fibroblasts from patients with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. The authors later found the two sample groups had been mislabeled during their computer analysis.

Because every later step built on those labels, the two conditions were swapped throughout: genes reported as switched on by low oxygen were in fact switched off, and the reverse. The corrected version swaps the terms in the affected passages. The authors apologize for the error and any confusion it caused.
pmc-13360302:
