The team asked whether the immune system's NKG2D pathway, which helps spot abnormal cells, shapes who gets this form. They compared gene variants in patients and healthy controls and read gene activity in blood stem cells.

One variant, called MICA*004:001, showed up more often in patients with CALR-driven disease than in controls. Other signals hinted at links with partner genes in the same pathway. Stem cells carrying the CALR fault also showed changed activity in these immune genes. The authors suggest this pathway helps the immune system watch for early cancer clones, and may one day guide risk checks.
pmc-13360802:
Manjula Nandakumar led a 2026 pilot study on blood clotting proteins in women with unexplained infertility. This form of infertility has no clear cause and may make up a large share of all cases. Odd clotting patterns are already linked to repeated pregnancy loss. The team asked whether the clotting and clot-clearing system also differs in unexplained infertility.

Blood from 11 women with unexplained infertility was compared with blood from 14 women whose infertility came from a male partner factor. A protein-scanning tool measured 20 clotting-related proteins in each sample. The team used careful statistics suited to a small, early study. If real differences exist, they could point to hidden causes of this frustrating diagnosis and to new tests or treatments worth chasing.
pmc-13361202:
Kyoung-Chan Park and co-authors studied jawbone death linked to medicines in a 2026 review of 812 patients. The condition, MRONJ, is a severe side effect of drugs that slow bone loss or blood vessel growth. It strikes the jaw, and cases that come back after treatment are a special worry. The team pulled records from Chosun University Dental Hospital for patients seen from 2020 to 2024.

Most patients were women, with an average age near 73, and the lower jaw was hit most often. The team gathered health, scan, and drug details and tested which traits independently raised the odds of the condition returning. A cohort this large can give firm answers about risk. Knowing who is prone to relapse helps dentists plan surgery, drug breaks, and follow-up with more care.
pmc-13361702:
Ferdinand Popp and co-authors present TelomereHunter2, an upgraded tool for reading telomeres from DNA data, in a 2026 paper. Telomeres are the caps on chromosome ends, and their length and makeup matter in cancer, aging, and genome stability. The original TelomereHunter is a standard tool in genome research and precision cancer care for studying how cancers maintain their telomeres. Bigger datasets and new file formats demanded a rebuild.

The new version is packaged in containers, so it installs cleanly in many computing settings. It also runs up to 74 percent faster than before. Support now extends to non-human genomes and single-cell studies, widening its reach. A sustainable, faster tool helps labs keep telomere analysis in routine cancer workflows as data keeps growing.
pmc-13362402:
Henrike Deissner and colleagues present a 2026 study of a rare cause of collapsed lung in women, drawn from 25 years of surgery records at one center. In this condition, called catamenial pneumothorax, the lung collapses near the time of a woman's period, often because womb-like tissue grows in the chest. The team checked how often doctors spotted it and why it was missed.

Among more than 4,500 treated cases, they found 15 such cases in 14 women, most with clear signs seen during surgery. These patients had far more repeat collapses than other women. The main gap was simple: staff often never asked about the timing of periods, so the study urges routine checks.
pmc-13363502:
Shaofeng Zhang and colleagues present a 2026 study on eco-friendly recycled concrete built from industrial leftovers. Their mixes swapped in steel slag, furnace slag powder, and polypropylene fibers across twelve recipes, then tested crushing and splitting strength and peered at the inner structure. An artificial intelligence model, a neural network tuned by a genetic algorithm, learned to predict strength from the recipe.

Steel slag alone weakened the concrete, but trading part of it for furnace slag restored and improved strength, above all at later ages, by driving more complete setting and tighter pores. Fibers clearly lifted splitting strength, which guards against cracking. The prediction model proved accurate, giving builders a design tool for greener mixes.
pmc-13363902:
Nikolaos Zarifis and Dimitrios Katsaros present a 2026 study on arranging wireless sensors over a sphere so the network watches everything, stays linked, and sips power evenly. Flat-map methods do not transfer to curved 3D surfaces, and single-goal fixes clash with each other. Their all-in-one algorithm works in three phases: place nodes for backup coverage, build a backbone with backup links, then layer a hierarchy that spreads energy use so no sensor dies early.

The design promises coverage that survives sensor failures and routes that hold when nodes drop. Even energy drain is the thread that ties the phases together, since a dead zone or a dead relay both break the system. The authors aim the method at real deployments on domes, tanks, and other curved structures.
pmc-13364102:
Jing Li and colleagues present a 2026 study on how augmented reality head-up displays in cars should present navigation cues, tested with eye tracking in a driving simulator. Thirty-eight drivers, sorted by thinking style with a standard test, drove goal-directed and surprise-driven tasks with two cue styles: fixed to the world outside or fixed to the screen. Reaction times, gaze measures, and pupil size were modeled together.

Surprise tasks slowed reactions and widened visual search for everyone. World-fixed cues sped visual work during lane changes, while screen-fixed cues grabbed attention better for pedestrian warnings. Drivers with a field-dependent style showed larger pupils, a sign of heavier mental load, at equal driving scores. The authors propose displays that adapt cue style to task and driver state.
pmc-13365402:
Ayşe Ömerli and others built a clear-space three-sized printed model of the pterygopalatine fossa for anatomy teaching, in 2026. This deep midfacial space serves as a major neurovascular crossroads, with confined edges and multidirectional connections that make it hard to visualise with usual items. Students often struggle to grasp its three-sized layout.

A digital model built from commercial bone models and refined in ZBrush software was printed as an enlarged clear-space model, showing the space itself rather than surrounding bone. Its impact on anatomical comprehension was tested educationally. Anatomy educators gain a reproducible teaching tool for one of the head's most confusing spaces.
pmc-13372202:
Daiki Kogetsu and co-authors write on end-of-life care in Japan in a 2026 case report. A man aged 68 with grave mind and body limits got cancer spread in his belly, with no known start point. He could not speak his wishes, so staff talked at length with his aunt, his legal guard.

The group chose comfort care over hard tests and strong drugs. Staff held a small concert of songs he loved in his care home. He showed clear joy, and far kin came back in touch. He died in peace a week later. The case shows how music, kin talks, and close watch can guide care when a patient cannot speak.
pmc-13373602:
Darcy A. Freedman and co-authors built a trust scale for health science staff in a 2026 study. The scale checks how sure staff feel in seven rules for fast, useful science that turns finds into health gains. A total of 158 staff at three large hubs in three states took the survey in 2025.

Study of the replies found four tight groups of items, with a high trust score for the whole set. One group was about bold acts for big gains. The scale gives hubs a way to mark where staff feel weak, train there, and check if trust grows. That helps turn good science into care more fast.
pmc-13377702:
Vincent Bouteloup and co-authors weigh two fixes for tool swaps in long brain studies in a 2026 paper. Blood marks of brain loss are read for years in such work. Mid-way, labs oft swap the test kit for cost or stock, which can bend the trend line.

The test bed is a French group tracked for mind loss marks. One fix bends the new reads to the old scale, and one lets each kit keep its own line in the sums. The pair is set on true trend fits for the marks. A fair call here guards years of work in many long studies, not just this one.
pmc-13380802:
Ariel Yuhan Ong and colleagues present a large real-world dataset for diagnosing and triaging macular disease, in a 2026 datasheet paper. Macular disease causes major vision loss, and timely triage matters, yet researchers lacked high-quality multimodal datasets mirroring routine clinics. The team curated records from adults attending Moorfields Eye Hospital retina service for the first time between February 2017 and July 2025.

The dataset centers on macula OCT scans from Topcon and Heidelberg machines, drawn from the INSIGHT Health Data Research Hub, a major ophthalmic imaging resource. Clinical and imaging data from routine care were processed and de-identified for secondary research. The resource lets teams build and test diagnostic tools on data that look like real clinic caseloads.
pmc-13382702:
Xiangdong Wu and co-authors report a 2026 study showing that fructose, a common sugar, blocks the formation of heat-producing brown fat cells. Excess fructose is linked to obesity, diabetes, and fatty liver, but its effect on brown fat was poorly defined. Brown fat burns energy as heat and is seen as a target against obesity.

Mouse precursor cells grown with fructose formed smaller, fewer fat droplets and lost a key brown fat identity protein. Thyroid hormone normally boosts that protein, but in fructose it could not, revealing hormone resistance. Fructose lowered the hormone's receptor by marking it for destruction. Adding extra receptor did not rescue the cells, suggesting a deeper block in the signalling chain.
pmc-13383402:
Karci and five co-authors study survival after lung cancer surgery, in work from twenty twenty-six. Their patients had non small cell lung cancer removed by surgery. Lab checks then showed spread to nearby lymph nodes, a stage called N1.

Sixty-six patients treated over a decade at one clinic were reviewed. Most were men in their early sixties. Surgery ranged from one lobe removal to whole lung removal. Survival curves and risk models tested which traits linked to longer life. Such data help doctors counsel patients whose node spread is found only after surgery, when choices on further therapy must be made.
pmc-13383502:
Şengül Üzen Cura's team tested whether resilience carries the link between AI attitudes and nursing values, in a 2026 study. AI-assisted tools are reshaping nursing care, and attitudes toward them may color how nurses view professional values. The team surveyed 301 nurses at a university hospital between June and September 2025 with validated scales for AI attitude, professional values, and resilience.

Positive AI attitudes correlated strongly with professional value perception, with a direct effect of 0.835. The indirect path through resilience was near zero and not significant, so resilience did not mediate the link. The result suggests value formation around AI tracks attitudes directly, and resilience training alone will not shift that relationship.
pmc-13385402:
Vinod Divya's team surveyed drug and care-product pollution in South Indian city waters, in a 2026 study. Medicines and care products persist in water and harm ecosystems, yet data for Bengaluru and Mysuru were sparse. The team sampled surface water and well water at 30 sites, testing five chemicals by SPE-HPLC with risk quotients.

All five chemicals appeared across the study area. Highest risk quotients reached about 2 for norfloxacin, 13 for diclofenac, 0.7 for naproxen, 8 for triclosan, and 16 for caffeine. Caffeine, diclofenac, and triclosan often passed the high-risk threshold, norfloxacin sat at moderate risk, and naproxen at low to middle risk, pointing to raw sewage.
pmc-13385802:
Mathilde Bizou's team mapped how nerve-vessel talk differs across growing mouse brain regions, in a 2026 study. Nerve-vessel unit talk guides vessel layout, barrier growth, and neuronal balance, but regional gaps during growth were unclear. The team joined spatial gene readouts with region-by-region vessel-cell reads in postnatal mouse brain.

Cortex and thalamus vessel programs split over time, tracking nerve and glial growth. Nerve-vessel TGF-beta2 talk proved vital for thalamus vessel growth in a defined window after birth. Losing vessel TGF-beta receptor 1 talk caused excess mTOR with thalamus-first defects and bleeding, rescued by mTOR blockade.
pmc-13386502:
Xiaochen Xue and colleagues unveil a sequencing method that reads two DNA marks at once, base by base, in 2026 work. The marks, 5mC and 5hmC, steer gene control, yet older methods infer one by subtracting the other. Their BRIGHT-seq approach converts each mark into a different DNA letter within the same molecule.

That direct readout removes the need for paired subtraction assays and sharpens both maps. Trials across human and mouse genomes showed the method can chart both landscapes together. The authors offer the tool for studies of how the two marks jointly shape gene activity and disease.
pmc-13386902:
Fattore's team surveyed Italian cancer screening staff on AI in national screening, in a 2026 survey. AI is more and more pitched for screening, but staff views on value, risks, and rollout barriers were little studied. The web survey, 39 questions, reached program leads through local chains and the FASO mailing list, covering use, gains, risks, barriers, and readiness to invest.

A total of 305 answered, covering all but one Italian region. About one-third noted AI use, most often in bowel polyp spotting and breast imaging support. About 75 percent showed strong keenness for AI, valuing test quality, workflow gains, and faster reports. Top concerns were legal risk, clarity and bias, and skill loss, while weak IT systems, missing rules, and limited funds topped barriers. Seen gains raised drive to invest, while risks lowered it.
pmc-13387402:
Papageorgiou Anastasios's team followed thirty-one patients who started clozapine, a drug reserved for schizophrenia that resists other treatment, at a psychiatric hospital in Athens between January 2022 and June 2024. Blood tests and heart tracings were checked at the start, after five to ten days, and again after one to two months.

Two patients developed inflammation of the heart muscle within three weeks and had to stop the drug at once. Four showed a lengthened heart rhythm interval, and eleven had raised immune markers. Enzyme rises in liver and muscle were also common, mainly when doses rose fast. The paper argues for slow dose increases and close early monitoring to catch these harms in time.
pmc-13388702:
Tatiana A. Mishchenko's team reviews how temozolomide, the standard drug for glioblastoma, an aggressive brain tumour, might be made to work better by steering tumour cells toward more immune forms of death. Resistance to the drug, driven by genes, epigenetics, and the tumour surroundings, remains a major barrier, and standard treatment pairs the drug with radiotherapy.

The review maps apoptosis, necroptosis, ferroptosis, pyroptosis, and cuproptosis, weighs how each one alerts the immune system, and warns that pushing inflammation too far can also help tumours. It closes by sketching combination strategies that could turn dying tumour cells into an immune signal instead of a quiet exit.
pmc-13390402:
Padmavathy Krishna Kumar's team analysed India's rural and tribal public health capacity from 2011 to 2021 using Rural Health Statistics on sub-centres, primary health centres, and community health centres. Tribal groups face limited care access, but no systematic nationwide comparison had been made.

Nationally, both the tribal capacity index and the tribal-rural disparity index fell over the decade, with facility-wise tribal-rural gaps narrowing for sub-centres, primary centres, and community centres. State patterns varied, and despite improvement in high-tribal-group areas, tribal access still lagged rural access overall, with capacity declining in absolute terms.
pmc-13391002:
Ya-Ju Hsieh's team checked a saliva marker panel for oral cancer spotting, using focused marker work with isotope tagging across 299 people. Oral flat-cell cancer results hinge on early spotting, but reliable salivary biomarkers had not been proved in full.

Twenty-six markers were counted in healthy controls, two stages of potentially harmful disorders, and cancer patients. Cadaverine, N-acetylcadaverine, and choline rose with disease stage while an amino acid fell, and a four-marker panel distinguished cancer from health with an area under the curve of 0.91, pointing to amine energy use in harmful change.
pmc-13391802:
Raakel Lintunen and Anselm Tamminen analyse, in 2026, whether a breast cancer diagnosis prompts women to quit smoking. Smoking raises breast cancer risk and worsens treatment outcomes, yet how quitting behaviour changes around diagnosis was not fully understood.

The retrospective study reviewed smoking status in more than six thousand consecutive patients treated from 2010 to 2022, focusing on the subgroup who smoked at diagnosis. Baseline questionnaires supplied smoking histories. The authors determine what share quit after diagnosis and which factors predicted quitting. Oncology teams gain timing evidence for a teachable moment, showing when cessation support after diagnosis is most likely to land.
pmc-13394102:
Vilja Vihtonen and others trace why induced births rose in Finland from 2005 to 2023 in a 2026 nation-wide birth file study. Induced birth aims to cut mother and baby harm, but gains for many common reasons are unsure, and rising rates tax health care.

All single, head-first births at or past 37 weeks went into the Finnish birth file across three spans. Shifts in mother traits, birth week, birth problems, and womb troubles were weighed, with induced births read apart. Policy chiefs gain a full account of what truly drove the national rise, from older mothers to new birth rules and risk habits.
pmc-13394202:
Leonardo Oliveira Reis uses Brazil's recent adoption of robot-assisted prostate removal into its universal public health system as a case study in surgical public health. The Unified Health System, known as SUS, covers the whole population, and taking on an expensive robot platform forced the system to weigh effectiveness, equity, and sustainability together. Reis connects that decision to wider lenses, including One Health and population health thinking across the patient journey.

Beyond buying technology, the rollout behaves like a learning health system: real-world evidence, implementation science, quality measurement, and policy feed each other at national scale. Reis argues the experience shows how a universal system can evaluate and spread complex innovation while generating lessons for diverse settings. The piece offers Brazil's governance of high-complexity surgery as a model for resilient, equitable cancer care.
pmc-13394802:
Kai T. Fox and colleagues review, in 2026, what cuff-based exercise may do to the brain paths that drive movement. Blood flow restriction pairs light loads with a cuff that partly blocks limb flow. It builds muscle much like heavy training, yet suits people who cannot lift heavy. Far less is known about its effects on nerve paths from brain to muscle.

The review gathers early proof that such training may reshape those paths. It weighs likely routes, from changed excitability to altered braking signals in the cord. The authors give tips for turning lab findings into rehab care. They also list the gaps that new studies must fill.
pmc-13395502:
Kyu-Ho Yi and co-authors test, in 2026, filler shots that make collarbones stand out, a beauty trend in East Asia. Forty-four women had both collarbones treated with a collagen-stirring filler through a blunt tube under the skin. Photos, three-dimensional scans, and satisfaction scores were tracked for six months. No major harms appeared.

Bruising and swelling showed in a fifth to a quarter of women and faded on their own. Projection rose by just under two millimetres at three months and held near that at six. Nine in ten women said they were pleased or very pleased. The authors call the method workable but early. Bigger, controlled studies must check lasting value.
pmc-13395902:
Jonathan de Brito Brum, José Walkimar de Mesquita Carneiro, and Leonardo Moreira da Costa compare, in 2026, computer solvent models for carbon capture by amines. Amines soak up carbon dioxide, a key climate gas, but the catch step turns on solvent effects. Four amines of unlike strength were modelled in fifteen solvents. Three solvation schemes were scored against known lab and theory data.

One scheme, SMD, tracked the known data best. Its edge came from sensing local hydrogen bonds between solute and solvent. The catch runs through a charged middle state, whose stability the solvent sets. The authors say picking the right model sharpens design of capture fluids. Cheaper screens can then guide costly lab work.
pmc-13396102:
Aurora Zanghì and colleagues describe three older adults with generalized myasthenia gravis, a disease where the immune system weakens muscles, who began treatment with the drug ravulizumab. Their 2026 case series looks past muscle strength to fatigue and thinking, two burdens patients report often but clinics measure rarely.

All three patients tested positive for antibodies against the acetylcholine receptor. Each went through a set battery covering daily activity limits, a scored strength exam, fatigue questionnaires, quality-of-life reports, and hands-on cognitive tests. By recording many domains side by side, the authors show how a fuller picture of this disease can be gathered in routine care.
pmc-13396302:
Tobias Hegelmaier and co-authors ran a six-month trial testing gut-based help for constipation in Parkinson's disease. That symptom troubles up to 90 percent of patients and can start years before shaking or stiffness. Their 2026 trial builds on the idea that an unbalanced gut and low short-chain fatty acids feed the problem.

Seventy-two patients were assigned at random, with neither side told the group, to added short-chain fatty acids, a prebiotic sugar called 2-fucosyllactose, or both together. Constipation and quality of life were scored with standard clinic questionnaires across the trial. The design separates the effect of feeding gut bacteria from supplying their products directly.
pmc-13396502:
Moyer and team extend, in 2026, the Shared Socioeconomic Pathways, the standard scenario narratives for climate-era futures, by projecting 188 socioeconomic measures for 188 countries all the way to the year 2150. Using the integrated International Futures model, they cover economics, conflict, demographics, education, health, infrastructure, and governance in one framework. That fixes earlier problems of narrative misalignment, disconnected models, missing gauges, and horizons that stopped at 2100.

Their projections correlate strongly with existing forecasts but run lower on economic growth, because the joint model lets conflict, governance, infrastructure, and human development drag on output from inside. Global population comes out 1.3 percent lower than current pathway figures for 2050 and 7.4 percent lower for 2100 in their comparisons. Gross domestic product runs 10 percent lower in 2050 and 11.4 percent lower in 2100 against the same benchmarks. The authors add sector-level government spending data to connect scenarios with climate planning.
pmc-13396602:
Jillian E. O'Carroll and co-authors describe a frightening snag during a routine tube change in a 62-year-old man, and how water pressure fixed it without surgery. Their 2026 case report comes from care for a man with an inoperable duodenal cancer who depended on a biliary drain passing through the bowel.

During a scheduled exchange under X-ray guidance, injected dye revealed that the duodenum had telescoped into itself. Such folding is a rare event, thought to follow traction on the bowel lining as the catheter was pulled back. Left alone, such folding can strangle the bowel. The team reduced it promptly by hydrostatic pressure, and the report argues for spotting the pattern fast whenever it occurs.
pmc-13396802:
Shuang Zhang and co-authors published an author correction in 2026 to a 2019 Nature Communications study of ovarian cancer origins. The study had argued that both the fallopian tube and the ovary's surface can seed the deadliest form of the disease. The correction lists a string of figure preparation mistakes in the original paper.

One microscope image in Figure 8 had been duplicated into a second panel meant to show a different drug. Some error bars showed standard deviation where the tighter standard error was intended. Source data for a tumor chart in Figure 3 listed wrong measurements. Plate reader values behind Figure 8 had been transposed and duplicated. A supplementary chart also carried the wrong axis scale. Corrected files replace the faulty ones.
pmc-13397102:
Ting Fu and co-authors pooled four long-running ageing surveys to ask whether having a hobby protects older adults against frailty. Their 2026 analysis spans 15 countries and the years 2010 to 2023, using national cohorts from China, England, the United States, and Europe.

The main analysis held 43,346 people aged 65 and over, each with hobby and frailty readings at the start and a frailty index at follow-up. Mixed models and a cross-cohort pooling estimated the link, and a second analysis asked whether more frequent hobby time adds benefit. Single-country studies had left open whether the pattern is universal or a local quirk of culture and wealth.
pmc-13397702:
Yixin Li and others show neuronal tetraspanin TSP-6 damping intestinal innate immunity in roundworms in a 2026 study. Immune tuning keeps balance and defends against pathogens, and tetraspanins, a conserved surface protein family, were suspected immune players.

From a family tree of 21 roundworm tetraspanins, chosen members were knocked down by RNA interference during pathogen infection. TSP-6 emerged as a neuronal damper of intestinal immunity acting through dense-core vesicle release. The paper bares a nervous system brake on gut defense with implications for neuroimmune regulation with wider lessons for worm and human gut health.
pmc-13397802:
Joseph Tang and colleagues measured how willing volunteers in a Kenyan HIV incidence study would be to join a future HIV vaccine trial. Their 2026 paper draws on people without HIV who reported multiple sexual partners in Kisumu County, a group whose participation future vaccine efficacy testing would require. Understanding willingness, and what shapes it, helps trial planners recruit fairly and avoid wasted outreach.

From February 2017 to May 2018, the team screened 940 people, and 97.8 percent said they would join a future candidate vaccine trial. Willing people more often had exchanged sex for goods or money and less often believed HIV status could be judged by appearance. Willingness stayed near 98 percent among those who enrolled and finished the cohort study. The paper supports strong community openness to trials, while noting that stated willingness is not the same as later enrollment.
pmc-13398102:
Ambika Choudhary and colleagues test whether spraying a sugar called trehalose shields mustard plants from arsenic poisoning. Their 2026 study grows Brassica juncea under arsenic stress and applies three trehalose doses (25, 50 and 75 mM) across 30, 60 and 90 days after sowing. Arsenic in soil slashes the green pigments plants need and floods cells with damaging oxygen by-products.

Arsenic cut chlorophyll a by up to about 72.91 percent in the worst readings and drove damage markers sharply upward. Sprayed trehalose softened those losses in step with dose, and the strongest mix lifted chlorophyll a by 49 to 88 percent above stressed plants. The work backs trehalose as a cheap shield for crops on tainted land.
pmc-13398502:
Chigign Mengiste and co-authors test ten barley types across Ethiopian highland sites to find lines that yield steadily on acid soils. Their 2026 study grows ten lines (eight accessions, a local variety and a released cultivar among them) on both untreated acid ground and lime-treated plots. Acidity caps barley output across the highlands, and tolerant varieties are scarce.

Environment swamped the results, explaining 60.45 percent of all variation, with genotype at 32.38 percent and their interaction at 7.18 percent in the AMMI analysis quoted. Two interaction axes captured most of the interplay, at 80.59 percent of its variance in the figures given. Sites in the Gumer district, limed and unlimed, helped separate lines that hold yield when soils sour.
pmc-13400102:
Massoud A. Leesar and Mehmet Cilingiroglu weigh the clinical gains and costs of imaging-guided coronary stenting. Their 2026 editorial addresses percutaneous coronary intervention, where plain angiography poorly shows vessel size, calcium, and stent expansion. Intravascular ultrasound and optical coherence tomography look inside the vessel before and after stenting.

Imaging before stenting reveals reference size, lesion shape, and calcium, while imaging after stenting catches underexpansion, missed segments, and edge tears at the strut level. Large trials show imaging-guided stenting improves optimization and lowers target vessel failure, heart attack, and stent clotting, prompting guideline support. The editorial balances those gains against device and time costs, urging selective, value-aware use rather than imaging for every case.
pmc-13400302:
Asmita Pathak leads a large group reporting in 2026 that a brain chemical signal, GABA, helps glioblastoma grow in female mice. Glioblastoma is the most common malignant brain tumor in adults and resists immune therapy. The effect ran through suppressor immune cells that damp down T cell attack.

In female mice, GABA receptor signals made those suppressor cells stronger by raising a pathway that uses the amino acid arginine. A drug boosting the signal sped tumor growth, while one blocking it lengthened survival, both only in females. Immune cells from women with the tumor also showed stronger GABA-linked gene patterns and more GABA than cells from men.
pmc-13400602:
Sukhman Singh, Michelle Peiffer, Gary W Felton and Flor E Acevedo test, in 2026, how grapevines defend themselves when spotted lanternflies feed on them. The invasive insect threatens United States vineyards by weakening vines and cutting yield. Whether vines mount whole-plant defenses after attack was largely unknown.

Potted Cabernet Franc vines were infested with zero to fifteen adult insects for up to 29 days. At high numbers and long durations, leaf green pigment fell, defense enzyme activity rose and protective phenolic compounds built up steadily. Tannin levels did not change. Lanternflies later placed on heavily infested vines survived less and gained less weight, showing that prolonged heavy feeding makes the whole vine a poorer host.
pmc-13400702:
Yuri Lopes Lima and colleagues test, in 2026, whether a field-based screening model can predict knee ligament injuries in women footballers. Anterior cruciate ligament tears strike women players several times more often than men. No prediction model had ever been checked in a fresh group of women.

Three hundred twenty players completed preseason tests of hopping, jumping and hip strength, then were followed for 18 months. The original model performed weakly in this new cohort and overestimated risk. The team rebuilt it with five variables, adding the hip strength ratio and trunk lean measures, which improved discrimination to a moderate level. Internal checks suggested some of that gain is optimistic, so further validation is needed.
pmc-13401302:
Çakır and colleagues audit, in 2026, intravenous albumin use in Turkish intensive care units against the 2024 international guideline, in a prospective one-week point prevalence study across seven hospitals. Of 385 ICU patients monitored, 56, or 14.5 percent, received albumin, with a median age of 68 years among them. The team recorded indications, whether clinical targets were met, guideline compliance, and costs.

The commonest stated reason for starting albumin was simply low serum albumin, at 41.1 percent of treated cases, followed by fluid shifts at 21.4 percent and sepsis at 14.3 percent in physicians' reports. The desired clinical target was achieved in 73.2 percent of cases, yet guideline compliance was exactly zero percent across all seven hospitals. Median consumption ran to 667 vials per 1,000 patient-days, costing an estimated 70,617.86 dollars on the same scale. Longer hospital stay and higher APACHE II severity scores predicted receiving albumin.
pmc-13401702:
Nahid Karamzad and co-authors wrote a 2026 integrated analysis of ischemic heart disease across the Middle East and North Africa from 1990 to 2021, using Global Burden of Disease 2021 estimates. Heart disease of this kind remains a leading cause of death and disability worldwide, and regional detail guides policy.

The secondary analysis covered all 21 countries and territories in the region, tracking prevalence, deaths, and disability-adjusted life years as counts and age-standardized rates. In 2021 the age-standardized prevalence sat above 6,400 cases per hundred thousand people, with the matching mortality rate a little above 200 per hundred thousand, each with stated uncertainty ranges. The single framework lets readers compare change over time and gaps between countries. It also supports gradients by sociodemographic development, plus the share of burden blamed on modifiable risk factors, split by sex and age.
pmc-13402102:
Christian Drerup and a broad team filmed how mosquito pupae swim at the water surface in 11 species from the Aedes, Anopheles, and Culex groups. Pupae are often treated as a still, inactive stage, yet mosquito pupae move through water on their own. Knowing how young mosquitoes behave matters for control work aimed at stopping deadly diseases they carry as adults.

The three groups swam in clearly different styles. Aedes pupae moved in slow but frequent bouts and ranged widely, as if exploring. Anopheles and Culex pupae moved less often, yet each bout was faster and covered more distance, most strongly in Culex. Drerup and colleagues link the styles to the waters each species favors. Control planners, they suggest, should count pupal behavior, not only larval habits, when designing measures.
pmc-13402802:
Yujin Liu and co-authors fuse tumor fluorescence and ordinary background imaging into one single-pixel camera, ending the misalignment that plagues two-camera surgical guidance systems. Their detector splits light by color using gradient-tuned perovskite layers: 520 nanometer fluorescence passes as one signal, 450 nanometer backscatter as the structural view. A suppression ratio of 57 between channels keeps the two pictures clean.

The system detected sodium fluorescein down to 50 nanomoles per milliliter in solution tests. Because one active pixel architecture captures both channels, field of view and pixel registration match perfectly with no correction software. In mouse tumor experiments the setup located and tracked fluorescence-tagged tumors in real time. The authors argue single-pixel fusion could sharpen image-guided surgery, where millimeter offsets carry real risk.
pmc-13403402:
Mohammed Ali Saghir and team weighed scope surgery against open surgery for plantar fasciitis, a wear-and-tear heel pain state common in adults aged 40 to 60. Their 2026 pooled review covers cases where rest care, therapy, orthotics, and shots have failed and surgery is on the table. Whether the smaller scope route matches open surgery on function and safety had been debated.

Pooling 19 studies with 646 patients, both routes gave strong gains in pain and function scores. Head-to-head studies showed no clear gap in pain or function scores between groups. The work backs scope surgery as a like-for-like option, while noting that complication rates and operating time details, plus study mix, should steer each surgical choice.
pmc-13403602:
Gillian Witten and colleagues reported two rare spinal cord tumors in 2026, both pigment-cell growths inside the cord itself. A 71-year-old man had back pain, weak legs, and bladder loss from a mass near the cord's lower tip. A 65-year-old man had back pain, unsteady walking, and spreading numbness from a chest-level mass.

The first man's tumor came out in part, and he regained some strength. The second man's tumor came out fully yet returned, needing more surgery and radiation. Gene tests in the tumors, covering BAP1 loss and GNAQ changes, may help forecast behavior and guide added care.
pmc-13403802:
Ashutosh Vashisht and co-authors checked a broad cancer gene test in 2026 that reads 1,080 genes and reports through a cloud platform. Labs often struggle with patchy gene coverage and tangled data steps. The team ran 119 tumor samples from 18 cancer types through the new test and a trusted older panel.

Agreement across shared genes was strong, with sensitivity above 99 percent in their runs. The test caught small gene changes present in as few as 5 percent of cells. Repeat runs gave the same answers every time. A built-in platform turned raw data straight into reports, cutting middle steps for clinic labs.
pmc-13404202:
Bartosz W. Bichalski and co-authors asked in 2026 whether two guard proteins in tumor tissue can forecast survival in bowel cancer. The study covered 103 patients who had surgery for the cancer. Stain tests on stored tumor samples checked for faulty p53 patterns and missing PTEN.

Each fault alone tied to shorter survival in simple comparisons. Patients carrying both faults fared worst of all. Once age and lymph node spread entered the math, neither protein kept a solo forecasting role. The pair may still flag a fierce subgroup worth watching. Larger fresh groups must confirm the signal before clinics lean on it.
pmc-13404302:
José Leonildo Fernandes de Queiroz led a 2026 word study of nursing terms tied to HIV prevention pills, known as PrEP. Standard terms help nurses record care in a shared language. The team swept databases and official papers with no limits on year or language.

From over 24,000 records, 18 works formed the final set for word analysis. Four word families emerged: putting PrEP in place, professional care, felt vulnerability, and decision-making. A nursing theory lens sorted those families into body, self-image, role, and tie modes. The shared word set can guide clearer care records and teaching for PrEP users.
pmc-13404402:
William Wical and co-authors spent long field time in 2026 with hospital programs that try to break cycles of violent injury in Maryland. The work covered Maryland's two busiest trauma centers. Survivors, their loved ones, and program staff all weighed in on how well the programs work.

A clear gap opened between program goals and survivor realities. Services, many said, do little to make daily life safer outside the hospital. Their reach against payback violence also struck users as thin. One survivor line gives the study its title in spirit: the help is nice, yet it cannot keep him safe. Long-term care and community change are the fixes urged.
pmc-13404502:
Joshua Epuitai and colleagues studied antibiotic use after straightforward vaginal births in eastern Uganda, reporting in 2026. Guidelines advise against routine preventive antibiotics after such births because overuse feeds drug resistance. The team wanted to know how often the drugs are given and why staff give them.

Questionnaires covered 370 women after discharge, and eight midwives and clinical officers gave longer interviews. Nearly every woman, 99 percent, left with preventive antibiotics, most often amoxicillin or ampiclox paired with metronidazole. Staff said the drugs guard against infection after tears or episiotomy and cover gaps where sterile conditions are hard to keep. Some saw the drugs as needed even without a medical indication, with little weight given to resistance.
pmc-13406802:
In a 2026 review, Eric A. Grin and Erez Nossek trace how ultrasound has been used to check brain bypass grafts after surgery. Such grafts reroute blood flow for people with complex aneurysms or poorly supplied brain tissue, so confirming that a graft stays open matters over many years.

Early checks relied on indirect Doppler signals from outside the skull or tools used during the operation itself. A newer method looks straight through a clear implanted skull plate, giving a direct view of the join without radiation. Reported series found full agreement with angiography for judging whether grafts stayed open, plus visible changes in flow shape and vessel width that matched later imaging. Standard scan routines and wider testing still lie ahead.
pmc-13407402:
Lianzhi Chen and co-authors, in 2026, followed people with rheumatoid arthritis to see whether blood fats predict later lung scarring. Interstitial lung disease is a grave complication of the joint condition, and disturbed fat metabolism is implicated in both diseases, so the team mined a large British cohort for answers.

Among 4,229 participants free of lung disease at entry, 152 developed it over roughly 14.7 years of follow-up. Higher apolipoprotein A and high-density lipoprotein cholesterol each came with substantially lower risk, cutting it by about three-fifths and one-half per standard step. The links were stronger in men, younger patients, and ever-smokers. A statistical mediation analysis assigned most of the protective association to lower body-wide inflammation, suggesting the fats work largely through calming immune activity.
pmc-13407902:
Dan Wang, Diedie Yang, and Haibin Wang propose, in 2026, a leaner quantum protocol for several parties to add secret numbers without revealing them. Earlier quantum summation schemes demanded full quantum powers from everyone, pre-shared keys, or extra trusted parties, all costly; the new design works in a semi-quantum setting where ordinary participants only measure.

The protocol builds on multi-particle high-dimensional entangled states whose built-in correlations generate random masks straight from measurement outcomes. Those masks cancel automatically when the partial results are combined, so nobody distributes mask material and no pre-shared keys are needed. Formal correctness and security analyses are supplied, and simulations on IBM's Qiskit platform demonstrated feasibility. Spin-off protocols for anonymous voting, auctions, and ranking illustrate the reach.
pmc-13408602:
Reham Abd El Hamid, Fawzia Barakat, Roshdi Seoudi, and Doaa Said compare in 2026 two ways of stabilising cobalt ferrite nanoparticles, tiny magnetic crystals with uses from electronics to water treatment. The particles were made by a sol-gel route, capped either with short ethylene glycol or with its long-chain cousin polyethylene glycol. That single choice rippled through every property measured.

Both products formed the expected cubic spinel structure. The long-chain cap gave better crystal quality, more even dispersion, stronger magnetisation, and higher electrical permittivity, while the short-chain cap produced smaller, clumpier particles with greater magnetic coercivity. Under ultraviolet light both destroyed a test dye almost completely, the short-chain version finishing faster. Materials readers get a clear lesson in how stabiliser chain length steers structure and performance.
pmc-13408702:
Hiroyuki Kojima and a Japanese endoscopy team report in 2026 their first dozen cases with an ultraslim catheter scope for looking directly inside bile and pancreatic ducts. Standard scopes are too thick for the narrowest ducts, leaving some stones, strictures, and tumours hard to assess. The new instrument measures only a few millimetres across at its tip.

Between late 2022 and mid 2024 the scope was used in eight bile duct cases and four pancreatic duct cases. The cases covered stones, strictures, one bile duct cancer, bleeding after liver surgery, and growths inside the pancreatic duct. Insertion reached the target every time, and the examination achieved its clinical aim in eleven of twelve patients. The narrowest duct entered measured under two millimetres. One patient developed mild pancreatitis that settled with conservative care, supporting cautious wider use.
pmc-13409102:
Joanna Snowball and colleagues publish in 2026 the plan for a trial that would once have sounded backwards: helping people with cystic fibrosis lose weight. Better treatments have changed the disease, and excess weight now threatens heart, metabolic, and lung health in this population. Yet deliberate weight loss sits uneasily beside decades of advice to eat high-energy food, and beside evidence linking higher weight to better lung function. Thirty adults from four British centres will test the water.

Two thirds receive a remote, dietitian-led programme of structured energy restriction, meal replacements, and behavioural support; the rest continue routine dietetic care. Twenty-four weeks of follow-up will judge whether recruitment, adherence, and safety make a full trial viable, with interviews capturing how participants experience the reversal of lifelong dietary messaging. The study measures feasibility, not weight loss itself.
pmc-13410302:
Eivind Lundgaard and co-workers report in 2026 on lung function in adults with cerebral palsy who pushed to their limit on a treadmill. Little was known about how their lungs respond at hard effort. The study also asked whether feeling breathless matches the air a person still holds in reserve.

One hundred adults with spastic cerebral palsy took part, and 89 finished all tests. Most, about 90 percent, had lung function in the normal range. At peak effort, though, 70 percent kept less than 20 percent of breathing reserve, which signals a real limit. Fitness was lowest in those with the most motor limits. Feeling breathless did not line up with measured reserve.
pmc-13411102:
Jiecheng Jiang and colleagues followed 3221 older Chinese adults from 2011 to 2018 to see how sleep and low mood travel together and what illness follows. Most earlier work froze both at one visit, so the team grouped repeated measures into four joint paths, from steady sleep with low mood to shrinking sleep with rising low mood.

The shrinking-sleep and rising-mood group faced the highest later risks, including memory disorders, stroke, and having several chronic diseases at once. Machine learning models also flagged who was likeliest to land on that risky path, giving prevention work an early target group to watch.
pmc-13411302:
Henrique de Aguiar Wiederkehr and colleagues review in 2026 machine perfusion, a method that keeps donor livers alive on a pump before transplant. Demand for livers outruns supply everywhere, and many donated organs are borderline. Pumping oxygen and nutrients through the organ can rescue some of those grafts.

Two modes dominate: cold perfusion and body-temperature perfusion. Both aim to prevent the damage that hits when blood returns to a starved organ, a process that can kill grafts early. Wider use could grow transplant numbers and shrink waiting lists. Cost is the open question, and Brazil faces extra hurdles, from donor support gaps to a ban on donation after cardiac death.
pmc-13411902:
Paul Iziomo and a large team dissect in 2026 six years of Lassa fever in Nigeria's Ebonyi State, where deaths from the rodent-borne virus run strikingly high. State health records from 2018 to 2023 held 1,910 suspected cases, of which 368 were confirmed. Survival predictors and case geography anchored the analysis.

About a third of confirmed patients died, and the death share rose year by year. Nearly half the cases clustered in one local government area around the state capital. Patients arrived a median of ten days after symptoms began, then waited about twelve more for diagnosis. Bleeding, sepsis, breathing trouble, and confusion each cut survival odds sharply. Faster presentation and testing in the hotspot are the authors' urgent prescriptions.
pmc-13412202:
Gerald Kizza and co-authors describe in 2026 the design and first month of a text-message support program in Uganda for adults who carry HIV alongside type 2 diabetes. Juggling two long-term conditions strains pill routines, clinic visits, and privacy. The formative study enrolled 64 people at Mbarara Regional Referral Hospital: 39 patients, 20 helpers they chose, and five health workers.

Patients received discreet SMS pill reminders, visit prompts, and learning messages, while helpers got their own nudges to check in. Over the month the system sent 1,092 medication reminders and 280 helper prompts among its message types. Those enrolled rated the program acceptable and workable, and interviews guided small fixes to wording and clinic links.
pmc-13412302:
Mohaddeseh Sadat Hafez Yousefi and colleagues compared two forms of gentle brain stimulation for motor learning in 39 older adults with mild cognitive impairment in 2026. Pulsed and direct current stimulation over the movement cortex were each paired with five days of a reaction-time task, against a sham treatment, with brain waves tracked to follow-up.

Both real treatments beat sham on speed, accuracy, and brain wave measures, while pulsed current gave stronger early gains that partly held two weeks later. The paper suggests pulsed stimulation deserves the larger trial, since early motor gains in this group could support daily independence.
pmc-13412702:
Ioannis A. Ziogas and colleagues use spatial transcriptomics in 2026 to ask why some infants with biliary atresia lose their native liver faster than others. The disease scars and blocks bile ducts in newborns and is the leading reason for child liver transplants. The team mapped gene activity by tissue region in livers removed at transplant from fourteen children, grouping patients by whether the native liver had survived under or over two years.

Children with the fastest course showed the most aggressive pattern: liver cells lost their normal zonation, scar tissue varied more, and immune-driven pathways ran hot. Genes tied to SOX4, a factor that pushes liver cells toward a bile-duct identity, were most enriched in that group. Samples taken at diagnosis confirmed the pattern.
pmc-13412902:
Feiyun Huang, Xi Xu, and Yanzhong Li identify in 2026 the fungus behind a new shoot dieback disease of pigeonpea in Hainan, China. The legume is a protein staple across Asia and Africa, and the dieback had hit between 30 and 100 percent of plants in affected fields around Danzhou. Isolates from dying shoot tips were purified, sequenced at two gene regions, and sprayed onto healthy seedlings to test whether they truly cause the disease.

The culprit proved to be Lasiodiplodia theobromae: sprayed seedlings sickened within six days, and the fungus was recovered again from them. Infection cut plant height by 45 percent and dry weight by about 76 percent in the trials reported. Among seven fungicides screened, two inhibited it best in dishes, and one controlled disease best in pots.
pmc-13413602:
Md Shamim Ahmed, Xianghong Ma, and Yu Jia build in 2026 a spinning energy harvester that adapts its working mode to speed without any electronics in charge. Rotation harvesters usually work only in a narrow speed band, a poor fit for wheels, turbines, and machinery that speed up and slow down. Their design leans on gravity-driven magnetic excitation when rotation is slow, then hands over to centripetal-force-driven nonlinear motion as speed climbs, with mounting orientation shaping the response.

Bench tests used vibration profiles from aerospace, automotive, building, and industrial settings to check realism. Pointing the cantilever downward peaked at an average 57.8 microwatts under the aerospace profile in their experiments. Pointing it upward proved tougher under random broadband shaking instead. The authors pitch the stator-free design for self-powered sensors.
pmc-13413702:
Reem Zabit and co-authors measure cancer risk in 2026 among adults with clinically recognized celiac disease in a nationwide Israeli health dataset. Reports on this risk have swung widely with referral patterns and study design. Propensity matching paired 1,006 patients with 7,137 controls similar in background, illnesses, and inflammation markers, and dated cancer outcomes were followed for roughly forty-nine thousand person-years combined.

Celiac patients carried a 61 percent higher hazard of an invasive cancer code than matched controls in the main analysis. The strongest signals clustered in blood cancers, especially lymphoma, and in gut cancers, which showed nearly triple the hazard. Breast and lung cancers showed no link at all. The gut-pattern T-cell lymphomas matched the type long tied to celiac disease. The authors advise vigilance, not wider screening.
pmc-13414602:
Haonan Zhang and co-authors test whether selenium nanoparticles can keep cadmium out of rice grain, in a 2026 pot experiment. Plants grew for a full season in contaminated paddy soil. Particles of 50, 100, and 200 nanometers were added at two rates, 20 and 50 milligrams per kilogram of soil.

Treatment shifted soil chemistry, lowered available cadmium, and moved cadmium into less mobile forms bound to iron and manganese oxides. Iron plaque on roots trapped more cadmium at the surface. Particles of 100 nanometers at the lower rate cut grain cadmium by about 89 percent. Grain selenium stayed within the accepted range for enriched rice.
pmc-13416202:
Fatemeh Majdolashrafi and colleagues map anxiety rates across the provinces of Iran for 2010 to 2021, in a 2026 ecological study. Age standardized rates came from a global health database, analyzed for space and time patterns. Anxiety disorders rank as the second leading cause of mental health disability worldwide.

Iran's rate rose by about 176 per hundred thousand people over the period, outpacing global trends. Women recorded higher incidence than men throughout. Southeastern provinces showed the highest rates in both sexes. One northern province emerged as a hotspot in the later years. Targeted mental health resources for high risk provinces are the practical takeaway.
pmc-13416902:
Yong-Jin Park and Moon-Il Park propose standard terms for emergency cervical cerclage, a stitch placed to hold a pregnancy when the cervix has opened early, in a 2026 framework paper. Membranes may bulge through the opening, which makes the operation the hardest form of cerclage. Older systems sort cases by reason, not by what the surgeon actually finds.

Their model grades three features: how far membranes bulge, whether they can be pushed back, and whether enough cervix rim remains. The last two decide if surgery is feasible at all. Three grades follow, from low complexity to not feasible. Shared terms should help teams compare cases and studies.
pmc-13417002:
Araceli Sánchez-Ortiz and co-authors profile the scent chemicals given off by whole olives, in a 2026 study of cultivar differences and fruit damage. Plants release volatile compounds, small airborne molecules, when stressed by pests or disease. Six olive varieties were compared, and healthy fruit was set against damaged fruit.

Lab tuning fixed the best heat, time, and sample size for trapping the volatiles. Varieties differed clearly in their scent profiles. Statistical models separated healthy from damaged fruit with about 90 percent accuracy, pointing to marker compounds from one fat breakdown pathway. Such fingerprints could help growers spot trouble early under a changing climate.
pmc-13418202:
Jiangpeng Yu and colleagues find how a soil microbe makes a useful acid called benzohydroxamic acid, in a 2026 study. The acid can help in drug design and crop care, yet no one had shown that nature makes it. A search of the microbe's genes found a three gene set that looked fit for the job. The product then showed up in the microbe's broth.

Feeding tests with marked atoms showed benzoic acid is the start point. One enzyme moves the key group in one step, with help from cell energy. When the three genes were placed in a lab strain, that strain made the acid too.
pmc-13418602:
Alrudayni and colleagues reported in 2026 a rare and fast-moving cancer case in a 42-year-old man. He had two months of worsening constipation, weight loss, belly discomfort, and dark stools. Scans found a mass growing from the anal canal into the lower rectum, plus spots in the liver. Tissue tests confirmed anorectal malignant melanoma, a skin-type cancer arising in the anus or rectum, which makes up under one in a hundred melanomas.

Surgeons made a colostomy, an opening for stool, because the bowel was close to blocking. Treatment with the immunotherapy drug nivolumab was started as first-line therapy. The patient declined quickly despite treatment and died while on comfort-focused care. The authors warn that this cancer mimics common benign anorectal problems, which delays diagnosis.
pmc-13418702:
Hiromasa Ishihara and colleagues track virus specific T cells that persist in HPV driven throat cancer, including in metastases, in a 2026 study. These cancers usually respond well yet can recur late. Gene profiling of 56 tumours and single cell analysis of tumour T cells, including a primary and lung metastasis pair sampled three years apart, hunted lasting defenders.

Nine receptors specific to viral proteins E6 and E7 were validated in lab tests. High strength receptors persisted in the metastasis, while weaker clones vanished, including one already in clinical testing. Persistent cells bore tissue resident marks and inhibitory features. Their presence linked to lower recurrence risk, suggesting biomarker and therapy value.
pmc-13419302:
Leyao Xu and colleagues screen skin treatments for teat hyperkeratosis, a rough keratin ring that builds at the teat tip of dairy cows under long machine milking. The lesion is the most common chronic teat problem on intensive farms, yet it draws little notice in daily checks. The study ran at a large commercial dairy with milking cows in full production.

Four store-bought topical products, each meeting national drug standards, were applied and compared on the same farm. Teat tips were watched for shape changes before and after treatment, and group differences were recorded. Urea ointment came out as the lead treatment in the results. A cheap, working cream matters to farms since sore teats can cut milk yield and raise infection risk.
pmc-13420302:
Maria Del Mar Ferrà-Cañellas and colleagues test a sequential micro-immunotherapy product on bone loss after menopause, using rats whose ovaries were removed to mimic hormone loss. Falling estrogen unbalances bone building against bone removal, driving the thinning that raises fracture risk. The study covered both early and established bone loss stages in the rat models.

Body composition, blood markers of bone turnover, strength testing, and fine scans of spongy bone structure all gauged the product's effect. Four blood markers, including two that report bone breakdown and formation, were tracked through the runs. Ultra-low-dose immune signaling products claim gentle, system-wide effects, a claim this design tests directly. Results here will shape whether the approach earns study in women facing the same bone loss.
pmc-13421002:
Hailin Xiong and colleagues built a reconstruction framework in 2026 for high-resolution diffusion MRI that sharpens images while using fewer scan blades. Their CORPUSE method joins multi-blade propeller data with distortion correction and field maps, aiming for cleaner diffusion-tensor images at higher acceleration.

Tests in healthy volunteers on a 1.5 Tesla scanner showed sharper images, better geometric fidelity, and stronger motion resilience than standard multishot methods across blade counts and trajectories. MRI teams gain a faster, more robust diffusion protocol for mapping white-matter structure for diffusion studies in busy clinics.
pmc-13421202:
Carling Robinson and colleagues tested in 2026 whether higher tau PET signals in women reflect real Alzheimer pathology or a measurement quirk. Women consistently show stronger tau PET signals, yet PET can mislead through off-target binding. The team compared PET against a spinal-fluid marker of aggregated tau, MTBR-tau243, in two cohorts totaling 665 people.

The fluid marker tracked PET burden strongly in both cohorts, and that link did not differ by sex, supporting the view that women's higher signals reflect genuinely greater tau aggregation. The paper strengthens confidence in sex comparisons of Alzheimer tau burden.
pmc-13421502:
Jasmin Ochs and nine colleagues report, in a 2026 study, that CD19 — a protein treated as an exclusive B-cell marker — passes between immune cells. When immune cells meet, they often swap membrane pieces, and this transfer blurs the line between cell identities in ways that matter for antibody therapies aimed at CD19.

In mouse and human cell cultures, T cells picked up CD19 while activating B cells, along with working antibody molecules that gave them B-cell-like abilities. In patients with chronic brain demyelination, such T cells looked pro-inflammatory and were removed by an approved anti-CD19 drug. Macrophage-like cells also gained CD19 after eating dead B cells. The authors warn that marker-based targeting needs this traffic in mind.
pmc-13421802:
Van Hamelsveld and colleagues built surveillance tools in 2026 for antimicrobial resistance in an urban river in Aotearoa New Zealand. Antimicrobial resistance is the ability of bacteria to survive antibiotic drugs. Resistance is not routinely measured alongside standard water testing.

Over two years the team measured resistant Escherichia coli bacteria and their resistance genes near homes and swimming spots, finding persistently high levels of both. They compared lab phenotyping, growing bacteria against drugs, with full genome sequencing and checked how resistance genes move between bacteria. One common resistance pattern acted as a sentinel for rarer, more worrying ones, probably because resistance genes travel together on shared DNA rings called plasmids. The authors offer the cheap phenotype test as a practical stand-in for costly sequencing in routine monitoring.
pmc-13422702:
Tierney and colleagues analyze in 2026 how the type of diagnostic test changes what Salmonella surveillance sees in the United States. Newer stool tests detect the bacteria's DNA without growing it, while the older culture method grows a living isolate.

Using the Foodborne Diseases Active Surveillance Network records from 2004 through 2024, the team found overall infection rates stable across two decades. Beneath that calm surface, culture-diagnosed and culture-confirmed cases steadily declined. Cases found only by the newer tests, and never confirmed by culture, steadily rose. The two routes caught demographically similar patients, but test-only cases tended to be milder and more scattered, suggesting such infections were once missed entirely. The authors warn that prevention wins against severe disease can look flat in headline numbers as detection of mild cases expands.
pmc-13423802:
Taylor Wild and colleagues reviewed delivery-room care in 2026 for 19 sets of conjoined twins treated from 2013 to 2025 at one center. The golden hour for conjoined twins demands a tailored team plan, yet published delivery-room data were sparse.

Thirteen sets received active resuscitation and six palliative care, and breathing support was frequent. Among ten sets that underwent separation, survival to neonatal intensive-care discharge reached 80 percent for twin A and 100 percent for twin B. Neonatal teams gain a benchmark for planning these rare, high-stakes deliveries at referral centers in future cases.
pmc-13423902:
Jenna Magri and colleagues report a 2026 case where a Kayexalate-related mass mimicked metastatic cancer outside the gut. The potassium-binding drug's gut side effects are well known, and its discontinued US use has not erased the risk, since masses can appear long after exposure.

A 65-year-old woman presented with a mass beside the ascending colon reaching the abdominal wall and nearby bowel, raising concern for spread cancer, and the paper reviews similar pseudotumor reports. Clinicians gain a reminder to keep this drug reaction in the differential for puzzling abdominal masses.
pmc-13424302:
Kaiyuan Ma and colleagues studied in 2026 how music and body motion each shape emotion judgments in traditional Chinese plucked-instrument performance. Expressive movement is a hard-to-read channel for embodied agents, so the team tested audio-only, visual-only, and combined presentations from professional performances.

Combined judgments tracked audio more than vision, motion alone gave weak and ambiguous valence readings, and motion may help only for low-arousal clips, with no systematic shift in average emotion. The team also released EMOSIC, over 7.5 hours of synced audio and motion capture, giving affect researchers a non-Eurocentric resource.
pmc-13426402:
Seyedzadeh and colleagues reported in 2026 on how tissue stiffness affects cytotoxic T lymphocytes, the immune cells that kill cancer cells. Tumors often sit in stiffened tissue, and it was unclear how much that stiffness alone weakens the T cells. The team printed the T cells and their target cells inside gel-like supports whose stiffness could be set, while pore size stayed the same across samples.

Seyedzadeh found that in stiffer supports the T cells moved more slowly and killed fewer of their specific targets. The cells still met their targets as often, but each contact lasted a shorter time because the immune synapse, the close junction between the cells, formed poorly. Calcium signals and a key activation marker both backed this picture. Stiffness thus harms T cell action at several steps, from movement to killing, which matters for designing cancer immune therapies.
pmc-13427402:
Rivkah Gardner-Frolick and coauthors studied industrial siting inequity across Canada in a 2026 environmental justice analysis. Facilities responsible for most fine particle and precursor emissions were checked for disproportionate placement near structurally marginalized groups, a pattern the authors call double disproportionality when both emissions and siting skew. Siting patterns differed sharply between urban and rural settings in their results.

Oil and gas extraction facilities disproportionately affected marginalized groups in cities. Mining and quarrying did so in rural areas. Urban Indigenous populations were heavily affected for both all emitters and high emitters. Low-income and Black residents were likelier to live near clusters of emitting facilities. Smoke and dust from mills and mines do not fall in fair shares, and this work counts that tilt town by town and group by group in hard terms.
pmc-13427502:
Andrew G. Georgiadis profiles his own practice in a 2026 reviewer profile for the journal JPOSNA, part of a series honoring the volunteer reviewers behind the publication. At Gillette Children's Hospital, his pediatric orthopaedics work splits into three parts. About forty percent goes to cerebral palsy care with gait analysis decision-making. Another forty percent goes to limb lengthening and deformity correction, and twenty percent to general pediatric orthopaedics and trauma. He notes subspecialty clinics have multiplied as the group grows.

Even with deep subspecialization, he argues pediatric orthopaedists must remain generalists to a degree, since the field's breadth is part of its reward. The profile humanizes the peer review workforce readers rarely see.
pmc-13428002:
Seána Duggan reviews how copper shapes meetings between fungi and bacteria across farms, animals, buildings, and the human body. She names this whole zone of copper influence the cuprosphere, and views it through One Health, which links human, animal, and environmental health.

Copper arrives through crop sprays, animal feed, manure, wastewater, and even the immune system's own defences, where it can kill germs. Duggan shows that such pressure kills sensitive microbes, favours copper-tolerant ones, and boosts genes that resist copper. In mixed mats of Candida yeast and Staphylococcus bacteria, the two partners handle copper in matching ways that keep the mat strong. She urges care with copper use across farming, infection control, and waste handling.
pmc-13429102:
Pihu Mehrotra and colleagues study GPR81, a receptor that responds to lactate, and its role in aging skeletal muscle. Their 2026 paper links loss of this receptor to myosteatosis, the build-up of fat inside muscle that harms muscle function.

In cell experiments, reducing GPR81 in young healthy muscle cells increased signs of aging, including DNA damage, harmful reactive oxygen species, weaker mitochondria, and faulty clean-up processes. Treating aged cells with drugs that activate GPR81 boosted fat burning, cut fat build-up, lowered DNA damage and reactive oxygen species, and improved the cells' ability to form muscle fibres. In mice with a rapid-aging condition, the same activating drugs improved muscle regeneration and overall health. The authors suggest GPR81 activation could help reverse age-related fat build-up in muscle.
pmc-13429802:
González-Mancebo and colleagues ask allergy experts to agree on what 'control' and 'remission' mean for patients on allergen immunotherapy. This long treatment retrains the immune system against triggers such as dust mites and pollen. For allergic rhinitis, conjunctivitis, and asthma, no shared definitions existed for routine care. Their 2026 study builds a survey from the literature and runs a two round Delphi process, a method that polls experts until views converge, with forty allergists.

Agreement, set at seventy percent or more, was reached on every item after two rounds. The panel's definitions blend symptom severity, medication use, validated questionnaires, and measures such as lung tests, separately for each of the three diseases. A controlled disease still shows on treatment, while remission marks a deeper, sustained quieting. The authors stress these are preliminary proposals, not validated endpoints, and call for studies to test whether the definitions predict real outcomes.
pmc-13429902:
Jing Mao and co-authors profile, in a 2026 study, the worn-out killer T cells inside pancreatic tumors, cell by cell and place by place. Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma resists immunotherapy because its inner environment suppresses immune attack. The team combined single-cell gene reading with spatial mapping that keeps each cell's location in the tumor. Samples came from tumors and matched blood of patients.

Exhausted CD8 T cells showed a raised signal gene and a lowered killing gene compared with fresher T cells. They talked most often with two partners: a macrophage type marked by a gene called INHBA, and the cancer cells themselves. Two molecular handshake pairs carried much of that traffic, confirmed by staining and docking models. High levels of both handshake molecules tracked with worse patient survival in a public atlas. Immunotherapy designers gain named contacts to interrupt.
pmc-13430202:
Tobias Heiri and Caroline F. Frey monitor, in a 2026 Swiss study, the parasites shared, or not shared, by reintroduced bison and the cattle grazing beside them. European bison are returning to forests across the continent, and moved herds can trade worms with livestock. Seven relocated bison and 25 suckler cows on neighboring ground gave monthly dung samples from April 2023 through March 2024. Lab methods ranged from sieving and flotation to antigen tests.

Eleven parasite groups turned up across both herds, with richer variety in the bison. Several worm and protozoan types appeared only in bison dung, and one only in cattle. Both herds carried gut strongyle worms constantly, though bison egg counts ran about ten times higher. Two cattle-leaning parasites also stood out statistically. No lungworms appeared anywhere. pmc-13433002:

pmc-13439802:

pmc-13455402:

pmc-13456602:

pmc-13456902:

pmc-13457002:

pmc-13457202:

pmc-13457302:

pmc-13457702:

pmc-13458602:

pmc-13459202:

pmc-13461402:

pmc-13462402:

pmc-13464802:

pmc-13465302:

pmc-13465502:

pmc-13465602:

pmc-13465902:

pmc-13466402:

pmc-13466602:

pmc-13466902:

pmc-13467002:

pmc-13467702:

pmc-13468002:

pmc-13468102:

pmc-13468402:

pmc-13468802:

pmc-13469302:

pmc-13469902:

pmc-13470002:

pmc-13470202:

pmc-13471002:

pmc-13471302:

pmc-13471402:

pmc-13471502:

pmc-13471602:
Hama and co-authors pooled community studies of deprescribing, the planned cutting of inappropriate medicines, to see whether it trims drug burden and saves money outside hospitals. Their 2026 systematic review covered 27 studies published before April 20, 2025, with nine of them feeding the meta-analysis.

The pooled result showed a moderate but statistically significant drop in potentially inappropriate medications, though studies varied widely in design and population. Economic evaluations pointed the same way: one Irish analysis estimated that halving inappropriate anti-inflammatory drug use, a 49.8% reduction, could save up to €1,971 per person. Polypharmacy itself affects 26 to 40% of older adults, the authors note, which is why community-level programs matter.
pmc-13471802:
Xukun Dang leads a twenty two author effort in 2026 to set veterinary breakpoints for ceftiofur, a drug used against E. coli infections in dogs. Breakpoints are the lab thresholds that declare a bacterium susceptible or resistant. None existed for this drug in dogs, despite its use for urinary infections, especially in China. Missing thresholds hamper both prescribing and resistance surveillance.

Three cutoffs were derived from separate evidence streams. One came from the spread of resistance in collected isolates. One came from drug exposure modeling with Monte Carlo simulation. One came from a treatment trial in dogs with bladder infections. The proposed urinary breakpoints declare isolates susceptible at or below one microgram per milliliter. They declare isolates resistant at four or above, with matching disk test zones. The authors offer the values for standards adoption.
pmc-13472302:
Barathi Palani, Ľubica Cenknerová, and Martin Pumera build in 2026 a five metal framework material that stores ammonium ions for water based batteries. Ammonium batteries are cheap and safe, but their cathodes suffer low energy and fast fading. Their framework mixes cobalt, nickel, iron, manganese, and molybdenum nodes with an amino decorated linker, an entropy engineered design meant to spread stability across many metals.

The amino groups add polarity and hydrogen bonding sites that welcome ammonium, while molybdenum tightens the metal linker grip and slows dissolution. The cathode delivered a high reversible capacity at modest current and beat its non amino sibling. Capacity actually grew over thousands of cycles, reaching well past its starting value. A full cell with an organic anode kept most of its capacity after a thousand cycles.
pmc-13472802:
Lim and colleagues reported in 2026 new lab models for a brittle bone disease caused by variants in the MBTPS2 gene. Osteogenesis imperfecta makes bones fragile; most cases involve collagen genes, but MBTPS2 causes a rarer form. They grew stem cells from patient skin cells and guided them toward bone-forming cells, and built an image tool to inspect collagen fibres in cell cultures.

The stem cell route let them watch bone development step by step with the patient's own mutation. The image pipeline measured collagen misfolding and fibre organisation in two-dimensional cultures. Together, the models revealed differences in how this gene's variants disturb collagen compared with classic forms. The authors say the tools complement existing qualitative collagen checks. Understanding the distinct mechanism matters because treatment logic may differ by gene.
pmc-13474002:
Moxley, Chialvo, and Scott Chialvo published a 2026 gene model for a fruit fly's detox gene. The gene, Cyp6a14, belongs to a family that breaks down plant poisons and insecticides. Their subject was Drosophila cardini, a cousin of the classic lab fruit fly. Student researchers built the model under a genomics education partnership protocol.

The team placed the gene within the fly's published genome assembly. Neighboring genes matched the layout seen in the classic lab fly closely. Both flies carry the gene on the same DNA strand direction. The model joins a growing dataset on detox gene family evolution. Comparing layouts helps trace how fly lineages handle new plant toxins. Classroom researchers annotated the gene using a shared partnership protocol.
pmc-13474502:
Shi and colleagues trialled in 2026 an oral simulated tube feeding method against nasogastric feeding in acute pancreatitis. Sixty patients with moderately severe disease were randomised: thirty-one to the oral simulated method, twenty-nine to a nose-to-stomach tube. Feeding tolerance at twenty-four hours was the main outcome, in a non-inferiority design testing whether the new method is no worse.

The oral method's tolerance rate was about ninety-seven percent, versus about sixty-nine percent for tube feeding, comfortably non-inferior. Tolerance scores were also better, and bloating and nausea occurred less often. Hospital costs were significantly lower with the oral method: only about thirteen percent of its patients exceeded the cost threshold, versus about half of tube patients. Length of stay did not differ. The authors conclude the oral simulated method is a safe, cheaper alternative for these patients.
pmc-13474602:
Chi Dai and five colleagues described in 2026 a combined approach for front teeth that are both badly damaged on top and infected at the root tip. Root canal treatment alone cannot fix the gum line or the crown shape, so the team paired root-tip microsurgery with gum reshaping surgery in a single coordinated plan.

In two cases of remaining crowns with apical infection, microsurgery cleared infection and encouraged bone healing, while crown lengthening set a healthy gum contour and crown length. Final crowns were fitted after more than six months, and follow-up beyond a year found the teeth symptom-free, though X-rays showed incomplete healing. The approach offers a reference for saving similar complex front teeth.
pmc-13474802:
Taş and Güleryüz tested porcelain veneer designs in a 2026 lab study on teeth that have a cavity on the side facing the next tooth. They compared three setups on model front teeth: a sound tooth, a tooth first repaired with tooth-colored filling material, and a veneer built to cover the cavity directly in one piece. Each group held 12 teeth, giving 36 specimens whose fit and strength the team measured.

Fit was checked at 19 points on each tooth using silicone copies viewed under a microscope, and strength was tested by pushing until the veneer broke.
