The one-piece veneer left a clearly wider gap at the edge beside the cavity and a thicker cement layer inside that region of the tooth. Its breaking strength, however, matched the other groups and even averaged highest, so the authors call the design promising but unproven for real mouths.
pmc-13477602:
Ismail, a family physician, reflects in 2026 on grieving her own father's death while professionally guiding other families through loss. In the consultation room she had long delivered bad news with a practiced, steady hand, yet medical training gave her no immunity when the loss was hers. She describes oscillating between the daughter at the bedside and the doctor explaining his condition to the family.

She names the experience disenfranchised grief, a sorrow not openly acknowledged because professionals are expected to stay stoic and return to work. Focusing only on medical details became her defense, an intellectualization that postponed the emotional reality and added to her burden, alongside rescue fantasies about whether she had done enough as a doctor-daughter. She concludes that physicians are allowed to grieve, may need help themselves, and can turn anguish into personal growth and better patient care.
pmc-13478602:
Remil and colleagues turned discarded olive pits into activated carbon in 2026 and tested it for removing tartrazine, a yellow food dye, from water. The pits were soaked in phosphoric acid and heated to open a pore network, then the carbon's surface and chemistry were profiled with several instruments. Batch tests varied acidity, dye strength, carbon dose, time, and temperature to find the best cleanup conditions.

Cleanup peaked in strongly acidic water at pH 2, using a 40 milligram carbon dose against dye at 40 milligrams per liter over 24 hours. The top measured capacity reached 47.18 milligrams of dye per gram of carbon, and the uptake speed fit a standard second-order model with a fit score of 0.9996 in the analysis. Heat values showed the process releases heat and runs spontaneously, and the authors pitch the waste-derived carbon as a cheap option for dye-laden wastewater.
pmc-13479602:
Lafata and colleagues interviewed 12 experts in 2026 to identify which features of a care organization, not of individual doctors, shape cancer patient outcomes. The panel mixed organization theorists, cancer clinicians, and the people who build clinical data warehouses. They were asked which organization-level traits matter, and whether those traits could realistically be captured in existing data systems for research and improvement work.

Four feature families stood out: leadership structure and culture, quality monitoring processes, outside incentives, and the support services an organization provides its patients. Experts stressed deliberate attention to equity, noting the same features that lift quality also tend to lift fairness in who benefits from care. Some features are easy to pull from public records, while others resist extraction, so the authors say progress needs healthcare organizations themselves to share data as partners.
pmc-13480202:
Jiahuan Li and co-authors present a 2026 field study of how soil microbes shape grassland plants on the steppe. The team tracked root fungi and root pathogens in thirteen grassland species, covering grasses and broader-leafed forbs, grown alone or in competition across overgrazed and restored soils. They then linked microbe levels to how strongly each species responded to its soil community.

Grass species tended to fare worse with their own soil microbes, while forbs tended to fare better. Forbs carried more friendly fungal partners in overgrazed soil, and stronger fungal ties matched stronger gains for them. Grasses carried more root pathogens, and heavier pathogen loads matched worse outcomes where grazing and solo growth combined. The split suggests that restoring steppe may call for different microbe strategies for grasses than for forbs.
pmc-13482302:
Wedgwood, Tuxworth, and Ahmed pooled in 2026 the lab proof for gene based cures of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, a disease that kills nerve cells and robs movement. No cure exists for people yet, so the team asked how well such cures work in rodents. They searched three databases for rat and mouse studies from 2015 to 2025. Of more than four hundred finds, fifty three fit their rules.

Across the pooled studies, gene cures beat no cure on most gauges. Treated rodents kept more motor neurons, the nerve cells that drive muscle. They also lived longer and held on better in a spinning rod test of muscle skill. One catch marred the picture: most studies had a high risk of bias, with weak design or loose reporting. The authors back the promise, but urge stricter lab work before clinic trials.
pmc-13482602:
Hiu Lam Athena Wu and co-authors offer a 2026 review of computer modelling for atopic dermatitis, the itchy, relapsing skin disease also called eczema. The disease mixes gene faults, immune skew, microbes, and triggers, and patient types vary so much that trial-and-error care wastes years. The review surveys maths models, statistics, and learning methods that pick apart this web.

Models can sort patients into biological subtypes, flag the drivers that matter most, and forecast who answers which drug, all while keeping a whole-system view that bench work loses. Skin models grown in dishes help, yet they cannot hold the full body context. The authors map where each method shines and where proof stays thin, then sketch steps to carry models into clinic use. Sharper subtyping may finally match the right therapy to the right skin.
pmc-13483202:
Tafreshi and colleagues tested whether computer analysis of brain scans could reveal hidden injury in obese children with obstructive sleep apnea, a condition where breathing repeatedly stops during sleep. Their 2026 study compared 23 affected children with 26 healthy peers. Standard scans look normal in these children, so the team measured fine texture patterns in MRI images of regions tied to memory, emotion, and self-control.

Texture features separated the two groups best in the left amygdala, where classification reached 87 percent accuracy in the reported analysis. The right hippocampus and left insula followed closely behind. Simple brightness-based features did most of the separating work. Two children treated with a nighttime air-pressure mask later showed texture values moving back toward normal. Tafreshi suggests texture analysis could help doctors spot injury early and track whether treatment is helping.
pmc-13483602:
Junyan Wang leads a 2026 forensic study on estimating sex from tooth size using automated image analysis. Teeth differ by sex, yet hand-measuring three-dimensional dental scans is slow and subjective. The team used a deep learning system to segment teeth automatically in 398 cone-beam scans from northern Han Chinese adults, keeping 357 cases for modeling.

All 16 measured teeth were larger on average in males than in females. Four machine learning models each predicted sex with solid accuracy, reaching 0.859 at best on held-out cases, with canine teeth contributing most to the decisions. Automated measurement removes much of the manual guesswork. The authors position the method as a practical aid for forensic, anthropology, and archaeology work in this population.
pmc-13483702:
Shuang Shang and co-authors review how chemical marks added to RNA molecules steer whether cells live or die. Published in 2026, the synthesis covers four mark types, including the widely studied m6A mark, and the writer, eraser, and reader proteins that place, remove, and interpret them. Each mark can alter how RNA is spliced, moved, translated, or broken down.

When the marking system goes off balance, several controlled death programs shift with it, spanning self-eating, inflammatory bursting, and iron-driven death among others. Those shifts can help tumors grow, hide from immunity, and resist treatment. Readers get a map of where a mark could serve as a cancer signal for diagnosis or outlook, and where blocking a marking protein might open a new treatment angle.
pmc-13483902:
Fawaier and team compared two solar wall panels that preheat ventilation air, testing whether adding a glass cover pays off. Both panels share a perforated steel plate that sun-warms incoming air, acting as insulation that also heats. Their 2026 outdoor study mounted glazed and unglazed versions side by side on a building in Amman, Jordan, through the clear winter months, sweeping airflow and sunlight levels.

The glazed panel converted sunlight to useful heat at 48 to 75 percent efficiency across the test range. The unglazed panel ran six to nine percentage points lower under the same conditions. The glazed version also reached higher efficiency on the stricter energy-quality measure the authors applied. The unglazed panel still recovered much wall heat at low sunlight. Fawaier concludes glazing is worth it where winter heating dominates, with exact payback depending on airflow settings.
pmc-13486502:
Zhuocheng Ding, Naizhong Xu, and Chang Su forecast roof pressure in a steeply tilted coal mine face with an attention-tuned deep network. Published in 2026, the study mines two months of hydraulic support readings from a Huaibei panel, repairing gaps and filtering noise before model comparison. Five modern architectures face simple persistence and classic neural baselines.

Pressure concentrated persistently from the middle to the upper face, a pattern any warning system must respect. The combined convolution, memory, and attention model won on every headline error measure, with fit close to 0.99 and average percentage error near 2.52 percent. Multi-step checks on four supports gave usable warning horizons of five to ten hours. Single-support forecasting can already feed graded alerts, while mine-wide spatial modeling remains the next step.
pmc-13488002:
Saeed, Attar, and Karlakki described in 2026 a small fix to a wound care device used after hip and knee joint replacement. The PICO system uses gentle suction through a dressing to guard high risk cuts, but its loose pump and tube can pull free when patients start to walk. Tubes snagging on crutches made early movement a chore. Their fix uses a Granuflex pad, a sticky skin friendly sheet, to strap the pump firm to the patient.

In their early test group, every one of the 24 patients reported no trouble with wound healing. The dressing and pump stayed put for the full set time in all but two cases. The team says the tweak lets patients move sooner and use walking aids with less fuss. They suggest wards in other fields of surgery could adopt the same strap on method.
pmc-13488202:
Menglu Li and co-authors speed up DNA reactions by mounting them on swimming algae in a 2026 nanotechnology study. DNA tests on still surfaces run slowly because molecules must drift to meet, which limits medical uses. The team attached DNA strands to living algal cells that propel themselves, turning each cell into a moving reaction platform. Several reaction types were timed, from simple strand pairing to enzyme-driven amplification used for detection.

Faster swimming meant faster reactions across the board in the reported experiments. Motion stirred the fluid around each cell, cutting pairing times to minutes and lifting detection sensitivity in complex biological fluids. The system also assembled cells on command. The authors present motion as a general fix for sluggish surface chemistry in future biohybrid tools.
pmc-13490202:
Mehmet Gulmez and a large surgical team evaluate dye-guided imaging during repeat pouch surgery in a 2026 matched case-control study. The operation rebuilds an ileal pouch, a reservoir made from small intestine after colon removal, and repeat surgery risks poor blood flow at the join, which can leak. A fluorescent dye called indocyanine green lights up blood flow under special cameras in real time. Forty-six patients at a high-volume bowel center were matched into dye and no-dye groups of twenty-three.

Imaging changed the surgical plan in two patients, prompting trimming of a poorly supplied pouch tip in one and pouch removal in the other. Major early complications ran lower with imaging, without statistical significance in this small sample. No dye reactions occurred.
pmc-13490902:
Vaishnavi and colleagues tested the probiotic bacterium Lacticaseibacillus rhamnosus GG against mouth thrush in diabetic rats, in a 2026 animal study. Diabetes weakens immunity and makes the yeast Candida more aggressive, so oral candidiasis is common and hard to control in diabetic patients. The team induced diabetes chemically in male rats, painted two Candida species onto their tongues for three days, then gave it daily for twenty-eight days.

Vaishnavi found treated rats carrying far fewer Candida colonies in mouth swabs, and their body weight stabilized instead of falling further as in untreated diabetic animals. Blood and biochemical measures improved, tongue tissue showed less inflammation under the microscope, and molecular signals from immune sensors and a probiotic surface protein shifted with treatment. The authors conclude the probiotic delivered antifungal and immune-calming benefits in this model, supporting it as a safe therapy candidate alongside antifungal drugs, pending human trials.
pmc-13491702:
Lv and colleagues tested flooding fields as a weapon against Fusarium wilt of watermelon and worked out why it succeeds, in a 2026 soil study. The soil-borne fungus survives for years and defeats control methods, yet farmers have known that a period under water suppresses it. The team flooded soil and tracked the pathogen, plant growth, soil chemistry, and the microbial community.

Lv found flooding cutting fungal numbers and wilt incidence while watermelon plants grew better. Soil chemistry shifted, with phosphorus and potassium rising and organic matter and nitrogen falling, and two enzyme activities increased. Bacterial diversity and richness rose while fungal diversity fell, genera as Bacillus and Penicillium became more abundant, and Fusarium dwindled by thirty days. Statistical modeling found potassium, nitrogen, and the richness of the bacterial and fungal communities as the channels through which flooding suppresses disease. That guides how growers can keep the soil ecology stable.
pmc-13491802:
Yi Yang and five colleagues survey in 2026 the quality of life of Chinese children treated for clubfoot with the Ponseti method, alongside the burden carried by their parents. An online questionnaire reached 180 families through parent groups on WeChat, using standard pediatric quality-of-life scales for the children and caregivers plus a short burden inventory.

Children in the youngest group scored below healthy norms on physical and social functioning, while children aged five to eighteen scored above the reference on every scale. Caregiver quality of life was lowest when children were one to two years old and highest in the oldest group. Burden rose during active treatment and eased after age five, with over half of caregivers reporting little or none. Complications hurt children's scores, and brace adherence supported caregivers' well-being.
pmc-13492002:
Mahmoud Mohammadi and others describe a child with Landau-Kleffner syndrome whose language loss finally responded to aimed therapy. In 2026, the case follows a boy with normal early development who lost speech and developed non-motor seizures around age three, with sleep-activated spike-wave brain action. Standard seizure drugs and repeated immune care gave no lasting benefit.

Genetic testing at age twelve found a gain-of-function variant in GRIN2A, a gene for an NMDA dock subunit key in speech and language areas. Treatment with memantine, which blocks NMDA docks, clearly improved speech and social interaction and reduced sleep-related discharges, though some deficits remained. The case argues for early genetic testing in refractory epilepsy-aphasia syndromes.
pmc-13492602:
Colleen C Mercado, Marcel P Fraix, and Devendra K Agrawal review in 2026 stiff person syndrome, a rare autoimmune disorder where the body's own defenses silence the nervous system's brakes. Muscles grow rigid, and sudden noises or touches trigger painful spasms. The review sweeps from the syndrome's antibody families and look-alike spectrum disorders to diagnosis and the newest immune therapies.

Attack antibodies target the machinery that makes the calming signal GABA, plus related receptors and proteins. Standard immune treatments help many patients, and cell-based therapies are being tried for stubborn cases. Yet daily function often stays limited, which is why the authors devote equal weight to rehabilitation: physical and occupational therapy, spasm management, and coordinated multidisciplinary care. Evidence for rehabilitation remains thin, and they call for standardized outcome measures to build it.
pmc-13493802:
Dinesh Kumar Yadav leads a fourteen-author team asking in 2026 which partner plants best help sandalwood survive drought. Sandalwood is a half-parasite that taps host roots for nutrients, so the host's identity shapes its chemistry. Roots from sandalwood grown with eleven different hosts were profiled for free amino acids and stress physiology under water shortage.

One host, Pongamia pinnata, loaded sandalwood roots with the highest levels of several amino acids, while Sesbania grandiflora left one key compound at rock bottom. Acacia and pomegranate partnerships kept leaves greener and better hydrated, with more of the protective compound proline. Statistical patterns confirmed that nitrogen-fixing hosts generally fed the stress response best. Choosing hosts deliberately, the authors argue, is a practical climate adaptation for sandalwood plantations.
pmc-13494102:
Pilleriin Sikka, Sherry Hu, and Boris D Heifets present a 2026 scoping review of dreaming during anesthesia, a topic studied for more than a century yet still poorly mapped. They gathered trials, observational studies, and lab experiments in adults, children, and healthy volunteers. The review covers how often dreams are recalled, what the dreams are like, who recalls them, and what brain signs go with them.

Across 157 studies with 87,866 people, recall rates swung widely, running much higher in lab settings than in large clinical trials. Ketamine and propofol were the drugs most often tied to recall. Most dreams were pleasant and drawn from daily life. Recall was not linked to waking during surgery, which undercuts the idea that a dream means the anesthesia was too light. The authors call for shared definitions and better ways to ask patients about dreams.
pmc-13494402:
Nabeel Sami and others describe transient severe mitral leakage set off by rapid pacing during tube-fed aortic valve fitting. In 2026, the case concerns a sixty-nine-year-old with severe tight aortic valve and normal pumping function, who got acute severe mitral leakage at once after rapid heart-chamber pacing for valve fitting. Pacing can for a time upset muscle-tip tension and leaflet closure.

Sound scans told apart this passing cause from shape troubles such as wire tangling or valve pressing, and the leakage cleared fully within minutes. The case warns doctors not to rush to fit a lasting pacemaker for pacing-linked leakage that fades as timing and muscle-tip tension return.
pmc-13495202:
Aapo Pikkujämsä and colleagues compare, in a 2026 cohort study, very long survival after two ways of doing heart bypass surgery. On-pump surgery uses a heart-lung machine, while off-pump surgery works on the beating heart. Trials had tracked the pair for five to ten years with mixed verdicts, and data past twenty years were scarce.

The team drew on one center's patients from 1999 to 2016 and matched 402 off-pump patients to 804 on-pump patients with like health profiles. Median survival landed near twelve and a half years in both groups, and heart-related deaths did not differ either. Follow-up stretched past two decades for some. The authors back choosing the technique case by case, based on the patient's state and the surgeon's skill, rather than any blanket rule.
pmc-13495302:
Anastasia-Vasiliki Madenidou and colleagues audit, in a 2026 study, how well a standard medical vocabulary covers systemic autoimmune rheumatic diseases. The Human Phenotype Ontology gives shared terms for patient traits and links them to diseases, which helps computers match traits to genes. Complex autoimmune diseases had never been checked against it. The team used gene data from 111 patients in a lupus-centered cohort.

Gaps proved common. Over a third of patients had at least one trait missing a term, and five traits, among them a lung-shrinking syndrome and a kidney crisis of scleroderma, had no term at all. One key term was wrongly defined, and six terms lacked links to diseases they belong with. A small test showed the gaps shift which gene variants a diagnostic tool ranks first. The authors have proposed the missing terms and links to the ontology's keepers.
pmc-13495502:
Lorena Rodrigues Sabino leads a large team setting out, in a 2026 protocol, the ORIGIN-1 trial for cystic fibrosis patients with rare gene faults. New modulator drugs have transformed the disease for common faults, yet people with rare ones are shut out worldwide because big trials cannot be run on so few. The trial first grows each patient's gut organoids, tiny lab replicas, to test whether the drug trio switches their faulty protein on.

Those whose organoids respond enter blinded treatment blocks: two weeks on the drug, a washout, then two weeks on placebo or the reverse, cycled at least twice. Each patient thus serves as their own control, a design called n-of-1. Interim looks decide whether more cycles are needed. The authors hope the pathway can win drug access for patients whose faults will never fill a standard trial, while spending costly medicine only where it works.
pmc-13499202:
Kuanbing Chen and colleagues review in 2026 how metal ions bind and act where drugs and materials meet living tissue. Metals serve in the body as enzyme helpers, structural elements, and signals, and their binding shape governs what metal-based medicines can do. The review organises the field around those biological interfaces, linking binding geometry, reaction speed, and chemical softness to interactions with DNA, proteins, fats, and sugar-coated molecules.

Those interactions shape cell powerhouses, signal chains, and forms of cell death, including an iron-linked type called ferroptosis, which the authors explain as death driven by iron-dependent damage. Clinically used metal compounds are surveyed beside newer designs such as porous metal frameworks, polymer carriers, and artificial enzymes built for targeted delivery. Attention to how the body absorbs and clears such agents, and to their toxicity, connects atomic chemistry with real treatment outcomes.
pmc-13499402:
Xingyue Wu and nine colleagues published this 2026 feeding study on how dietary energy levels affect growing broiler chickens. They varied metabolizable energy, the usable energy in feed, and tracked growth, liver metabolism and gut microbes. Energy is a major feed cost, so finding the right level matters for poultry producers. The birds were male AA broilers raised under standard conditions.

From day 21, 480 birds were split across four diets holding 3,050 to 3,350 kilocalories per kilogram of feed. Growth did not change: body weight, daily gain, feed intake and feed conversion were alike across groups. Higher energy did raise antioxidant defences, shown by stronger enzyme activity, and lowered a marker of inflammation. It also changed gene activity in the liver and gut, and altered the size of immune organs such as the spleen. The authors suggest moderate energy levels support stable metabolism without faster growth.
pmc-13500402:
Roberto Cirocchi leads a 2026 Italian consensus effort fixing shared definitions for appendiceal abscesses, pus collections arising from appendicitis, are defined and diagnosed. Abscess cases vary widely in what drives them and how scans show them, and loose wording has kept studies hard to compare. Two national surgical groups ran a four-round Delphi process, a structured method for building expert agreement, ending with a meeting in Rome in November 2025.

Panellists agreed 22 statements in total. The first seven map the range from simple appendix inflammation through swollen, gangrenous, and burst forms, and they separate true abscesses from appendix masses. A companion imaging framework built on CT descriptors ties scan wording to tissue findings. The authors offer the shared scheme to improve how surgeons, radiologists, and pathologists talk to each other and to make future studies comparable.
pmc-13501602:
Safdar Masoumi leads a nine-author team reporting a 2026 effort to build a severity score for cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic syndrome, a framework tying heart, kidney, and metabolic problems. Existing staging sorts patients into categories with fixed cut-offs that can hide differences within one stage. Using 7,343 adults aged 20 to 80 from the Tehran Lipid and Glucose Study, the team applied confirmatory factor analysis to build age- and sex-specific latent scores. Validation followed in a later wave and in the US NHANES survey, 1999 to 2018.

The score identified stages well, with area-under-curve values at or above 0.83 for stage 2 or higher and 0.90 for stage 3 or higher in later-wave validation. Each standard-deviation rise in the score carried a hazard ratio of 3.2 for all-cause death and 4.7 for cardiovascular death in the Tehran cohort. Within stage 2 alone, the score split patients into thirds whose mortality risk climbed steeply.
pmc-13501702:
Ser Hon Puah leads a six-author team with a 2026 mixed-methods study of how intensive care training builds residents' confidence in managing ventilators. Twenty final-year internal medicine residents who had finished three-month ICU rotations at Tan Tock Seng Hospital in Singapore took part. A self-efficacy scale and a six-item proxy measure captured perceived access to the sources of confidence: mastery experiences, watching others, encouragement, and emotional state. Eight focus groups supplied the discussion strand.

Residents reported moderate to high confidence scores, and mastery, learning by watching, and calm states were all seen as available. Timely feedback, the social persuasion channel, looked scarce in the survey yet rich in the discussions, a gap the authors flag. Seven themes in three categories described an arc from fear of the ventilator toward confidence, powered by mentorship and workplace teaching. The authors credit taking part in ICU work.
pmc-13501802:
Xinyu Fan leads a four-author team reporting a 2026 analysis of whether the kind of sitting matters for the ageing brain. Data came from 2,516 Americans aged 60 or older in the 2011 to 2014 national health survey NHANES. Wrist accelerometers measured sleep, sitting, and activity, while questionnaires split sitting into television watching, computer use, and other forms. Three standard tests scored memory, language fluency, and executive function, merged into one global cognition score. Compositional models treated the day as a fixed time budget.

More relative time in vigorous activity and in total sitting both linked to better cognition in the simple model, while sleep and light activity linked negatively. Splitting sitting apart changed the story: computer use was positively tied to every cognitive domain, while television watching dragged global cognition and language down. Swapping time into activity or computer use predicted gains, and cutting those behaviours predicted steep losses.
pmc-13503702:
Victor M Aguilera and three colleagues study plankton blooms off the coast of Chile in a 2026 paper. The site is the Humboldt Archipelago, near 29 degrees south, where deep water rises to the surface all year. That rise feeds the plant plankton that support fish and sea life.

The team paired 21 monthly boat surveys over two years with data from space and weather records. A base model using water depth mix and wind-driven flow explained most shifts in green pigment, a sign of plankton mass. A broad Pacific wind pattern added more skill. The work shows how far-off climate swings tune the strength of local rising water, and space images hint that plankton mass can drift from bays out to the islands.
pmc-13503802:
Myeounggon Lee and four colleagues build an index to catch early loss of strength and function in older adults, in a 2026 study. Frailty spans body, mind, and social life, yet many tools need clinic tests that are hard to scale. The team aimed for a score drawn from daily-life measures.

They studied 729 adults aged 65 and over who live at home. The index blends grip strength, walking speed, and activity into one score from zero to one, with higher meaning worse function. Scores drew on health history, self-reports, gait tests, thinking tests, and quality of life. People with a fall history scored far worse. The top-risk quarter also slept worse and felt more stress, which supports use in early screening.
pmc-13505102:
Xuesong Liu leads a team linking insomnia to higher death risk in people with depression, and tracing part of that path through blood proteins, in a 2026 UK Biobank study. Sleeplessness is near universal in depression and has been tied to worse outcomes, but the biology in between was blank.

Among nearly four and a half thousand depressed participants, those who usually had insomnia faced about a third higher death risk and lost over two years of life expectancy at age forty-five. A signature of twenty sleeplessness-linked proteins carried its own risk signal. Joint analysis credited the protein set with over a third of the insomnia effect, with three proteins standing as solo mediators. The signature also improved risk forecasts past standard clinical factors.
pmc-13507102:
Sunidhi Garg and colleagues develop, in 2026 work, a machine learning method that predicts phase change charts for uranium alloys while respecting physical shape rules. The charts, called time-temperature-transformation diagrams, show how fast a solid phase changes at each heat level. Lab mapping of each alloy is slow and costly, which limits alloy search.

They tested four training goals, from plain error fitting to versions that enforce the classic C-curve bend and nucleation physics. Shape-aware models gave realistic curves that matched lab data well. The best model flagged five uranium mixes with molybdenum plus a third metal as more stable than the base mix. Faster screening could focus costly lab work.
pmc-13507202:
Stanisław Kurzyna and colleagues demonstrate, in 2026 work, a microwave sensor built from Rydberg atoms that resists signal loss at readout. Rydberg atoms have hugely swollen electron orbits, which makes them exquisitely sensitive to electric fields. The team measured a very short microwave pulse in a single shot with fine precision.

Atom-to-atom interactions then ran a protection step before readout, a step that itself adds a lossy channel yet shields the stored information. Usable information tripled compared with unprotected sensing. The trick borrows from quantum computing without needing a full quantum computer. Practical quantum sensors for communications and field mapping could gain real-world toughness from built-in interactions.
pmc-13507502:
A Ozakgul and four co-authors study sexual health in younger stroke patients and how it links to mood and quality of life, in 2026 work. Their case-control study enrolled 30 stroke patients and 30 matched people without stroke. Each person completed scales on sexual experience, stroke-related quality of life, anxiety, and depression. Sexual health is often left out of rehab for this age group, the authors note.

Patients scored worse on sexual function than controls, and far more of them met the mark for dysfunction. Their reported satisfaction also fell sharply after stroke. Poorer sexual function tracked with lower energy, thinking, and language scores, and with more depression symptoms. It did not track with physical ability, so the authors urge routine screening and care for mood and fatigue in rehab.
pmc-13508102:
Peng Zou and eight co-authors report a light-driven way to build a useful family of alcohol compounds, in chemistry work published in 2026. The starting materials tend to waste light energy through a fast internal process that blocks useful change. The team locked those materials into a rigid shape by tying them to boron-based partners. That lock shut down the wasteful path and let light drive a shift of atoms instead. The reaction ran under mild conditions with no metals or added bases.

The method produced 61 different products, with yields reaching 81 percent in the best cases. It worked with several classes of boron partners and kept a clean choice between two possible paths. Fast light-based tests and computer models showed the reaction passes through a short-lived excited state. The approach also suited late tweaks to complex drug-like molecules.
pmc-13508202:
Jingcheng Chen leads a ten-author team building a simple score to predict whether an irregular heartbeat returns within a year after catheter treatment, in 2026 work. The rhythm problem, persistent atrial fibrillation, often comes back after the procedure. Records came from four Chinese hospitals for 1,689 patients having the treatment for the first time. Patients were split into a larger group for building the score and a smaller group for testing it. Follow-up covered the year after treatment.

About one in four patients saw the rhythm problem return within that year. Return was tied to older age, a larger left heart chamber, longer illness duration, and female sex. The resulting ALADS-AF score, built from those four traits, runs from 0 to 30. Its sorting accuracy was modest, which the authors state plainly. Even so, a quick score can help set honest expectations and plan follow-up before the procedure.
pmc-13508302:
Safak Necati Donertas and Selcen Ozcan Bulut compare a modern guided cleaning method with standard tools for early gum disease, in 2026 work. Standard care uses hand curettes and an ultrasonic device to clean below the gumline. The guided method, called Guided Biofilm Therapy, follows a set sequence built around showing and removing the bacterial film. Eighty non-smoking, healthy volunteers with stage 1 or 2 disease were split at random between the two methods. Gum measures and fluid from the gum crevice were checked before care and again at one and three months.

Both methods improved every measure over time. The guided method pulled ahead on gum redness, plaque scores, and one key inflammation marker in the fluid. Other fluid markers did not differ between groups. The authors call the guided route a strong choice, above all where motivation and plaque control matter most.
pmc-13508402:
Aydın Balcı and six co-authors compare entering the airways through the nose versus the mouth for an ultrasound-guided needle test, in 2026 work. The test samples glands in the chest for cancer staging and diagnosis. Mouth entry is standard, yet the nose may hold the scope steadier and suit patients better. Records covered adults treated at one center from 2019 to 2023. The team compared vital signs, drug needs, sampling yield, diagnosis, and problems by entry route.

Nasal entry was used in 158 patients and oral entry in 246. Oxygen levels after the test ran higher in the nasal group. Oral entry brought bigger heart rate jumps, more sedative use, more pauses for low oxygen, and more repeat tests. Nasal procedures ran a bit shorter and sampled slightly more gland stations. The authors present the nose as a safe, workable alternative route.
pmc-13508502:
Prabakar VaittinadaAyar leads a fifteen-author team testing a six-question geriatric check as a fast risk tool for older emergency patients, in 2026 work. Older arrivals are rising in emergency departments, and quick sorting tools are scarce. The study ran in 36 European departments over seven straight days and enrolled 4,657 patients aged 65 and older with any complaint. Nurses scored the brief check at arrival, sorting patients into low, moderate, or high risk. Models then linked risk level to admission, stay length, and death.

Admission odds and stay length matched between low and moderate groups, yet both jumped in the high group. Moderate-risk patients died at about double the low-risk rate, and high-risk patients at about triple. The authors say the six items can flag frailer elders fast and support standard triage. They still call for forward trials before routine use, since this was an observational snapshot.
pmc-13509002:
Inomata and colleagues sorted left- and right-handed crystals of a family of potassium lanthanoid nitrates. They measured how strongly each metal ion inside responds to the twisted crystal setting. Their 2026 study covers seven lanthanoid elements in fully inorganic salts. The salts form crystals in handed space groups even though their building blocks are not handed, an effect called spontaneous resolution.

Inomata recorded circular dichroism spectra, which measure unequal absorption of left- and right-handed light. They found sharp bands from inner-shell electron transitions for the praseodymium, neodymium, samarium, and europium salts. The distorted surroundings partly switch on transitions that are usually forbidden, boosting both absorption and the dichroism signal. Samarium showed the largest anisotropy factor. It is the ion that reacts most strongly to a chiral crystal field in this family, a result that guides design of inorganic optical materials.
pmc-13509302:
Okura and co-authors reported a 2026 cell study on melatonin, the sleep related hormone, protecting skin cells from ultraviolet B light. Sunlight's UVB rays damage the surface skin cells called keratinocytes and drive ageing and cancer. Melatonin gathers inside mitochondria, the cell's energy producers, where it fights oxidative damage.

In human keratinocytes grown in the lab, UVB cut cell survival in step with dose and flooded cells with reactive oxygen species. Okura found pre-treatment with melatonin blunted that damage across the board. Treated cells kept their mitochondrial voltage, kept making energy, and showed less of the self destruct signal caspase-3. Markers of DNA damage and cell ageing also rose less, tying protection to preserved mitochondrial balance.
pmc-13509502:
Zeyuan Li, Linzhe Chen, Haoqiang Liu, and Kelin Lu propose a 2026 guidance method that lets a drone locate a target from direction readings alone while steering clear of no-fly zones. Direction-only sensing gives no distance, so the drone must keep moving into positions that make the target location easier to pin down. The method takes cues from flying insects that adjust their paths in response to what they sense.

A mapped field of uncertainty guides the drone toward informative positions, and local sensitivity within that field widens or narrows the safety margin near forbidden zones. A shaping step then keeps each move within the allowed space. Computer trials covered open airspace, a single bent forbidden zone, and crowded zones, and the drone avoided all zones while its target estimate settled to a stable answer in each setting.
pmc-13509602:
Milan Lackovic, Dejan Nikolic, Jovana Kuzmanovic Pficer, and Sladjana Mihajlovic follow 400 pregnant women with migraine treated at a Belgrade hospital between 2024 and 2026, in work published in 2026. The team tracked whether migraine attacks stayed steady, eased, or grew worse during pregnancy. They then compared those patterns with fetal growth, blood pressure problems, diabetes in pregnancy, weight gain, and early birth.

Lasting or worsening migraine appeared more often in pregnancies with poor fetal growth and several other complications. Migraine worsening alone raised the odds of abnormal growth in simple comparisons, yet the link faded once other maternal and pregnancy factors were counted. High blood pressure in pregnancy and poor weight gain stood out as stronger factors in the adjusted results. The authors say migraine change works better as a warning flag than as a direct cause to blame.
pmc-13511302:
Daisy Duan and five co-authors report a 2026 feeding trial of time-restricted eating in adults with obesity and prediabetes. Thirty-nine participants finished a twelve-week program where all food was supplied and calories were held equal. One group ate within a ten-hour window, while the other kept a sixteen-hour usual pattern. Eating behavior, appetite hormones, and inflammation markers were measured before and after.

Both groups lost a similar small share of body weight. Both also reported stronger restraint over eating plus lower loss-of-control eating and hunger by the end. No clear between-group gaps appeared in behavior scores, appetite hormones, or inflammation markers. The authors say any edge for the shorter window was not visible at this size and calorie match, and larger forward-looking studies must judge whether real differences exist.
pmc-13512202:
Panuvit Rienpradub and eleven co-authors grow bacterial cellulose membranes in coconut water and blend in a second bioplastic to make them flexible enough for medical handling, in 2026 work. Pure bacterial cellulose is clean and strong yet rigid and brittle. A Komagataeibacter strain fermented mature coconut water, and a response-surface search tuned sugar level and growing time.

Seven days at a set sugar level gave the most even, intact membrane. Adding the bioplastic powder during growth lifted stretch at break from about twenty-three to twenty-eight percent, with only a slight drop in peak strength, and the composite held more water. A cradle-to-gate life cycle check found the warming footprint about three times lower than bovine collagen membranes. The authors pitch the material as a greener base for tissue engineering dressings.
pmc-13512602:
Leshata Winter Mokhwelepa and Gsakani Olivia Sumbane map the literature on family-centred approaches in mental health care for people with psychiatric disorders, in a 2026 scoping review. Involving families can lift treatment results and social inclusion, and solid proof exists for single interventions such as family work in psychosis. No earlier synthesis, though, traced how family-centred care is framed and used as a system-wide route to inclusive practice across diagnoses and settings.

The review gathers how such approaches are defined, put into practice, and tied to inclusivity at several evidence levels. Findings aim to push practitioners toward family-inclusive habits that raise engagement. For policy makers, the map supports funding and rules that treat families as care partners rather than bystanders. The authors also frame family-centred care as a lever for narrowing mental health disparities in whole populations.
pmc-13514602:
Jiaqi Tang, Huichao Bi, and Jun Wei present a 2026 systematic review of how schools spot STEM talent among gifted children. With science and technology skills in high demand, finding able pupils early matters, yet schools lack well-tested, shared methods for doing so. Following a standard review protocol, the authors gathered 26 peer-reviewed studies from nine databases and compared the identification approaches on offer.

Most studies came from the United States, peaked around 2018, and focused on high school students. Methods ranged widely: intelligence and spatial tests, school achievement, creativity and problem-solving tasks, portfolios, subject competitions, and teacher or parent nominations. Reasoning, creativity, spatial ability, and problem-solving stood out as the core traits worth measuring. Family income, culture, adult support, and gender expectations all bent who got noticed.
pmc-13515502:
Jing Zhao and five colleagues present a lightweight vision system in a 2026 study for inspecting shallow grooves cut into metal by a controlled electrochemical method. The grooves, only micrometres deep, steer how precision surfaces perform, yet they are faint, irregular, and hard to spot in grey microscope images. Manual inspection is slow and subjective, so the team built a network that expands each grey image into three channels: the original, a contrast-enhanced version, and edge maps at several scales.

Wavelet-based shrinking inside the network keeps fine edge detail while cutting the model's size and computing cost. Extra parts, an attention module and a boundary-aware training loss, were tested piece by piece, along with data tricks that stretch the training set. On the team's own groove dataset, the system segmented the grooves well enough for automated inspection.
pmc-13516002:
Juin Yee Kong leads a thirteen-author team presenting the Singapore Neonatal Resuscitation Guidelines 2026. Reviving newborns who struggle to breathe at birth demands tight teamwork along a standard sequence. The subgroup of the Singapore Resuscitation and First Aid Council rebuilt the national guidance by comparing the newest global consensus reports and the American and European guidelines against Singapore's 2021 edition.

Local conditions shaped the final advice, which follows the steps of the newborn flow chart. Preparation receives strong emphasis: briefing the team before delivery, checking equipment, assigning roles, and agreeing a cord management plan with the wider care team. The guidelines cover babies born anywhere, plus newborns who need reviving again during their first hospital stay. Kong's team presents the update as the working standard for delivery rooms across Singapore until the next evidence cycle.
pmc-13518002:
Sakamoto reported a 2026 emergency case where a visual clue in a patient's hair pointed to the overdose drug before any history was available. A 28-year-old woman was found collapsed at home and arrived unable to speak for herself, with severely impaired consciousness. Clinicians noticed bright yellow granular material with a medicinal smell stuck in her hair during the initial examination.

Sakamoto explains that in Japan that residue suggests granules from an over-the-counter cold medicine containing acetaminophen, prompting an immediate blood acetaminophen measurement, which came back markedly elevated. The antidote N-acetylcysteine was given promptly, and she recovered without liver injury and was discharged. The author is careful that the residue alone proves nothing and was never chemically analyzed. argues that amid rising over-the-counter overdoses among young Japanese women, such bedside clues can trigger the one test and treatment that prevent liver failure.
pmc-13518302:
Aditya Aggarwal and four colleagues rebuild a young woman's ear from her own forearm tissue in a 2026 case report. Her left ear was torn off in 2011, along with scalp, cheek, and eye injuries. A synthetic implant version later infected and had to come out, and heavy scarring ruled out the usual local flaps for a second attempt.

The team chose a pre-laminated radial forearm flap. First they parked a rib-cartilage ear framework under the forearm skin to let it settle and take shape. Then microsurgery moved the whole composite, cartilage, skin, and its artery supply, to the side of her head. Aggarwal's team chose the method because scarred local tissue could not drape a framework on its own. They present the rarely used route as a workable answer when old avulsion injuries leave surgeons nothing nearby to build with.
pmc-13518602:
Luis A Huerta Díaz and three colleagues review the return of weight after bariatric surgery in a 2026 article. Obesity behaves as a chronic, relapsing disease, and regain after surgery springs from hormone adaptation, behaviour, metabolic pushback, and anatomical change together. Re-operation was once the default answer, though it is technically harder and riskier than the first procedure.

A new drug wave changes the order of play. GLP-1 medicines deliver meaningful loss after surgery in trial after trial, above all when no fixable anatomical fault exists. The dual-action tirzepatide outperformed the older drugs and may suit selected patients best, with triple-action and oral agents behind it. The authors propose a step-wise path: check anatomy, rebuild lifestyle, add proven drugs, and reserve revision surgery for true anatomical failure. Modern medicines, they argue, can shrink, delay, or better target the return to theatre.
pmc-13518802:
Christian Doh Dinga, Sander van Rijn, Laurens J. de Vries, and Milos Cvetkovic examine in 2026 how to schedule flexible energy use across systems that link electricity, heat, and other carriers. Homes and firms now control heat pumps, electric cars, and similar assets, so central planners cannot simply command them. Privacy and independence matter alongside cost.

The team proposes coupling separate models at runtime instead of merging everything into one giant optimization. They test a price-response version and a market auction version against central co-optimization at several problem sizes. Coupling gave up little efficiency while scaling far better and keeping provider data private. Open-source software accompanies the comparison for other modelers.
pmc-13519002:
Miao Shi and a large team map a bacterial immune weapon in 2026: dGTPase enzymes that starve invader phages by draining a DNA building block. How the enzymes work was known, while their spread across life stayed murky. Mining genomes from bacteria, archaea, and eukaryotes showed the enzymes are widespread and often fused to other immune domains.

One Vibrio enzyme, Vdg, was imaged by cryo-electron microscopy in groups of 8 and 16 parts, plus filaments. Only the 8-part ring proved needed for antiviral defense on its own, while bigger stacks were extra. A related molecule, dAMP, tuned the enzyme's activity. Shi's team ties enzyme switching to how the parts group, widening the picture of nucleotide-depletion immunity.
pmc-13520302:
Stefania Canneva and colleagues describe in 2026 a single patient whose stable myasthenia gravis flared after two different bone-strengthening treatments. Myasthenia gravis causes fluctuating muscle weakness, while long-term steroid use for the condition can thin bones and prompt bone treatment.

The patient was a 78-year-old woman with long-standing, stable disease. Weakness worsened after an infusion of zoledronic acid and again after one dose of denosumab, and each flare needed a temporary rise in steroid dose. Bone drugs were then stopped, while vitamin D continued. The authors note that a denosumab-linked flare had not been reported before, so clinicians may want closer watch after dosing.
pmc-13520402:
David Livingstone Ejalu leads a 2026 study of young people with HIV in East-Central Uganda who still had unsuppressed virus and then received intensive adherence counselling. Prior work counted suppression after counselling, while this study asks which personal, clinic and social factors shape the outcome.

Programme records covered 580 people aged 10 to 24 years across 32 facilities, each with a repeat viral load after counselling. Median age was about sixteen years. Adjusted analysis using a modified Poisson approach then weighs each factor while allowing for facility clustering. The results aim to show programmes where extra support beyond counselling is most needed.
pmc-13520502:
Jesse S. Leavitt and colleagues profile in 2026 chemical decorations on transfer RNA across nine archaeal species living in hot, acidic, salty and mild habitats. Such decorations keep transfer RNA stable and accurate, yet their evolution in archaea was poorly charted.

A sequencing method that reads full-length transfer RNAs while recording modification signals revealed position-specific patterns that varied by lineage. Hot-loving species showed coordinated or mutually exclusive marking at paired stem positions. Enzyme family shapes also diverged by lineage, matching substrate habits. The multi-species atlas links enzyme evolution with translation tuning in extreme environments.
pmc-13520702:
Michele L Lemons and colleagues interviewed biology teachers about how they judge, comment on, and grade student work. Published in 2026, the study held one-to-one video interviews with 27 instructors of introductory biology at two-year and four-year colleges in the United States. Teachers were asked what assessment, feedback, and grading should achieve and to share examples from their own courses.

Goals proved varied and at times at odds, with some teachers treating grades as motivation and others as a drag on it. Lines between the three tasks blurred, since grading was sometimes described as feedback and feedback as grading, and stated beliefs did not always match classroom practice. The authors argue that sharper distinctions among the three roles could improve talk among teachers, students, and researchers. Readers get a grounded portrait of grading as lived, not just theorized.
pmc-13521902:
Sandra Rukobo leads a 2026 study of antibacterial immune recovery in young children healing from complicated severe malnutrition in Zambia and Zimbabwe. Recovering children still face high infection risk, which may reflect slow immune repair lagging behind weight gain.

Blood samples covered 125 hospitalised cases under age five plus 73 nourished community controls. Early immune responses did not predict later death, readmission or relapse in caseload comparisons. Stronger inflammatory responses to bacterial triggers instead tracked with better arm circumference gains. Follow-up sampling to 48 weeks after discharge charts how defence recovers over time, testing whether immune repair trails nutritional recovery.
pmc-13522502:
Kyuhyeon Im and colleagues design a solar module that can recover waste heat without losing power in a 2026 engineering study. Solar panels lose output as they heat up, and attaching a thermoelectric generator, a device that turns heat into electricity, can add resistance that wastes power. The team reasoned that running at low current and high voltage would shrink that loss.

A shingled module made of fourteen narrow strips wired in series achieved exactly that operating pattern. Coupled to a field-scale thermoelectric unit, the module delivered useful power with a power loss reported as near zero. The design can be applied to several solar cell types, including newer tandem cells, giving builders a practical route to combined solar and heat recovery systems.
pmc-13522802:
Hyun Jung Hong and co-authors silence a brainstem receptor to treat cancer wasting in mice in a 2026 study. Cancer cachexia is a life-threatening loss of weight, muscle, and fat, driven in part by a tumor signal acting on a receptor found only in a small brainstem area. A designed antisense molecule, a short strand that blocks one gene's message, was delivered once into the brain fluid.

Treatment sharply reduced the receptor and calmed abnormal nerve cell activation in models of colon and pancreatic cancer. Body weight, muscle mass, and fat stores recovered, and grip strength improved more than with a body-wide antibody against the tumor signal. Survival of tumor-bearing mice lengthened substantially. The authors propose central receptor blockade as a promising approach to cancer wasting.
pmc-13523302:
Mei Guo, Huan Duan, Daoping Ru, Shuai Yang, and Wenqiang Yu review how small RNAs may carry the lasting damage of high blood sugar in a 2026 article. Metabolic memory means that cells keep showing harm from earlier high glucose even after levels normalize, a pattern linked to diabetic vessel complications. MicroRNAs, tiny regulators of gene activity, are known contributors through chemical tagging of genes.

The review also covers a newer proposal: some microRNAs inside the cell nucleus may switch genes on rather than off by interacting with enhancer regions. That activating role is established as a concept, yet the authors note it still awaits validation in diabetic systems. The article maps established mechanisms and emerging ideas for diagnosis and treatment of diabetic complications.
pmc-13523502:
Bing-Ru Shao and colleagues report a 2026 chemistry study on catalyzing the Diels-Alder reaction with externally applied electric fields. The Diels-Alder reaction, a workhorse for building ring structures, has long been the test case for electric-field catalysis. Practical use under normal synthesis conditions had remained out of reach, despite elegant model systems and theory.

Working in microfluidic capacitors, the team assembled functional Helmholtz layers, thin charged layers at a surface, that translate applied voltage into strong local fields. Yields climbed in a nonlinear way from zero to 90 percent as voltage rose. Layers built from chiral, or handed, charged molecules also steered product handedness, reaching 31 percent enantiomeric excess at very low catalyst loading. The authors present chiral layers as both catalyst and sole source of handedness.
pmc-13524602:
Sadiq Alaqaili and colleagues compare, in a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis, partial against full repair in large to massive rotator cuff tears in the shoulder. Such tears, at least three centimeters wide, are hard to fix fully, and surgeons debate whether a partial repair that restores some tendon coverage does as well as a complete one.

Three databases were screened through June 2025 under standard review rules, and nine comparative human studies with 508 patients qualified. Complete repair gave greater strength recovery after surgery. Forward flexion and internal rotation were similar between approaches, while external rotation showed no difference amid wide variation. Patient-reported scores were mostly similar, although one shoulder score favored complete repair. Structural failure on imaging was also compared, and the authors weigh tear size when choosing a technique.
pmc-13524802:
Debajit Dey leads a large team in a 2026 study on how a gut bacterium digests colonic mucus. Akkermansia muciniphila, linked with good metabolic health, feeds on mucin, the gel that shields the gut wall. Mucin sugars are heavily sulfated, and the enzymes that strip those sulfate groups were poorly understood.

Combining digestion assays, proteomics, and structural biology, the team found the bacterium's sulfatases carry rare adaptations aimed at known sulfated mucin structures, including extra modular parts and a previously unknown mucin-binding domain. Smaller glycoproteins supported growth well. Location studies showed one sugar type was desulfated inside the cell's periplasm compartment, while another was handled outside the cell as well. The results refine how this microbe balances mucus use against gut protection.
pmc-13526102:
Irena Dajic leads a large Vienna team in a 2026 feasibility study of a steady-infusion PET method for measuring dopamine D2 and D3 receptors across the whole brain at once. These receptors sit in both deep and cortical regions, and quantifying them together with one tracer has been difficult. The tracer used, PHNO, prefers these receptor types.

Five healthy men each underwent two scans using a bolus plus constant infusion design, with an intravenous amphetamine challenge midway to displace the tracer. Baseline binding values were reproducible for most regions, with test-retest variation under ten percent. Amphetamine lowered binding in cortical and several deep regions in both scans. Two dopamine-rich areas had not reached equilibrium before the challenge, so the authors recommend protocol refinement there.
pmc-13527102:
Mustafa Tahsin Yilmaz, Enes Algul, and Ishak Pacal benchmark, in a 2026 comparative study, thirty deep-learning architectures for two lung cancer tasks on chest CT scans. Sorting tumors by tissue subtype and judging nodule malignancy need different visual cues, one broad and contextual, the other local. Fifteen convolutional networks and fifteen vision transformers were trained under one unified setup.

Two public datasets supplied images, one covering three cancer subtypes plus normal scans and one covering normal, benign, and malignant cases. A transformer model led subtyping with an F1 score near 0.973, closely followed by a leading convolutional model. For malignancy classification, three models tied at the top near 0.982. Heat-map visualizations suggested the best models attended to lesion and lung regions that matter clinically.
pmc-13527902:
Nay Htut and three colleagues report a 2026 study of adults whose sunken chest, called pectus excavatum, was repaired with the Nuss procedure. That operation lifts the sternum with a metal bar. The team tracked the thoracic Cobb angle, a measure of spinal curve, in 186 patients. All were treated at Taipei Tzu Chi Hospital between 2014 and 2024, and the review looked back over their records.

Chest X-rays showed the curve rising slightly one month after surgery. It then eased while the bar stayed in place. After bar removal the angle fell below its starting level, and every subgroup showed the same drop. The authors conclude the operation does not worsen spinal alignment. They note the gain itself was small.
pmc-13528002:
Franck Ale and seven colleagues reconstruct a measles epidemic in Yakusu Health Zone, Democratic Republic of the Congo, in a 2026 study. The outbreak ran from January 2018 to June 2019. A household survey covered 8,968 people. About fifteen percent reported having had measles. The team scaled the results to the whole zone.

They estimate roughly 22,000 true cases. Routine surveillance had caught only about twenty-eight percent of them. Among children under five, the attack rate was near forty-six percent. About five percent of young cases died within a month. Infants fared worst, and deaths kept coming after the standard cutoff. A reactive vaccine campaign arrived over a year into the outbreak. It mostly reached children who were already vaccinated. The authors stress faster response and better routine coverage.
pmc-13528102:
Lucas Martins and three colleagues link heart MRI signs with fingertip vessel damage in systemic sclerosis in a 2026 study. The disease scars skin and organs and harms small vessels. Forty patients had heart scans with a cold stress step. They also had nailfold vessel checks under a microscope. Heart involvement was judged by flow defects, strain, and scar patterns.

Twenty-two patients, fifty-five percent, showed heart involvement on MRI. Flow-related lesions appeared in about thirty-eight percent. Fibrosis-type lesions appeared in twenty percent. Patients with the late vessel pattern had more fluid around the heart. They also had more scar-type heart lesions. Fewer fingertip capillaries and more bare zones tracked with worse heart findings. The authors suggest the fingertip window mirrors the heart. Nail checks could flag who needs heart imaging most.
pmc-13528202:
Aakanksha Jha, Elizabeth R Lawlor and Cole A DeForest published this 2026 study building a gel that mimics the soft tissue where Ewing sarcoma, a childhood cancer, spreads. Flat cell cultures cannot reproduce the matrix signals tumours feel, and animal models cannot isolate matrix ingredients. Their hydrogel is built on a degradable polyethylene glycol network. It is decorated with binding peptides from collagen and fibronectin, plus a peptide from tenascin-C, a matrix protein enriched at metastatic sites.

Ewing sarcoma cells grown inside the gels changed their growth and cell state according to the matrix recipe. Adding the tenascin-C peptide drove tumour behaviours and shifted cells into states matching those produced by the native protein, validating the peptide as a stand-in. A built-in enzymatic release mechanism lets researchers recover the cells for assays. The authors offer the platform as a way to dissect how matrix composition steers metastasis.
pmc-13529802:
M. Aparicio and six colleagues compare three ways to teach medical students patient education in a 2026 study. Fifth and sixth year students all took the same theory lessons. One group then practiced with real patients in primary care. A second practiced with simulation in intensive care teaching. A third had no practice round. Knowledge tests and a judged practical exam measured the payoff.

Theory scores rose for everyone after the lessons. The simulation group topped the practical exam, scoring just over eight points. Real-patient practice came next, at about seven and a half points. The no-practice group trailed near seven points. Students also rated themselves higher than their teachers did. The authors crown theory plus simulation as the best mix. Simulated patients give safe, repeatable reps, they note. Self-confidence should be checked against outside judgment.
pmc-13530502:
Vu Thi Hoang Lan and colleagues tracked pregnancy care in Vietnam in a study published in two thousand twenty-six. Counting clinic visits alone can hide whether mothers actually received key checks. Using national survey data from three survey years, they built an index covering both visit numbers and the content of care.

Every measure improved over the decade, including skilled care and core services like blood pressure checks and blood and urine tests. Gaps by wealth, place, and ethnic group were also tracked over time. Health officials gain a fairer yardstick: progress counts only when mothers receive the full set of recommended services, not just appointments.
pmc-13530602:
Bryant and colleagues present in 2026, as conference poster 126, a prospective study of response shift after hip arthroscopy. Response shift is the phenomenon where patients' internal yardsticks move over time, so their later memory of how bad things were before surgery no longer matches what they reported then.

Fifty-six patients completed hip questionnaires before surgery and at one and two years, also re-rating their pre-surgery state from memory at each visit. Scores improved significantly at both time points. Yet meaningful response shift appeared in about half to three fifths of patients depending on the scale. Most often they remembered their earlier health as better than they had said, which shrank the measured size of the surgical benefit. Negative coping styles and adverse events predicted worse final scores, but nothing consistently predicted the size of the shift itself.
pmc-13531202:
Julio Echarte-Morales and co-authors present a 2026 catheter replacement of a leaking mitral valve using a device built solely for that valve. The 77-year-old man had worsening breathlessness and fatigue from severe leakage and faced high surgical risk. His anatomy also suited the clipping alternative poorly.

CT planning mapped the route and guarded against blocking the outflow path after placement. The fully leg-delivered system crossed into the left atrium and seated a new valve, cutting leakage effectively. The case supports replacement as a real choice when repair geometry fails and surgery looms too risky.
pmc-13532002:
Zhiyin Wang and co-authors measure in 2026 a small RNA in blood cells of children newly diagnosed with immune platelet loss. Eighty-seven patients, split into severe and non-severe groups, plus 40 healthy controls gave samples for RNA measurement and T-cell subset counting by flow methods. The disease destroys platelets through misdirected immunity.

The RNA ran higher in patients than controls and higher still in severe cases. Helper cell balance tilted toward inflammatory types and away from regulatory cells, tracking the RNA level and platelet counts. A three-part combined score sorted severe cases with strong accuracy, pending prospective checks.
pmc-13532202:
Simon Roques and co-authors explore in 2026 what blocking methane production in dairy cow stomachs does to microbes and body chemistry together. Twelve cows received a methane inhibitor for six weeks while thirteen served as controls. Rumen microbe genes and activity were read alongside blood metabolite profiles from earlier work.

The overall microbe-to-body link proved moderate. A handful of quieted microbial pathways for sugar use, hydrogen handling, and protein building correlated with one-carbon metabolites in blood, alongside a dip in one bacterial order. The patterns raise fresh questions about hydrogen buildup when methane making stops.
pmc-13532302:
Leus and colleagues report a 2026 study comparing three ways to tell poultry E. coli strains apart, a key task in outbreak control. The team typed 200 isolates from four Dutch poultry farms. Two methods read the full genome, using Nanopore and Illumina sequencing. The third, the IR Biotyper, reads an infrared light fingerprint of each strain's surface chemistry.

Infrared grouping matched the genome-based grouping closely, with agreement scores in the high range, especially for type and core-genome clusters. Sequencing still gave the finest detail, but typing all 200 isolates took twelve to twenty-eight days, against a maximum of six days by infrared. The infrared route also costs less per strain. For farm outbreaks, where days matter, a fast fingerprint that agrees with genomes could guide action while sequencing confirms the details.
pmc-13532602:
William H Wu, Joanna K M Ng, and Joshua J X Li report in 2026 a rare case of clear cell sarcoma found in body fluids. The cancer is uncommon, grows in soft tissue, and can look much like melanoma or other cancers under the microscope. Their patient had spread to sputum plus fluid around the belly and heart.

Cell traits varied, and stains for pigment-linked marks gave mixed results across cases in past reports. Gene tests for a known fusion helped confirm the diagnosis. Readers learn why fluid samples from this cancer need cell study, stains, and gene proof together.
pmc-13533302:
Güven and colleagues scanned the retinas of children with accommodative esotropia, an inward eye turn driven by focusing effort, looking for blood vessel changes at the macula. The macula is the center of sharp vision. Their 2026 prospective study imaged 34 affected children and 35 healthy controls with a vessel-mapping scan. The patients were divided into the condition's three subtypes, adjusting for glasses prescription and eye length.

Güven found the superficial vessel layer unchanged, but deeper layers showed thinning of vessel density in the upper quadrant of the macula. The changes survived strict statistical correction in the choroidal layer for the high-convergence and partially accommodative subtypes. They also survived in the outer retina for the high-convergence subtype, while other apparent differences faded after correction. Because patterns differed by subtype, the authors suggest chronic focusing and convergence effort shapes retinal microcirculation, a hypothesis needing confirmation in larger groups.
pmc-13534202:
Sue-Yeon Song and Wei-Lin Chen study in 2026 how school tracks and parenting shape self-esteem from age 13 to 19 in South Korea. Status and pressure around school paths are strong there, yet family and school effects were rarely studied together. Data came from a national panel with 1,484 youth across three waves from 2010 to 2016.

Youth on some non-university paths reported lower self-esteem across all waves. Warm affection linked to higher self-esteem, while excess expectations and interference linked to lower scores. Parenting effects grew stronger for one technical path, pointing to school and family partnerships.
pmc-13538402:
Jovana Periša and co-authors turn tomato waste into glowing carbon dots for copper sensing in a 2026 study. Stems and fruits served as separate carbon sources, with a nitrogen helper added to tune surface chemistry. The dots formed stable nanoscale clusters in water and glowed strongly under ultraviolet light, with brightness depending on excitation color. Detailed surface checks linked starting material to glow behavior.

Precursor choice shaped defect levels and surface groups, directly steering glow strength. Both dot types dimmed sharply when copper ions bound to surface groups, enabling detection at very low levels with slightly better sensitivity for stem dots. Surface oxygen and nitrogen groups drove the strong metal grip. The authors present farm waste conversion as a cheap, green route to useful sensors.
pmc-13538502:
Jan Jansen and colleagues released a large expert-labeled set of Antarctic seafloor photos. Published in 2026, the photo set pulls together images from 21 Antarctic research trips between 1985 and 2019. Seafloor photos offer cheap, gentle data on ocean life, yet steady labeled sets were rarely shared in public.

The set holds 52,491 place-tagged downward photos, of which 3,599 carry labels totaling 632,252 expert marks under a shared sea-life sorting scheme. Each mark's pixel spot is stored, so views can be tuned to a user's focus. The set serves studies of species spread, group patterns, change over time, and teaching programs to label sea life. Readers get a rare Southern Ocean baseline for guarding sea life and tracking change.
pmc-13538602:
Ximena Ruden and colleagues test a two-stage stress response in placental stem cells in a 2026 gene activity study. Stem cells first mount a cell-level survival program, then may shift to a development-linked program favoring the whole organism. Mouse placental stem cells faced strong salt stress. Gene activity was profiled from half an hour through a full day to watch for the same staged shift seen earlier in embryonic stem cells.

Early hours were dominated by building and metabolism genes typical of cell-level adaptation. Later hours swung toward development and differentiation pathways, matching activation of the second program. The authors read the pattern as evidence that the staged shift is a general feature of stressed developmental stem cells. Candidate markers are proposed for fertility care, miscarriage study, and regenerative medicine.
pmc-13540402:
Özkocaman and colleagues laid out in 2026 a practical guide to preventing and treating invasive fungal infections in blood cancer patients. Chemotherapy and stem cell transplants leave these patients with weak immune defenses. Such infections kill many patients, yet the right drug at the right time depends on each person's risk level. New targeted cancer drugs have added fresh twists, since several clash with standard antifungal medicines.

The guide sorts patients into high, middle, and low risk groups. High-risk patients, such as those starting treatment for acute leukemia, get mold-active preventive drugs, while low-risk patients get none. It gives dosing adjustments when antifungals meet drugs like venetoclax, and care pathways for cell therapy patients. Chest scans and fungal blood markers drive decisions on when to start, escalate, or operate.
pmc-13540902:
Siddharth Nahar and five colleagues present, in a 2026 software paper, a graphics-processor version of MitoGraph, a popular tool that traces mitochondrial networks in three-dimensional microscope images. New live-cell microscopes produce four-dimensional movies far too large for the original processor-bound program.

The rewrite pushes the heavy filtering maths onto graphics hardware and speeds up skeleton extraction. On yeast cells it ran up to eleven times faster, and on human lung organoid frames up to thirty times faster, with segmentation matching the original almost exactly. One organoid workload dropped from roughly five hundred hours to twenty. The authors offer the tool for large-scale studies of mitochondrial shape over time.
pmc-13542102:
Qiaoyun Liu and colleagues propose a text classifier in a 2026 study. The tool sorts agricultural news with large language models. It needs no labelled training examples. Farm vocabulary is sparse, and annotation is scarce. Single-prompt methods judge from one angle only. That weakness drives the design.

The framework builds several prompts for each text. Each prompt views the text at a different level. Levels run from local terms to overall theme. A consistency check then compares decisions and confidence scores. Disputed items go to a second judgement round. Tests used French pest reports and a humanitarian news set. Accuracy beat the strongest rival by several points.
pmc-13543602:
Rodrigo Sánchez-Jiménez's team turned the SCImago group's Integrity Risk Indicators into a working measurement system for universities in 2026. Instead of judging misconduct by one person, the framework asks how exposed an institution is to integrity risks. It looks at incentives, authorship patterns, citation dynamics, choice of publication venues, and transparency habits. The indicators are built from bibliometric data for institutions in the SCImago rankings.

The paper's advance is normalisation: each indicator is turned into a standard score centred on the global average, so unlike readings can share one scale and unusual outliers stand out by size. The authors insist the signals flag possible risk, never guilt. Read rightly, the system works like a smoke detector for research culture, helping universities strengthen their own defences rather than feeding another league table.
pmc-13547402:
Bisma Ali and colleagues benchmarked in 2026 three deep learning architectures for predicting how much life a lithium-ion battery has left and how its health fades. They used two public aging datasets from NASA and Oxford. Honest comparison is the point of the exercise, so every model received identical preparation and training. A strict leave-one-cell-out rule meant each model was always tested on battery cells it had never seen.

Sequence models, a convolutional variant, and a transformer variant were scored on errors across repeated runs, with extra statistics separating luck in training from true differences between cells. Performance swung with degradation complexity and cell-to-cell variety. The authors argue that rigorous cross-cell testing and reliability reporting matter more than any single leaderboard number.
pmc-13548602:
Yiyang Zhu, Changlin Zhai, and Jingjing Wang follow more than three thousand Chinese adults over time, in a 2026 cohort study. They ask how two blood markers, alone and together, relate to future heart and vessel disease. All participants had early-stage cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic syndrome, a clustering of risks gaining attention. One marker gauges inflammation, while the other summarizes fat-related risk in the blood over time.

During five years of follow-up, 495 participants developed cardiovascular disease. High inflammation scores raised risk by over a third, and high cumulative fat-index values raised it by about forty percent, each after full adjustment. People high on both markers faced roughly eighty percent greater risk than people low on both, with the combined pattern stronger in men. The authors propose tracking the pair together when judging risk in this syndrome's early stages.
pmc-13548702:
Yu Qi and colleagues expose a livestock bacterium to an antibiotic and read its genome, genes, and chemistry to learn how tolerance takes hold, in a 2026 multi-omics study. Pasteurella multocida, a common farm pathogen, was pressured with enrofloxacin, a fluoroquinolone drug. Tolerance, surviving without true resistance, is a suspected stepping stone to resistance, so the team compared the adapted strain with its parent.

The tolerant strain idled longer before growing, grew more slowly, formed less biofilm, and stretched into elongated shapes.
