A gene called dusB had been partly deleted and broken, and removing it deliberately reproduced the slow, tolerant style. A second regulator, cpxR, added tolerance when deleted, acting through ribosome-related genes, while the cell's central energy cycle switched on during adaptation. The authors name both genes as possible targets for blocking tolerance before it hardens into resistance.
pmc-13548902:
Bengt H. Gless and colleagues disarm Staphylococcus aureus by destroying its chemical chatter before the signal reaches the bacteria, in a 2026 study. These bacteria switch on their attack genes when a secreted peptide signal builds up, a process called quorum sensing. Earlier blockers jammed the bacterial receiver. The new approach uses simple relatives of the amino acid cysteine, carrying a reactive sulfur group, to eliminate the signal peptides outside the cells.

Reporter strains confirmed the compounds shut the sensing system down across different staph types. Two chosen compounds then reduced skin infection by drug-resistant MRSA in mice. Because the strategy mops up signals rather than killing bacteria, it may press less toward resistance than antibiotics do. The authors see a path toward simple topical molecules for staph skin infections, with delivery methods still to be worked out.
pmc-13549802:
Kazunori Ohashi and colleagues build a dedicated test dummy, or phantom, for checking prostate MRI sequences, in a 2026 technical study. Diffusion-weighted imaging is central to spotting prostate cancer, yet gas in the rectum warps the images, and scanners vary. Their phantom mimics prostate tissue, tumor-like lesions, and rectal gas, letting six diffusion techniques be compared at two magnet strengths under identical conditions.

The team measured signal quality, warping artifacts, and geometric distortion against standard images, then had clinicians judge matching patient scans and technologists judge the phantom scans. Readers agreed strongly with each other on the phantom, and the artifact patterns seen in the dummy echoed those in real patients sequence by sequence. The authors offer the phantom as a reproducible stand-in for routine quality checks without scanning volunteers.
pmc-13550602:
Wanling Zhang, with eleven colleagues, published a 2026 longitudinal study of how obsessive-compulsive symptoms and psychotic-like experiences develop together in young people. Both often appear in late childhood, yet it was unclear whether their overlap reflects lasting personal differences or changes within a child over time. Data came from four waves of a large adolescent brain study with 7,451 participants.

Growth models showed the two symptom types followed distinct but partly linked paths. Early links mostly reflected stable differences between children, although psychotic-like experiences predicted later rises in obsessive-compulsive symptoms from ages 12 to 13 within the same child. Intrusive thoughts and worry repeatedly bridged the two sets of symptoms, so the authors stress timing and symptom-level checks.
pmc-13550902:
Olga Sivell, with a large consortium of co-authors, published a 2026 genome assembly for Melanomya nana, a small black blow fly. The fly measures only 3 to 4.5 millimeters and belongs to the family Calliphoridae. Sequencing came from a single male specimen as part of the Darwin Tree of Life project, which builds reference genomes for species in Britain and Ireland.

The assembly presents two haplotypes, the two inherited copies of the genome, each near 1,400 megabases long. Nearly all of the first haplotype sits in five chromosome-scale pieces, while the second was assembled to scaffold level. A mitochondrial genome of 27.12 kilobases was also completed, giving researchers a full genetic reference for the species.
pmc-13551402:
Anton C. de Groot, with three colleagues, published a 2026 patch test study on Brazilian propolis. Propolis is a bee product used in health goods. It often triggers positive skin reactions in routine tests. The team had earlier found 98 chemicals in the test material. They built a test set from some of those chemicals and used it on 224 patients.

Forty-two patients in the group reacted to propolis itself. A few single chemicals drew reactions in small shares of patients. Benzyl acetate and one called δ-cadinene led that short list. Reactions occurred in propolis-positive and propolis-negative patients alike. No one chemical explained most reactions. The team presents the set as a step toward finding the true culprits.
pmc-13551802:
Hui-qi Kang, leading eight colleagues, published a 2026 cross-sectional study sorting fear of falling among older adults with sarcopenia into distinct profiles. The survey recruited 356 community-dwelling people aged 60 or older with sarcopenia between December 2023 and December 2024, using questionnaires on fall confidence, anxiety and depression, family function, and social support. Latent profile analysis searched for subgroups.

Four profiles appeared, from low fear in about a fifth of participants to severe fear in about a tenth, with the middle groups largest. A decision tree singled out physical activity level, family function score, and anxiety as the key classifiers in the reported model. Regression agreed that more active people clustered in lower-fear profiles, guiding tailored prevention programs.
pmc-13552602:
Evgenia Gurevich leads a six-author team in a 2026 Israeli study linking a blood enzyme to kidney harm in sick children. The enzyme, alkaline phosphatase, was tracked in children aged up to eighteen with sepsis, a severe body-wide infection. Records came from four hospitals across more than two decades. The sepsis group held 701 records, set against matched children with fever alone.

Enzyme levels, adjusted for age and sex, sat lower in sepsis than in fever alone. They fell lower still in the near one quarter who developed acute kidney injury. Those children also stayed in hospital longer, a median of seven days against four. After other blood tests were weighed, low levels still pointed to kidney risk.
pmc-13553302:
Daniel Persaud and eleven colleagues build MAP-E, a self-run high-throughput platform for electrochemistry. Corrosion testing is slow, hands-on, and shaped by operator technique, which limits large, high-quality data for materials work. MAP-E pairs robotic liquid and sample handling with multi-channel voltage control. It extracts corrosion metrics with no human step.

Checks against an ASTM G61-analog benchmark showed steady results, with pitting potential varying by 75 mV across 32 runs. The team then used MAP-E to map pH-chloride stability maps for 304 stainless steel, guided by uncertainty-driven sampling on a Gaussian process model. The platform cuts operator input and speeds search of new settings.
pmc-13554102:
Gaddam Lakshmi and Perumalla Swetha present a 2026 defence system against phishing, the fake messages that trick people into giving up secrets. Crooks now use smart tools to craft fakes that look almost real. Their system reads wording, looks at page images, and checks hidden data all at once. Plain rules sit beside the learning parts, so choices rest on clear grounds as well as patterns.

Fake attack samples made by a diffusion tool hardened the system during training. A replay memory lets it keep learning as attack styles drift. A helper module names the features behind each warning, so analysts can follow the logic. Across public test sets the system scored high and beat rivals on new data by a clear margin.
pmc-13554202:
Poramaporn Luangprasert leads a nine-author team automating counts of lens cells tied to cataract in a 2026 study. Cells lining the lens help keep it clear, and their density may track cataract growth. Hand counting is slow and varies between counters. Their software learned to count these cells in microscope photos of lens capsules removed during surgery.

More than 43,000 cells were checked across twenty test images. The software matched expert consensus counts with accuracy above ninety-eight percent. Its error ran about half that seen between two human experts. Agreement scores also topped the human pair's marks. The authors offer the tool for fast, steady, repeatable density measures in clinic studies of cataract patients.
pmc-13556102:
Yannai DeJonghe and four colleagues surveyed care workers in 2026 about care left undone in nursing homes and the toll it may take on staff. Ageing populations and heavier workloads raise the risk that essential tasks slip, which earlier work tied to exhaustion in nurses. Their cross-sectional study drew survey data from 56 Belgian nursing homes collected in 2021, covering 1,054 nurses, assistants, and allied health staff.

Every domain of unfinished care linked to higher emotional exhaustion and depersonalisation, and to a weaker sense of personal accomplishment. Supportive management softened the link with depersonalisation, while unsupportive management appeared to sharpen the strain. The authors read the findings through a demands and resources lens. Tasks left undone act as a demand on staff. A good manager counts as a resource that can offset part of the damage.
pmc-13557902:
Tong Wu and Yun Jiang review how fat metabolism rewiring in tumour-associated macrophages drives resistance to immune checkpoint therapy in lung cancer. Their 2026 narrative review integrates mechanisms and possible counter-strategies.

Checkpoint drugs transformed non-small cell lung cancer care, yet many patients resist them, and response rates stay limited even in favourable marker groups. Macrophages inside tumours form a key part of the suppressive environment shielding cancers. Their lipid metabolism changes deeply affect their function and gene activity. The review explains how those changes promote immune suppression and therapy resistance. It then outlines therapeutic strategies aimed at the macrophage fat pathways to restore treatment sensitivity.
pmc-13558602:
Sushmita Kumari, Somnath Mandal, and Sajad Nabi Dar charted in 2026 two decades of land change in Saharsa District, Bihar, using satellite images from 2002 to 2023. The district sits on a flood-prone river fan in the Kosi Basin, where ecological stress was suspected but unmapped. The team classified land cover at four time points with a standard supervised method and built an ecological vulnerability index to locate stress hotspots.

Built-up land grew by about one hundred square kilometres while forest cover shrank by more than seventy. Vulnerability mapping showed ecological quality sliding from moderate toward poor and very poor, concentrated in the district's centre and southeast where clearing and building ran fastest. The authors urge sustainable land management, replanting, and flood-resilient town planning, and they suggest sharper imagery plus machine learning for the next assessment round.
pmc-13558702:
Darebe Yohannes and three colleagues redesigned in 2026 the animal-drawn tillage tools that Ethiopian smallholders use to furrow light wheat soils. The traditional maresha plough works, yet it is heavy and slow. Working in Misrak Bedawacho District, the team used pairs of oxen under real farm conditions. They built lighter multi-share tools with a shallower rake angle. Comparisons covered depth, pulling force, field capacity, and structural safety.

Working time for a quarter hectare fell from nearly seven hours to about two, and field capacity more than tripled, with efficiency approaching ninety-nine percent. Extra shares raised draft force slightly, while the pull stayed within what oxen can manage, and stress analysis kept every part inside safe limits. Treated soil also held moisture and shaped better for planting. The authors recommend local manufacture plus farmer training.
pmc-13559102:
Lei Wang and four colleagues report a 2026 study that built a prediction model for refractory Mycoplasma pneumoniae pneumonia in children, the form that responds poorly to standard treatment. Their approach leans on measurable features from chest CT scans, combined with ordinary clinical and laboratory data. The records came from children first scanned between January 2019 and December 2021 across four hospitals.

The study group held 197 children, 60 with the refractory form and 137 with the general form. One hospital supplied the training set, while the other three formed an outside validation set. Four measures stood out as independent predictors: C-reactive protein, lactate dehydrogenase, the share of lung volume taken by lesions, and the share of ground-glass opacity. A nomogram built from them discriminated well in both sets. The authors offer the tool as an aid for earlier recognition and planning of care.
pmc-13559402:
Gu and colleagues published a 2026 narrative review and policy analysis on lung nodule risk tools for people who never smoked. Screening rules were built around age, smoking history, and scan appearance, so never smokers rarely qualify for low dose CT screening. East Asian women face notable lung cancer risk despite never smoking, the authors stress.

Mapping guidelines, prediction models, and cohort studies, Gu found that smoking centred entry rules shut never smokers out of screening. Chinese and Taiwanese studies instead flagged local predictors such as family history, past tuberculosis, and chronic lung disease. A Taiwanese trial in never smokers found invasive cancers that scans could catch early. Models built on screening groups also lost accuracy in hospital patients, and delays in diagnosis cut survival chances.
pmc-13560302:
Laurens Léger and colleagues review blood microRNAs in depth as blood-marker leads for three inherited heart muscle diseases: hypertrophic, arrhythmogenic, and dilated cardiomyopathy. Their 2026 review searched electronic databases and applied strict filters, keeping only studies with healthy controls and proof the test separates sick from well. Nineteen papers survived for analysis.

One microRNA stood out as overexpressed in each disease across different studies: miR-29a-3p in hypertrophic disease, miR-185-5p in the arrhythmogenic form, and miR-454-3p in dilated disease. Beyond those leads, consistency crumbled. Attempts to tie microRNA levels to heart features or genetic background yielded no stable profiles between studies. The authors warn that sudden death can be these diseases' first symptom, which makes a blood test valuable, yet the field is not ready. Larger cohorts using shared methods must validate the candidates first.
pmc-13560402:
Musa Abbas Waziri and colleagues measure nontraumatic ileal perforation, a spontaneous hole in the small intestine causing obscure peritonitis, across three Ugandan hospitals. Their 2026 multicenter cross-sectional study uses a structured checklist on 149 consecutive gut perforation patients. The condition kills often and burdens low-income settings most, where hygiene and HIV shape its causes.

Typhoid fever caused the overwhelming majority of the perforations studied, about four in five cases. Most holes sat twenty to thirty-nine centimeters from the junction with the colon, measured half to one centimeter wide, and appeared singly on the antimesenteric border. Men, farmers, and rural residents carried the heaviest share. HIV-positive patients had far higher odds of this perforation type in the adjusted analysis. Using an open or closed pit latrine, rather than a flush toilet, also raised the odds sharply. The authors tie prevention to sanitation and typhoid control.
pmc-13560802:
Farah M. Babakurd and colleagues link the severity of anterior crossbite, where lower front teeth bite in front of the uppers, to appearance-based bullying in schoolchildren. Their 2026 cross-sectional study examines 2,080 children aged eight to twelve in Damascus public schools, sampled by clusters. Occlusion was scored with the ROMA Index, and bullying with a modified standard questionnaire.

Anterior crossbite appeared in 19.6 percent of the children, while 34.4 percent reported dental appearance bullying at victim frequency in the reported shares. Every form of crooked bite raised bullying likelihood, and crossbite did so most strongly. Crucially, bullying intensity climbed step by step with crossbite severity. Teasing and mockery dominated the abuse types, and playgrounds hosted most incidents regardless of dental group. The authors propose adding crossbite severity screening to school prevention programs for both oral and psychosocial health.
pmc-13563702:
Ahmed Emara and seven colleagues pool the trial evidence for orforglipron, a daily pill that mimics a gut hormone used against obesity and diabetes. Injected versions work but deter many patients, so an oral option could widen use. The 2026 review searched four databases to January 2026 and found three randomised trials with 2,505 adults who had both obesity and type 2 diabetes. Effects were pooled against placebo, split by dose, and graded for certainty with a standard framework.

Every outcome improved in a clean dose-response pattern. Extra weight loss over placebo ran from 2.43 percent at the 3 milligram dose to 7.80 percent at 24 milligrams. Long-term blood sugar fell by 0.80 to 1.67 percentage points across the dose range, and waistlines shrank significantly from 6 milligrams up. More people quit the drug over side effects, while serious harms matched placebo. With only three trials and some low-certainty ratings, the authors urge caution until bigger studies land.
pmc-13563902:
Hao Wang and twelve colleagues trace a self-feeding circuit in osteosarcoma, the bone cancer of teenagers, where sugar burning and gene switching keep switching each other on. The link is lactylation, a chemical tag built from lactate, the waste of glycolysis. Their 2026 study found these tags raised in tumour tissue over matched healthy tissue. Tag mapping showed the H3K9la mark sitting on the promoter of DHX9, a helicase, and proteomics found DHX9 carrying a lactyl tag at one spot, lysine 1024.

Cutting DHX9 slowed the cancer cells' growth, migration, and invasion, and shrank mouse tumours; adding it back did the reverse. Mutating the 1024 site so it cannot accept the tag broke the loop: glycolytic enzymes fell, lactate tags faded, and malignant behaviour ebbed. A tag-mimicking mutation restored the engine. The authors name the loop a metabolic-epigenetic interface and nominate that lysine as a target.
pmc-13568202:
Diana Castro Paupério and colleagues report, in a 2026 feasibility study at a Portuguese hospital, an automated digital tool that collects patient-reported outcomes for people awaiting heart and chest surgery. As part of a patient blood management program, 221 patients received scheduled questionnaires about health, pain, and mood over their care journey during 2024.

The two-stage digital journey was built in under two months, and patients completed about seventy-two percent of planned interactions. Mood screening flagged five severe and nine moderately severe depression cases for attention. Scores for general health and pain changed little by ninety days. The pilot shows automated outcome tracking can work inside a busy surgical pathway.
pmc-13569702:
Benjamin Wajsberg and colleagues tested a silk-and-hyaluronic-acid injection for voices weakened by incomplete vocal-fold closure. Glottic insufficiency, often from vocal-fold paralysis or age-related thinning, leaves voices breathy and weak and can cause swallowing trouble. Their retrospective study at one academic voice centre reviewed 33 patients who received 44 silk-HA injections between June 2022 and August 2025, mostly in the office.

About 86 percent reported at least minimal vocal improvement, and about 79 percent reported partial to significant improvement, matching plain hyaluronic acid in patients who had received both. Operative revisions were more frequent with silk-HA, though serious adverse events did not rise. The authors present silk-HA as a viable office-based option, with independent-centre evidence backing earlier claims.
pmc-13571802:
López-Rodríguez Larissa and colleagues review, in a 2026 article with two new cases, what is known before birth about spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia congenita caused by the collagen gene COL2A1. This skeletal disorder affects the spine and bone ends. Published prenatal cases were gathered with a planned search, and two further cases from a referral center were described with later gene proof.

First detection ranged from eleven to twenty-eight weeks of pregnancy. Several families carried the condition, while others appeared sporadic, and extra imaging was often needed to clarify spine and bone hardening defects. No gene pattern foretold severity. Diagnosis before birth, the authors stress, needs imaging, genetic testing, and close teamwork together.
pmc-13572402:
Jiachen Liu, with three colleagues, presents a 2026 computer framework for naming aircraft types in satellite and aerial images. Fine splits between look-alike planes matter for defence work, yet deep learning models rarely show why they choose a label. That gap limits trust when the stakes are high.

The framework, EC-AT, pairs transfer learning with checks on whether three explanation tools point at the same image zones. Eight plane types came from the MAR20 data set. Models that started from pre-trained weights, then had their last layers tuned, reached accuracy up to 99.9 percent. A new overlap score measured how well the three tools agreed. A trust scorecard then rated the whole setup on accuracy, logic, and clarity of display. The checks also flagged background clutter that can sway a call.
pmc-13572502:
Lais Takata Walter, with ten colleagues, details a 2026 study of nitric oxide in the wiring of the young rat retina. Nitric oxide is a gas that cells use as a signal. The team asked whether it shapes circuits through the retina's own waves of activity or through a route apart from those waves.

Work began at postnatal day 10, when the enzyme that makes the gas first appeared in two cell types and gas output was first detected. Blocking that enzyme left the timing and shape of stage III waves intact. Still, the network grew denser, with more links per cell. Gene levels for both chemical and electrical synapse parts fell, and their layered layout broke down. Cells grown in dishes grew longer fibres. The team reads the gas as a brake on wiring that acts apart from wave patterns.
pmc-13573402:
Senem Askin Ekinci, with three colleagues, reports a 2026 mapping study of jaw fractures from CT scans. Knowing where jaw breaks cluster helps surgeons plan care and helps engineers design better plates. The team rebuilt fracture lines in three dimensions for a hospital cohort treated from 2018 to 2025.

The cohort held 158 patients, near two thirds men, with a mean age in the late thirties. In all, 239 fractures and 267 fracture lines were drawn. Breaks clustered behind the molars, at the jaw joint neck, at the canine socket, and near the chin hole. The angle and ramus zone broke most often, and assault was the top cause. Impacted wisdom teeth went with more angle breaks and fewer joint breaks. The heat maps show where the jaw is weakest in this group.
pmc-13573702:
Shi and co-authors find a clock gene that drives spread in KRAS G12D pancreatic cancer. This KRAS type sits in about 40 percent of such cancers. It also carries the worst outlook of KRAS types. Data mining plus lab tests flagged ARNTL2 as a partner factor. ARNTL2 binds the SERPINE1 promoter and switches it on.

That axis drove shape change and spread in cells and mice. Rescue tests proved SERPINE1 was the needed link. Protein levels of both tracked together in patient samples. Joint levels split patients into distinct outlook groups. The axis also shifted reply to KRAS G12D drugs.
pmc-13575402:
Elizabeth Dapre leads a 2026 report on how to draw South Asian women into diet trials for diabetes in pregnancy, and keep them taking part. Diabetes in pregnancy affects about one in five UK pregnancies at most, and South Asian women face roughly double the risk of white British women. A planned trial of an intermittent low-energy diet needed better recruitment.

Seventeen women in Greater Manchester who knew the condition personally or through family reviewed the study materials. Three priorities emerged: easing feelings of vulnerability and loss of control, making the trial easier to reach and join, and cutting the mental load from family duties and emotional strain. Contributors also named research fatigue and low trust. The feedback reshaped the trial design and recruitment plans.
pmc-13576102:
Charles Ntalika and Eric Umar gather nurses' views on their ongoing training at Malawi's Zomba Central Hospital for a 2026 qualitative study. Ongoing training keeps nurses current, yet little was known about how programmes match daily needs in a low-resource hospital. Fifteen nurses were interviewed in depth.

Five themes came out of the talks. Nurses spot their own learning needs through practice, often with weak coordination from the hospital. Training was valued for knowledge, skill, and confidence, yet many sessions missed practical gaps and offered no mentoring afterwards. Facilitators often lacked teaching skill, according to participants. Time clashes, heavy workloads, and costs such as transport and mobile data blocked attendance. The authors call for training shaped around nurses' stated needs with follow-up support built in.
pmc-13576202:
Behnam Kiani Kalejahi and Mohammad Javad Rajabi retest a thyroid cancer diagnosis model under stricter rules in a 2026 study. Papillary thyroid carcinoma is the most common thyroid cancer, and diagnosis before surgery blends ultrasound images with needle biopsy cell samples. A recent paper reported near-perfect scores from classic methods on one random split of the data.

The pair held back 77 of 384 patients as an untouched test set and built a deep learning model joining both data types. On the held-out patients it scored 0.977 on the ranking accuracy measure, with sensitivity of 0.977 and specificity of 0.939 at the chosen cut-off. Its probability estimates were far better calibrated than a simpler baseline. It also beat the re-run classic methods on the same patients. The authors argue strict holdout testing gives a fairer picture.
pmc-13576302:
Michela Destito leads a 2026 study testing whether CT scan patterns can predict a key immunotherapy marker in lung cancer without a tissue sample. The marker, PD-L1, guides drug choice in non-small cell lung cancer, yet biopsy can miss tumour variety or be impossible. Radiomics turns scan texture into numbers a model can learn from.

Scans from 55 patients with confirmed cancer were analysed, and several learning models were trained with repeated cross-checks. A support vector machine did best, with median accuracy of 0.77 and a ranking score of 0.83 for spotting high PD-L1 levels. Texture features carried most of the signal, and adding clinical data did not help. The authors call the virtual biopsy idea feasible, as a partner or fallback for tissue testing.
pmc-13578002:
Iris Mulder and four colleagues measure blood flow markers in eye tumours and other inner-eye lesions with MRI scans, in a 2026 exploratory study. Telling a uveal melanoma from a harmless mole or a benign blood vessel growth inside the eye can be hard. Perfusion imaging tracks how contrast washes through tissue, giving numbers that may separate the types.

Thirty-eight patients covering twelve diagnoses had 3 tesla dynamic scans. A standard model produced flow and leakage values, while simpler curve measures were taken for comparison. Blood vessel tumours showed by far the highest flow values. Melanomas sat above moles and metastases on the main measures. Simple and model-based numbers tracked each other well, and patterns matched a dye-based eye test. Small group sizes blocked firm comparisons between single diagnoses.
pmc-13578502:
Zora Arum and colleagues describe a meningioma program launched in September 2024 that joins treatment, research, and patient support under one roof. Meningioma, the most common primary brain tumor, leaves many patients with quality-of-life and thinking problems after diagnosis and treatment. The program combined a weekly tumor board, a multidisciplinary clinic, clinical trials, prospective registries, and a dedicated support group.

In its first fifteen months, the board discussed 602 cases and the clinic saw 142 patients in consultation. Twelve percent of board cases were offered trial enrollment and 84 percent were offered registry enrollment, while support-group members reported informational and emotional benefits. Consultation and treatment volumes rose sharply across departments, suggesting the model can streamline care for a complex tumor.
pmc-13578702:
Zhang and a large team combine brain imaging with gene expression atlases in this 2026 study of Alzheimer's disease, focusing on the white matter hugging the cortex. They measured free water fraction, a diffusion MRI signal reflecting tissue disorganization, across 68 such regions in 194 patients with amyloid-confirmed Alzheimer's and 153 cognitively normal controls.

They then asked which of 15,633 genes, their expression mapped from the Allen Human Brain Atlas, track the regions where water accumulates. The linked genes clustered in lipid metabolism, neuron insulation, and synaptic signaling, and were expressed mainly in oligodendrocytes, the insulation-making cells, plus two neuron types. The enrichments replicated in two additional datasets. Mediation analysis added a functional twist: free water fraction partly carried the effect of the APOE4 risk gene on cognition, in a domain-specific pattern, positioning the imaging marker between genes and symptoms.
pmc-13584502:
Eigo Kawahara and colleagues use mice to show how a common bacterium can turn a viral lung infection far worse in this 2026 study. The virus is RSV, a leading cause of chest disease in babies, and the bacterium is a form of Haemophilus influenzae often found alongside it in severe cases. Whether the bacterium truly drives the harm, or merely shows up, was unknown.

Mice first caught RSV, then received live, ultraviolet-killed, or heat-killed bacteria into the windpipe. Only the live bacteria brought sharp weight loss, lung injury, and a flood of white cells and inflammatory signals. A signal called IL-6 tracked closely with how sick the mice became. Removing one T-cell type eased matters a little, which suggests those cells help the damage but cannot explain it alone.
pmc-13589002:
Alessio Frisone and five colleagues review contrast ultrasound for sorting salivary gland lumps before surgery. Telling a harmless lump from a cancer in these glands is notoriously tricky, and contrast imaging adds a live view of the tiny vessels inside. Their 2026 systematic review gathered ten studies covering 663 lumps, the clear majority benign, all checked against tissue diagnosis afterward.

Cancers tended to light up unevenly with blurred edges and dead-looking dark patches. Their contrast also rushed in faster, peaked higher, and washed through with steeper curves than benign lumps showed. Blurred margins were a highly specific cancer sign, while uneven lighting was sensitive but less specific. Because study methods and cut-offs varied so much, the authors stopped short of pooled numbers and call the tool an adjunct, not a replacement for biopsy.
pmc-13589502:
Vivek Behera leads a twelve-author team in a search for shared organizing principles across tumors, in a study from two thousand twenty-six. Tumor microenvironments mix cancer, immune, and support cells in bewildering variety. If a common architecture lies at the base of that mix was not known. The team set out to find one if it is there.

Spatial transcriptomics profiled 262 solid tumors, and it mapped gene activity in place. The team found these spaces split into discrete sub-regions of many cells, set in a hierarchy. They call these spatial groups. Pathologists and independent measurements confirmed the groups match real biological domains. To set tumors side by side through these groups gave a pan-tumor classification. Its dominant axis was spatial variation in immune biology. A small lung cancer cohort hinted the scheme ties to how well immunotherapy works.
pmc-13592302:
Christopher R B Swanson and three colleagues use enzymes, in 2026, to tag therapeutic DNA strands with radioactive hydrogen late in their making. Drug developers need such tags to track where a medicine travels in the body. Older chemistry demands costly radioactive building blocks, yields weak tags, and leaves much radioactive waste. Their platform borrows methyltransferase enzymes, which naturally add methyl groups to DNA with exact aim.

The enzymes tagged strands at preparative scale with sharp site control, reaching record tag strength for this class. Both stable heavy hydrogen and radioactive tritium versions were made. Swanson and the team expect the method to cut cost and waste by orders of magnitude and to spread to other drug types that need whole body tracking studies.
pmc-13593702:
Lidia Mendes de Aquino and a large team followed ninety-eight cow and calf pairs in a tropical beef herd for two years to track tick fever, a disease complex carried by ticks. Blood tests searched for three agents, one Anaplasma bacterium and two Babesia parasites, from birth until the males were slaughtered and the females had their first calves.

Passage from mother to calf before birth was found only for Anaplasma, in a small share of pairs. Yet by twenty days of age most calves already carried the agents' DNA, showing very early exposure, and antibody rates across the herd passed three quarters. Tick load was the one factor clearly tied to active infection. Clinical illness still broke out in animals of several ages despite widespread antibodies, which leads the authors to urge a rethink of tick fever control in tropical herds.
pmc-13594502:
Nurit Zusman, Martine Denise Freeman, and Caryn Scheinberg Andrews surveyed 260 Israeli healthcare workers. They asked about resilience, positive mood, and quality of life during a period that combined the pandemic's aftermath with active warfare. Their cross-sectional study used standard scales for bouncing back from hardship, for positive and negative feelings, and for quality of life.

Both resilience and positive mood predicted a better quality of life on their own. The two also interacted: positive mood mattered most for staff whose resilience ran low, easing the drawback, while among upbeat staff the resilience gap flattened. The authors advise managers to build positive feeling deliberately, through peer support and praise, aiming most at workers with thinner reserves. They also call for broad system-wide plans rather than resilience training alone. Long-term studies of effects on keeping staff are needed too.
pmc-13594702:
Jyoti Srivastava and Sanjay Premi reviewed in two thousand twenty-six how a chemical tag placed on proteins by nitric oxide may shape melanoma outcomes. Modern melanoma drugs can shrink tumors without lasting control. The tag, called S-nitrosylation, has been linked to drug resistance and to weaker immune attack on the tumor.

Blocking the tag in lab work raised stress signals on dying tumor cells and drew in immune cells. Still, proof that specific tagged sites control how visibly tumor cells die is missing. The authors propose a two-gate model to test next. Cancer researchers get a careful sorting of proven facts versus promising guesses.
pmc-13596402:
Yuan Ren and colleagues published a 2026 study of how five common burdens of rheumatoid arthritis in older adults influence each other over time. They are pain, fatigue, anxiety and depression, poor sleep, and limits on daily function. One hundred seventy-seven patients were assessed in hospital and again one month after going home.

Network analysis mapped which symptoms sat at the center of the web at each point. Limits on function and fatigue mattered most at both times. Fatigue was also the only symptom that predicted later problems, worsening sleep afterward. The results suggest that treating fatigue early may protect several other parts of patients' lives.
pmc-13598902:
Toma Shinkai, Koki Ogawa, Mohamed S. Mohamed, and Tetsuya Ozeki systematically exposed mRNA-carrying lipid nanoparticles, the delivery system behind the COVID vaccines, to the hazards of the digestive tract, a first step toward an oral mRNA medicine. Injections are the only proven route today, and the team tested digestive enzymes, stomach-like fluid, and acidity one by one.

Pepsin, the stomach's protein-cutting enzyme, slashed the particles' protein-making ability and swelled their size, while amylase left them alone. Fat-cutting lipase at high concentration also damaged function, and rebuilding the particles around a lipid without the vulnerable chemical bonds blunted that damage, identifying the mechanism. Simulated gastric fluid crippled the particles, with the harm traced to extreme acidity near pH 1 rather than milder levels. The authors convert the findings into design rules for particles that might survive swallowing.
pmc-13599702:
Zainab Naaran and Amit Yashar published this 2026 study on how autistic adults search a visual scene and how much mental effort that search costs. Earlier work often found a search advantage in autism, but the effort behind it was unclear.

In one experiment, forty-eight autistic and forty-five non-autistic adults hunted for a colored target while their pupils were measured. Reaction times were similar, yet pupil responses were smaller in the autistic group, suggesting less effort. In a harder second task with brief, masked displays, autistic participants were more accurate. Both groups used recent trial history to guide attention, so the difference lay in how effort and accuracy shifted under pressure.
pmc-13608802:
Luis Ramalhete leads a seven-author team stress-testing a blood-scan score meant to predict kidney transplant rejection before surgery. The score comes from infrared spectroscopy of pre-transplant serum, and an earlier study had linked it to later biopsy-proven rejection. The extension reused the same single-center cohort, 79 recipients of whom 40 rejected and 39 stayed rejection-free for five years. It asked whether the frozen score still separated patients at many horizons without retraining.

Discrimination held up, with area-under-curve values of 0.780 at thirty days, rising to 0.860 at one year, and 0.850 at five years. Each standard-deviation rise in the score nearly doubled the rejection hazard. Models retrained for single rejection types gave mixed results. The authors treat those findings as hypothesis-generating only, since nothing here establishes distinct spectral signatures. Independent external validation is the next step, they conclude, before the score can inform transplant decisions.
pmc-13616002:
Angelika Buczyńska-Backiel and colleagues reviewed how stress and swelling disturb placenta blood-vessel growth when diabetes starts in pregnancy. The condition means high blood sugar, yet it also drives body-wide stress and swelling that reshape the placenta. Their 2026 narrative review pulled together lab and clinical evidence on stress, swelling, and vessel signals in these cases.

These cases as a rule showed higher stress and swelling in blood and placenta, tied to vessel-wall trouble and odd vessel rebuild. Gene risk mainly shaped mother's sugar handling, while placenta changes followed sugar-linked stress plus gene-switch tuning. Trials of antioxidant pills partly eased balance and sugar markers. Buczyńska-Backiel and colleagues propose tackling stress and swelling as an add-on to sugar control.
pmc-13616402:
Xinjing Gong and colleagues present DRIVE, a computer framework for picking out the true driver genes of cancer from the crowd of harmless passenger changes. The hunt is hard because gene interaction maps mix unlike neighbours, the many data types disagree, and confirmed drivers are few. DRIVE fuses four evidence kinds: mutation frequency, copy number shifts, chemical silencing, and gene activity, all laid over interaction networks.

The system splits each gene's neighbourhood into tight and loose views to stop signals bleeding across types, and separates evidence shared across data kinds from evidence unique to one. Training mixes self-teaching with penalties tuned for rare, lopsided labels. Across six benchmark networks it beat ten rival methods. Better driver lists mean experiments and drug trials aim at genes that truly run the disease.
pmc-13617302:
Suguru Nishiuchi and four colleagues describe a stepwise method for finding the source of extra heartbeats that arise outside the pulmonary veins, a known trigger of atrial fibrillation. Such stray beats can be rare or brief, which makes them hard to catch with standard mapping. Their approach uses the Affera mapping system, which records heartbeats of mixed rhythms into a single voltage map.

After collection, beats are separated by their cycle length into sinus and early-beat activation maps from the same dataset. Stepwise filtering by signal steepness removes far-away interference, and a close look at local signal shape, seeking a QS-like pattern, pinpoints the origin. The authors illustrate the workflow with a seventy-five-year-old man returning for repeat ablation, in whom a drug challenge provoked renewed fibrillation. They present the method as a way to localize stubborn triggers without extra mapping steps.
pmc-13617402:
Andrej Belančić and co-authors checked the transformed treatment landscape of spinal muscular atrophy in 2026. The disease is a genetic mess in which a missing survival motor neuron protein, caused by mutations in the SMN1 gene, destroys the motor neurons of the spinal cord. Within a few years, three approved disease-modifying treatments have changed its course: an injected antisense drug, a one-time gene treatment, and a daily oral drug.

The review summarizes trial efficacy and real-world effectiveness for all three, finding major gains in survival, motor milestones, and quality of life, strongest when treatment starts early. Safety data from trials and post-marketing surveillance show manageable side effects. The harder chapter is economics: prices are high and cost-effectiveness strains standard thresholds, though context matters. A section surveys the workflow of next-generation treatments aiming at the missing protein and independent targets such as muscle itself.
pmc-13620102:
Hikaru Ogi and four colleagues screened tissues from wild game animals in Japan for useful proteins and health-linked activity after digestion. Wild sika deer and boar are culled in large numbers to limit farm and forest damage, yet little of each animal gets used. The team compared eight tissues from deer and boar with matching cattle and pig tissues, running them through a lab model of stomach and intestinal digestion.

Protein and peptide yields differed by tissue and species in six of the eight tissues compared. Boar stomach, liver, and round cuts scored well in several matchups, while deer spleen lagged behind. Two lab tests measured antioxidant power and the ability to block an enzyme tied to blood pressure. Boar liver and loin and deer spleen each stood out on one of those measures. The authors flag those three tissues for deeper study as ingredients with added value.
pmc-13620302:
Xin Du and Jingwei Li explored whether fatty liver worsens thinking after a stroke, and whether blood inflammation signals carry that effect. Their study enrolled 247 patients with ischemic stroke, split by how severe their nonalcoholic fatty liver disease was, a condition where fat builds up in the liver without alcohol. Every patient took a standard thinking test and gave blood for cytokine measures.

Patients with worse fatty liver scored lower on the thinking test and carried higher levels of four inflammation signals. Statistical modeling showed liver grade itself predicted both thinking scores and two of those signals. A mediation analysis, which tests whether one factor explains another's effect, singled out TNF-alpha: part of the liver's link to poor thinking ran through that one signal. The authors propose treating fatty liver and calming inflammation as early targets against post-stroke cognitive decline.
pmc-13620402:
Rafat Hossain Rafi and eight colleagues tested whether two old drugs can rescue antibiotics against a diarrhea-causing gut bacterium. Silybin, a milk thistle extract, and diclofenac, a common painkiller, were paired with several antibiotics against enteropathogenic E. coli in dishes and in infected mice. The gentamicin pairings came out strongest.

Both combinations kept killing bacteria longer than gentamicin alone in timed tests. In mice, the pairings protected the gut lining's crypt cells better and calmed colon inflammation and swelling more effectively, alongside checks of weight, blood counts, and stool scores. Computer docking studies pointed to two bacterial proteins as the likely helpers' targets, one that ferries outer membrane parts and one that clamps DNA during copying. The authors frame drug repurposing as a practical answer while new antibiotics stall.
pmc-13621702:
Taifur Rahman, Satyajit Kundu, and Ahmed Hossain report a 2026 case-control study of childhood tuberculosis in rural Bangladesh. The study asks whether the BCG vaccine, given at birth, still protects children, and how much recent tuberculosis inside the home raises a child's risk. It focuses on Moulvibazar District, including poor tea-garden communities.

The team compared 207 children aged two to fourteen who had newly confirmed tuberculosis with 207 matched children from the same neighbourhoods who had no breathing symptoms. Older children, boys, and children whose family had tuberculosis in the prior six months faced higher odds of disease. Vaccinated children had much lower odds, with vaccination linked to a drop of more than half. The authors urge wider BCG coverage and careful checks of household contacts, above all for older boys.
pmc-13623502:
Franziska Messirek and Stephan Getzin track how desert trees in Namibia choose their ground along streams flowing only a few days a year. In the hyper-arid Namib, trees line these dry channels like a green ribbon and shelter other species. Using drones over six years, from 2020 to 2025, the pair mapped three species against fine terrain models.

Along the Kuiseb River, one species hugged the low riverbed while its partner grew higher up the bank. The second is known for roots reaching tens of metres down to groundwater, freeing it from the channel. In a valley site, moringa trees favoured low drainage lines that catch rain runoff, and they store water in thick trunks. Dead wood told a story: where trees crowded low ground, dead trees were rare, while a site of bank-side trees showed far more. The authors link survival strategy to each species' water plan.
pmc-13625202:
Vinaya C Iyer, Lilach O Lerman, Alfonso Eirin, and Satabdi Datta Choudhury review how narrowed kidney arteries sabotage the kidney's own repair crews. Renovascular disease tightens the arteries feeding the kidneys, driving high blood pressure and chronic kidney damage in older adults. The kidney leans on three repair systems, vessel-growing progenitor cells, mesenchymal stromal cells, and tubule renewal paths, and the review traces how each one falters.

Low blood flow, stretch, hormone surges, and low oxygen all converge on the same cell harms, from rust-like chemical damage and failing power plants to cells aging early or dying. Heart and metabolic illnesses pile on. The authors survey rescue ideas, including cell-free vesicle therapies and drugs that shield cell power plants, as ways to keep repair alive.
pmc-13629302:
de Souza Junyor and coauthors study a protein that may shape Parkinson harm. Clumps of a brain protein kill nerve cells in that illness. What makes some brain zones prone to that harm stays unclear. A cell surface protein may act as a gate for the clumps.

Gene data from human brain tissue showed the gate gene switched up. That held in the deep brain zone most hurt by the illness. Mouse work then raised and lowered the protein in the brain. More protein meant more nerve harm from the clumps. Less protein meant less harm in the same tests. The gate may be a drug target.
pmc-13629802:
He Huang and three colleagues examined how body mass index relates to exercise capacity in 405 patients with chronic coronary syndrome, stable heart disease, at a hospital in Taizhou, China. Each patient took a cardiopulmonary exercise test, and the team compared results across weight groups and between the sexes.

Higher body mass came with greater absolute peak oxygen uptake, yet lower uptake once body weight was factored in, a two-way pattern with no bend in the middle. Sex modified both arms: the positive link ran stronger in men, while the weight-adjusted penalty pressed harder in women. The authors warn against reading body mass as simply good or bad for fitness in these patients, and they argue for sex-aware interpretation of exercise tests.
pmc-13631602:
Zubaydah Abdi and colleagues reported a rare womb vessel condition in two thousand twenty-six. A woman in her early thirties had stubborn pelvic pain. She also suffered heavy menstrual bleeding. Standard treatments failed to control her symptoms. Surgeons removed her womb and tubes by keyhole surgery. Lab examination then revealed the surprise cause.

Blood vessels had grown diffusely through the womb wall. Only a handful of such cases exist in print. Scans and scopes usually miss this condition. Diagnosis almost always comes after surgery. Medicines appear largely ineffective for symptom control. Most reported patients ended with hysterectomy. Follow-up watching is advised afterward.
pmc-13634002:
Yago Medeiros Dutra and six colleagues published this 2026 study of how running in heat reshapes recovery afterward. Twelve trained participants ran to exhaustion at a hard, set pace in a mild room and in a hot room. The team tracked leg muscle function with voluntary and stimulated contractions. They also followed heart rate patterns and blood markers of muscle damage for three days after each run.

Heat cut the time to exhaustion by more than half. Muscle function and heart control dipped in the first hour under both conditions, then normalized within a day. Across three days, though, the hot run left deeper low-frequency muscle fatigue and stronger withdrawal of the heart's calming vagal influence. One surprise ran the other way: the rise in a muscle damage marker at one day was smaller after the hot run. Coaches misread recovery if they trust that single marker alone.
pmc-13635002:
Phan and colleagues publish in 2026 an experimental dataset for engineers who model and control a dual-phase gas-liquid pressure system. In the system, carbon dioxide and water flow on opposite sides of a porous membrane. Such systems need accurate dynamic models before controllers can be designed.

The data come from a laboratory rig with gas and water channels separated by a PTFE membrane module. Its valves were driven while industrial sensors logged pressures once per second under a programmable controller. Three water flow rates were crossed with three excitation patterns, sine wave, sawtooth, and multi-step. That gave nine twenty-minute experiments and 10,800 synchronized samples in total across the nine spreadsheet files released with this data article. Each file records valve commands alongside gas inlet and water outlet pressures, ready for system identification work.
pmc-13635602:
Uri Gabbay, Shai Fein, and Michael J Drescher review cardiovascular reserve and the tools that try to measure it. Reserve means the circulation's spare capacity to keep tissues supplied as stress rises. Standard vital signs show only the present state, so a patient can look stable while compensation quietly runs out. Two technologies aim to estimate remaining reserve: one metric built largely on bleeding experiments, one index tested across wider stress types.

The bleeding-focused metric performs strongly in animal and experimental hemorrhage work and is the most studied of the two. The broader index has thinner evidence, from exercise testing, bleeding, and heat stress, yet seems to track reserve draining across stresses. Both rest on small clinical groups with mixed designs and little independent checking. The authors map the physiology behind reserve monitoring and list what research must settle before such tools guide bedside care.
pmc-13638202:
Tiffani Matos Oliveira and Franciele Marabotti Costa Leite examine whether childhood adversity predicts depressive symptoms in adult women, using a population survey from Vitória, Brazil. Eleven hundred women answered an international childhood adversity questionnaire covering neglect, abuse, and household dysfunction, plus a standard depression scale. Statistical models tested which early experiences still echoed decades later, adjusting for other factors.

Three experiences stood out. Women who had been physically neglected as children carried notably higher odds of depressive symptoms in adulthood. So did women who had suffered sexual abuse, and women who had lived with an incarcerated family member. The links survived adjustment, marking them as durable rather than incidental. The authors call for public policies across sectors that protect children and cut economic inequality, arguing that harm done in childhood taxes mental health across the whole life course.
pmc-13638702:
Ugljesa Malicevic and two colleagues present a 2026 animal study on how long-term high blood sugar inflames the gut in diabetes. They used Yucatan mini pigs made diabetic through a rich diet plus a drug that damages insulin production, then examined tissue from the small and large intestine.

Diabetic pigs showed damaged villi, lost goblet cells, and more immune cells in the gut wall. Genes tied to inflammation, cell stress in the endoplasmic reticulum, and autophagy, the cell's recycling system, were all raised. The findings suggest these stress pathways could be targets for treating diabetes-related gut problems.
pmc-13639502:
Jingyi Huang, Tessa Kaufman, and Susan Branje studied peer bullying reports in two thousand twenty-six. Sexual and gender diverse youth face more peer victimization. Their well-being suffers as a result. Reports came from youth, parents, and teachers in a British cohort. The team compared who noticed the bullying. Four patterns emerged, from no victimization to agreed victimization.

Adults usually underestimated what youth experienced. Most incidents were visible only to the youth. Diverse youth were more often in the agreed group, though. Their bullying was more visible to adults. Agreed victims reported the worst mental health. That pattern explained much of the well-being gap.
pmc-13645602:
Wen-Yuan Yang and Hui-Ru Chi present a qualitative study of older women living in rural Hakka areas of northeastern Guangdong, China. The pair interviewed eighteen women at length about hardship and coping in later life. Their method built a model from the interview material in stages. The central question is how weakness and strength interact in these women's daily lives.

The women faced risks stacked from personal, family, community, and cultural pressures, including lifelong gender expectations and quiet institutional neglect. Yet they also rebuilt their thinking, reshaped support networks, and drew on local resources to keep going. Hardship and resilience appeared woven together rather than as opposites, and resilience often rested on unnoticed extra labor. The authors argue policy should rebuild support systems around such women instead of only aiding individuals in crisis.
pmc-13646302:
Whether testosterone therapy raises the risk of atrial fibrillation is appraised by Traish and two colleagues. Atrial fibrillation is an irregular heart rhythm linked to stroke and heart failure. It has become a flashpoint in care for men with low testosterone, with a few studies suggesting therapy raises risk and many others suggesting the opposite. The team reviewed the medical literature on testosterone treatment in hypogonadal men, weighing studies that blamed therapy against studies that blamed testosterone deficiency itself.

Closer reading, they argue, shows confounding factors behind several claims that therapy increases fibrillation. A larger body of work links low testosterone to higher fibrillation rates and finds no increased rate with treatment. No trial so far has made fibrillation its primary outcome, since it usually appears only as a secondary measure. Traish and colleagues conclude that current evidence favours deficiency, not therapy, as the risk factor, pending dedicated trials.
pmc-13646502:
Shuxia Liang, Lu Xu, and Zheng Hu review recovery after takotsubo syndrome, a temporary weakening of the heart often triggered by stress. Doctors usually declare recovery when the heart's pumping percentage returns to normal. The trio argue that this single number misses much of convalescence. Their state-of-the-art review gathers registry and imaging evidence across mechanical, functional, and biological layers of recovery.

Some survivors keep symptoms or exercise limits after the pumping number normalizes, while others show quiet abnormalities in muscle motion, tissue character, energy use, or blood flow. The authors propose a staged framework that separates unresolved heart recovery from competing risks such as cancer or nerve disease. Extra tests, from strain imaging to exercise testing, should answer a defined question rather than run by routine. The framework is meant to organize follow-up and trial design, not to serve as a finished risk score.
pmc-13649402:
Yihan Chen and three colleagues studied what drives Chinese shoppers to buy organic food. Buyers cannot check farm claims on their own, so they lean on labels, seals, and facts they seek out. The team surveyed 412 screened shoppers and tested a model that joins planned behaviour theory with trust cues.

Seeking facts raised what shoppers knew, and more knowledge warmed their view of organic food. Good views, peer norms, a sense of control, social media, eco-labels, and faith in state support all raised the wish to buy. A step-by-step path ran from fact seeking through knowledge and views to purchase plans. The authors offer tips for shops, seal bodies, and policy makers.
pmc-13649702:
António Luís Vidinha Pereira and five colleagues weigh how Portugal's health system must adapt to one of the world's fastest aging populations. The national health service dates to 1979, an era when Portugal ranked among the youngest lands in Europe, and it focused on mother and child health. That focus no longer fits the country.

Care for older adults now centres on disease lists and deficits, and few staff hold deep training in old-age care in the community. The authors explore a World Health Organization approach called ICOPE, which screens for drops in core abilities and builds care around them. Their team is piloting the approach. They weigh its promise for joined-up primary care against time and staffing costs.
pmc-13651602:
Ehsan Rahimi and five co-authors let machine learning read the scattered literature on micro- and nanorobots, the swimming devices being developed for drug delivery, sensing, imaging, and therapy inside the body. Reports in the field vary so wildly in setup and readouts that design lessons refuse to build up.

A dataset gathered from published systems was grouped by structure and correlation. Three descriptor kinds stood out: the setting of use, how drive and sensing couple, and the design intent. Trained models found learnable patterns in how drive methods are chosen. Forecasts of raw swimming speed carried over only somewhat, betraying deep shifts between materials, drive physics, body fluids, and lab protocols. The authors argue that the field's immediate gift from AI is a map of itself. It charts the design landscape, exposes reporting bias, and pushes all labs toward shared datasets that future forecasts can trust.
pmc-13658302:
Sheridan Hoy profiles linerixibat, a new drug for the severe itching that comes with primary biliary cholangitis, a liver disease. The drug blocks the ileal bile acid transporter in the gut, cutting the recycling of bile acids that drives the itch. Developed by GSK, it won its first approval in the United States for this use. Becoming the first therapy approved there for cholestatic itching in this disease, with approval in the United Kingdom following.

Regulatory reviews were still running in Canada, China, and the European Union when the profile was written. As part of a first-approval series, the article traces the milestones of the drug's development, from its mechanism through the trials that supported licensing. Clinicians treating a symptom that ruins sleep and daily life for many patients get a compact account of where this option came from and where it stands.
pmc-13663902:
Liu and co-authors review a plan to shield T cells from oxidative harm so they can fight solid tumors better. Adoptive T cell therapy struggles in solid tumors, where the local setting suppresses immunity. A build-up of reactive oxygen species drives much of that resistance. Blanket antioxidant treatment lacks aim and can disturb normal signaling. The review instead maps how T cell types differ in their defenses.

Effector, memory, and regulatory T cells vary in fuel use, power plant behavior, and defense genes. Other immune cells in the tumor add to the suppressive web. The authors argue for boosting the antioxidant strength of the therapy cells themselves. Aim matters more than dose.
pmc-13670502:
He and co-authors test a leaf extract that eases drug-induced liver injury in mice by reshaping gut microbes. The leaves of Eucommia ulmoides are rich in flavonoids with liver-protective hints. Excess acetaminophen is a classic cause of acute liver damage. The team built that injury model in mice and dosed the extract. Liver function tests and tissue checks measured the damage. Gene sequencing mapped gut bacteria, and a targeted scan tracked bile acids.

Antibiotic arms tested whether microbes carry the benefit. Gut barrier strength was also checked. The extract calmed the disorder in microbe-driven bile acid handling. The work joins plant, microbe, and liver in one chain.
pmc-13685602:
Shanique Sterling-Lovy and seven co-authors ask whether replacing the pulmonary valve improves overall heart function in patients whose tetralogy of Fallot was repaired in childhood. A combined index of both ventricles' function predicts bad outcomes in this population, but its response to valve replacement was unknown. One hundred thirty-three patients had cardiac MRI within a year before and two years after their first valve replacement, compared against one hundred thirty-six controls.

Patients' index values ran well below controls', and nearly half were subnormal before surgery. After replacement, the mean index did not significantly change, while the right ventricle's own index fell. The study hunts pre-operative factors predicting severely depressed function afterward, complicating assumptions that valve replacement restores global function.
pmc-1852402:
Hellemans, Mortier, De Paepe, and co-authors present qBase, a free program for handling real-time PCR data. PCR tests that track DNA growth are used to measure gene activity. Raw output from many samples and genes is hard to manage and easy to mishandle by hand.

qBase organises that data and automates the relative quantification step, which compares gene activity between samples. Automated, standard handling cuts errors and makes results easier to repeat. For labs running gene tests daily, shared software of this kind raised the reliability of reported changes in gene activity.
pmc-3412702:
Ye, Coulouris, Zaretskaya, and co-authors present Primer-BLAST, a tool to design target-specific primers for PCR. Primers are the short DNA pieces that start copying in a PCR test. Choosing them well is probably the single most important factor in whether the reaction works.

Specific copying requires primers that do not match other targets in the wrong orientation or at the wrong distance. Primer-BLAST checks candidate primers against sequence databases for such stray matches. The free tool saves labs from failed reactions and false results, and it is built into routine test design.
pmc-3965102:
Law, Knox, Djoumbou, and their team presented DrugBank version four in 2013. DrugBank is a free online database that holds deep detail on drugs, how they act, and what they target in the body. First described in 2006, it had grown fast as users asked for more.

The new release put fresh weight on drug metabolism, the way the body changes and clears a drug. Entries link a drug to its targets, enzymes, and chemical facts in one place. Doctors, chemists, and drug makers use that joined-up view to check safety, plan trials, and hunt for new uses of known drugs.
pmc-4029002:
Rosano and Ceccarelli reviewed in 2014 how to make proteins in the bacterium Escherichia coli. This microbe is one of the top choices for producing recombinant proteins, meaning proteins from genes placed into it on purpose. Its use as a living factory is well established and very common.

The review covers the many tools and protocols built for high-level production in this host. It also faces the hard parts, such as proteins that fold badly or form clumps. Clear guidance on strain choice, gene design, and growth conditions helps labs raise yields. Such proteins are used in research, medicine, and industry.
pmc-4383202:
Wan, Wang, Liu, and their co-authors tackled a common problem in meta-analysis in 2014. Reviews often need to pool the mean and standard deviation from similar clinical trials. Many trials, though, report only the median, the range, or the quartiles instead.

The authors give formulas to estimate the mean and spread from those reported values. Their methods were tested and compared so users can pick the best fit for each case. Without such estimates, many trials would be dropped from a review, wasting their evidence. The paper is a practical aid used by review teams across medicine.
pmc-4748402:
Atanasov, Waltenberger, Pferschy-Wenzig, and their colleagues reviewed plant-derived natural products in 2015. Medicinal plants have a long record as sources of molecules with therapeutic value. They still form an important pool for finding new drug leads today.

For some decades, industry focused mainly on libraries of synthetic compounds instead. The review covers both discovery of active plant products and the resupply problem, since a rare plant may not yield enough material. Solving supply through farming or synthesis decides whether a lead becomes a drug. The paper supports renewed investment in plant sources for future medicines.
pmc-5641502:
The GBD 2015 Neurological Disorders Collaborator Group published this large study in 2017. It measures how much illness, disability, and early death brain and nerve disorders caused around the world. The work covers global, regional, and national levels for the years from 1990 to 2015.

Readers get comparable figures for conditions such as stroke, dementia, epilepsy, and Parkinson disease across many countries and years. Health planners need numbers like these to decide where staff, beds, and money should go. The study shows that the share of disease linked to nerve disorders grew as populations aged, which makes planning harder.
pmc-6602502:
Stephan Greiner, Pascal Lehwark, and Ralph Bock presented OGDRAW version 1.3.1 in 2019. Chloroplast and mitochondrial genomes are small circles packed with genes. Drawing clear maps of them is a routine need as sequencing floods in.

OGDRAW turns genome annotation into publication-ready circular maps automatically. The update expands the toolkit and eases work on many genomes at once. Users can tune colors and layout without drawing by hand. Plant and organelle researchers use the maps in papers and teaching to show gene order at a glance. Maps can be exported in formats ready for journals, posters, and genome database pages.
pmc-6678302:
Laura Doyle and Matthew Wang gave an overview of extracellular vesicles in 2019. Cells release tiny vesicles, including exosomes, that carry markers of their state. Those parcels show up in blood and other fluids, which makes them tempting for tests.

Clinical use is held back by a lack of standard ways to isolate and measure vesicles. The authors review origins, contents, and the main separation methods, with the strengths of each. They stress reporting standards so studies can be compared. The overview helps newcomers avoid the field's common traps. Practical tables compare yield, purity, and cost across the main isolation methods.
podmore-modern-spiritualism-1902:
Frank Podmore wrote the chief cool past of a faith in Modern Spiritualism, his two tome work of 1902. Podmore was the top doubt voice in the band that made such things its study. He knew the dark room from the in side. Here he tells the faith's tale from the Fox girls to his own day, fraud by fraud.

His tone is fair, dry, and oft wry. He grants some strange scraps, yet finds fraud at the root of most fame. All pasts of the theme since cite his work. It is the faith judged by its best foe.
recollections-of-the-private-life-of-nap: A plain-text publisher's header is the whole of the opening matter for the second volume of Constant's Private Life of Napoleon Bonaparte. It records the title, credits the work to Constant, and marks the language as English. Beyond those facts the pages at hand are blank of the work itself: no chapter heading, no table of contents, and no line of memoir appears. What this second part covers, and where its story picks up, cannot be told from what is printed here.
rhodes-last-will-testament-1902:
Cecil John Rhodes built a vast fortune in South African diamonds and gold, and he died in 1902 leaving a series of wills. Those wills set out how his money should be used after his death. Journalist W. T. Stead edited the wills for print that same year, adding long notes to explain them.

Readers find the actual terms Rhodes left behind, including money for scholarships and for grand plans in Africa. Stead's notes spell out the secret aims Rhodes attached to some gifts, aims later tied to the Round Table movement. Few books show so plainly how one rich man hoped to shape an empire from the grave.
richard-carvel-volume-02:
Winston Churchill's Richard Carvel continues in a second volume of five chapters, from Over the Wall to News from a Far Country. Under False Colours and The Red in the Carvel Blood stand between them, with A Festival and a Parting. The volume opens in Richard's voice, rueful over Dorothy Manners.

Dorothy, he says, treated him ill that spring, since she had tasted power at Carvel Hall. Suitors crowd her house, Dr. Courtenay and Will Fotheringay among them, while gentlemen call on her mother to see her. Richard, an awkward old playmate, gets scant attention. She teases him for knowing every twist of his nature, and bids him make her jealous instead.
rilke-buch-der-bilder-1902:
Das Buch der Bilder, The Book of Images, is Rainer Maria Rilke's early book of poems, published in German in 1902. The text here is the German original, since no English translation is in the public domain. Rilke was still in his twenties, fresh from Russia trips and deep study of art.

The poems picture saints, angels, lovers, beggars, and quiet rooms, each held in a tender, watchful gaze. Things in Rilke are never mere props; they seem to look back at the reader. His lines favor soft music over bold statement, and images over argument. The book stands at the source of modern German lyric poetry. Later came the sterner Elegies, but the seeds are here.
rob-roy-volume-02:
Sir Walter Scott's Rob Roy opens its second volume at chapter first, under a verse from Bürger about the dead riding fast. A picture of Helen MacGregor serves as frontispiece. The narrator, Frank, weighs two sorrows at once in the opening passage.

He grieves at parting from Miss Vernon, yet his father's troubles press on him too, with news of Mr. Tresham between them. Man can give only a fixed share of distress to each cause, he reflects, like a bankrupt's divided funds. His father's letter, not very distinct, bids him meet Owen at Glasgow, at the merchants MacVittie, MacFin and Company in the Gallowgate. Earlier letters seem to have miscarried or been intercepted.
run-to-earth-a-novel-pg9102: Run to Earth, a novel billed only as by the author of Lady Audley's Secret, Aurora Floyd, Ishmael, Vixen, and Wyllard's Weird. It opens with a picture of Honoria murmuring that she is in the power of a maniac. The contents list chapters headed Warned in a Dream, Done in the Darkness, and Disinherited. A fourth is headed Out of the Depths.
scheible-das-kloster-vol02:
Band two of Das Kloster, issued by editor Johann Scheible in 1845, gathers cells five through eight. Scheible's plan was bold for its time: rescue the cheap print of past ages before it rotted away. Whole texts went back into print under his Stuttgart imprint, in German, for any buyer to own.

Folk magic fills much of the space, from charms spoken over wounds to full spell books. Faust tales and Höllenzwänge, the hell-compelling grimoires, keep their full wording here. Chapbooks of popular story stand beside them without apology. Scholars still mine these pages when a lone copy elsewhere has crumbled or vanished.
scientific-phrenology-being-a-practical-: Pages shown here are for a work headed by its record title as a practical mental science from 1902. They consist of a publisher's list and press opinions. The opinions concern a related book by the same author. That related book, The Mental Functions of the Brain, is described as an investigation into their localisation and their manifestation in health and disease.
serapis-volume-02:
Georg Ebers wrote this historical novel of Alexandria; volume two opens at chapter five. Karnis has been long away from the boat, and young Dada frets through the wait with little Papias. When Karnis returns at sunset, she begs for the promised walk to see Alexandria.

Herse, her foster mother, forbids the trip until the next day. Dada bursts into tears, flings her distaff over the boat's side, and vows to run away. Karnis calms her by pleading his own deep weariness. Family warmth and a girl's restless spirit carry this middle volume's opening scenes.
serge-panine-volume-02: Volume two of Serge Panine, Georges Ohnet's French novel, stands behind these pages. Its English issue forms part of a series of Academy-crowned romances from France. Only the publisher's header appears here. The header repeats the title and Ohnet's name. It adds the series note and file data. Not one scene from this middle volume is shown. The tale's state at this point stays beyond fair statement from such thin front matter.
sketches-by-seymour-volume-02:
Robert Seymour's comic plates carry this second part of his sketches, opening at scene nine with verse. Two urchins, Tom and Bill, get hold of a pistol, powder, horn, and shot one day and set out on sport. A hare would crown their hopes, till Bill spots mother Tibbs's tabby cat instead.

Puss makes as good a mark as any bull's-eye, Bill argues, while the cat's mistress shrieks from above the wall. The shot leaves poor Tink finished and his mistress in a stew, while both boys flee. Cruel boy humor of the 1830s fills the plate's rhymed tale.
slave-narratives-a-folk-history-of-slave: Slave Narratives, a folk history of slavery in the United States from talks with former slaves, was typed from records made by the Federal Writers' Project in 1936-1938. The Library of Congress project put the set together, with photos, at Washington in 1941. One part is Volume IV, the Georgia Narratives, Part 1. Its list of those who spoke begins with Rachel Adams, Uncle Wash Allen, Hannah Austin, and Celestia Avery.
sombart-moderne-kapitalismus-vol1-1902:
Werner Sombart published the first volume of Modern Capitalism in German in 1902. Sombart, a German economist of the historical school, set out to explain how the modern economic system was born. The scale of the attempt, a full history of capitalism from its roots, matched the ambitions of its age.

Volume 1 traces the system's growth from medieval trade through the early crafts and the first great merchants. Sombart sorts economic life into stages and asks what spirit drives each one, the quiet craftsman against the bold entrepreneur. His answer gave later writers the phrase capitalist spirit to argue with. Weber, his younger rival, answered Sombart in famous essays of his own. The volume opens the most ambitious economic history of its time, and the argument it started has never fully closed.
sombart-moderne-kapitalismus-vol2-1902:
The second volume of Sombart's Modern Capitalism followed the first in 1902, completing the original design. Sombart had traced capitalism's birth in the opening volume; now the system stands full-grown. The German scholar's panorama widens to the whole industrial order of his day.

Volume 2 carries the tale into the industrial age: the factory system, the great firms and trusts, and the world market that bound them together. Sombart weighs the costs of the triumph, the uprooted crafts and crowded cities, beside the gains in wealth and power. His historical method piles up evidence where pure theory would argue. Economic history on the grandest scale ever attempted closes here, with capitalism triumphant and troubled at once. Later editions tripled the work, but the 1902 pair remains the statement that made his name.
strindberg-the-dream-play-1902:
August Strindberg wrote The Dream Play in 1902, here in Edwin Björkman's English translation for Western readers. The daughter of Indra descends to earth in the dream-drama that invented expressionist theatre for the modern stage. Strindberg's preface bids actors imitate the disjointed but seemingly logical shape of a dream in performance throughout.

Indra's daughter, as Agnes, marries, suffers, and watches human life repeat its pains in shifting scenes. An Officer waits for a singer who never comes, and a Lawyer wears mankind's grievances in his face. A castle grows from a dung heap, and a door with a cloverleaf hole guards life's secret. Humanity's refrain, men are to be pitied, tolls through scene changes that melt like thoughts in sleep. Björkman's version seeded the play's immense influence on theatre, film, and the modernist stage.
tales-and-novels-of-j-de-la-fontaine-vol:
Four verse tales fill the second volume of La Fontaine's Tales and Novels. They are The Cudgelled and Contented Cuckold, The Husband Confessor, The Cobbler, and The Peasant and His Angry Lord. A note from the producer points readers to a short list of bookmarks for sampling the author's ideas before making a whole meal of them.

The first tale follows a younger brother homeward from Rome. His travels have not improved him. He falls at once for a fair lady in a country town. He sees her safely home with gallant attention. Pardons from Rome he has in plenty; the virtues, the verse jokes, he left with His Holiness behind.
