La Fontaine's cuckolds, confessors, and craftsmen play out the old comedy of desire and deception in brisk rhymes.
tales-from-the-arabic-volume-02:
Payne's Tales from the Arabic continues in Volume the Second. A Delhi edition carries the printing, dated 1901. The Breslau text of the Thousand Nights and One Night goes on. Its frame is King Shah Bekht and his vizier Er Rehwan. It resumes from volume one.

Within that frame the contents list a pious woman accused of lewdness, a journeyman and a girl, and a weaver who became a physician by his wife's commandment. A run of sharper tales follows. Two sharpers cheat each his fellow in one. Sharpers deal with a money-changer and an ass in another. A sharper and the merchants come next. The hawk and the locust sit nested inside that tale. A king and his chamberlain's wife, an old woman and a draper's wife, and a foul-favored man with a fair wife keep the volume's world of tricks, lust, and sudden fortune turning.
the-adventures-of-ferdinand-count-fathom: Tobias Smollett wrote The Adventures of Ferdinand Count Fathom, and this second volume holds Part Two of the novel, with the author's preface and an opening essay by G. H. Maynadier of Harvard University. Chapter heads start at thirty-nine and trace fresh scenes of life, Renaldo's deepening distress as Fathom's plot thickens, the art of borrowing, and Monimia's honor guarded by a stroke of heaven.
the-antiquary-volume-02: Volume Two of The Antiquary by Sir Walter Scott is present only as cover and contents matter, with a second-volume title page and frontispiece named. Its chapters are counted in words from first to sixteenth and beyond, with no heads or summaries attached. No story text appears in these pages, so nothing of the novel's cast or course can be grounded from what is shown here.
the-arabian-nights-entertainments-volume: Contents pages list the second Aldine volume. Pickering and Chatto printed it at London in 1890. It has pictures by S. L. Wood, from Dr. Jonathan Scott's text. The volume centers on the little hunchback. A ring of tales surrounds him, told by a merchant, a purveyor, a physician, a tailor, and a barber. The barber's six brothers each get a story. Later come Aboulhassen Ali Ebn Ecar and Schemselnihar. Noor Ad Deen and the fair Persian close the list.
the-attache-or-sam-slick-in-england-volu: Volume two of Haliburton's Attaché repeats the front matter of the first. It has the motto and Slick's threat of the mitten for printed talk. It also has the author's London letter of July 3, 1843. That letter sends the attaché ahead to Edmund Hopkinson at Edgeworth. It pleads for indulgence of his eccentric ways. Its own contents then begin afresh, with The Nose of a Spy as chapter one and The Patron as chapter two.
the-bride-of-the-nile-volume-02:
Volume 2 of The Bride of the Nile, by Georg Ebers, opens at Chapter VI with a governor in deep unrest. Soul pangs and doubts of conscience drove him to buy a costly hanging as a gift. The dearer the gift, the stronger his hope of grace from the man who got it. He has cause to ask if he acted rightly.

Revenge is no Christian virtue, he knows, yet he could not let the Melchites' evil go unpaid when the chance to crush them came. His two bright young sons were murdered by them, and since that blow he has felt himself slowly dying. Greeks and Melchites were driven from Egypt in shame, some slain by crowds who hailed the Moslems as saviors. His revenge is complete, and now conscience lifts its voice.
the-burgomaster-s-wife-volume-02:
Volume 2 of The Burgomaster's Wife, by Georg Ebers, opens at Chapter VII in a spell of rain over Leyden. A second and third rainy day follow the first. White mists and grey fog hang over the meadows. The cold north-west wind drives heavy clouds together, and water in the canals grows turbid and rises toward the banks. Men and women hurry past each other, dripping and freezing, with no greeting.

Talk in the tap-rooms sounds anything but hopeful, and some men are heard calling resistance folly. Others demand aloud the desertion of the Prince of Orange and liberty. Three days have passed since Peter's departure, and the fourth nears noon. No message has reached his family. Maria, his wife, has put on her light-blue dress with Mechlin lace, for he must surely return today.
the-caxtons-a-family-picture-volume-02:
Part II of The Caxtons takes up the family tale again. Pisistratus, the son of the house, narrates his own youth in the first person. His father, a bookish scholar, presides over the household at the tale's center.

The chapter opens with the narrator at the head of his preparatory school at age twelve. His parents then look for a wider field for his studies. Love of study has come back to him in a keen, rival-driven form, and his father no longer tries to curb it. The father honors scholarship too much to block a son who might become a scholar.
the-celebrity-volume-02:
Volume 2 of Winston Churchill's novel opens at Chapter V, at the resort of Asquith. Its hero, the famed Mr. Charles Wrexell Allen, is known in the tale as the Celebrity. Society life by the northern lake frames this stretch of the story.

Knowing voices at Asquith find it small wonder that Allen is drawn to Irene Trevor. Lake breezes have brought color to her cheeks and spring to her step. Bit by bit it grows plain that Miss Trevor is gaining ground with the Celebrity, to the neglect of the other young women there. Word that he will lead the cotillon with her settles the matter for local gossips, and the narrator watches the match form.
the-confessions-of-jean-jacques-rousseau:
Book II of Jean Jacques Rousseau's Confessions stands here as volume II of the twelve-book set, privately printed for members of the Aldus Society at London in 1903. The book opens at the moment of the boy's flight from home and apprenticeship.

Rousseau contrasts two views of the same act. The moment when fear drove his flight seemed no more terrible than the moment of carrying it out seemed delightful. Yet reason draws a grim picture: a child leaving relations and resources midway through his training, before he could earn a living. Such a start runs toward misery and danger, toward vice, despair, snares, slavery, and death. How different, he says, was the idea he actually entertained, which was one of independence. Book II thus turns on the gap between a boy's dream of freedom and the hard world that waits for a runaway apprentice.
the-crisis-volume-02:
Volume 2 of Winston Churchill's The Crisis opens at Chapter VIII, Bellegarde. Miss Virginia Carvel comes down the steps in her riding habit while Ned waits in the street with the horses. She leaps into Vixen's saddle and canters off, neighbors waving from opened windows, to visit the Russell girls at their father's country place on Bellefontaine Road.

Her errand is to announce her hatred for a certain young Yankee upstart, a feeling she confided the day before to Anne Brinsmade and Eugenie Renault. At the Russells she finds a guest, Elise Saint Simon from New Orleans, and will not stay, pleading dinner at Bellegarde though it is only ten o'clock. Puss Russell presses her about a new young man in town as the chapter turns.
the-disowned-volume-02:
Volume two of Edward Bulwer Lytton's The Disowned begins at chapter eleven, with Clarence Linden settled in small lodgings at a house called Copperas Bower. His first morning there brings a thin, weak breakfast tea and sharp, funny talk from Mr. and Mrs. Copperas. Mr. Copperas works in stocks and loves a joke, while his wife prides herself on fine manners.

Clarence watches this odd household with dry amusement. The chapters mix social satire with the hero's slow rise in the world. Talk at the table hints at money, pride, and the schemes that will soon test him.
the-divine-comedy-by-dante-illustrated-h:
Cantos three and four fill part two of Hell in Dante's Vision, rendered into English verse by the Rev. H. F. Cary. At the gate of Hell, Dante reads the stern words that end with a call to leave all hope behind. Inside, he sees the souls who lost the good of the mind, and his guide steadies him for what lies ahead.

The part moves from the gate to the first circle. Dante meets crowds of the dead and learns how each soul is placed. Cary's blank verse keeps the scene grave and clear.
the-emperor-volume-02:
Volume two of Georg Ebers's The Emperor opens at chapter five, in the hall of the Muses at Lochias. Pontius the architect, back in good humour after a spat with the steward, calls the sculptor Pollux to supper. Pollux begs off: his mother has cooked cabbage and sausages, food of the gods, and his father has brought the bowl in.

Work for the emperor's visit drives the days, while Pollux jokes through his hunger. Clara Bell's rendering keeps Ebers's mix of craft talk, family warmth, and looming courts. Supper scenes ground the grand tale in daily bread.
the-history-of-don-quixote-volume-1-part:
Volume 1, Part 02 of Don Quixote comes from Cervantes, in Ormsby's English rendering. Chapter four tells of what happened to the knight when he left the inn. Day was dawning as Don Quixote rode out, so happy and gay at finding himself dubbed a knight that his joy seemed ready to burst his horse-girths.

On the road he recalls the advice of his host at the inn. The part continues the first sally begun in the earlier chapters, with the new knight fresh from his dubbing and full of delight. Cervantes keeps the tone light here, letting pride and pleasure carry a man who has no true idea of the road ahead.
the-honor-of-the-name-pg4002:
Emile Gaboriau wrote The Honor of the Name. Chapter one opens on the first Sunday of August 1815, at ten o'clock precisely, in the parish church at Sairmeuse. The sacristan sounds three strokes of the bell to warn the faithful that the priest is mounting the altar steps for high mass.

The church stands more than half full, and peasant women hurry in with shoes in hand, put on in reverence at the door. Most men stay outside to talk crops and news in the porch and yard, treating Sunday mass as a weekly market of talk. A sibling record in the library shows only the title page and contents for the same title.
the-innocents-abroad-volume-02:
Part 2 of Mark Twain's Innocents Abroad finds the travelers in France. The text comes from the 1869 first edition. Chapter XI opens the part. The party is getting foreignized rapidly, Twain says. Stone floors ring to the heel here. They kill all sentimental musing. Noiseless waiters hover like butterflies at the elbow. Ice comes made by artifice in bottles. One hardship stands beyond bearing. They must ring for soap at every wash.

He walks readers through the table d'hôte. Soup comes, then fish after a wait. Roast beef, peas, and lentils follow in turn. Snail patties and roast chicken arrive. Strawberry pie and ice cream close the meal. Wine stands with every course, this being France. His joke about Marseilles caps the chapter. Its people make hymns, vests, and soap for the world. They never sing, wear, or wash with them themselves.
the-inside-of-the-cup-volume-02:
Volume 2 of Winston Churchill's novel opens with chapter V. The rector has more food for thought here. Sunday after Sunday, Hodder surveys the same scene at St. John's. Winter light falls through stained windows. It colors the marble of the center aisle. The choir's voices echo among the arches. Certain landmarks fill the pews. Eldon Parr sits rigid in his empty pew. Everett Constable settles pompously into his own. His white-haired wife takes the far end. Their children once filled the space between.

Churchill catalogues the flock with malice. The Fergusons and the healthy Plimptons appear. Young Gordon Atterbury is forty-five and unmarried. His eyeglasses hang from a gold chain. The widowed Mrs. Larrabbee agitates any air she enters. Even prayer cannot settle her presence. Hodder feels her interest as almost personal. His discomfort hints at the crisis gathering below.
the-last-of-the-barons-volume-02:
Book Two, called the King Court, forms the portion in this record of Edward Bulwer Lytton novel of Earl Warwick. Young men ride along the Strand past half fortified mansions and merchants houses with orchards. They head for Marmaduke hostel in East Cheap.

Marmaduke Nevile, kinsman to a great minister, changes plain provincial dress for court finery sewn with seed pearls and gold fringe. The chapter shows London wealth and display under Edward IV. Private ambition enters a court famous for gorgeous dress and restless intrigue, display, and sudden shifts of favor among the great.
the-lerouge-case-pg3802:
Emile Gaboriau opens his detective novel on Thursday, March 6, 1862, shortly after Shrove Tuesday. Five women from La Jonchere village visit the police station at Bougival in France. Their neighbor, the Widow Lerouge, has not been seen for two days.

Knocks at her isolated cottage went unanswered, with shutters and door closed tight. The police commissioner resists at first, then sends gendarmes and a locksmith to force entry. Gaboriau builds one of the early modern detective novels from village alarm, careful police work, and a hidden family past. Village gossip gives the inquiry its first push.
the-lion-s-skin-pg2702: Rafael Sabatini's The Lion's Skin appears here with only a title page and a contents list, so the novel itself does not appear. The list runs to twenty-two chapters, four more than the contents shown for the companion record of the same title. Early chapters include The Fanatic, The Witness, and Moonshine, while the closing titles name The End of Lord Ostermore, Mr. Caryll's Identity, The Lion's Skin, and The Hunters.
the-memoirs-of-count-grammont-volume-02:
Volume 2 of Anthony Hamilton's Memoirs of Count Grammont, edited with notes by Sir Walter Scott, opens at Chapter Fourth, the Chevalier's arrival at the court of Turin. Hamilton argues that military glory is only half a hero's equipment, since love must give the finishing stroke. Fresh from the siege of Trino, Grammont and his companion Matta plan new sieges against the beauties and husbands of Turin.

Hamilton compares the pair to Amadis of Gaul and Don Galaor, then notes their real advantages. Unlike those silent knights of romance, Grammont and Matta are adepts at cards and dice. They are young, handsome, witty, and free with money, so Turin receives them warmly. The court, Hamilton says, was then the seat of gallantry and love. Readers get courtly intrigue told with open amusement at its heroes.
the-parisians-volume-02:
Volume 2 of Edward Bulwer-Lytton's The Parisians opens with Book II. Several weeks have passed, and the lime trees in the Tuileries are green. Graham Vane sits absorbed in thought at a writing table in a ground-floor apartment in the Rue d'Anjou. The narrator pauses to give his parentage and position.

Vane's father inherited a fair squire's estate and about half a million in investments, free of entail. A man of brilliant, irregular genius and princely generosity, he turned his hall into a ducal palace, then stood for the county and won early success in Parliament. The son's striking forehead marks him out in the Paris scenes that follow.
the-prince-of-india-or-why-constantinopl: Volume II of Lew. Wallace's The Prince of India, or Why Constantinople Fell, carries the same Longfellow verses as the first volume. The pages shown give the title page and contents, not the novel itself. The contents open at Book IV, The Palace of Blacherne, continued from the earlier volume. Chapters include The Princess Hears from the World and Lael Tells of Her Two Fathers. The Prince of India Preaches God to the Greeks stands at the centre. Later entries name The Imperial Cistern Gives Up Its Secret.
the-project-gutenberg-faq-2002:
Jim Tinsley's Project Gutenberg FAQ 2002 announces itself as a historical reference, not a current guide. Readers wanting up-to-date answers are sent to the project's site. A first answer tells questioners where to ask: the Volunteers' Board for production questions, the gutvol-d list for matters of general volunteer interest. Sections then cover Project Gutenberg itself, its publications, and more.

The opening questions ask what the project is, where it came from, and what it has achieved. They continue to who runs it, how many people take part, and how to help. Relations with Projekt Gutenberg-DE, Project Gutenberg of Australia, and Project Runeberg get their own question. The FAQ preserves the project's self-description at the start of the century.
the-red-lily-volume-02: Anatole France is named as author on the electronic edition header, which labels the text volume two and gives an April 2003 release. Here only that edition header and its general notices are present, so no part of the novel itself appears and nothing about its story can be told from these pages. A companion complete record in the set carries a biographical preface instead.
the-right-of-way-volume-02:
Gilbert Parker's second volume joins the story at chapter nine, where Jo Portugais runs a small raft downriver at night against the law of the river. Jo, a young man of many gifts who works as driver, woodsman, hunter, carpenter, or guide as whim takes him, has come alone from far upriver.

Contents for the volume promise old debts, a raised curtain, Rosalie's coming, Charley's adventuring, a mark in paper, a mission, a tailor's midnight foray, and a stolen cross. Habitual defiance of custom defines Jo at once. The volume listing overlaps the combined contents given in the complete record in the set.
the-story-of-my-life-volume-02:
Volume two of Georg Ebers's autobiography, translated by Mary J. Safford, opens at chapter six with his introduction to art among the neighbours of the Lennestrasse in Berlin. The Drakes of his sister's journal were a sculptor's family. Berlin owed splendid works of art to Drake. He was a warm friend of Ebers's mother. He welcomed the children into his studio. He gave them clay to shape.

Ebers watched statues, busts, and reliefs grow from rude clay and plaster casts turn into marble, while the calm master explained everything with unfailing patience. He credits those childhood hours for later characters in his novels: little Pennu in Uarda, Polykarp in Homo Sum, Pollux in The Emperor, and the cheery Alexander in Per Aspera.
the-thirty-years-war-volume-02:
Frederick Schiller opens Book Two of his History of the Thirty Years' War with Ferdinand's fateful resolution. That decision gave the war a new direction, a new scene, and new actors. What began as a Bohemian rebellion and the chastisement of rebels now spreads across Germany and then Europe. Schiller pauses to survey the balance between Roman Catholics and Protestants across the empire.

Catholics were more numerous and favoured by the constitution; Protestants held compact, populous territories, warlike princes, free towns, and command of the sea. Spain and Italy stood behind one side, Venice, Holland, and England behind the other. Schiller shows a continent balanced for catastrophe, then blames private interests for dissolving the Protestant union at the decisive moment.
the-wandering-jew-volume-02:
Volume two of Eugene Sue's Wandering Jew carries book two, opening with an interval titled The Wandering Jew's Sentence. Contents chapters move through an ajoupa, tattooing, a smuggler, the ruins of Tchandi, an ambuscade, a tempest, and a shipwreck. Paris draws nearer through Dagobert's wife, Agricola Baudoin, Adrienne at her toilet, and a closing interview.

The interval passage itself is printed after the contents. Its scene is a wild, rugged eminence of sandstone boulders, birch, and oak under a red western light left by the sun. Below lies a deep, fertile valley veiled in evening mist, with ripe corn gathered, church steeples rising, and a high-road running north to west. The hour of repose settles over the cottages.
thomson-bible-1808-vol-02:
The second volume of Charles Thomson's 1808 Bible carries the story from the first book of Kings through Esther. It then adds the wisdom books, from Job through the Song of Solomon. Thomson translated from the Greek Septuagint, and Jane Aitken printed the volumes at Philadelphia.

Readers meet Solomon's temple, the split of the kingdom, exile and return, and the court tale of Esther. Then the tone shifts to poetry: Job's debate, the Psalms in Greek order, Proverbs, and the Song. Because Thomson worked from Greek, names and lines often differ from the King James text. The volume shows the Bible as the Greek church read it.
tob-0102:
Abraham of Worms left an account of learning sacred magic from Abramelin, an Egyptian mage he met in his travels. Book one of the Sacred Magic of Abramelin tells that story. Abraham writes for his son, explaining why the true magic differs from the frauds and dark rites around him.

The prize is the Knowledge and Conversation of the Holy Guardian Angel, won through many months of prayer and a purified life. Book one sets out the journey, the teacher, and the rules of conduct. Few magical books demand so much of the reader. Later magicians, Crowley among them, treated the work as a summit.
tob-0202:
The Kybalion opens with a key line: as above, so below. The 1908 Hermetic classic teaches mental transmutation. That is, the art of changing one's inner state to change one's world. Seven rules, said to come down from Hermes of old Egypt, carry the whole teaching. The Three Initiates wrote for doers, not for scholars.

Mind, matching, rhythm, the pull of opposites, cause and effect: each rule is stated, then glossed, then put to use. The book is the New Thought world's most lasting handbook, still in print and still quoted. Its plain style is the point. Seven rules, meant to be used each day.
tob-10102:
Johann Arndt published True Christianity in the seventeenth century, in German as Vier Bücher vom wahren Christentum. His argument rebuked comfortable churchgoers: real Christianity is not attendance or correct doctrine alone. It is an inward transformation of the heart that changes how a person lives.

Arndt calls readers to repentance, prayer, humility, and daily practice of faith rather than mere profession. The book proved hugely popular, was carried by missionaries around the world, and shaped Protestant piety for generations. Its stern, searching tone still explains its influence: Arndt measured religion by fruit in ordinary conduct, not by labels.
tob-10402:
Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, spent much of his life fighting the teaching of Arius, who said Christ was a created being, not fully God. His discourses Against the Arians form his fullest defense of the Nicene faith. Enemies exiled him five times, yet he kept writing.

He argues from scripture that the Word is true God, of one being with the Father, and that only a divine savior can save mankind. The discourses mix close Bible reading with sharp attacks on his foes. They helped secure the doctrine of the Trinity in the church and remain a base text of early Christian theology.
tob-10802:
Charles Squire retold the myths of the British Islands, drawing on medieval Irish and Welsh sources. Cuchulain's heroics, the voyage of Bran, Arthur's court, and the old gods behind the tales all appear. Squire aimed at the general reader rather than the Celtic scholar.

Working as a storyteller with a scholar's conscience, he separates story from history where the evidence allows and admits where it does not. Gods become kings in some tales, heroes shrink or grow across versions, and Squire tracks the changes. V1 evidence calls the result the best single doorway into Celtic mythology; readers get narrative first, with learning carried lightly.
tob-14502:
Jalaluddin Rumi, the thirteenth-century Sufi master of Konya, composed the Masnavi, a vast poem in six books in Persian. He dictated it to a disciple over many years. Persian speakers have called it the Quran in Persian for its depth.

Story follows story: kings, fools, lovers, and animals act out lessons on the soul's longing for God. The opening song of the reed flute, cut from its reed bed, sets the theme of separation and return. Rumi breaks off tales to comment, joke, and pray. It is the most read poem in the Muslim world and a summit of Sufi teaching.
tob-3002:
Augustine of Hippo's Confessions, in E. B. Pusey's translation, trace his path from restless North African youth to Christian bishop. A stolen pear, a brilliant career in rhetoric, years with the Manichaeans, and a mother's prayers fill the early books. Conversion comes in a Milan garden, under a child's voice chanting take up and read.

Late have I loved thee, O Beauty ever ancient, ever new, runs his famous cry. The final books turn from story to memory, time, and Genesis, in thirteen books that effectively invented spiritual autobiography in Western literature. Pusey, an Oxford churchman, keeps the passion of the Latin in dignified English. The examined life starts here for many readers.
tob-4002:
Niccolò Machiavelli wrote The Prince in 1513 after his fall from Florentine politics cost him office, freedom, and nearly his health under torture. Addressed to a Medici ruler, the manual asks how new princes gain and keep power in a dangerous Italy of rival states and foreign armies. His answers shocked Christendom.

Power, Machiavelli argues, is kept by being feared rather than loved when both cannot be had, promises are tools to be judged by outcomes, and fortune favors the bold who act. He describes power as it is practiced, not as moralists said it should be. Five centuries of argument over his name began with these chapters.
tob-4102:
Kenneth James Saunders, scholar and missionary, translated the Dhammapada from the Pali under the title The Buddha's Way of Virtue. His 1919 edition carries introduction and notes for the general reader. The 423 verses of the original form the best-known summary of the Buddha's teaching.

Mind goes before all things, the opening verse declares; a trained mind brings happiness like a shadow that never leaves. Saunders renders the Pali with respect and a light touch. His notes explain terms from Buddhist practice for Western ears. Verified from the 1919 edition, the little book serves as a gentle, scholarly first step into Buddhist ethics.
tob-9102:
Melody rules the Sama Veda, the Veda of chants, in Griffith's translation verified from the 1919 scan. Its verses are mostly Rigvedic lines reset for singing at the soma sacrifice. Priests stretched and ornamented the words until the chant became an art of its own.

As a book of words, the Sama Veda is the shortest of the four Vedas. As a book of music, it is the root from which Indian classical singing claims descent. Griffith prints the verses in the order singers used them. Readers meet the Veda that exists to be heard, the liturgy behind the hymns found elsewhere.
travels-in-the-interior-of-africa-volume:
Volume two of Mungo Park's Travels in the Interior of Africa, in the 1887 Cassell edition, completes his account of the 1795-97 journey. Its introduction picks Park up where volume one left him. He had reached the Niger, then fallen sick, alone, and stripped of nearly everything.

The editor praises the tale as one of the most gripping in English travel writing. Park's good temper, courage, and kindness toward the people whose help kept him alive draw special notice. A half-starved man robbed in a forest still stops to admire a tiny moss, the introduction recalls. That eye for detail carries the homeward journey here.
trunko-watauga-democrat-1925-04-02:
A strange bulk fights the sea in the Watauga Democrat piece of April 2, 1925. The North Carolina paper reprints a tale from Margate, on the coast of South Africa, from the year past. There, guests watched a vast hairy beast fight two whales for hours. It looked like a polar bear grown huge. It then lay dead on the sand, lost ere it could be gauged for science.

Locals named the beast Trunko in lore since then. No proof of it was kept at all. The reprint is the root source of the whole tale. Its loss is the point.
uarda-a-romance-of-ancient-egypt-volume-:
Volume two of Georg Ebers's Uarda begins at chapter five, on the morning after Princess Bent-Anat knocked at the gate of the House of Seti. Dawn's freshness gives way to heat pouring from a cloudless sky. The limestone rocks of the Necropolis glare, and the air quivers as if over a flame.

Below, the harbor where boats cross from eastern Thebes crowds with barks waiting to return. Boatmen attached to priestly and noble houses rest, play at morra, and dispute eagerly. A vendor of food, drink, and cooling acids sets up under a sycamore. Ebers builds ancient Thebes from heat, dust, and the working riverfront before the plot resumes.
un-ga-res-president-george-w-bush-s-rema:
George W. Bush addressed the United Nations General Assembly on September 12, 2002, and turned the hall's attention to Iraq. A year after the September 11 attacks, he warned of a grave and gathering danger from Saddam Hussein's regime. The speech began the public march toward the invasion that came six months later.

Bush lists Iraq's breaches of past Council resolutions on arms and terror. He challenges the UN to enforce its own demands or risk fading into irrelevance. He pledges to work with the Council while reserving the right to act alone. The address frames the case that shaped a war.
un-sc-res-102:
Resolution 102 sets the terms for Japan to join the Statute of the International Court of Justice. The Council adopted it on 3 December 1953. The vote was ten to none. The Soviet Union abstained. Japan was not yet a UN member. So the Charter required the General Assembly to fix the terms. It would act on advice from the Council.

Japan would join once it filed a signed statement with the Secretary-General. The statement also had to be ratified under Japanese law. In it, Japan would accept the Statute in full. It would accept the duties in Article 94 of the Charter. It would also agree to pay a fair share of the Court's costs. The Assembly would set that share after talks with Japan.
un-sc-res-1302: Adopted by the Security Council and numbered 1302, this formal text is catalogued under the year 1995. Such texts can call for cease-fires, set up missions, impose duties, or settle points of UN procedure and membership. Its value lies in the primary wording: the decision as adopted, kept through the Wikisource transcription of the record. No summary replaces it; the record itself is the content of the entry.
un-sc-res-1402:
The second Palestinian uprising reached a grave point in March 2002. Suicide bombings had struck Israel. Israeli forces had attacked the headquarters of the President of the Palestinian Authority and moved into Palestinian cities. Resolution 1402 was adopted in March 2002, days after the two-state text, Resolution 1397.

The Council called on both parties to move at once to a meaningful cease-fire. Israeli troops were called on to withdraw from Palestinian cities, including Ramallah. Both sides had to work with the United States special envoy and others on the ground. Their first step was to carry out the Tenet security work plan in full. The Council also repeated the demand of Resolution 1397. All acts of violence had to end at once, including terror, provocation, incitement, and destruction.
un-sc-res-1502:
A bomb had destroyed the United Nations headquarters in Baghdad days before. On 26 August 2003 the Security Council spoke on the safety of aid and United Nations workers. It recalled the attack on the Iraq mission of 19 August. It voiced grave concern at violence against humanitarian staff in many places. Such attacks, it stressed, break the laws of war.

The Council condemns murder, abduction, hostage-taking, and attacks on aid convoys. It urges states to punish crimes against relief workers. It demands safe access for aid staff to all people in need. It also asks host countries to write stronger safety rules into their agreements with the United Nations.
un-sc-res-1602:
Burundi's operation was extended as elections neared on 31 May 2005. The Arusha Agreement's transition was moving toward its close. Burundians had approved a post-transition constitution in the referendum of 28 February 2005. On 15 May the president and the last rebel group's leader signed a Dar es Salaam declaration. They pledged an instant halt to fighting and a permanent ceasefire within a month.

The Council extended ONUB's mandate until 1 December 2005. All Burundian parties were called to work harder to make the elections a success. The Council looked forward to the Secretary-General's advice, due by mid-June, on the mission's future shape. He was to keep reporting on events as they unfolded. ONUB's work on a zero tolerance approach to abuse by its own staff was welcomed. The renewal carried the mission through the polls and the new government's birth.
un-sc-res-1702:
MINUSTAH was renewed behind an elected government on 15 August 2006. Haiti had completed a peaceful move to elected rule, with a new president and parliament. The government's program covered modernizing the state and creating wealth. A social relief program answered the country's urgent needs. The Secretary-General's report of 28 July set out the mission's next phase.

The Council extended MINUSTAH's mandate, as set by resolution 1542 (2004), for six months. The mission would keep a military part of up to 7,200 troops and a police part of up to 1,951 officers. Sixteen correction officers, seconded from member states, were authorized to help the prison service. Haiti's authorities were urged to finish the run-off legislative and local elections without delay. States were asked to supply well-qualified police. The Council restated its call for the mission to back the constitutional and political process and the rule of law.
un-sc-res-1902:
The Security Council adopted Resolution 1902 on Burundi on 17 December 2009. Burundi was preparing presidential and legislative elections for 2010. Rights abuses and limits on free assembly still drew concern. Youth groups tied to parties had clashed, and talks on justice for past crimes were under way.

The text extends the United Nations Integrated Office in Burundi, called BINUB, until 31 December 2010. The office should focus on the elections, fair rule, peace, and the return of former fighters. The government must create fair conditions for the 2010 vote. It should also keep fighting graft, set up an independent rights body, and avoid steps that could raise tensions again.
un-sc-res-2002:
Somalia and Eritrea are the subject of United Nations Security Council Resolution 2002, adopted on 29 July 2011. Drought and famine were gripping Somalia that summer. Armed groups blocked aid and taxed trade through ports they held. Weapons kept crossing borders in breach of two arms embargoes.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council widens who can face travel bans and asset freezes. Recruiting child soldiers now counts, as do attacks on schools, hospitals, and civilians. Blocking aid and stealing public funds also qualify for listing. Trade through Al-Shabaab ports may count as backing a listed group. The Monitoring Group gains twelve more months, and urgent aid payments are shielded from the freeze for a year.
un-sc-res-202:
Southern Rhodesia's drift toward a breakaway declaration met a warning on 6 May 1965. Elections under the rejected 1961 constitution were set for 7 May. The minority government was threatening a unilateral declaration of independence. The General Assembly and its special committee had long pressed Britain to free political prisoners and repeal repressive laws.

The Council noted Britain's stated terms for any grant of independence. It backed the majority view that Britain should call a constitutional conference of all parties. Britain and all member states were asked to refuse any unilateral declaration of independence. Britain had to act to prevent one from coming. No powers or armed forces were to pass to the Rhodesian government as it stood. The question stayed on the Council's agenda. The warning failed, and the Smith regime declared independence that November.
un-sc-res-2202:
Resolution 2202 gave the Security Council's backing to the Minsk agreements, the ceasefire deals meant to end fighting in eastern Ukraine. Rebels backed by Russia held parts of the Donetsk and Luhansk regions. The Council adopted the text days after the second Minsk deal was signed.

Inside, the members endorse the full package: a ceasefire, withdrawal of heavy weapons, local elections, and changes to Ukraine's constitution. They call on all sides to carry out every step. The resolution matters because it put the world's top security body behind a peace plan that both Ukraine and Russia had accepted.
un-sc-res-302: The library catalogues Resolution 302, a Security Council decision, under the year 1971. Voting in the Council requires support from its permanent members, so each adopted text marks a point of agreement. Readers will find the full wording here, taken from the English Wikisource transcription of the UN official record. The entry belongs to the library's DECLASSIFIED group of public official records.
un-sc-res-402: Preserved as Resolution 402, this Security Council text carries a 1981 date in the catalog record. A resolution may address a conflict, a court vacancy, a new member, or the running of the United Nations itself. Anyone studying UN practice can read the decision itself here, in the Wikisource transcription of the official record. The catalog places it in the DECLASSIFIED group of official public records.
un-sc-res-502:
Argentina's invasion of the Falkland Islands was met with a withdrawal order in April 1982. The Council's president had called on 1 April for both governments to shun force in the region. Reports then told of an invasion by Argentine forces on 2 April. The Council judged that a breach of the peace existed in the region of the islands.

The Council demanded an immediate end to hostilities. It demanded the immediate withdrawal of all Argentine forces from the Falkland Islands (Islas Malvinas). Argentina and the United Kingdom were called to seek a diplomatic answer to their differences. Both were told to respect the purposes and principles of the United Nations Charter in full. The text gave Britain the legal ground it stood on through the war that followed. Argentina did not withdraw, and the fighting ended only with its surrender in June.
un-sc-res-702: North and South Korea both sought United Nations seats in 1991. On 8 August 1991 the Security Council examined their applications separately. It recommended to the General Assembly that the Democratic People's Republic of Korea be admitted. It made the same recommendation for the Republic of Korea. The decision was taken without a vote. Both states joined that September. Their joint entry ended a long dispute over Korean representation.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci: Security Council resolution 102 was adopted on 3 December 1953, by 10 votes to none with one abstention. It recommends terms on which Japan could become a party to the Statute of the International Court of Justice, without joining the United Nations. Japan would deposit an instrument accepting the Statute and the obligations of Article 94 of the Charter. It would undertake to contribute an equitable share of the Court's expenses. The General Assembly would assess that share.

Iraq's oil-for-food programme gets another six months of life here, in a text passed on 8 June 2000. The programme let Iraq sell oil under United Nations control while wide sanctions stayed in force. The money paid for food, medicine, and other basic goods for Iraqi civilians.

Acting under Chapter VII of the Charter, the Council kept the rules first set in 1995 in force for 180 days from 9 June. Food, nutrition, and health kept first claim on the funds, with a fixed share set aside for the north of the country. The Council also pressed for fair sharing of goods in every part of Iraq and for stronger United Nations checks on the ground.

As Israeli tanks ringed the Palestinian leader's compound in Ramallah, the Council called for a ceasefire. On 29 March 2002, it adopted Resolution 1402. Fourteen members backed it and none opposed it. Syria took no part in the vote. The text voices grave concern at suicide bombings in Israel. It also cites the attack on the Palestinian Authority's headquarters.

Both parties must move at once to a real ceasefire. Israeli troops must pull out of Palestinian cities, Ramallah included. The text repeats the demand made in Resolution 1397 days before. All violence, terror, and wrecking must stop at once. It backs the envoys then working to restart the peace track.

A bomb at UN headquarters in Baghdad pushed aid worker safety onto the agenda in 2003. On 26 August, the Council adopted Resolution 1502 without dissent. The blast a week before killed the mission's chief. Twenty-one others died with him. The attack is named in the text itself.

The Council condemns in strong terms the violence aid staff now face. Murder, abduction, and attacks on convoys all count. States must make sure such crimes do not go unpunished. All parties must let aid workers reach people in need in safety. The text pledges steps of its own as well. Host states should adopt the safety pact's key guards. The text still anchors debate on aid worker safety.

Resolution 1602, adopted on 31 May 2005, extends the UN operation in Burundi as the country's transition nears its vote. Burundians had approved a post-transition constitution by referendum in February. In May, the sitting president and the leader of the last big rebel group, the Palipehutu-FNL, signed a declaration in Dar es Salaam moving toward a ceasefire. The Arusha peace agreement of 2000 was the framework everything rested on.

ONUB's mandate was extended for six months, to December 2005. The Council assured all Burundian parties of its determination to see the transition end successfully through free and fair elections. It also restated support for the Arusha process and called on the parties to honor their commitments in full.

Haiti's fresh start under an elected government is the backdrop for Resolution 1702, adopted on 15 August 2006. A new president and parliament had been chosen in a calm transfer of power. The UN Stabilization Mission in Haiti, MINUSTAH, was a key support. The government had approved a police reform plan and set social programs in motion, but gangs, weak courts, and crowded prisons still plagued the country.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council extends MINUSTAH until 15 February 2007. It sets the force at up to 7,200 troops and 1,951 police, plus 16 corrections officers to help fix the prison system. It asks MINUSTAH to shift its disarmament work toward a community violence reduction program with jobs for former gang members and at-risk youth. It also urges fast completion of run-off and local elections.

Burundi's integrated UN office is renewed by Resolution 1902, adopted on 17 December 2009. The Palipehutu-FNL had become a political party under the December 2008 agreements, an electoral commission and revised electoral code were in place, and elections were due in 2010. Continuing rights violations, curbs on opposition assembly and expression, and violence by party youth groups remained concerns.

The Council extends the mandate of the UN Integrated Office in Burundi, BINUB, until 31 December 2010. BINUB must focus on the electoral process, democratic governance, peace consolidation, reintegration, and gender issues, and be ready to give the electoral commission logistical support at key moments. The government is pressed to protect the commission's independence, finish the disarmament and reintegration strategy, set up an independent national human rights commission, and end impunity. A briefing on the elections is due in May 2010 and a full report in November 2010.

Somalia's targeted sanctions are sharpened and the monitors renewed in Resolution 2002, adopted on 29 July 2011. The Monitoring Group's July 2011 report documented embargo violations and revenue streams, drought and famine were worsening, and armed groups were obstructing humanitarian aid. The Council judged the designation criteria of Resolution 1844 (2008) needed reaffirming and strengthening.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council confirms the travel ban, asset freeze, and arms embargo reach those threatening the peace or the Djibouti process. They reach those violating the embargo, blocking humanitarian aid, recruiting children, or attacking civilians. Misappropriating transitional funds counts as a threat, and non-local commerce through Al-Shabaab-controlled ports counts as supporting a designated entity, so traders can be listed. It extends the Monitoring Group for twelve months with eight experts, tasked with investigating seaport operations raising revenue for Al-Shabaab. It exempts urgent humanitarian payments from the asset freeze for a year.

Southern Rhodesia's white rulers are pressed in Resolution 202, adopted on 6 May 1965 by seven votes to none with four abstentions. The General Assembly and its decolonization committee had repeatedly asked Britain, the colonial power, to free political prisoners, repeal repressive laws, and open political life. Two laws drew special dislike: the order law used to crush protest, and the land law that split farms and fields by race.

The Council endorsed those Assembly requests. It also flagged the danger in elections set for 7 May under a constitution most Rhodesians had rejected. The vote went ahead, the settler government won, and six months later it declared independence unilaterally, defying exactly the pressure this text applied.

Fighting in eastern Ukraine had caused heavy loss of life when diplomats reached a deal in Minsk in February 2015. Resolution 2202, adopted on 17 February 2015, endorses that deal. The Council said the crisis in the Donetsk and Luhansk regions could only be settled in a peaceful way.

The Council endorsed the Package of Measures signed in Minsk on 12 February 2015. All parties were called on to carry it out in full. The package is attached to the resolution. It ordered a cease-fire from 15 February and a pullback of heavy weapons to create wide safety zones. The OSCE would monitor the cease-fire. The package also covered talks on local elections, a special status for the area, and an amnesty law.

A special mission sent to investigate Portuguese attacks on Senegal reported back in 1971. Portugal had refused to cooperate with the mission. Resolution 302, adopted on 24 November 1971, is the Council's response to that report. It follows up Resolution 294, passed the previous July.

The Council thanked the mission and welcomed its proposals. It condemned once more the violence and destruction carried out since 1963. Portuguese forces from Guinea-Bissau had attacked Senegalese villages again and again. Portugal was criticized for refusing to help the mission, and it was told to act at once to respect Senegal's land and people. The Council also called on Portugal to honor, without delay, the right of the people of Guinea-Bissau to govern themselves and be free.

Lesotho, a small country entirely surrounded by South Africa, paid a price for a brave stand in 1976. South Africa had closed several border posts with Lesotho. The closures were meant to force Lesotho to recognize the Transkei. The Transkei was a so-called independent bantustan created under apartheid, and Lesotho refused to recognize it. Resolution 402 was adopted by consensus on 22 December 1976.

The Council praised Lesotho's refusal. It endorsed the General Assembly's call for all governments to deny the Transkei any recognition. South Africa's attempt at coercion was condemned, and it was told to reopen the border posts at once. The closures were causing Lesotho urgent economic harm. The Council therefore appealed to all states for immediate aid. United Nations agencies were asked to organize financial, technical, and material help for the country.

Resolution 502 was adopted in April 1982, right after Argentine armed forces invaded the Falkland Islands, called the Islas Malvinas in the text. The Council had already urged Argentina and the United Kingdom on 1 April to avoid using or threatening force in the area. Members said the invasion deeply disturbed them.

The Council rules that a breach of the peace exists in the region. It demands that fighting stop at once and that all Argentine forces leave the islands right away. It then calls on both governments to settle their differences through talks and to respect the UN Charter in full. The text became the Council's core legal statement on the opening of the Falklands War.

Two states share the Korean peninsula, but for decades neither sat at the UN. The Cold War kept both out. Each had a great-power backer blocking the other. That logjam broke in 1991. Resolution 702 passed without a vote on 8 August 1991. The Council had weighed each bid on its own.

The text backs both bids in turn. First comes North Korea, the Democratic People's Republic. Next comes South Korea, the Republic of Korea. The Assembly admitted both that September. The joint entry was a sign the Cold War was done. Rivals could now sit in the same hall. The door stayed open for talks, though the peninsula's split itself stayed firmly in place.
uslaw-cfr-t1-s426-102:
Section 426.102 of Title 1 of the Code of Federal Regulations sets out definitions for its part. It sits in Part 426, on the National Commission on Military, National, and Public Service. The definitions in part (a) of the Privacy Act, at 5 U.S.C. 552a(a), apply to the part. More terms are then defined for use in the part.

Business day means a calendar day other than a Saturday, Sunday, or legal public holiday. Chair means the Chair of the Commission or the person he or she names in that place. Commission means the National Commission itself. Commission system means a system of records kept by that body, as the text goes on to state. The text is drawn from the eCFR as of October 2026.
uslaw-cfr-t1-s500-102: Section 500.102 of Title 1 of the Code of Federal Regulations states the reach of its part. It sits in Part 500, on the bar against bias based on handicap in programs run by the National Commission for Employment Policy. The rule is a single sentence. It states that the part applies to all programs or activities run by the agency. The text is drawn from the eCFR as of October 2026, an unofficial compilation. The official edition is the yearly Code of Federal Regulations.
uslaw-usc-t2-s2002:
Section 2002 of Title 2 of the United States Code deals with the gain of buildings for a time of need. It sits in Chapter 30, on the work of the Capitol complex, in a part on the House. The rule stands even if a second law says the reverse. In order to meet a state of need, the Chief Administrative Officer of the House may gain buildings and plant. Those buildings are for the use of the House of Representatives.

The gain may be made if funds for the end are free for use. The ways of gain are named in the text. They are a lease, a buy, or a second form of pact that the officer holds to be fit. One such form is a pact of shared views with the head of an agency of the state.
uslaw-usc-t2-s4102:
Section 4102 of Title 2 of the United States Code covers the purchase of supplies for the Senate and the House of Representatives. It sits in Chapter 41, on officers of Congress and their work, in a general subchapter. The Code text is current through Public Law 119-134, as issued by the Office of the Law Revision Counsel.

The whole provision is a single sentence. It permits supplies for either chamber to be bought under one shared source: the schedule of contract items and prices kept by the Administrator of General Services. No other buying route is named in the section.
uslaw-usc-t2-s4702:
Section 4702 of Title 2 of the United States Code covers notice of limits on work after leaving Congress. It sits in Chapter 47 of that title, on congressional ethics. Part (a) deals with notice of those limits. The duty arises after a Member of Congress or an elected officer of either House leaves office. It also arises when the work of a covered staff member ends.

The staff covered are those named in named parts of section 207(e) of Title 18. The Clerk of the House gives the notice, after talks with a further officer, as the text goes on to state. The text is current through Public Law 119-134, as issued by the Office of the Law Revision Counsel.
uslaw-usc-t2-s4902:
Section 4902 of Title 2 of the United States Code covers the John W. McCormack Residential Page School. It sits in Chapter 49 of that title, on congressional pages. Part (a) clears the building of a dormitory and classroom complex for the school. The site must be approved by two bodies acting jointly. They are the Senate Office Building Commission and the House Office Building Commission.

Plans for the complex are to be drawn up by or under the Architect of the Capitol. Those plans must be sent to both commissions and approved by them jointly. The part goes on with more terms for the project, as the text states. The text is current through Public Law 119-134, as issued by the Office of the Law Revision Counsel.
uslaw-usc-t2-s5502:
Section 5502 of Title 2 of the United States Code covers House emergency operations positions. It sits in Chapter 55 of that title, on House officers and administration. Part (a) creates new posts with effect from fiscal year 2002 and each year after. Two added posts are created in each of three named House offices.

The three offices are the Office of the Clerk, the Office of the Chief Administrative Officer, and the Office of the Sergeant at Arms. Part (b) of the section takes up the duties of the staff named to those posts. The text is current through Public Law 119-134, as issued by the Office of the Law Revision Counsel.
uslaw-usc-t2-s5602: Section 5602 of Title 2 of the United States Code deals with the term of the Sergeant at Arms of the House. It sits in Chapter 55, on House officers, in a part on that office. A man duly chosen for the post and sworn is the subject. Such a man is to stay in the post till the man who is to take his place is chosen and sworn. The House keeps the right to take the post from him at any time.
uslaw-usc-t2-s6102:
Section 6102 of Title 2 of the United States Code deals with grants for the costs of the heads of the Senate. It sits in Chapter 61, on the heads of the Senate, in a general part of the chapter. From the year of funds 1978, and each year from then on, a change is made. The grants for the costs of the Majority and Minority Leaders of the Senate are raised. They are raised to $40,000 in each year for each such head of the Senate.

A first bar deals with the grants of two more posts. From the year of funds 1983, the grants for the costs of the Majority and Minority Whips may not top $10,000 in a year for each Whip. A second bar deals with a span of time that starts on 3 January 1977.
uslaw-usc-t2-s6302:
Section 6302 of Title 2 of the United States Code deals with the wages of Senators. It sits in Chapter 63, on Senate members, in a part on the pay of members. The rule in chief deals with Senators named to fill a gap in the Senate. The wages of such a Senator start on the day of the naming. They run on till the man's heirs in the post are chosen and sworn in their place.

The text then adds rules for the men chosen to take the place of those named. If such a man is chosen in a break when the Senate is not in session, his wages start on the day after the poll. If he is chosen while the Senate sits, his wages start on the day he is sworn.
voltaire-philosophical-dictionary-1802:
Voltaire published his Dictionnaire philosophique in 1764, a pocket book of short articles meant to be carried and quoted. The London English edition of 1802, The Philosophical Dictionary, is the text here. He wrote many entries himself and shaped them all into an alphabet of the Enlightenment, from Abraham to Zoroaster.

Toleration, fanaticism, and superstition take the sharpest hits, while common sense gets the warmest praise. Each article is a small raid: a definition, a story, a sting in the tail. Voltaire meant the book to change the way his century thought, one entry at a time. It remains the most readable of his weapons, and the most quoted.
voyages-of-samuel-de-champlain-volume-02: Volume two of Samuel de Champlain's Voyages covers the years 1604 to 1610, in Charles Pomeroy Otis's rendering from the French, for the Prince Society. The Rev. Edmund F. Slafter edited the volume and wrote its memoir of Champlain, and twenty local maps appear as heliotype copies. Pages present here hold transcriber's notes, the title page, and the first lines of the preface only. That preface explains that two French poems of praise, printed with Champlain's 1613 edition, are left out here as having no historical worth. The voyages themselves are not shown.
what-will-he-do-with-it-volume-02:
Book two of Lord Lytton's What Will He Do With It? follows Lionel Haughton on a trip by rail and carriage. Lionel asks the way to Fawley Manor House, five miles off. The road runs through rough, empty country with wide commons and beech woods. No village, spire, or lodge comes in sight along the way.

Lytton contrasts this older, wilder England with the neat suburbs of his own day. Knights Templar or fleeing fighters of the Wars of the Roses might have ridden here, he muses. The quiet land shapes the minds of those who live in it, by his claim. Lionel rides toward Guy Darrell's house and a fateful meeting. The volume's mood turns grave and lonely.
works-of-john-bunyan-volume-02:
George Offor edited this second volume of John Bunyan's works, again covering experimental, doctrinal, and practical writings. Pages present here open with a treatise on the saints' knowledge of Christ's love. Offor's remarks say Bunyan left the piece ready for the press at his death. It first appeared in a folio gathering in 1692. Offor praises its depth and clear Christian thought.

Friends Ebenezer Chandler and John Wilson called the treatise excellent. It aims to help Christians grow in grace and win others over. Readers get mature Bunyan, writing on Christ's riches for believers. Devotion and doctrine stay tightly joined.
young-journal-of-discourses-vol02:
Liverpool printed Volume II of the Journal of Discourses in 1855, one more year of Utah sermons set in type. Brigham Young speaks often, joined by his counsellors, members of the Twelve, and other elders. Shorthand reporters caught the words as spoken, so the record keeps the rough edge of live preaching.

The talks mix high doctrine with farming, building, and conduct in a desert kingdom taking shape. Together the volumes form a year-by-year account of what the Saints heard from their pulpits. For students of the movement, few sources put them so close to the voices that led it.
young-theory-light-colours-1802:
Thomas Young, an English doctor and sage, read this Bakerian Lecture on light and hues across 1801 and 1802. Most men of his day held that light was a stream of tiny parts. Young held that light moves in waves, like sound through air.

His proof rests on the way light bands form when rays cross and mix. He showed the bands fit waves that add and cancel, not parts that fly straight. The wave view made a stuff called the ether seem a need, since waves must wave in something. The talk is still the root text of the wave view.
zicci-a-tale-volume-02:
Edward Bulwer-Lytton is named as author in the pages present here for this second book of the tale. Chapter ten opens on a mountain at night. Merton and his Italian guides reach the mules safely, then worry over missing Glyndon. Two forms approach through starlight. Zicci carries Glyndon, who was overcome by crater fumes. One more minute of vapour would have killed him, Zicci says.

The Italian guide trembles, claiming Zicci's face looked inhuman nights before. Zicci calmly notes his prophecy of the meeting came true. Rescue and dread arrive together. Readers get the tale's middle, with its start and end held in sibling records.
